apple-tv-military-discount: There is no verification path for an Apple TV streaming military discount because no such discount exists. Apple’s hardware military program uses ID.me: you verify your veteran or active-military status with an existing or new ID.me account to shop the special Veterans and Military storefront, where the 10% discount applies to eligible products and accessories. That storefront’s pricing does not extend to the Apple TV subscription or other Apple services — so don’t expect the ID.me verification to lower your streaming bill.

The ways to reduce Apple TV cost are open to everyone, including service members: the 7-day free trial; 3 months free when you buy a qualifying Apple device (the offer appears automatically in the Apple TV app when signed in with the associated Apple Account, subject to eligibility); free Apple TV access with an Apple Music Student plan for eligible students; and the Apple One bundle (Individual $19.95/mo, Family $25.95/mo, Premier $37.95/mo), which combines Apple TV with iCloud+, Apple Music, and Apple Arcade. One Apple TV subscription can also be shared with up to five family members via Family Sharing.

If a real military streaming discount matters more than the specific service, some competitors publish dedicated offers verified through SheerID — reporting suggests Paramount+ around 50% off and Hulu around 40% off the ad-supported plan. Those figures come from secondary sources, so confirm current terms on each service’s official page before relying on them. And note this page is about the Apple TV subscription — Apple’s hardware military discount is a separate program.
ringconn-military-discount: There is no military or verification path anywhere on ringconn.com — not in the shop, product pages, support center, or footer — and RingConn integrates no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or student-verification service. One coupon aggregator even states plainly that RingConn "currently does not provide a military discount." So rather than chase a code that isn’t a real military offer, the smart move is to use the legitimate savings levers RingConn actually has.

The single biggest legitimate saver is paying with HSA/FSA funds. RingConn is HSA/FSA eligible, and at checkout you can choose "Pay with HSA/FSA," which is handled by Flex. Because you’re spending pre-tax dollars, the effective saving is your marginal tax rate on the purchase — often 22–32% — which typically beats any public promo code. It’s a payment method rather than a coupon, so it applies to the final total regardless of any code you’ve entered.

If you have an old smart ring or wearable, RingConn’s trade-in program gives up to $70 credit — $70 for a RingConn Gen 1/2/2 Air, and $60 for an Oura, Galaxy Ring, Ultrahuman, Apple device, or Galaxy Watch — provided you send the old device within 30 days of receiving your new ring. Trade-in credit and promo codes generally compete for the same single checkout field, so compare which one saves more on your order rather than expecting to stack both.

Be cautious of the "RingConn military discount code" listings on coupon and deal sites (for example "CNRCEWD — $15 off" or "military discount up to 50% off"). No such official military offer exists; these are ordinary public sitewide codes relabeled as "military" for SEO, they aren’t gated to service members, and the advertised percentages are often inflated or expired. Any working code is a public code anyone can use — verify it live at checkout rather than trusting a listicle.
dbrand-military-discount: Verification is not applicable here: dbrand uses no military verification provider because it has no military discount to verify against. If any site claims you can "verify with ID.me or SheerID for a dbrand military discount," it’s inaccurate.

dbrand is the "anti-discount / irreverent-brand" archetype — it deliberately does not offer identity-gated discounts, and it doesn’t run a standing "enter a coupon code" program at all. Its Terms of Use and FAQ describe no coupon-code system, so the public sale price is generally the final price.

For math, take a representative ~$40 order (a phone skin plus a Grip case). During a public sitewide sale that might fall to roughly $28-$36, the same for every customer. A first-order/newsletter offer can shave a little more when live, and a "Grab Bag" mystery item lowers the unit price — but none of these depend on or reward military status.
longhorn-military-discount: The honest headline is confirmed by Darden’s own partner: ID.me states "We’re not aware that LongHorn Steakhouse offers Military discounts," and Darden publishes no company-wide military policy. Because LongHorn’s U.S. locations are company-owned by Darden (not franchised), the common "ask your local franchise" boilerplate is doubly misleading — any everyday percentage is a manager’s courtesy at a company restaurant, not a brand rate. Treat "10% off, show your ID" as a possible courtesy to confirm at your restaurant, never a guaranteed program. Sites promising "25% off" or "$10 off" LongHorn "military promo codes" are generic coupon noise.

The one recurring, documented military offer is the Veterans Day promo. In 2024 and 2025 it was reported as 10% off the meal plus a free appetizer or dessert for the table, for active-duty, retirees, and veterans with proof of service, dine-in or call-in. Darden’s own 2013 newsroom release shows the offer’s long history but a shifting format (that year it was a complimentary Texas Tonion appetizer and non-alcohol beverage over Nov 11–14). The format varies year to year, so re-verify each fall — and never treat a past year as a promised future offer.

For everyday value anyone can rely on, the LongHorn eClub is the move: a free-appetizer welcome coupon (with an adult entrée) that reliably arrives within about 24–48 hours of signup. Separately, a seasonal Darden gift-card bonus ("buy $500, get a $50 bonus card," roughly 9% off) can prepay meals across all Darden brands — verify a bonus event is live before relying on it. Neither is a military benefit, but each beats chasing an unverified register discount.
hers-military-discount: The discount is a standalone program price for the GLP-1 weight-loss line, not a coupon you stack on other offers, and it does not extend to any other Hers category. It was announced September 18, 2024 as an ongoing program rather than a one-time holiday sale.

Per secondary reporting, eligibility is confirmed through SheerID using an ID card, pay stub, or current licensure document; the primary press release did not name the provider, so treat the mechanic as "eligibility verification" and confirm the exact flow on the program page.

Because compounded semaglutide is a regulatory moving target, the offer’s availability and exact terms are volatile. Re-check forhers.com/appreciation before relying on any specific price, and compare annual versus monthly billing on the subscription.
publix-military-discount: Publix uses no digital verification service — no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute. Eligibility is confirmed the old-fashioned way: you show a physical veteran or military ID card, discharge documents, or a driver’s license with a veteran designation to the cashier on Veterans Day. There is no account to create and no online military portal.

The 10% comes off your pre-tax grocery total, which already reflects that week’s BOGO and shelf pricing, so on November 11 an eligible shopper effectively gets 10% on top of sale prices. Publix’s exclusions are item categories — prescriptions, alcohol, tobacco, gift cards, lottery, postage, and money services — not "sale items," so BOGO groceries appear to qualify. Interaction with manufacturer coupons on the same trip is not spelled out, so confirm at the register.

Publix has run the Veterans Day discount at a steady 10% every year from 2022 through 2025, and it is expected to recur on November 11, 2026, but it is never promised in advance. Because Publix controls the terms, treat the figures here as a starting point and confirm the current-year newsroom release before you shop.
houston-zoo-military-discount: The Zoo uses flex pricing, so the standard adult rate varies by date and time; the 50% military discount comes off the applicable general-admission price for your chosen date. Children (3–12) and seniors (65+) already receive an automatic 20% off at checkout, but the 50% military rate is the deeper discount for eligible guests within the 5-guest cap.

Verification is via SheerID online (which issues a one-time discount code) or by presenting a valid military ID at the gate. Either way, you must show proof of military service when presenting your ticket. There is no ID.me or GovX integration reported for the Zoo.

For repeat visitors, a Houston Zoo membership can beat repeated single-day military pricing if you will visit two or more times a year, and it adds parking and member perks. SNAP/WIC households should also compare the separate Lone Star $9 ticket rate.
dennis-kirk-military-discount: There is nothing to verify at Dennis Kirk — it has no military-verification partner because it has no military offer. Any site prompting you to “verify for a Dennis Kirk military discount” is not offering a real Dennis Kirk program. Military Markdown’s own investigation reached the same conclusion and debunked the fabricated 10–85% “military” codes that circulate on aggregator pages (orangeoffer, valuecom, worthepenny, knoji).

The real levers are open to everyone. The biggest is the Low Price Guarantee: if you find the same in-stock item cheaper at a qualifying competitor (on select categories and items over $100), Dennis Kirk beats it by a dollar — which can beat any percentage a military program would have given. Free shipping kicks in at $89, an easy threshold on a typical parts order, and same-day shipping applies to orders placed before the daily cutoff.

Watch the public promotions calendar rather than a military offer. Dennis Kirk runs seasonal public sales (riding-season, Black Friday) open to everyone, and a one-time email sign-up welcome offer for new subscribers. There is no documented military-specific Veterans Day discount.
american-eagle-military-discount: We lead by correcting the record because the honest answer is "no official program." American Eagle’s own promotion and help pages list no military discount, and ID.me’s American Eagle page states plainly that it is "not aware that American Eagle offers Military discounts." That means there is no online discount and no account-based verification (no ID.me, SheerID, or GovX brand-run percentage offer) for service members at AE or Aerie.

The single offer with any outside corroboration is a store-level ~10% off with a military ID, documented on a Tanger Outlets mall-landlord listing marked "See store for details." Because that is a third party rather than AE, treat the 10% as store-reported and unverified at the corporate level: the percentage, the eligible groups (aggregators claim active duty, veterans, retirees, and Reserve/Guard; spouses and dependents are not stated), and whether it runs at all are all store-dependent. Call ahead before relying on it.

Two marketplace listings can look like AE military discounts but are not: WeSalute’s "American Eagle" deal is a BenefitHub gift-card marketplace offer behind a paid WeSalute+ membership, and GovX is a members-only marketplace that may resell AE goods — neither is an AE-run percentage discount. If you want a confirmed apparel military discount, brands like Levi’s, Gap, and Old Navy publish one via ID.me; verify current terms at each.
frigidaire-military-discount: Frigidaire verifies eligibility through SheerID. You submit your eligibility details on the SheerID form; on approval Frigidaire issues a single-use code you enter at frigidaire.com checkout. This is a per-purchase code, not a permanent account status, so you re-verify for each future order. There is no ID.me and no GovX route for Frigidaire.

Two myths are worth killing. First, aggregator pages blur the tiers into a single "25% off Frigidaire military" — that is wrong: 25% is parts, accessories, and filters only and explicitly excludes appliances; appliances are 10%, and there is no combined "35% off." Second, "verify with ID.me" is wrong — the provider is SheerID, and ID.me publicly says it isn’t aware of a Frigidaire military offer.

On a whole appliance, do the math before using the code. A deeper public or clearance price frequently beats the 10%, and on a big-ticket unit a tax-free Exchange purchase can flip the ranking if AAFES/NEX actually stocks the model — so price-check first. For parts and filters, skip the comparison: the 25% SheerID code is the best deal, full stop.
hilton-military-discount: For the Military Family Rate, Hilton does not use an online verification partner — eligibility is confirmed by showing a valid military ID at check-in. No special account is required to book, though a Hilton Honors account is needed to earn points. For Hilton’s government per diem rates, you show valid government identification at check-in.

Hilton’s readable official page does not publish a fixed percentage; many third-party sources cite "up to 10% off," but that figure is not clearly confirmed on the live offer page, so this guide does not state a number. Check the actual rate on Hilton.com for your specific hotel and dates.

Hilton also runs a separate Hilton All-Inclusive military offer that is verified online through ID.me (and lists additional audiences such as nurses and first responders). That is a different promotion from the Military Family Rate covered here.
disneyland-hotel-military-discount: The Disneyland Hotel military offer is not gated by ID.me, SheerID, or GovX. You book on your word by phone, and Disney verifies at check-in: the eligible service member or spouse must present a valid military identification and be an occupant of the room. If valid ID isn’t presented at check-in, the non-discounted room price is charged for the duration of the stay. (This is separate from the military ticket offer, which does use GovX or U.S. military base ticket offices.)

Disney publishes no percentage for the hotel rate — only "great rates on select rooms" on a limited, date-variable allotment. Aggregators and travel blogs confidently quote "up to 35% off the Disneyland Hotel" (and up to 40% / 30% for the Grand Californian and Pixar Place), but those figures come from Disney’s retired 2009–2017 Armed Forces Salute structure (fixed 30% value / 35% moderate / 40% deluxe off rack). Disney replaced that with variable "up to" maximums that can be smaller — or zero — on any given date, so treat "35%" as an unverified third-party estimate, never Disney’s current rate.

The military hotel rate is "not valid in combination with any other hotel discounts or offers," so the military rate, the Disney Visa rate (up to ~25% on Sun–Thu windows), the AAA rate (up to ~25% at the Disneyland Hotel on 4+ consecutive nights in summer), and any public offer are mutually exclusive — ask the phone agent to quote every rate you qualify for and book the single lowest. That "no combining" rule applies only within hotel discounts: it does not stop you from separately buying discounted Disney Military Promotional Tickets, so do both. There is no exchange, GovX, cashback-portal, or pro-deal path for an on-property Disney hotel room — booking is direct with Disney by phone.
boden-military-discount: Boden uses SheerID. You verify your status once through SheerID — which checks authoritative records for your group — and receive a unique coupon code to enter at checkout. Codes are single-use and tied to the offer window; SheerID states your personal info is used only for identity confirmation and isn’t sold or shared. Boden USA does not use ID.me, GovX, WeSalute, or VerifyPass for this offer.

The 20% hero code cannot be combined with any other Boden offer, so you pick one Boden code per order — the hero code or a public sitewide code, whichever is larger. It also doesn’t touch Sale, Clearance, Multibuy, or Gift Card items. A cashback portal is different: it’s a separate rebate paid by the portal, not a Boden discount, so it layers on top of whichever single code you use. Standard caveat — some portals void the rebate if you apply a non-approved code, so confirm the order tracks.

Ignore the "40% Boden military discount for in-store use" claim seen on aggregator sites: Boden USA has no US retail stores (the US channel is online and catalogue only), and Boden’s own page publishes a single 20% figure with Military as one of five equally-weighted groups. There is no separate or larger military-only rate.
pandora-military-discount: Pandora uses ID.me to confirm military eligibility. You verify through ID.me (a free account is required), and on success Pandora issues a promo code that is single-use, limited to one per customer per 24 hours, and expires 60 days after you receive it. ID.me may periodically require re-verification per its own policies, so don’t assume a one-time, permanent verification. For verification problems, use ID.me support; for code or order issues, contact Pandora. In-store redemption is available only where the store supports ID.me.

The exclusions are specific: the code doesn’t apply to 14K gold, Lab-Grown Diamonds (Diamonds by Pandora), or gift card/e-card purchases, and it can’t be combined with any other offer or used on prior purchases. Because Pandora also runs frequent sitewide sales (e.g., "up to 50% off select styles"), and those can’t be stacked with the military code, compare the 10% against the current sale price to see which saves more on your item. If the code won’t apply, check that your bag has no excluded items, that the code is under 60 days old, and that no other promo is applied.

Two disambiguations worth keeping straight. First, students get a separate 10% discount via Student Beans (online only), not this military offer. Second — and most importantly — the Pandora music-streaming service (pandora.com) is a completely different company; its 20% "Pandora Premium" military deal (via SheerID) is not this jewelry discount. This page is the 10% ID.me jewelry offer at pandora.net.
jegs-military-discount: Coupon aggregators advertise "10% Off JEGS Military & Veteran Discounts," "up to 10–25% via ID.me," and codes to "verify with your Military ID at checkout." None of it holds up against primary sources: ID.me itself says it is not aware of any JEGS military discount, there is no ID.me, GovX, or SheerID verification gate at jegs.com, and a full-text search of JEGS’ help center returns no military program — only the APO/FPO shipping FAQ. Treat every "JEGS military discount code" as fabricated until JEGS itself says otherwise.

The real either/or that coupon pages never explain: JEGS’ promo codes and its Price Match Guarantee cannot be combined on the same order. The price match — a self-serve "Lowest Price Guarantee" button on product pages — matches listed prices at Summit Racing, items Sold by Amazon, and verified eBay stores, and is often the biggest single lever. The recurring public promo codes run in sitewide-style dollar-off tiers, but they default to JEGS-brand (555) products only unless noted and exclude engines, blocks, transmissions, and all clearance. The live code and its tiers change constantly, so verify the current one on jegs.com/Deals rather than trusting a coupon site.

For a genuine military-specific edge in this category, cross-shop Summit Racing: it runs a real ~10% manual military discount (arranged through customer service, non-combinable, clearance excluded) on much of the same catalog. JEGS has also historically run public Veterans Day sale pages (2023 and 2024) — themed public promos open to everyone, not verified military-only rates. The one military accommodation JEGS does document is APO/FPO shipping, arranged by phone at 1-800-345-4545.

teva-military-discount: Teva is a Deckers Brands label, a sister brand to Hoka and UGG, and Deckers brands generally do not run direct military discounts. A search of ID.me, GovX, and Teva’s own site turns up no military, veteran, or first-responder program: ID.me’s Teva page states plainly, "We’re not aware that Teva offers Military discounts," and Teva does not appear as a GovX marketplace store. So the honest question for a service member is not "what is the Teva military rate" but "which public savings path wins."

Be cautious of aggregator pages that advertise a "Teva military discount." No verified military rate is published, and the ID.me entry that surfaces for Teva is the general ID.me Shop cashback and free-shipping perk — available to everyone through the shopping portal, not a military-gated discount. We do not repeat any circulating "military percentage" here because doing so would imply an offer Teva does not run.

The reliable ways to save are all public. Teva.com’s Sale and outlet are the deepest reliable markdowns (often 20–40% off, best at end-of-season and around summer holidays like Memorial Day, July 4, and Labor Day). A public email/SMS welcome code gives about 10% on a full-price pair but usually cannot be stacked on already-reduced sale items. Routing a full-price order through ID.me Shop (or another cashback portal) adds a small rebate — just do not add a non-portal code that voids it.

If you already shop REI, that is often the best substitute path: REI stocks Teva widely, and a $30 lifetime Co-op membership earns a roughly 10% annual dividend on eligible full-price purchases, plus member sales, REI Outlet, and generous returns. Approved ExpertVoice pros can access a Teva pro store with deeper pricing, but that is industry/invite-gated and personal-use only — not a military benefit, and military is not a guaranteed eligible category.
champs-sports-military-discount: Champs uses SheerID for online orders: select the military discount at checkout, upload documentation showing your name, branch, and current military status, and SheerID confirms eligibility — usually within about 20 minutes. In stores, you simply show a valid military ID at the register. Note the guardrails: four SheerID verifications per rolling 30 days and a $100 maximum discount per verification. Despite what some aggregators claim, Champs does not use ID.me — ID.me's own site says it isn't aware Champs offers a discount — and no GovX path is published either.

The honest strategy is timing, not the badge. The 10% doesn't combine with other offers, and Champs runs frequent public sales at 20–40% off — historically deep around Veterans Day, Memorial Day, Black Friday, and back-to-school. When one of those is live, the public sale price beats the flat 10% outright. Use the military discount when no better sale or code is running and your items aren't excluded.

Champs Sports is a Foot Locker, Inc. banner, and the identical 10% SheerID military program runs at Foot Locker and Kids Foot Locker — same discount, same verification, same exclusions — so check the sister stores if your size is sold out. Repeat buyers can also join FLX, the Foot Locker family loyalty program, to earn rewards on whatever they pay. And if you're after one specific brand, Nike, adidas, and others run their own military discounts on their own sites, sometimes with better stock.
gymshark-military-discount: Verification is handled by WeSalute, Gymshark’s military verification partner since 2019. You create or sign in to a WeSalute account and confirm your eligibility, and WeSalute then unlocks access to Gymshark’s private member store where the 10% applies at checkout. Gymshark’s pages don’t state an exact re-verification cadence; one aggregator cites a 12-month renewal, but that is not confirmed by Gymshark or WeSalute, so we don’t assert it.

An important correction: widely circulated coupon-site claims that Gymshark verifies a "Military and First Responder Discount" via "ID.me or SheerID at checkout" are not confirmed by any primary source. Gymshark’s own US Discounts page lists only WeSalute for military, and ID.me’s shop page states it is not aware that Gymshark offers a military or first-responder discount via ID.me. There is no US first-responder, teacher, nurse, or government offer on Gymshark’s page.

On where it works: Gymshark and WeSalute describe the 10% as an online-checkout benefit that can’t be applied retroactively. In-store or app redemption is claimed by some third-party sites but isn’t confirmed by Gymshark, so don’t rely on it — ask in-store staff if you’re shopping a retail location. Gymshark separately runs a student discount (12% via Student Beans or UNiDAYS in the US), which is its own program, not the military offer.
darn-tough-military-discount: VerifyPass handles all four groups — military, first responder/government, healthcare, and teacher — with separate application flows. Per Darn Tough’s FAQ, a status document is generally sufficient, and work-email verification is accepted for some fields; re-verification frequency is not stated. The provider debunk matters: several aggregators say the discount runs "via ID.me," but ID.me Shop’s Darn Tough page is just an affiliate/cashback listing that links back to this program — the verification is VerifyPass. Likewise, the "30–50% off Darn Tough codes" on coupon sites are confirmed by no official source.

The stacking rules are simple because they’re absolute: Darn Tough’s promotion terms allow exactly one offer or discount code per order, codes can’t buy gift cards, and codes don’t combine with warranty credits. Treat "20% + cashback portal" as unreliable too — portals commonly void payouts when a non-portal code is applied (no Darn Tough-specific ruling is published; that’s the standard portal risk). Cashback is the fallback for shoppers who can’t verify: ExtraBux paid 8%, TopCashback 4.04%, and Rakuten 3% on the public price as of July 4, 2026.

Two channels can beat 20% for the right reader. ExpertVoice hosts an active Darn Tough store advertising up to 60% off MSRP for qualified experts — ExpertVoice hosts military-affiliation groups, but which groups unlock the Darn Tough store is confirmed only after login, so check before assuming. And retailer closeouts on discontinued colors regularly go past 20%: REI’s outlet had the Hiker Micro Crew at ~27% off during its July 4, 2026 sale window. GovX runs a member storefront too (pricing gated behind login — compare its net against the 20% path), and AAFES and the Navy Exchange both stock Darn Tough tactical styles tax-free.

The quiet total-cost lever is the guarantee: every Darn Tough sock is unconditionally guaranteed for life, with free replacement and no receipt needed — over years of wear that beats any coupon. Layer the free stuff too: Micro Crew Rewards pays 5 points per $1 (plus 150 signup points), the referral program gives a friend 10% off a first order and earns you points worth up to 15% off, and the brand’s only recurring blowout is the in-person Vermont Sock Sale in Northfield, VT each November (2025: November 22–23) — steep discounts on seconds that keep the lifetime guarantee.
mount-vernon-military-discount: The everyday military and teacher discount runs through ID.me. You create or sign in to a free ID.me account, verify your status once, and receive a single-use discount code — "one ticket per ID," so it’s a per-person gate discount rather than a code you can multiply across a party. The Purple Heart and Veterans Day free-admission benefits are handled in person at the ticket window by self-identification; Mount Vernon states no additional proof is requested for Purple Heart recipients.

One source wrinkle worth knowing: ID.me’s own Mount Vernon landing page shows an inconsistent "$3 off" headline against "save $4 on general admission" in the body, plus a stale ticket price. Mount Vernon’s own pages describe the benefit as $4 off, so that’s the figure we carry — and it’s worth a quick re-check on the official page if a dollar matters to your plans.

Also watch out for coupon aggregators advertising "$20 Off Mount Vernon Military & Veteran Discounts" codes. There is no $20-off ticket code. The only real $20 is the military membership discount — a one-time reduction on a membership that then includes a year of free daytime admission. For anyone visiting twice or more in a year, that membership beats repeat gate fees; for a single visit, the real everyday ticket benefit is $4 off via ID.me, and the free Purple Heart and Veterans Day offers beat everything when you qualify.
take-5-military-discount: The offer itself is refreshingly simple: 25% off any oil change, all year, with no third-party verification service to sign up for. Take 5 doesn’t use ID.me, GovX, or SheerID for this — you just show proof of service or a valid government-issued military ID to the technician at the shop. Because Take 5 is a stay-in-your-car, drive-up service with no online checkout, there’s no code to enter and nothing to redeem on the web; verification happens in person at each visit.

The eligibility wording is where to be careful. Take 5’s coupon tile is labeled "Veterans & Military" and its 2024 press release headline honors veterans, but the groups the company actually enumerates are "active, reserve, or retired." That leaves separated veterans who didn’t retire in a gray area — plus spouses, dependents, and National Guard, none of which the official sources address by name (Guard most likely falls under "reserve," but Take 5 doesn’t say so). If you’re in one of those groups, the honest move is to confirm with your local shop before counting on the discount.

Two mechanics trip people up. First, the coupon is only "valid if emailed or texted," which means you have to opt into Take 5 marketing to receive it — you can unsubscribe afterward. Second, coupons "typically cannot be combined with other offers," so the 25% military discount won’t stack with Take 5’s general "$15 off" coupon; bring whichever saves more on your service. A delivered coupon may also show an expiration date even though the underlying discount is year-round, and because Take 5 runs 1,000+ company-owned and franchised shops, participation and exact terms can vary location to location.
trijicon-military-discount: Trijicon runs no verification at its own checkout — verification happens on the partner platforms. Its official page says: "We partnered with ExpertVoice to put a program together to give you special pricing on select optics… We also offer a program with Guidefitter which offers special pricing to Military and Law Enforcement." No exact percentage is stated anywhere on Trijicon’s site. Guidefitter uses your LES, a @mail.mil address, or discharge-status confirmation; ExpertVoice verifies partner-org affiliation; GovX runs its own free eligibility check. Each is a separate account.

The pro programs are real but not open to the general public. Guidefitter’s Trijicon Pro Program is "a membership program reserved for qualified outdoor professionals and other select individuals," covering military (active/reserve/veteran), first responders (LEO, retired LEO, Fire, EMS/EMT/paramedic, 911 dispatch, search & rescue), and outdoor/government/conservation pros — with verification typically under 3 business days. ExpertVoice offers MIL/LE pricing on select optics, with quizzes that unlock top-tier pricing. In both, depth is gated behind login and acceptance into a specific brand program is not guaranteed.

The most important insight for a shopper: on a hot commodity like the RMR, the open street price often matches the gated pro price. The RMR Type 2 RM06 routinely sells ~$569–$599 at OpticsPlanet, Brownells, and similar retailers versus the $779 MSRP, with no verification. Firearms forums report that pro-program pricing on Trijicon flagships is "real but modest," and that the street price frequently ties it — so always price-check the specific SKU before assuming a pro program wins.

The deepest documented lever isn’t a military percentage at all — it’s Trijicon’s periodic public factory rebate. In 2026 Trijicon ran a $100 rebate on eligible RMR LED models (April 3–May 31, 2026), excluding RMR Green Dot, Dual Illuminated, RMR HD, RMRcc, and RCR, claimed at MillionthRMR.com. It stacks on a normal retail purchase, so street price minus $100 (~$469–$499 net) is the best price we found — and it’s open to everyone. Trijicon runs these RMR/MRO rebates in periodic spring and fall windows; watch its promotions page.

lg-military-discount: Verification is handled by ID.me. You select the military group affiliation and complete ID.me’s prompts; verification is free. After your status is confirmed you register for the LG Store. LG says returning members can sign in directly, but it does not publish how long a verification lasts before re-verification is required, so do not assume it is permanent.

The headline percentage is a floor, not a ceiling. LG guarantees a minimum additional 10% (15% for LG STUDIO/LG SIGNATURE) off LG.com sale prices and does not publish a maximum, so actual savings can be higher when in-store bundle promos and seasonal markdowns stack on top.

Members can buy up to 100 items per year, with category limits, and free installation is available on many categories (excluding the LG STUDIO Refrigerator SRSXB2622S). LG’s official copy does not address combining the Partner Store discount with promo codes, gift cards, the Referral Program, or MyLG Rewards.
orvis-military-discount: Verification runs entirely through WeSalute (formerly Veterans Advantage), Orvis’ longtime partner — not ID.me, SheerID, or GovX. The catch is that verification is bundled with the paid WeSalute+ tier: $59.95 the first 12 months, $119.98 per 12 months after (multi-year plans and a $4.95 auto-enrolling 30-day trial also exist). WeSalute covers active duty, veterans, retirees, current and former Guard and Reserve, and immediate family — but on a $200 full-price cart, the 10% returns $20 against a $59.95 membership, so joining just for this discount loses money until you spend roughly $600 per year on qualifying full-price Orvis items. On top of that, the offer page itself said the benefit was "currently being updated by the partner" as of July 13, 2026, so there may be nothing to redeem right now at all.

Be skeptical of what coupon and aggregator pages claim. Several describe the 10% as available "in-store and online every day" — the WeSalute offer terms say online at orvis.com only, and no primary source verifies any everyday in-store military discount (Orvis ran in-store "$25 off $50" military weekends around Veterans Day circa 2012–2014, but no recent recurrence is verified). Sites advertising "70% off Orvis promo codes" are dressing up the public sale section; the only sitewide code we could verify is the 15% new-subscriber welcome code. And pitches to "verify with ID.me for an Orvis discount" are dead ends — ID.me itself says it is not aware of one.

Nothing at Orvis stacks. The WeSalute offer cannot be combined with any other promotional offer, and orvis.com/exclusions repeats the rule for all promos: one code per order, full price only, nothing on sale items or at the Orvis Outlet. Fishing gear is excluded from the military discount, the welcome code, and general promo codes alike — so fly anglers should watch the sale section, where fly gear does appear at real markdowns. The one legitimate payment-side play is the Orvis Rewards Visa: roughly 5% back in Orvis gift cards (5 points per $1; 2,500 points = $25 gift card) plus free standard shipping, and because it is a card benefit rather than a promo code, it applies even on sale prices.

Other routes are ruled out or unverified. There is no Orvis storefront on GovX, and the military exchanges (AAFES, NEX) do not stock Orvis, so no tax-free channel exists. An ExpertVoice Orvis brand page exists, but whether military members can access it could not be verified. Orvis’ own Pro Program is for fishing and wingshooting industry professionals — guides, instructors, media — and is not a military program. Cashback portals showed a top rate around 3% per CashbackMonitor as of July 13, 2026 (Rakuten has no Orvis store), but that rate could not be confirmed portal-by-portal — verify it live before counting on it.
mac-cosmetics-military-discount: MAC uses SheerID, a third-party verifier — not ID.me, despite some aggregator claims, and not GovX. You confirm eligibility once; SheerID may ask for a document upload if it can’t verify instantly. Approval issues a single-use promo code. This is not a permanent account discount: each redemption cycle (every 30 days) requires a fresh code. Ignore coupon sites advertising a "35% military discount" — that figure is fabricated; MAC’s own Appreciation Discount page states 15% for military.

Because the code stacks with nothing, timing is the real lever. MAC historically runs sitewide Friends & Family and seasonal sales around 25–30% off a few times a year (spring, summer, holiday/Black Friday). When one of those is live, it beats the 15% code — and since they can’t combine, you simply use whichever is bigger. The 15% is evergreen, so it’s always there when no larger sale is running.

A few extra moves layer value without breaking the no-stack rule. MAC Lover (free loyalty) adds points, a birthday gift, and free-shipping tiers on any price you pay. A cashback portal like Rakuten or TopCashback may pay back a few percent, but many portals exclude appreciation-code orders — verify the portal’s MAC terms before counting on it. And if you have exchange access, AAFES/NEX shopping is tax-free, though MAC brand stock at the exchanges is unconfirmed.
ticketmaster-military-discount: For GovX offers, eligibility is confirmed through GovX’s own free membership and proprietary verification — you create a GovX account once, and GovX confirms your military/government status before granting access to offers. Re-verification frequency is not stated by Ticketmaster; GovX governs its own rules. Ticketmaster does not document an ID.me or SheerID flow for military discounts, and ID.me’s shop page indicates it is not aware of a Ticketmaster military discount. For venue box-office discounts, verification is whatever ID the venue requires in person. For Vet Tix, eligibility is verified by the Veteran Tickets Foundation at registration.

The key thing to understand is that there’s no fixed number. Because each organizer sets whether a military offer exists and what it’s worth, Ticketmaster publishes no standard percentage — so treat any coupon-site "10%," "25%," or "up to 50% off" as unverified. Many events simply have no military offer, so the honest approach is to check the specific event page (or GovX) rather than expecting a guaranteed discount.

The two channels serve different needs. GovX surfaces event-specific paid discounts for a broad eligible community (military, first responders, law enforcement, government, EMS), while Vet Tix gives active military and veterans free tickets to eligible events with availability. For venue-run pricing not shown online, contacting the box office directly is worth it. And for general (non-military) savings, Ticketmaster’s ticket deals and official presale/onsale timing help, while SeatGeek, StubHub, and league/team programs occasionally run their own military offers worth comparing per event.
adobe-military-discount: The honest core fact: Adobe does not publish a direct military or veteran discount. Its Special Offers page shows intro pricing, education pricing, and business plans — but no military rate at all. That makes the education price (for students/teachers) or the public intro the real starting points for a service member shopping Adobe, not a military code.

Why the "military %" claims keep circulating. Coupon aggregators and "military law" listicles confidently advertise an "Adobe military discount" of 13%–30%, including a "30% off Acrobat Pro for military." No official Adobe source confirms any of it. The 15% (Creative Cloud) and 20% (Premiere Pro) figures that do exist are WeSalute member benefits requiring a paid membership — not Adobe-direct — and the "30% Acrobat" claim could not be confirmed on Adobe.com.

Where the real savings are. Adobe’s genuinely large published discount is the education (student/teacher) price — over 71% off, ~$19.99/mo the first year, verified via SheerID. It is not a military benefit, but it is widely usable: it applies to anyone in the household who currently qualifies as a student or teacher, and it crushes the WeSalute 15%.

When WeSalute makes sense. The WeSalute+ Adobe offer (15% Creative Cloud, 20% Premiere Pro) is a real benefit, but it lives behind a paid WeSalute+ membership and is verified by WeSalute, not Adobe. It only saves money net of your annual dues — so it makes sense mainly if you already pay for WeSalute+ for its travel and other perks. Otherwise Adobe’s own promos often win.
smith-and-wesson-military-discount: Eligibility is gated by a GovX ID — you verify military, law-enforcement, or first-responder status with GovX once, then use it to submit the rebate. There’s no in-store percentage to verify; the value comes after purchase as a prepaid card, typically issued weeks later. Confirm the current qualifying purchase-date window before you buy, because rebates run in windows and the amount can change.

The rebate’s big advantage is that it’s a post-purchase manufacturer rebate, so it stacks on whatever retail price you pay a dealer — the discount and the rebate aren’t mutually exclusive the way a store coupon would be. That makes the maximum-savings path clear: shop the lowest online price, transfer to a local FFL (typically a ~$20–$40 fee), and file the $150 rebate on top.

Two cautions from the brief: don’t confuse the periodic public consumer rebates S&W runs (open to everyone) with the military/LE rebate — check which program a given gun qualifies for, and if both overlap, take the larger single rebate rather than assuming they stack. And ignore aggregator claims of an "S&W military discount 15–20% off" at checkout — Smith & Wesson doesn’t sell firearms at a point-of-sale military percentage.
revzilla-military-discount: RevZilla verifies eligibility through GovX ID, a free verification account for military and first responders. You build your cart, click the GovX ID banner in the cart, and verify once with your service documentation; RevZilla then recognizes the verified account at checkout on future orders. The discount applies automatically — so read the order total before paying, because that’s the only place the actual percentage appears and the only way to confirm your items weren’t silently excluded.

The no-stacking rule is absolute. RevZilla’s own terms say the discount "may not be stacked with any other promotion, code and/or offer" — no sign-up code, no sale price, no RPM member pricing on top. Pick one savings path per order. And the exclusion list is long: 70+ brands, including Alpinestars, Dainese, REV’IT!, Shoei, Arai, AGV, HJC, Shark, and every tire and wheel manufacturer, because some manufacturers don’t allow RevZilla to extend a discount.

One thing to watch: aggregator sites quote hard numbers RevZilla never states. WorthEPenny headlines "5% Off RevZilla Military," others claim 10–25% for military "including veterans and immediate families." RevZilla’s own pages publish no percentage and no veteran or family eligibility — the offer is for active-duty or retired police, military, fire, and EMS, with the amount revealed only after GovX ID verification at checkout. Treat every quoted number as unverified until you see your own cart.

Because the amount is unpublished and community reports put it around 5%, the smarter plays are often elsewhere: the public 10% email code on a first order, the Closeout section (20–50% off, which the military discount won’t beat or join), the RPM membership (reported $39.99/yr for 5% RPM Cash back plus 10% off 70+ brands across RevZilla, Cycle Gear, and J&P Cycles), or Cycle Gear’s in-store version of the same GovX ID program, which is published at 20% off exclusive brands and 10% off third-party brands with valid ID.
athleta-military-discount: Athleta’s military discount is a discretionary in-store benefit: you show a valid military ID at the register and, where the store participates, get 10% off. There’s no third-party provider and no account to create, so there’s no re-verification cycle — but there’s also nothing to redeem online. Because Athleta doesn’t publish the discount, the figure comes from a secondary military-discount directory (Medium confidence), so treat the 10% as “ask and confirm locally,” not a guaranteed rate.

The online reality is a myth to correct. ID.me’s Athleta page plainly states, “We’re not aware that Athleta offers Military discounts,” and Athleta’s own coupons page lists no military offer or verification step. Some low-quality aggregators claim Athleta “redirects you to SheerID” for a sitewide online military discount — that is not verified; the generic shop.sheerid.com military landing page is not an Athleta-confirmed offer.

The one legitimate online-adjacent layer is GovX, which sells Athleta gift cards at about 5% off — you buy discounted gift cards, then spend them on a sale-priced order, effectively stacking ~5% under a public sale. It’s a small payment-side layer, not a sitewide military percentage.

For most shoppers the public offers win: a 20% email-signup code, deep sale/clearance, Rewards free shipping on $50+, and Athleta Preloved resale all typically beat a 10% in-store discount. On a $150 cart, the 20% signup code lands you at $120 versus $135 with the in-store 10% — so online shoppers should skip the hunt for a military code that doesn’t exist.
anker-military-discount: Anker verifies military eligibility through GovX ID, not ID.me. You create a free GovX account, verify your service once against your records, and receive a single-use code to apply at checkout on the brand site. The code is one-time — it is not a permanent status — and the program’s availability is set by Anker, which paused it on the main U.S. store on March 18, 2026. ID.me itself confirms it is not aware of an Anker or Anker SOLIX military offer, so any "ID.me Anker discount" you see elsewhere is inaccurate.

Because the flagship charger store’s program is paused, the practical move depends on what you’re buying. For a full-price Anker SOLIX power station, eufy security device, or soundcore audio product with no sale live, the up-to-20% GovX code on that brand’s own GovX page is worth verifying at checkout. For chargers and power banks from the main store, the GovX route is currently unavailable — lean on the public sale or Amazon price instead.

That public-sale path is usually the cheaper one regardless. Anker runs deep seasonal events — up to 46% sitewide in its Summer Sale and up to 65% off SOLIX at Earth Day — and Amazon coupon-clip pricing frequently ties or beats anker.com (the SOLIX C1000 hit a record-low roughly $399 against a $799 MSRP). Anker’s codes don’t combine with sales or with each other, so you generally pick the single lowest price rather than stacking.

Exchange-eligible shoppers have one more lever: the Navy Exchange stocks Anker tax-free, and AAFES typically does too. On big-ticket items, skipping sales tax can flip the ranking, so compare the tax-free Exchange price against Amazon and any live anker.com sale. Anker controls all of these terms and can change or restore them at any time, so confirm the current offer at the source before you buy.
pods-military-veteran: PODS’ model is a container you load at your own pace: the company drops a weather-resistant container at your door, you pack it over your included first 30 days, and PODS moves it to your new home or holds it at a secure Storage Center. The military discount layers onto that — up to 10% off the delivery and first month’s rental locally, and up to 10% off storage, delivery, and transportation on a long-distance move between PODS company-owned and/or franchise locations.

There are three ways to claim it: enter promo code SERV10 at online checkout, verify your military status with ID.me in your cart, or call PODS and have an agent apply it. A free ID.me account is the cleanest path because it confirms your status without you ever handing over a copy of your ID — and you should never email or send a photocopy of a military ID or CAC, which is not how legitimate verification works. The discount is "up to" 10% and cannot be combined with other PODS offers, so compare it against any general promotion running at the time.

Military families with USAA should also check USAA Perks, which has an alliance with PODS for savings on the move and monthly storage — a separate path you would compare against SERV10 rather than stack. As with any PCS, keep every receipt: a personally procured move (PPM/DITY) is reimbursable through your transportation office, so the container, mileage, and storage costs may come back to you regardless of the discount.
weber-military-discount: Weber verifies eligibility through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA and many major retailers. Verification happens inside weber.com checkout: you authenticate once with ID.me and the 10% applies to the order. Weber’s consumer-care article "What is the Weber.com Military Program?" is the official reference — its full terms load in a browser session, so check it for any caps or category exclusions before a large order. Military.com also reports a phone option for special military pricing (800-446-1071); that number isn’t confirmed on a readable Weber page, so verify it with Weber support before relying on it.

The discount is weber.com-only. Weber’s own blog states plainly that "any in-store discounts or sales advertised by a retailer are not controlled in any way by Weber" — so what a hardware store does at the register is that retailer’s policy, not Weber’s. The practical upside: Lowe’s and The Home Depot both carry Weber and run their own everyday 10% military programs, which match Weber’s rate if you want the grill assembled or picked up locally. And the military Exchange stocks Weber Spirit II and Genesis models tax-free on shopmyexchange.com.

The stacking rule that matters most: the military 10% does not combine with promo codes or promotional pricing. When Weber runs 20% off select grills — a public offer listed right alongside the military discount on ID.me Shop — the sale beats the 10%, and you have to pick one. Cashback is a similar story: an ID.me-gated checkout commonly breaks portal tracking, so treat military-10% orders as no-cashback; a no-code sale-price order is the portal-safe play (Rakuten paid 2.5% on weber.com as of July 14, 2026).

One thing to watch: aggregator sites inflate Weber’s program to "up to 10–25% off for military." The verified figure is 10%, via ID.me, on weber.com — the 20–25% numbers are Weber’s public promos on select grills, open to everyone. And GovX’s "Weber Tactical" storefront is a firearms-holster company, not Weber grills; there is no Weber grills storefront on GovX.
kennedy-space-center-military-discount: The Visitor Complex is operated for NASA by Delaware North and is not government-funded, which is why admission is charged and priced dynamically. That dynamic pricing is also why no honest guide can quote a fixed dollar figure here: pull the live adult one-day price before relying on any number.

Verification differs by channel. On-site, KSC accepts a physical military or veteran credential — an active-duty or retired military ID, a Choose VA card, a driver’s license with veteran designation, or a DD214 — at Will Call or Information. Online and at the front-of-park kiosks, verification runs through ID.me. A veteran who is not set up with ID.me can still redeem in person with a qualifying document.

Beyond KSC’s own channels, military and government tickets are also sold on GovX (a closed marketplace — compare its live price to the on-site military rate rather than stacking a code), and WeSalute lists "up to 30% off" admission, but that is WeSalute’s own paid-membership figure, not a KSC counter price. Aggregators confidently quote a flat "10%," "25%," or "up to 30%" year-round KSC military discount; KSC’s site confirms a discount exists but publishes no percentage, so treat those numbers as unverified. The only precisely documented, KSC-stated military offer is Armed Forces Week.
simplisafe-military-discount: Verification runs through VerifyPass, a third-party status-verification service. You select your eligible group at SimpliSafe.com/Protectors, submit proof through VerifyPass (creating a free VerifyPass account if prompted), and on approval SimpliSafe issues a one-time coupon to use at checkout. Treat the coupon as single-use per the terms, and re-verify if you need a new code.

The catch is stacking. SimpliSafe Support states the Protectors offer "may not be combined with other discounts or promotions or be applied retroactively." Because SimpliSafe’s public "up to 50% off" sale runs most of the year and frequently hits the same 50% — often adding a free camera with a one-month monitoring opt-in — the Protectors code’s marginal value is often $0 during an equal public sale. Its real worth is as a guaranteed floor when no public sale is running.

The official Protectors path is VerifyPass — not ID.me, GovX or SheerID. Some coupon and editorial pages claim ID.me verification; ID.me lists SimpliSafe only under its own separate cash-back program, which is not the official Protectors discount. Ignore aggregator claims of a "15% off" SimpliSafe military discount — the verified figure is 50% off a new system.

For the lowest real price, compare against the live public sale first, wait for Black Friday / Cyber Monday if you can (historically up to 70% off plus a free camera and a free month of monitoring — the best deal of the year), and consider a refurbished system (up to ~60% off, with a lifetime warranty when you add monitoring).
garmont-military-discount: The debunk is simple: any aggregator claim of a "Garmont military discount code," a flat "% off for veterans," or an "online via ID.me" Garmont offer is not verified. ID.me itself says it is not aware of a Garmont Tactical military discount, and the brand’s own site publishes no such program. The only verified identity-gated path is GovX member pricing, which is per-item and visible only after you log in.

How the paths compare depends on the item. Buying a single pair and you’re a verified GovX member? Price-check the T8 on GovX against brand retail and buy the lower — GovX pricing is login-gated, so we can’t quote the exact number. Buying two pairs (a T8 plus a Nemesis G-DRY)? The brand’s public "Buy 1 T8, get 35% off" bundle is likely the deepest. Not a GovX member and buying one pair? There’s no military discount — wait for a public sale or buy at brand retail.

A few caveats. GovX is a separate marketplace with its own account and checkout, so you can’t layer it onto a garmonttactical.com order, and cashback portals generally don’t track GovX checkouts. The public bundle and socks promos are open to everyone and rotate. And if you have base access, it’s worth a check whether AAFES/NEX stocks Garmont for a tax-free buy — but that carriage is unconfirmed, so verify in-store first.
milwaukee-tools-military-discount: Verification never happens at Milwaukee, because there’s nothing to verify — Milwaukee has no military program and no partnership with ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute (ID.me Shop lists no Milwaukee Tool store). At The Home Depot, you enroll once in its Military Discount Benefit and verify through SheerID, then use your account online or scan the app in-store. Northern Tool’s discount is a simple military-ID check at the register — no online account, and no online option.

Watch out for the fakes. Aggregator pages advertise a "Milwaukee Tools Military Discount – 10% Off" or a "FALL = 30% off" military code. The real 10% is The Home Depot’s retailer discount, misattributed to Milwaukee; codes like "FALL" are public promos open to everyone. No primary source shows Milwaukee Tool operating any service-verified discount.

For the math, take a ~$399 Milwaukee M18 FUEL kit. At Home Depot with the military discount, that’s about $359.10 — and enrolled military also skip sales tax on eligible HomeDepot.com products, which is worth roughly another $24–$40 depending on your state and often outweighs the 10% on larger carts. The 10% is capped at $400 in savings per calendar year (about $4,000 of eligible spend); the tax benefit has no cap. A deep public sale or "Milwaukee Days" kit deal can beat 10%, so compare before assuming the discount wins — and add a live E-Rebate on top whenever one covers your kit.
secretlab-military-discount: Secretlab uses ID.me to confirm military status. You verify once through ID.me and the $20 applies at checkout. There is no GovX storefront and no separate, larger military tier — the $20 is the offer, and it is the same amount Secretlab hands anyone through a referral link or a first-order newsletter credit.

The honest takeaway is that the military route is not special. If a seasonal sale is live, the marked-down price is almost always the better deal, and a $20 code typically will not add on top of it. If no sale is running, grab whichever single $20 offer you can — military ID.me, referral, or newsletter — because they are equivalent and cannot be combined.

Ignore the coupon-aggregator headlines promising "$150 off," "60% off," or "50% off Secretlab military." Those numbers are fabricated or are scraped from unrelated public sitewide-sale banners — they are not a military rate. The documented military offer is a flat $20 via ID.me.
frontier-military-discount: Coupon and aggregator pages often describe a "Frontier military discount," and Frontier’s own page title is literally "Frontier Military Discount" — but the body of that same page says "Frontier Airlines does not offer military discounts." The actual benefit is a baggage waiver, not a fare discount, and no ongoing "% off fares" appears anywhere on Frontier’s official pages. Treat any such claim as inaccurate unless Frontier itself republishes it.

The bag waiver is stated to apply "for all types of tickets, free of charge" — including Frontier’s cheapest basic fares, which normally bundle nothing but a personal item. That matters because Frontier is an unbundled, ultra-low-cost carrier: checked bags typically run roughly $40–$99+ each depending on route and when they’re purchased (cheapest at booking, most expensive at the airport), so waiving two checked bags plus a carry-on can be worth more than $100 round trip for an eligible traveler.

Eligibility is active-duty only as Frontier defines it: "current members of the military who are serving or may be called to serve," which explicitly includes the National Guard and Reserves and academy cadets, plus PHS Commissioned Corps/Ready Reserve Corps and NOAA Officer Corps. Separated veterans and retirees are not listed for this everyday benefit — they were named only in the historical Veterans Day fare promo, which is a different, limited-time offer with its own dates and restrictions.

The historical VETS promo (50% off base fares) ran with a specific booking window (Oct 24–27, 2024), travel window (through Dec 18, 2024), blackout dates, and route exclusions, and applied to base fare only. It is not an evergreen benefit — if you see "50% off" claimed as a standing Frontier military discount, that is the stale, out-of-context remnant of a since-expired seasonal promo, not a current offer.
carhartt-military-discount: Carhartt verifies eligibility through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. You create a free ID.me account and confirm your community — Military, First Responder, Nurse, or Medical Provider. Online, you click the ID.me button during checkout; in store, you present your validated ID.me eligibility card.

Carhartt states your ID.me account does not expire, so you can reuse the discount on later orders, though ID.me may ask you to re-confirm your identity or status at sign-in under its own policies. For verification problems, Carhartt directs shoppers to ID.me support.

One thing to watch: many coupon and aggregator pages still advertise a 25% Carhartt military discount. That figure is outdated — Carhartt reduced the discount to 15%, which is the only rate confirmed on Carhartt’s official page and on the ID.me store page.
biltmore-military-discount: Verification is a physical Military ID shown at the Reception & Ticketing Sales Center — there’s no ID.me, GovX, or SheerID app. You can also buy in advance by phone at 800-411-3812, handled by Biltmore’s guest services. The admission discount applies to regular adult daytime house admission, and the offer language extends it to the service member’s guests.

Be aware the $25 figure is elevated and time-framed. Biltmore describes it as increased "in honor of America’s 250th anniversary" and running through Labor Day; Military.com and older Q&A threads reference a smaller standing rate around $10. After the promotion window, the discount may revert, so re-verify the current dollar amount before each visit. Coupon sites advertising "25% off," "70% off," or "$8 off military" are stale or aggregator bait — the verified benefit is a flat dollar amount off admission plus 10% off dining and shops.

For the best total cost, buy adult daytime admission in advance (advance pricing typically beats the gate) with the military discount, and use the 10% at restaurants and shops for the rest of your visit. If you’ll visit more than twice a year, compare an Annual Pass against repeated $25-off day tickets.
equinox-military-discount: Note a common name collision: many "Equinox military discount" search results are actually about the Chevrolet Equinox EV (GM’s vehicle incentive) or the Minelab Equinox metal detector — neither is the Equinox fitness club. This guide is about Equinox gyms and the Equinox+ app, and for those there is simply no military, veteran, or first-responder discount and no verification partner.

The Amex Platinum $300 Equinox credit is the practical everyday saver. It’s a card benefit, not an Equinox discount, so it needs no Equinox-side eligibility — it applies to Equinox+ or an eligible club membership when you pay with the card (enrollment required). For eligible active-duty service members, Amex waives the card’s annual fee under the SCRA/MLA, so the $300 credit effectively makes the Equinox+ app free most of the year or takes $300 off a club membership at no card cost. The credit can even layer on top of a corporate/EFT rate, since it’s tied to your payment card — confirm your membership type is "eligible" with Amex.

The other levers are a corporate/EFT membership (an employer-negotiated payroll-deduct rate that commonly waives the ~$300-$500 initiation fee), timing your join to one of Equinox’s periodic public waived-initiation windows, and the free on-base MWR gym. If you want an actual gym military discount and Equinox isn’t essential, competitors like YouFit (~20%) or participating Anytime Fitness locations (~10-25%) run real ones.
tory-burch-military-discount: The single biggest public savings window is the Semi-Annual Sale, which Tory Burch runs roughly mid-June through early July and again in December–January. It marks down sale-section styles up to about 70%, with an extra 25% applied in-cart on eligible sale items and free shipping. It is open to everyone — no verification, no code — and when it is live it is usually the cheapest way to buy, so a shopper flexible on style should check toryburch.com/sale first.

For a specific current-season item on a first order, the 15%-off email/text welcome code is the play. Sign up for Tory Burch email or text and you get 15% off your first full-price purchase of $250+ (some variants show a $225+ threshold). It is full-price only — it excludes sale and final-sale items — and it is one-time use, so it cannot be stacked on the Semi-Annual Sale. There is also a $50-off-$200 birthday offer for account/birthday-club members.

You can layer a small cashback portal on top of a standard full-price welcome-code order: Rakuten shows 2% cash back on Tory Burch as of July 11, 2026. Portal rates move, and cashback commonly reduces or voids on scraped or exclusive-coupon orders, so confirm it tracked in your account after purchase. Treat that 2% as a stamped rate, not an evergreen number.

The one genuinely military-linked route is the Exchange. The online Exchange (shopmyexchange.com for AAFES, mynavyexchange.com for the Navy Exchange) carries Tory Burch sunglasses and select handbags at tax-free, exchange-set prices for authorized shoppers — including honorably discharged veterans who qualify for the Veterans Online Shopping Benefit. On a ~$298 bag, skipping roughly 7–9% sales tax is about $22–$27 saved. It is not a Tory Burch discount and it is a substitute, not a stack: you cannot add a toryburch.com code or Rakuten cashback on top of an Exchange order, so compare it net-of-tax against the brand-site route.
uppababy-military-discount: Start with the myth, because it’s everywhere: aggregators like WorthEPenny and Coupert claim UPPAbaby "provides a discount for military personnel — verify through VerifyPass on the UPPAbaby Military Discount page." That page does not exist — uppababy.com/military-discount returned a 404 on July 14, 2026 — and no VerifyPass offer for uppababy.com could be found. The claim appears to be boilerplate that conflates UPPAbaby the brand with the VerifyPass hero programs at two retailers that sell UPPAbaby: Albee Baby and Bambi Baby. Do not expect any percentage off at uppababy.com for military status.

The retailer path is real but conditional. Albee Baby’s Hero discount offers up to 20% off plus free shipping on qualifying orders to active duty, veterans and dependents, first responders, medical staff, and teachers, verified through VerifyPass with a one-time code — but it excludes sale items, price matches, furniture, items under $99, and "certain brands," and it can’t stack with other codes or registry-completion discounts. Bambi Baby’s 15% covers military and first responders on full-price items, with the store reserving the right to restrict brands from any discounting. Neither store publishes its excluded-brand list, and UPPAbaby is exactly the kind of price-controlled brand those clauses exist for — so the only reliable test is the cart: apply your code to the UPPAbaby item, and if the total doesn’t drop, the brand is excluded.

Why is this so locked down? UPPAbaby enforces MAP (minimum advertised price) across every authorized retailer, which is why a Vista V3 shows the same price everywhere it’s sold. The brand’s sanctioned discount channel is its own Last Chance page — markdowns on previous-generation models and colorways, historically around 15–20% off — plus a handful of historical sale windows: prior-gen markdowns around January–March and select items in the Nordstrom Anniversary Sale each July/August (historically ~20–25% below retail on select items). Those are past patterns, not promises.

Two more paths worth knowing. If you’re expecting, major baby registries offer a one-time completion discount (typically 10–15%) — the most reliable mainstream path, though UPPAbaby’s eligibility varies by registry, so check your registry’s brand terms. And the tax-free exchange route is unconfirmed: a Navy Exchange category page surfaces for the brand, but no UPPAbaby listings were verifiable on July 14, 2026, and no cashback-portal rate for uppababy.com could be verified either — we don’t promise either path.
build-a-bear-military-discount: We checked Build-A-Bear’s own pages — Current Promotions, the Customer Service help topics, the Bonus Club FAQ, the Birthdays page, and its investor-relations releases — and found no military or veteran discount and no military-status verification of any kind. Build-A-Bear does not appear on ID.me’s military directory, has no GovX storefront, and its make-your-own experience isn’t stocked through the military exchanges. In short, there is no first-party military route to claim.

Be cautious of coupon and deal sites (worthepenny, knoji, hotdeals and others) that advertise a current "20% off any purchase, verify through SheerID/ID.me" for Build-A-Bear. That figure is lifted from the expired 2010 in-store event, and the SheerID link attached to it resolves to Clinique’s Canadian Armed Forces program — not Build-A-Bear. We deliberately don’t repeat the percentage here, because doing so would imply an offer Build-A-Bear does not actually run.

The most reliable everyday saver is the free Bonus Club. You earn 1 point per $1 and get $10 in rewards for every 100 points — about 10% back as store credit toward a future order — plus a birthday reward and early access to sales. It costs nothing to join, needs no military status, and its points earn alongside public promos rather than competing with them, so it layers under almost everything else.

For a birthday, Pay Your Age (also run as Count Your Candles) is the single biggest saving here: a Bonus Club member buying in store during the child’s birth month, with the birthday child present, gets the special Birthday Treat Bear for the child’s age in dollars — turning 4 means a $4 bear, for ages 1 to 14. It applies only to that bear, not to outfits or accessories. Layer whatever public promo is live (Buy One, Get One for $15; 2-for-$30 charms; a $10 gift card for $5 with $25+ spend) for siblings or add-ons, and watch May and Veterans Day in case Build-A-Bear ever revives a military appreciation event — historical, not guaranteed.
childrens-place-military-discount: The verification question has a simple answer: there is none, because there is no everyday military offer. ID.me shows "not aware" pages for the military, nurse, first responder, teacher, government, medical, and student communities alike, and no GovX or SheerID storefront exists. ID.me members can still get member cash back and see public sale offers, but that is a portal benefit, not a military percentage off.

The reliable savings come from the brand’s frequent, deep public sales plus its loyalty wallet. Uniforms run 50% off, clearance up to 70% off, and joining text alerts unlocks a 30%-off welcome code. On top of that, My Place Rewards gives a $5 Discount per 100 points (usable on sale and clearance, up to $50/day) and PLACE Bucks earn $10 per $20 spent. The rules that govern stacking: one web code per order, codes don’t combine with a site-wide percentage-off event, and PLACE Bucks are their own lane that can’t ride on a % or $ coupon.

On a $100 regular-price cart, a single public % code lands you around $80, a deep seasonal sale event around $60, and uniform/clearance doorbusters can reach $30–$50 — all of which beat the historical 25% Veterans Day one-off (about $75, in-store only and not guaranteed). If you’re Exchange-eligible, note that ShopMyExchange carries only a Children’s Place gift card tax-free; the apparel itself isn’t stocked there, so there’s no tax-free apparel channel to change the math.
blackstone-military-discount: Blackstone’s discount is verified through GovX ID, a third-party service that confirms military, first-responder, and government eligibility. You log in to (or create) a free GovX ID account, prove your status through GovX’s real-time check, and receive a single-use code tied to your group. Each community — military, first responder, government — gets its own code, and because the code is single-use you re-verify for future orders. This is GovX ID specifically, not ID.me, SheerID, or WeSalute.

The catch is stacking. The 5% code doesn’t combine with sale or clearance items, gift cards, other promo codes, or Blackstone’s auto-applied "Deal of the Week" and bundle pricing — checkout takes one code per order. So the discount only helps on a full-price, direct-site item.

That’s why retail usually wins. Blackstone is a mass-market brand, and third-party retailers price the same griddles well under the direct MSRP — a 28-inch model listed at $349 direct has been seen around $224 at Walmart and roughly $300 in a Costco bundle. If you’re eligible for the military Exchange, Blackstone is stocked at AAFES (shopmyexchange.com) and the Navy Exchange (mynavyexchange.com) tax-free, with price-match — typically a better deal than the direct 5%.

Blackstone also runs public seasonal sales (Memorial Day, July 4, Black Friday) that are open to everyone and are usually deeper than 5%. They don’t stack with the GovX code, so take whichever discount is bigger. Because Blackstone controls the terms, confirm the current offer on its official GovX ID page before you buy.
discovery-cove-military-discount: Discovery Cove’s military benefit is powered by ID.me (also branded TroopID), the same free identity-verification service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. You verify your active-duty, reserve/Guard, veteran or retiree status once online, and your personalized discounted rate is then revealed inside the booking flow. Verification is done online, not at the gate — but you must still present a valid physical military or veteran ID at park reception.

Because Discovery Cove publishes no military percentage or price, treat any specific figure you see quoted on coupon or listicle sites as unverified. Some of those pages also conflate Discovery Cove with SeaWorld’s free active-duty admission — that is inaccurate for Discovery Cove, where the Waves of Honor benefit is always a discount, never free entry. The only reliable way to learn your rate is to verify with ID.me and view it in the booking flow.

The Waves of Honor rate is standalone: it cannot be stacked with public promo codes, seasonal sitewide sales, AAA, Florida-resident, annual-pass, or reseller pricing. Discovery Cove regularly runs public seasonal deals (historically around 30% off, open to everyone) that frequently match or beat the hidden military rate and cover your whole party rather than just four people. Base ITT/MWR ticket offices often sell SeaWorld-family tickets below gate price as well, so the smart move is to compare all three and book the single lowest option for your travel date.

Every Discovery Cove package also bundles 14 consecutive days of admission to SeaWorld Orlando or Aquatica Orlando. That is not a military perk — it comes with every booking regardless of status — but it is real added value, and active-duty members can separately claim free SeaWorld, Busch Gardens and Aquatica admission through Waves of Honor at those parks.
skims-military-discount: The "no military discount" finding is well supported. ID.me lists SKIMS but states plainly, "We’re not aware that SKIMS offers Military discounts," and no SKIMS military storefront exists on GovX, WeSalute, or VerifyPass. SKIMS’s own email/SMS signup page promises early access to drops and sales — not a percentage off and not a welcome code — so the "15–20% off your first order" line circulating on aggregators is not supported by the brand.

Because there’s no identity discount, the honest maximum-savings answer is a stack of public paths. Join SKIMS Rewards free for access perks (early sale access, waived US return fees, and free shipping at the ONYX tier — none of which is a percentage discount). Then route the purchase through a cashback portal: USAA MemberShop is the military-affiliated option at roughly 1.5% (as of May 26, 2026), while a public portal has run about 2%. Cashback portals sit on top of the purchase price and generally still track on full-price SKIMS orders, but they don’t create a bigger discount on a Sale price.

The real money is only in shopping the SKIMS Sale section during public sale events (Black Friday, seasonal drops), where select styles run 20–40%+ off — the one path that beats cashback on a full-price cart. Note SKIMS excludes Sale and final-sale items from promo codes, so you can’t code-stack on a marked-down style. If you carry an Amex, check your Amex Offers for a rotating SKIMS "+points per $" deal before buying.
cobra-golf-military-discount: On cobragolf.com there is no military discount to unlock: no ID.me, GovX, or SheerID military gate, and no brand checkout code for service members. Cobra Golf does not verify military status because there is no offer behind it. Any coupon site or golf blog stating "Cobra honors military with 10% via ID.me" is repeating a brand mix-up — that offer belongs to Cobra Electronics at cobra.com, a separate radios-and-radar company. We omit that figure here because repeating it would imply an offer Cobra Golf does not run.

ExpertVoice is the only military-relevant channel, and it is a separate professional-verification platform, not a Cobra program. Cobra runs a pro store on ExpertVoice where verified members see member pricing reported around 25% off full-price items, and active military is among ExpertVoice’s eligible communities. It is not a blanket veteran discount, though: eligibility and access to the Cobra store follow ExpertVoice’s own rules and can require an accepted affiliation, and the program is personal-use only with purchase caps and no resale.

The honest nuance most sources miss is that ExpertVoice is frequently beaten by Cobra’s own prices. Cobra’s checkout explicitly flags marked-down items as "on sale now — lower than your ExpertVoice discount / not eligible for ExpertVoice discount," because sale items are excluded from ExpertVoice. So for a service member the smart move is to compare the live public sale price against the ExpertVoice price for the same club and buy whichever is lower — on sale items, the public price wins.

Even without a military discount, there are strong ways to save on Cobra: public promo codes and price drops run frequently at 25–45% off prior-generation clubs; last-generation and certified pre-owned gear deliver the lowest cost per club; the deepest markdowns land at Black Friday / Cyber Monday and at new-model launch windows when older lines clear out. Cobra also runs public seasonal deals around Memorial Day and Veterans Day, but none is verified as military-gated — they are open to everyone.
garage-military-discount: Garage is a young-women’s fast-fashion apparel brand (Groupe Dynamite) whose savings live in loyalty, sale-stacking, and cash back rather than in an identity discount. There is no military/veteran/first-responder/nurse/teacher program on Garage’s site, and Garage is not listed on ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute. If that ever changes, this page will be updated with the official details.

Be cautious of coupon and deal sites that claim military members "unlock 10% off with code GET10" or get "military savings during Labor Day or Independence Day." There is no military-specific offer: the ~10% is the ordinary loyalty/newsletter welcome code any shopper can get, and the holiday markdowns are public, everyone-eligible sales. We do not present either as a military benefit.

The Garage Collectif loyalty program is free to join and gives a ~10% welcome code, a birthday gift, and a higher-spend VIP tier. Rakuten cash back (2% as of July 13, 2026) is a post-purchase portal rebate that layers on top of the sale price or any code — the one exception being gift cards and purchases made with gift cards. Free standard shipping kicks in at $75+ after discounts and before tax, and it is threshold-based, not a code, so it does not consume the single-code slot.
