Because Garage typically allows only one discount code per order, the winning move depends on the item. If it is on the sale rack, buy the sale price and route through Rakuten — sale + cash back usually beats the ~10% welcome code. If you are buying full-price as a member, apply the ~10% Garage Collectif welcome code, then Rakuten on the paid total. If you are a verified student, a third-party Student Beans code (online) can beat both, but that is a student path, not a military one.
staccato-military-discount: Staccato’s discount is verification-gated: eligibility is confirmed through VerifyPass, where you upload documentation proving your service or first-responder status. On approval, Staccato emails a single-use discount code, typically within one business day, which you apply on a direct Staccato2011.com order. Contact heroes@staccato2011.com or (512) 686-3613 with questions.

The two programs do not stack, and neither combines with a third-party dealer’s pricing — the code only applies on a direct Staccato order. Active-duty law enforcement should always use Blue Line (20% / $800 off), which no other path beats. For the Heroes 10% audience, the catch is that the discount is off MSRP: because Staccato pistols routinely sell below MSRP at FFL dealers, the genuine best move is to price the Heroes 10%-off-MSRP against the cheapest street price and take whichever is lower after transfer fee and tax.

Staccato pistols are not sold through GovX or the military exchanges (AAFES/NEX) — only third-party Staccato holsters and accessories appear on GovX — so the Heroes and Blue Line programs are the mechanism for the firearm itself. Because Staccato controls the terms and can change them at any time, confirm the current offer on the official program page before you buy.
trugreen-military-discount: Verification is handled by ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. You confirm military status once, receive a one-time code with no expiration, and a TruGreen representative applies it to your account. The discount continues in subsequent years and remains active even if your status changes to retired or veteran.

Coupon sites advertise "TruGreen military discount 25%–50% off" and "$92 off" codes. The verified military benefit is 10% off annual residential plans via ID.me. The larger numbers are public new-customer promos — such as 50% off the first application — open to everyone, not a standing military rate. The 50%-off-first-service figure specifically was a launch promo, not the ongoing military discount.

Because the military discount can’t stack with those public promos, the decision is durable-versus-front-loaded: the military 10% renews every year and survives your separation from service, while a public first-application promo can beat 10% in year one but reverts to list price after. The 10% is worth more on larger properties, since plan price scales with lawn size — get a custom quote, and bundle services so the discount applies across more applications.
ge-military-discount: GE Appliances (the consumer appliance maker, a Haier company since June 6, 2016 — not GE Aerospace or GE Vernova) gates its military program behind ID.me. Verification is a one-time process per GE’s page; afterward you only sign in to the member store at myapstore.com/GEStore/GEA. ID.me’s own offer page confirms the military discount exists but states no percentage, and notes store offers "can change at any time based on the store."

The same member store serves parallel programs for nurses and healthcare professionals, first responders, and teachers and students, each with its own GE landing page, the same $99 floor, and the same Monogram exclusion. GE’s military page names "members of our U.S. military, nurses, first responders, and others" without itemizing veterans, retirees, or dependents — Military.com’s offer page lists those groups, but final eligibility is determined at the ID.me gate.

How deep is member pricing? GE doesn’t say. Shoppers on Slickdeals have reported roughly 20% off list on some models — a community report, not a guaranteed rate. On hot SKUs, that has landed near big-box sale prices, which is why the smartest move is always a two-tab price check: the member store versus the public geappliances.com sale price (which does stack with portal cashback — Rakuten was at an elevated 10% and TopCashback at 8% on July 7, 2026).

Two more paths worth knowing: exchange-eligible shoppers (all honorably discharged veterans can shop online under the Veterans Online Shopping Benefit) can buy major appliances tax-free with free shipping through the Home Depot storefront on shopmyexchange.com. And GE’s public Innovation Rebate offers up to a $2,000 prepaid card on four or more eligible GE Profile appliances bought direct from GE between July 1 and December 31, 2026 — Home Depot, Lowe’s, and Best Buy purchases are excluded from that rebate. Note that Home Depot’s and Lowe’s own 10% military discounts both exclude major appliances entirely.
fabletics-military-discount: The discount is a single identity discount applied automatically after ID.me verification; there is no separate "military promo code" to enter, and the coupon-site "Fabletics 60–88% off" codes are overwhelmingly the new-VIP intro offer or generic sale banners, not stackable military codes. Fabletics does not allow stacking promo codes, and codes generally can’t be applied to already-discounted or sale items — so the 15% is essentially either/or versus the new-VIP intro or a sale, not additive.

If you’ll actively manage the VIP program — logging in to skip the charge every 1st–5th — the new-VIP intro pricing (2-for-$24, up to ~70–80% off the first order) is dramatically cheaper than 15% on order #1, and ongoing VIP prices beat 15% too. If you won’t manage a monthly subscription, take the free 15% via ID.me on non-member prices and skip VIP entirely. The membership is the real discount — and the real catch.

Verifying for the discount does not, by itself, enroll you in VIP, but be careful not to accept a new-VIP intro offer during checkout unless you intend to join the $69.95/month subscription. Whether the 15% applies on top of VIP member pricing is unverified — assume it applies to the price displayed (non-member for non-members) rather than compounding, and confirm at checkout.
applebees-military-discount: The one company-confirmed military offer comes from Applebee’s own Veterans Day press release: on November 11, U.S. veterans, active duty, reserves, and National Guard who dine in at participating restaurants get a free full-size entrée from an exclusive Veterans Day menu, plus a $5 Bounce Back Card to use on a later visit. You verify in person by showing proof of service — there is no online code and no ID.me, GovX, or SheerID flow.

The everyday "10% off" figure that circulates on coupon sites does not appear anywhere on applebees.com. It traces back to WeSalute and similar aggregators, which themselves note it "varies by location" and is not a guaranteed partner offer. With 1,500+ U.S. restaurants run by independent franchisees, any everyday military discount is at each restaurant’s discretion — so the honest read is "possible but unconfirmed; call ahead."

A note on timing and freshness: Applebee’s confirms the Veterans Day program each fall via press release (the terms here are from the October 27, 2025 release for the November 11, 2025 event). The exclusive Veterans Day menu and the Bounce Back Card’s redemption window can change year to year, so re-check Applebee’s newsroom or its Veterans Day page in late October for the current year’s details before you go.
delta-airlines-military-discount: The honest core: the real, quantifiable value here is free bags and early boarding for active-duty travelers, not a headline fare percentage. Delta’s own pages reference a "military discount on flights" but publish no number, and the fare is booked only by phone or message. Because it is unpublished, it is not guaranteed to beat a public sale fare — so an active-duty member should price the agent’s quote against the lowest online fare before booking.

Bags are where the math is clearest. On personal travel, active-duty members get 2 free checked bags in Main Cabin/Comfort and 3 in Premium Select, First, and Delta One. On military orders, the allowance is more generous still — larger dimensions (up to 80 linear inches vs. 62 for personal) and heavier weight tiers — which makes a PCS move the single biggest saving. All travelers still get one free carry-on plus a personal item.

Who is covered matters. Delta scopes these perks to active-duty status; separated veterans generally do not qualify for the bag/boarding perks or the fare discount. Aggregator sites frequently get two things wrong: they quote a confident fare percentage (Delta publishes none) and they extend the perks to veterans (Delta’s pages scope them to active duty). Reserve and National Guard eligibility tracks active-duty status, so confirm your specific status with Delta.

Verification is simple and offline: Delta confirms active-duty status at booking and/or check-in with a military ID (and your orders for on-orders travel). There is no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute flow for the military fare — you book through a Delta agent by phone or message. Bag benefits apply on Delta-marketed tickets, including flights operated by listed partners (Aeromexico, Air France, KLM, Korean Air, LATAM, Virgin Atlantic).
made-in-military-discount: Made In’s "Discount Eligible" collection is a generic sale landing page, not a military program — there is no military tier or verification gate anywhere on the site. A search of GovX and ID.me turns up no Made In military store either, unlike some other cookware brands (Dalstrong, 360 Cookware, Field Company, Magma) that do run verified military offers. So the honest verdict is simple: no military discount exists at Made In.

Be cautious of coupon and community pages that assert Made In "provides a standing discount to verified military personnel" and tell you to contact customer service. That claim is unverified, is not stated on Made In’s own site, and is contradicted by other sources. If Made In ever honors a quiet, discretionary courtesy case-by-case, it is unpublished and unverifiable — so we don’t promise it.

For a first order, the New Customer Welcome Offer (email signup) is the simplest saving. Aggregators report it as roughly 10% off regular-priced items with a ~$149 minimum, not valid on Sets — but those figures are low-confidence, so confirm the live terms when you sign up. If you can wait, a holiday sitewide sale (~25% is common) or a "The Seconds" factory-second drop (often 30–66% off select items) will usually save more, and both are open to everyone with no verification.

If your goal is specifically a verified military price on cookware, Made In won’t give you one — a comparable brand that runs a real GovX or ID.me offer, or the tax-free military Exchange (AAFES/NEX) for a similar product, is the better military-specific value.
lovesac-military-discount: Lovesac verifies eligibility through SheerID, not ID.me or GovX. Each Heroes group has its own SheerID verification flow linked from lovesac.com/heroes, and passing issues a single-use code. The brand doesn’t state a re-verification cadence — treat each code as one order and re-verify for the next.

One eligibility nuance most pages gloss over: Lovesac’s wording is "active or retired U.S. Service Members and their registered dependents." Military retirees clearly qualify; separated non-retiree veterans are not named, and whether SheerID’s Lovesac gate passes them is unconfirmed.

The stacking truth, tier by tier: during the live "Couch Goals" sale (July 7–12, 2026), Heroes 5% and Refer-a-Friend can each combine with the 35%-off accessories tier — on a $500 accessories cart that compounds to about $308.75, roughly 38.25% off. The 40%-off seating tier combines with nothing. Heroes also combines with Lovesac Credit Card promotional financing (0% APR over 24 equal monthly payments; 34.99% purchase APR after the promo).

Watch out for aggregator spin: "Lovesac military discount 40%" claims recycle time-boxed windows (25% around Veterans Day 2022; a 40% heroes window listed through November 6, 2025) or plain public sales. The standing military rate is 5%, and Groupon’s "$100 off" coupons are just the Refer-a-Friend reward ($100 off a $350+ purchase) dressed up as a code.
melin-military-discount: melin routes its discount through GovX. You create a free GovX account and verify your eligibility once via GovX ID; GovX confirms your status and issues a code that unlocks 30% off full-price items on melin.com. There is no confirmed ID.me, SheerID, or WeSalute path for melin — GovX is the named partner (an editorial claim of "ID.me" appears to be an error). melin and GovX can re-verify eligibility and change or end the program at any time.

The 30% is deep for headwear, so for an eligible shopper buying at full price it is almost always the best route. The one thing that can beat it is a genuine melin sitewide sale of 30%+ — because the GovX code is full-price-only and non-combinable, you would take the sale price in that window rather than the code. The two never stack, so it is always a "pick the lower price" decision.

Beyond the standard GovX storefront, melin runs a separate "Melin Open Box" GovX storefront with discounted returned/open-box inventory that can undercut new-unit pricing. Because melin.com was rate-limiting automated fetches on the verification date, confirm the exact 30% figure and current terms on melin’s official First Responders page before you buy.
airbnb-military-discount: Airbnb operates no military verification. It does not use ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute for any military discount, and ID.me itself states it is "not aware that Airbnb offers Military discounts." If an individual host chooses to give a military discount, that host sets their own evidence rules — for example, asking you to mention your service in a message — which varies host to host and which Airbnb does not standardize or guarantee.

The mechanic to know is the "special offer." After you message a host and they agree to a rate, they send a custom price in your message thread; you have 24 hours to accept, and it covers the nightly rate, cleaning fee, and extra-guest fees — not taxes, the Airbnb service fee, or a security deposit. Be skeptical of any coupon site advertising a fixed "Airbnb military discount" code: Airbnb issues no such code, so those are not reliable.

The savings that are real and open to everyone are the length-of-stay discounts: hosts can set weekly (7+ nights) and monthly (28+ nights) discounts, and Airbnb sometimes adds extra monthly-stay savings it funds itself — often a bigger price cut than any occupation-based rate. If a guaranteed military discount matters more than a specific listing, some hotel chains (Hilton, Marriott, Wyndham) and military-focused booking platforms run verified military rates worth comparing. Note too that Airbnb’s nonprofit, Airbnb.org, runs emergency and temporary-stay programs (e.g., for people displaced by disasters) — that’s humanitarian housing assistance, not a consumer military discount.
kohls-military-discount: There is no online verifier and no account requirement. Verification happens in person at checkout: you show a military ID card, a state-issued ID marked with veteran status, or Form DD 214. Because there’s no third-party service (ID.me/SheerID/GovX), there’s nothing to enroll in ahead of time — but you must have acceptable physical ID with you each time you redeem.

The best way to deepen the discount is to stack Kohl’s Cash and dollar-off coupons, which are applied before the 15% is taken. You cannot combine it with another percent-off coupon (including the senior discount), so on a given trip, compare which one saves more. The 15% is Monday-only; plan trips accordingly.

Around Veterans Day, Kohl’s has run an enhanced 30% in-store offer for a short window (Nov 10–11 in 2025). That’s a recurring seasonal pattern rather than a guaranteed year-round term, so re-check Kohl’s for the current year’s dates and rate. Kohl’s Rewards (free) earns Kohl’s Cash you can then stack.
shark-military-discount: There is no U.S. military verification for a Shark discount because no such discount exists. ID.me and Rakuten don’t verify military status here — they give cashback to any member. The "up to 40% for Military/Veterans/Nurses" line on ID.me is generic store boilerplate, not a Shark-set rate; the actual ID.me benefit is ordinary ~2% cash back available to everyone. UNiDAYS verifies student status for the 10% offer, and WeSalute verifies military status but only unlocks gated BenefitHub marketplace offers behind paid membership.

The realistic best path for a U.S. service member is Shark’s own frequent public sale, which routinely runs 30–50% off the same flagship (a Shark PowerDetect Speed Cordless was observed at $279.99, reg. $429.99 — 35% off — on July 10, 2026). Stack a cashback portal on top, and for the absolute floor consider certified-refurbished (Shark-renewed via Back Market, Walmart, eBay, or Amazon Renewed, with a 1–2 year warranty) or the military exchange for tax-free pricing if it stocks your model.

If a monthly military "code" is what you’re chasing, the honest answer is to skip the hunt: the aggregator claims of a "10%," "20%," or "40% Shark military discount" are wrong. Those are generic public promo codes or ID.me boilerplate, not a verified military offer.
thrive-market-military-discount: Thrive Market fits the membership/subscription-retailer archetype — a warehouse-club analog where the "discount" is a waived fee rather than a code at checkout. Thrive Gives runs a one-for-one model: each paid annual membership sponsors a free one for a qualifying group, including active-duty military, veterans, nurses, teachers, first responders, students, EBT/SNAP cardholders, and families in financial need.

Verification is handled by ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA and dozens of retailers. You prove military or veteran status once; most approvals are instant, though some users report a 1–2 day wait. SNAP EBT holders are approved instantly through Thrive’s own flow without ID.me.

Watch the framing on coupon and aggregator sites. "25–50% below retail" is Thrive’s general member value claim that applies to every member, and "30–40% off" is a new-member first-order promo open to anyone opening an account. Neither is a military-only discount. The only military-specific benefit is the waived $59.95 membership fee.
Because the free membership auto-renews at $59.95/year after the first year, set a reminder near your anniversary. Nothing in Thrive’s published terms promises an automatic second free year.
uniqlo-military-discount: There is nothing to verify — UNIQLO runs no military or identity verification and partners with no verification provider. Any page claiming a UNIQLO "ID.me military verification" is wrong; no such flow exists on uniqlo.com. UNIQLO’s coupons require only a free account, the app, or email/SMS signup.

The one rule that shapes every UNIQLO savings decision is that only one coupon can be used per order — coupons do not combine. You cannot layer the app, email, SMS, and birthday coupons; you choose the single best one for your cart. A coupon does apply on top of a Limited-Time / app-member sale price (the sale is the item price, not a coupon), but the coupon’s minimum spend is checked against the discounted subtotal.

The real stacking lever is cashback. Because UNIQLO’s coupons are first-party (not third-party codes pasted into the field), a web coupon plus a cashback portal such as Rakuten is generally portal-safe — but the $10-off-$75 app coupon requires in-app checkout, which portals do not track. To capture cashback, use a web coupon (email/SMS/birthday) instead. Verify the live cashback rate, as rates change weekly.
norton-military-discount: Verification works differently here than on a true military-discount page: Norton itself runs none. There is no ID.me or GovX gate on norton.com’s own checkout. Verification only happens on the third-party channels — GovX uses GovX ID, ID.me Shop uses ID.me, and WeSalute requires a paid WeSalute+ membership. Norton isn’t the verifier for any of these, which is exactly why no norton.com percentage should ever be called a "military discount."

The debunk matters because coupon sites present Norton’s public pricing as a military benefit. Aggregators claim "10%–25% off at norton.com for military," a "15% military" code like "SEMLLNBNFCREDIT," and "20% first order for military." None of these is a Norton-published military benefit — the discounts you actually see at checkout are the public first-year intro prices available to everyone, and generic promo codes are not military-gated. Meanwhile the genuinely military-verified channel, GovX, advertises "up to 45% off" — which is essentially the same ~47% first-year intro Norton already gives away publicly.

For the math, take one year of Norton 360 with LifeLock Select as the baseline: $99.99 public intro vs $189.99 renewal. Buying at the public price already saves about $90. Routing that same purchase through a cashback portal — ID.me Shop for verified military, or TopCashback/USAA MemberShop for anyone — is the only path that beats it, because the portal pays a rebate on top without touching Norton’s checkout price. Portal rates on Norton swing widely (roughly 20–50% across portals and dates per CashbackMonitor), so treat any single figure as promotional and confirm it live inside the portal before counting on it.
hollister-military-discount: We lead with the honest answer because that’s the useful one: Hollister’s promotions page lists no military discount, and ID.me — which gates military offers for many retailers — explicitly says it is not aware of a Hollister military discount, and Hollister is not listed among its partner brands. There is no online or account-based way to verify military status for a Hollister discount.

The only military offer with any corroboration is an in-store, manager-discretion ~10–15% with a military ID, and it comes solely from shopping-mall tenant directory pages (CBL Properties), not Hollister. Because it’s a third party rather than the brand, treat the percentage and availability as unverified and store-dependent — some locations may honor something, many won’t, and Hollister publishes nothing about it.

For real savings, everyone — including service members — uses the same routes: House Rewards (free), frequent 25%–50%-off sales, periodic app-only offers, and free shipping over $59. Hollister also runs an official student discount (verified through a third-party service) for enrolled students, which is separate from military status. If a verified military discount is the priority, apparel brands that run ID.me/SheerID-gated offers are more reliable than Hollister.
aerie-military-discount: Some aggregator sites claim Aerie offers "up to 10–25% off for military." That range is not supported by any AEO or ID.me source — AEO publishes no military discount at all, ID.me confirms none, and there is no online military code for aerie.com. Treat any percentage above the reported store-level 10% as fabricated or conflated with another brand’s program, and do not expect it to work at checkout.

The store-level 10% itself comes from third-party mall-landlord listings (e.g. Parkway Place, Tanger), not from AEO. Because AEO never states this as corporate policy, whether a specific store honors it — and whether it stacks with sales or clearance — is entirely up to that location. Shoppers report the practice is inconsistent: some AE/Aerie locations apply it, others don’t.

GovX may resell AEO goods, but its listing is JS-rendered with no confirmed brand-run military percentage. WeSalute lists a BenefitHub gift-card marketplace deal behind a paid membership — that is a gift-card resale arrangement, not an Aerie-run military discount, and neither counts as verified brand terms.

Because there is no official discount to chase, the highest-value move for a service member is the same one available to any shopper: watch for Aerie’s frequent public sale and clearance events, stack Real Rewards, and consider the AEO credit card for repeat purchases. These require no ID or verification and typically outsave the reported 10%.
dsw-military-discount: DSW verifies military status through BeansiD (Student Beans, operated by Pion) — not ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute. From DSW’s special group discount page, selecting the military offer launches a Student Beans widget; you create or log into a free BeansiD account and prove eligibility, and BeansiD issues a one-time DSW code to use at checkout. Some third-party listings reference ID.me, but DSW’s own page routes through the Student Beans widget.

The code is single-use and limited to one per customer. How often BeansiD requires re-verification for a new code is not stated in the official source. For help, DSW directs shoppers to the shoephoria! Center at 1.866.DSW.SHOES or customerservice@dsw.com.

Because the military discount is online-only, in-store shoppers should rely on DSW’s free VIP Rewards program and posted sales instead — seasonal sales and clearance can exceed 10%. DSW also runs separate 10% BeansiD offers for first responders, teachers, and healthcare workers under the same terms.
ping-military-discount: PING sells through a dealer network rather than a discounted direct checkout, so there is no “military price” to select online. The benefit is post-purchase: you pay the dealer’s price, then claim a fixed-dollar rebate per eligible club. The rebate attaches to the purchase and pays back as a virtual prepaid card mailed 6–8 weeks later.

Verification runs through ID.me at the rebate step — the same identity service used by the VA and many major retailers. There is no permanent account discount and no GovX or SheerID path for this program; you verify per claim, then complete the rebate form. Eligible groups are Active, Active Reserve, Retirees (and spouses), and honorably discharged veterans across all six services, including Space Force.

Because the rebate is fixed-dollar and modest, the biggest savings often come from where and how you buy rather than the rebate itself. A PING Trade-In / Move-Up credit for old clubs frequently beats the flat rebate; prior-generation or certified-used PING can run well below new (though it isn’t rebate-eligible); and if your on-base pro shop is an authorized PING dealer, a tax-free purchase can rival the rebate. The rebate does sit on top of a dealer’s own sale price, so a dealer markdown plus the rebate is the best new-club combo.

Aggregator sites sometimes advertise a flat “PING military discount up to 10–25% off” or a coupon code. PING publishes no percentage-off military discount and no checkout code — the only official military benefit is the fixed-dollar rebate above, claimed after a full-price authorized-dealer purchase.
kate-spade-military-discount: The offer aggregators keep surfacing is real, but it’s British: gocertify runs a Kate Spade UK military offer of 10% off, explicitly limited to "anyone in the UK who works for the Armed Forces" with a "Valid R.A.F, Army, Navy or Armed Forces Dependents Card," and it’s online-only and "not valid in conjunction with other codes/offers." None of that reaches a U.S. shopper on katespade.com. On the U.S. side, ID.me plainly states it isn’t aware of a Kate Spade military discount, and there is no SheerID or WeSalute military checkout for the brand.

So the real question isn’t "what’s the military discount" — it’s "what’s the cheapest valid path to a Kate Spade bag." For the exact full-line bag, the tax-free Exchange wins: both AAFES (shopmyexchange.com) and the Navy Exchange (mynavyexchange.com) carry Kate Spade handbags, and every Exchange order is tax-free for eligible shoppers, which is often the best "military" deal available on the identical item. Anyone can also stack a cashback portal (~8% on katespade.com, ~12% at the outlet) on a normal order.

For maximum savings overall, Kate Spade Outlet’s public sales — up to 70% off plus an extra 20% — crush every identity route and are open to everyone; a comparable Knott can land in the $60–$150 range. GovX runs a Kate Spade marketplace storefront (mirrored by the VA’s Veterans Canteen Service) whose member price sits behind a free login, but designer goods there are often near-retail. Ignore the fabricated "40% off," "80% first-responder," and "code 2000025991" claims — even one of the aggregators admits "there is no official Kate Spade military program."
away-luggage-military-discount: Away’s discount is powered by ID.me, the same identity network used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of major retailers. You verify once through ID.me’s flow; military eligibility covers active duty, veterans, retirees, spouses, and dependents (ID.me’s full military eligibility list governs). Re-verification follows ID.me’s standard cadence — if your session lapses, re-authenticate through the same ID.me button.

Be precise on who qualifies. Away lists the military/veteran community, medical personnel (nurses and medical providers), teachers, and students. It does not list a first-responder tier, so police, firefighters, and EMTs should not expect the Away 10% the way they might at brands that include a responder community. Coupon aggregators sometimes scrape fake "Away military codes" implying 15–20% or a GovX storefront — the official offer is a flat 10% via ID.me, there is no Away store on GovX, and the 10% cannot be stacked on a sale or code.

The counterintuitive part is timing. Because Away runs 20–25% sitewide sales several times a year (its Black Friday 2025 event was 25% off, "the biggest of the year"), the public sale price often beats your 10% — and the two never combine. On a regular-price day, verify with ID.me for the 10%. During a 20%+ sale, buy the public price instead and layer a cashback portal, since a no-code public sale keeps portal tracking intact.
space-needle-military-discount: Verification is a simple in-person ID check at the Box Office — no third-party provider (no ID.me or GovX). Because the rate is discretionary and unpublished, confirm current eligibility (for example, whether separated veterans qualify) and the price at the counter before buying.

Per the FAQ, the rate covers anyone in the party who shows an ID, not just the service member. Bundle passes (CityPASS/C3) are a separate purchase path and are not combined with the Box Office military rate.
Coupon aggregators advertise Space Needle "codes" for 20–50% off — these are generic/unverified claims, not the military rate. The only verified military benefit is the in-person Box Office rate.
urban-outfitters-military-discount: Coupon sites (Goodshop, LifeSaverSavings, WorthEPenny, Knoji) advertise a "military code SOS30 — 30% off" and a "10% first-responder in-store discount." Neither appears on any Urban Outfitters primary source; "SOS30" is a scraped, generic promo string, not a verified military benefit. Some pages also imply UO "uses ID.me / SheerID / GovX" — the only verified identity gate at UO is the student discount via UNiDAYS/Student Beans. Do not confuse urbancred.com (a separate brand with a GovX military page) with Urban Outfitters.

The student path is the one standing identity discount here: 15% off in the US, verified by confirming current enrollment through UNiDAYS (or Student Beans), delivered as a single-use code or linked offer at checkout. For a service member using the GI Bill or tuition assistance, that is the best evergreen discount on full-price, non-excluded items — but it is a student benefit, and it re-verifies on the provider’s normal student-status cycle.

For everyone else, the public math wins. On a $100 full-price cart, the 15% signup or student code brings it to $85, while a Sale item at 40% off is about $60 — so the Sale section is usually the single cheapest path, and it needs no code. UO Rewards points still accrue on promo-priced orders, making Rewards the one benefit that layers under a sale. Single-use codes do not stack on each other or on already-reduced Sale prices.
amazon-military-discount: Many coupon and military-info pages frame Amazon as having a "military discount" or a recurring "Veterans Day Prime discount." That is not confirmed by Amazon. The on-site "Amazon Military Discount" pages are simply keyword search results for products third-party sellers have tagged "military discount" — not an Amazon program — and the $40-off Prime promo people remember was a one-time event in November 2019 that has not returned.

The real discounted tier is Prime Access. It costs $6.99/month versus the standard $14.99/month and carries the same benefits as standard Prime — Prime Video, fast free delivery, Amazon Pharmacy pricing, and Amazon Family sharing. Eligibility is by government assistance or income, not service. Amazon’s official list of qualifying programs includes SNAP EBT, Medicaid, WIC, SSI, Direct Express, TANF, the National School Lunch Program, LIHEAP, and Tribal assistance programs; the income path is a household income at or below 200% of the Federal Poverty Guideline.

Verification for Prime Access is handled by Amazon directly — you income-verify or upload proof of participation in an eligible program at amazon.com/getprimeaccess — and must be reconfirmed every 12 months, with an emailed reminder. There is no military verification because there is no military offer to verify against.

On pricing, treat older figures with caution: Amazon’s own current page states $14.99/month standard and $6.99/month Prime Access, but an older Amazon help page still shows outdated $119/year and $12.99/month numbers. We do not quote an annual standard-Prime price here because it was not confirmable on a clean Amazon primary page — confirm it live on amazon.com/amazonprime before relying on any annual dollar figure.
turtlebox-military-discount: Turtlebox routes its discount through GovX, an identity-verification marketplace used across the military, first-responder, government, and teacher communities. You create a free GovX account and verify your eligibility once; GovX confirms your status and unlocks the 10%. There is no confirmed ID.me, SheerID, or WeSalute path for Turtlebox — GovX is the partner named on Turtlebox’s own page.

Be cautious of coupon and deal sites that advertise Turtlebox "military" savings of 20%, 25%, 30%, or even 40% and push codes like FATHER25, MOBILE10, EMAIL10, or WELCOME10. None of these is a verified military discount. FATHER25 was a past Father’s Day seasonal code, and MOBILE10/EMAIL10/WELCOME10 are ordinary email/SMS signup offers (about $10 or 10% off a first order) — not a military rate.

Because Turtlebox seldom discounts deeply, the free GovX 10% is usually the ceiling, not the floor. The one thing that beats it is a genuine Turtlebox seasonal event (Father’s Day, Black Friday), and those public codes won’t combine with the GovX discount — so if a real 25%+ sale is live, use it instead. On the $430 Turtlebox Original (Gen 3), the GovX 10% works out to about $387.
evo-military-discount: evo verifies eligibility through its own military discount program page and issues a discount code on approval. The exact third-party verification provider (GovX, ID.me, or SheerID) is not confirmed from a primary source in this research pass, so we do not state one as fact. For eligibility help, evo customer care is 1-866-386-1590.

Watch out for two common mix-ups. Aggregator sites inflate the rate ("up to 50% off," "10%–25%") — the only verified rate is 10%, full-price and eligible-category only. And the "Evolution Outdoor" storefront on the GovX marketplace is a different company (hunting/tactical storage), not evo.com the ski, snowboard, bike, and surf retailer — don’t conflate them. There is no verified public evo military promo code; the discount is issued per-account after verification.

For the categories the discount never touches — bikes, bike components, surfboards, surf hardgoods, and evoTrips — lean on evo’s public sales and its Lowest Price Guarantee (evo beats a lower US authorized-retailer price by 5%, though that can’t combine with the military discount). Joining evo Rewards is free and earns roughly 10% back in deferred credit (1 point per $1; 200 points = a $20 reward), which you can bank even on discounted orders and redeem later on full-price items.
dish-military-discount: DISH's offer is a value-add "appreciation" bundle rather than a percentage discount. The Stars & Stripes Pack (free for 2 years, a $240 value) includes channels like American Heroes Channel, Smithsonian, Crime+Investigation, Destination America, getTV, The Cowboy Channel, REELZ, and STARZ Encore. The free monthly movie rental draws from roughly 20,000 rentable On Demand titles, and the free Hopper Smart DVR upgrade lets you stream local content to your mobile device. The 2-Year TV Price Guarantee — "no hidden fees, no sports fees, or HD fees" — is DISH's standard term, though taxes, add-ons, DISH Protect, and transactional fees sit outside it.

Be skeptical of aggregators framing this as a "military discount on your bill." It is not a percentage off — the verified benefit is the free programming, the monthly movie, and the DVR upgrade, not a lower rate. Third-party "authorized retailer" sites (usdish.com, infinitydish.com, and others) resell the same DISH offer; none has a secret deeper military rate. There is also nothing to stack: the perks come instead of the equivalent public promo bundle, and no cashback-portal or GovX layer applies to a contracted subscription billed directly by DISH.

Verification runs through SheerID or ID.me during online signup — select "Military and First Responder Discount" at checkout and upload your service documentation — or a military ID shown in a DISH store. DISH does not publish a re-verification cadence for active accounts, so treat it as tied to account setup.

The real money question is whether a 2-year satellite contract beats no-contract streaming at all. If you want a full satellite package, the military bundle is genuine free value. If minimizing cost matters more, no-contract streaming — Sling TV (an EchoStar sister service, roughly $40–60/mo), YouTube TV, or Hulu Live — avoids the 2-year term and is usually cheaper than a DISH commitment, because the military offer doesn't lower DISH's base price.
famous-footwear-military-discount: Online verification is handled by SheerID, a third-party service that confirms military status on Famous Footwear’s behalf. You may be asked to provide basic personal information and upload supporting documentation; verification typically takes a few minutes, after which you receive a single-use, non-transferable promo code. If your code doesn’t arrive or doesn’t work, check spam and contact Famous Footwear Customer Service at 1-888-869-1053. Online codes expire at 11:59 PM CST on December 31 of the year issued, and you may receive up to five codes per 30 days — so re-verification is required over time rather than being a permanent, one-time benefit. In store, verification is done at the register each time by showing ID.

The most important limits are the exclusions. The discount can’t be stacked or combined with any other promotions or offers — only Rewards Cash — and it doesn’t apply to gift cards or prior purchases. A long list of brands is excluded, including Nike, Birkenstock, Crocs, Brooks, Dr. Martens, and Vans, plus many "select" brands (see the official Exclusions page). So confirm your specific shoe qualifies before counting on the 10%, and compare it against a sitewide promo (e.g., an "Extra 20% off online" code) since you can’t use both — whichever saves more.

One eligibility nuance to plan around: the online program lists spouses, dependents, and Gold Star families as eligible, but the official in-store FAQ names only active duty, reservist/National Guard, and veteran/retiree. If you’re a spouse or dependent hoping to use it in store, check with the store or Customer Service first. To stack legitimate savings, join the free Famously YOU Rewards program — its Reward Cash is the one thing that does combine with the military discount — and note Reward Cash also works with BOGO 1/2 Off events (the military code does not).
directv-stream-military-discount: Verification is handled by WeSalute, not ID.me or SheerID. You enroll in WeSalute+, verify your military, veteran, or nurse status once, and receive a secure WeSalute+ ID card so you don’t share your military ID directly with DIRECTV. The benefit is tied to your active WeSalute+ membership — if the membership lapses, the eligibility basis for the perk goes with it.

On a CHOICE streaming package at $94.99/mo, a full year is about $1,139.88 before the device lease, fees, taxes, and activation. The WeSalute $5/mo discount trims about $60 off the year — almost exactly the first-year WeSalute+ fee, so it’s roughly a wash on base tiers. On the top PREMIER tier the discount scales toward ~$20/mo, where the "$480 over 2 years" figure comes from and the membership clearly pays off.

Every aggregator claim of "25% off," "$29/mo off," or "up to 75% off" DIRECTV for military is fabricated — no such percentage discount is published on any primary source, and there is no military promo code entered at checkout. Separately, AT&T wireless customers may have a Signature Program / bundle discount, but that originates with AT&T, not DIRECTV, and we don’t assert figures for it here.
rep-fitness-military-discount: The military discount is gated by GovX ID: verify your military or veteran status once through GovX, then shop repfitness.com, the REP app, or participating retail at 5% off. REP’s GovX storefront page is JS-rendered, so the exact 5% figure is corroborated here by REP’s own GovX listing together with a secondary aggregator summary rather than read directly off a static page — treat the mechanic (GovX-gated discount) as solid and the precise percentage as confirmed-but-worth-a-periodic-recheck.

ExpertVoice is a separate program with its own verification, typically tied to a qualifying military or pro credential. It is a substitute for the 5% GovX discount, not an add-on, and it is frequently worth more — REP’s checkout shows an "ExpertVoice deal" price when it applies. Some items are excluded from ExpertVoice, and already-discounted sale items can beat the ExpertVoice price, so compare before assuming it wins.

One thing to watch: coupon and aggregator sites advertise "REP Fitness 10% off codes." REP explicitly says it does not run coupon codes and keeps prices direct — what those sites are usually picking up is either the 20% apparel welcome code (apparel only, via email sign-up) or the tiered cart/showroom discounts, not a stackable 10% military code. Also don’t conflate the two REP tier schedules: online cart tiers are 5%/7%/10% at $5,000/$7,500/$10,000+, while local-pickup/showroom tiers are a separate 10%/12.5%/15% schedule for REP-branded products picked up at a showroom.

Buyer reports say REP’s first-responder discount was dropped around 2023. That is not confirmed on REP’s current official pages one way or the other, so this page treats it as reported, not fact — check directly with REP or GovX if you’re a first responder hoping to use it.
corsair-military-discount: Corsair’s discount is powered by ID.me, the same identity-verification service used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of major retailers. You verify your community once through ID.me at checkout; ID.me confirms eligibility and Corsair issues a discount code. ID.me controls the offer amount. This is not a permanent account discount on Corsair’s side — it is a code per verified checkout — and it is U.S.-only.

The category split is the whole game. Corsair’s public 10% newsletter/SMS code excludes Gaming PCs, laptops, monitors, graphics cards, memory, and storage, while the ID.me 5% includes Gaming PCs. So on those excluded categories the 5% is usually your best (and often only) code; on peripherals the 10% code or a live sale wins — and none of these stack. Any time a 15%-or-better sale is live, take the public price: it beats the 5% and needs no verification.

There is no in-store or phone Corsair military program — the discount is online-only at corsair.com. If you are Exchange-eligible, note that the Exchange (AAFES/NEX) stocks Corsair peripherals like the K70 and K55 tax-free; gaming-PC carriage there is not confirmed. Because Corsair controls the terms and can change them at any time, treat the numbers here as a starting point and confirm the current offer on the official ID.me Corsair page before you buy.
ring-military-discount: The mechanic is the thing to get right. Ring verifies through VerifyPass — not ID.me, GovX, or SheerID. You start on ring.com/give-back, pick your group, and confirm your status in the VerifyPass widget. When it clears, you get a single-use code for one order; there’s no permanent account-level discount, and you can request a fresh code no more than once every 24 hours. VerifyPass notes codes are "subject to ID verification in our sole discretion." If verification fails, use VerifyPass’s support flow inside the widget; for checkout problems, use Ring Help.

On eligibility, Ring is precise about the headline groups but vague about the edges. Its pages name "military and veterans," first responders, government employees, healthcare workers, teachers, and students — all at 20%. What Ring does not spell out on its own pages is whether Reserve/National Guard, retirees, military spouses, or dependents qualify; those determinations happen inside the VerifyPass military verification flow. Aggregator sites contradict each other on this (one claims Guard/Reserve are excluded; another says included), and none is authoritative — so the honest answer is to run the VerifyPass check and see which categories it accepts.

The exclusions are where the real money math lives. The 20% code applies only to eligible products, and it excludes bundles and anything already on sale. Crucially, it can’t be combined with other discounts and is "not valid during sales events" — so during a Black Friday or Cyber Monday event, the code simply won’t work, and Ring’s advertised sitewide savings (up to 50% at times) can beat 20% on specific devices. It also can’t be stacked with the separate 10% subscriber discount, can’t be applied to subscriptions or Ring Assist+, and can’t be used retroactively. Free shipping and free returns on US orders apply to everyone regardless. Bottom line: verify, but check the current sale price on your exact device before you spend the code.
navy-federal-military-discount: Eligibility is the widest of any military-gated issuer. NFCU’s join page puts it plainly: "All branches of the military, Veterans, Department of Defense employees and their immediate family members can join our credit union." That means active duty of every branch (including Guard and Space Force), veterans — "no matter how long you served, you’re in!", with no published discharge-type gate — DoD civilians "including employees, contractors, retirees and annuitants," and immediate family defined as "spouses, siblings, parents, children, grandparents and grandchildren." Joining costs nothing beyond a $5 minimum balance in the Membership Savings Account. That family reach — down to grandchildren, no established-member requirement — is materially broader than USAA’s pass-down rule.

The card lineup competes on structure, not promos. Six of the seven personal cards charge $0 annual fee: More Rewards American Express (3x at restaurants and food delivery, supermarkets, gas, and transit), cashRewards (1.5% cash back, or the 2% cashRewards Plus when your credit limit is $5,000 or more), GO REWARDS (3x restaurants, 2x gas), Platinum (the low-APR card, 10.24%–18.00%), and cashRewards Secured (1% back, credit-building). Lineup-wide: no foreign-transaction fees, no balance-transfer fees, and NFCU’s own statement that "for all Navy Federal credit cards, APRs currently don’t exceed 18%." The Flagship Rewards ($49/yr, 3x travel, 2x everything else, APR 14.74%–18.00%) is the only fee in the family — and right now it is self-liquidating: an annual statement credit covers the Amazon Prime annual membership ($139 value) when you pay it with the card, and up to $120 in Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credits every four years stacks on top, along with a 35,000-point welcome bonus ($350 value on $3,500 spend in 90 days) for applications through January 3, 2027.

The statutory story is the part every coupon page gets wrong, in both directions. What NFCU does better than the law requires: its SCRA program caps interest on pre-active-duty debt at 4% — below the federal 6% — and waives account fees, covering credit cards, consumer loans, education loans, checking lines of credit, mortgages, and business loans opened before active duty began. It is not automatic: request it via eMessage, fax, mail, or a branch no later than 180 days after your active-duty end date, and NFCU applies it within up to two billing cycles. What NFCU does not do: waive annual fees under the Military Lending Act for cards opened during service. NFCU publishes no MLA fee-adjustment policy, its SCRA page limits relief to pre-service accounts, and independent military-finance coverage lists it among issuers that do not adjust annual fees — so a Flagship opened on active duty pays the $49. One genuinely open question: NFCU’s SCRA page says "account fees" are waived on eligible pre-service accounts but never itemizes whether that includes the Flagship’s annual fee — ask specifically when you file.

Two more layers most members miss. First, rank: the Senior Enlisted Reward Program — active-duty, Guard, and Reserve E-7 through E-9 only, proof of rank required — adds a $0 intro annual fee on the Flagship for the first year, 0% intro APR offers (purchases for 6 months; balance transfers made within 60 days, 12 months), a 1% rate discount on many consumer loans, and a $250 loyalty card on a first mortgage or home-equity close; retirees, warrant officers, and spouses are excluded, so enroll (1-877-720-7121) before applying for the card. Second, the banking stack: Free Active Duty Checking pays military pay one business day early, rebates up to $20 per statement period in ATM fees, and includes free military checks, while active-duty and retired members with direct deposit get a 0.25% APR discount on select loans. NFCU has also historically stepped in during crises — over $350 million in emergency shutdown loans to 82,000 members in 2025. And one thing you will never find: a Navy Federal promo code. Credit-union products have no coupon field, so every "Navy Federal promo code" list is fabricated. If you can’t pass the membership gate, PenFed Credit Union serves everyone, and the Amex/Chase MLA fee waivers hinge on active-duty status, not any credit union’s field of membership.
apple-military-discount: Apple verifies eligibility through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. You create or sign in to a free ID.me account and confirm your military or veteran status; immediate family members in the same household verify through the program flow as well. After verifying, you shop the dedicated storefront where the 10% pricing appears.

The most important caveat is the channel: this is an online-only benefit. Apple’s own terms say that purchases made at an Apple Store location or through the regular Apple Online Store are not eligible for the program’s discounted pricing, so you have to order through the verified storefront to get the 10%. You can still visit an Apple Store for hands-on setup or support, but the discount itself is applied online.

A note on purchase limits: many coupon and guide pages publish specific annual per-item caps (such as three Macs, three iPads, three iPhones, three Apple Watches, and ten accessories per year). Those numbers are not stated on Apple’s official program page or in the ID.me program terms. The only limit Apple actually states is that the program is for personal use and not for resale, so we don’t assert the numeric caps here.
handm-military-discount: How verification works: it doesn’t — H&M has no military verification. The only identity-verified discount H&M runs in the US is the student 10%, verified through Student Beans (H&M’s US site links directly to the Student Beans hosted page). Any site claiming H&M "verifies military ID for 10–20% off" is describing a program that does not exist. Note for readers of stale guides: UNiDAYS handles H&M in some other countries, not the US.

The honest math on a $100 full-price cart: the 15% signup code lands at $85 (about $83.30 net if portal-listed and cashback tracks); the member welcome 10% at $90; the garment-recycling reward at $85 and repeatable; and a 50%-off sale hit at roughly $49.50 net with 1% cashback — the sale beats every code, every time.

Membership is the only true "stack" at H&M: member prices, points (1 per $1), and the $5-per-250-points reward accrue alongside any purchase — sale items and portal-tracked orders included — while promo codes are one per order.

No military-holiday pattern exists to wait for: H&M is absent from the major Veterans Day and Memorial Day military-discount roundups. Its real calendar is public — holiday-weekend flash sales, Black Friday (reportedly up to 30% sitewide), and Cyber Monday (reportedly up to 60%). Historical, not promised.
universal-orlando-military-discount: The Freedom Pass is a promotional product, not a code you enter at checkout. You buy it at a base Information, Tickets & Tours (ITT) or Leisure Travel Services (LTS) office — or from an online outlet like Shades of Green or Patrick SFB ITT if you don’t have a base nearby — and you receive vouchers. You then bring those vouchers and your DEERS ID to Universal’s front gate, Guest Services, or a Destination Universal hotel desk to exchange and activate them. The eligible member or spouse must be present for both purchase and activation, and must show the DEERS ID again on first entry, where Universal uses a biometric scan. After that, each activated pass behaves like a normal ticket assigned to one person and can’t be transferred.

On price and value: the 2-Park pass is $220 adult / $215 child (ages 3-9) and the 3-Park pass (adding Volcano Bay) is $255 adult / $250 child — both giving unlimited admission from November 13, 2025 through December 18, 2026, minus blockout dates. That’s year-long access at roughly the price of a couple of regular days, which is the whole appeal. It is explicitly not a Universal Annual Pass, so it doesn’t come with Annual Passholder perks like lounges or the passholder store, and it doesn’t include Epic Universe — that park is a separate, date-priced 1-Day add-on you can only buy once your Freedom Pass is activated.

A few limits matter. You can buy up to 6 passes per eligible DEERS ID, but one of the six must be used by the member or spouse, and any extras must come from the original selling office. Eligibility is stricter than most theme-park military offers: general veterans who aren’t retired or 100% service-disabled are excluded, as are NOAA, Public Health Service, DHS, contractors, and retired DoW civilians. The pass excludes separately ticketed events (like Halloween Horror Nights), parking, and food or merchandise discounts. Universal does separately advertise military hotel rates — the press release confirms 40% off Cabana Bay Beach Resort — and military vacation packages bookable through base ITT or by calling 1-877-801-9720; other hotel percentages float around secondary sources, so confirm those on the official military page before counting on them.
comfrt-military-discount: Comfrt routes its discount entirely through ID.me — not SheerID and not GovX. You create a free ID.me account and verify your eligibility (military, first responder, government, medical, nurse, student, or teacher) once; ID.me saves your status so you generally will not re-verify on future visits, and there is no cap on how many eligible orders you can use it on. The GovX "Original Comfort" storefront that some aggregators cite is a different company (comfort footwear/insoles), not comfrt.com.

Because the ID.me discount excludes sale items and Comfrt’s everyday prices are sale prices (anchor $120 struck to ~$39), the public sale is almost always lower than any 15% path. You do not stack them; you take whichever is lower, which is nearly always the sale. The narrow case where ID.me does real work is a genuinely full-price item excluded from any sale — then 15% off beats nothing.

For repeat buyers, ComfrtClub is the one meaningful everyday layer: its credit-back is a loyalty credit on the amount paid, not a coupon, so unlike ID.me and welcome codes it is not blocked by sale pricing. Credits are store credit toward a future order rather than instant cash off the current one, and they cannot be combined with the ID.me discount on the same order.
geico-military-discount: The core fact: GEICO’s own military-discounts page states an "up to 15%" military discount, and its military FAQ restates it — "GEICO can offer up to a 15% discount for current and former military members, including the National Guard." Because the discount is applied to a rated quote rather than a cart, the 15% is a ceiling: "discount amount varies in some states," and it’s "not available in all states or all GEICO companies." Your realized percentage may be lower.

How verification works: GEICO doesn’t use ID.me, SheerID, or GovX for its insurance military discount. It’s applied when you state your eligibility during the quote or enrollment process. The fastest route is the dedicated line, 1-800-MILITARY (645-4827), or a local GEICO agent, who can confirm which discounts you qualify for in your state.

The two military-specific extras. The Emergency Deployment Discount is an additional reduction for members deployed to a DOD-designated imminent-danger-pay area, available when the vehicle is stored under an approved GEICO storage plan — GEICO doesn’t publish the exact percentage, and some operations/areas are excluded. Separately, membership discounts tied to AUSA, AFBA, or the Navy League are "applicable in most states" and may stack with the military discount; amounts vary by state.

A common myth to ignore: aggregator and coupon sites confidently quote a "25% GEICO military discount" or an "extra 25% emergency deployment discount." GEICO’s own page states the standing military discount as up to 15% and describes the Emergency Deployment Discount without publishing any percentage. Treat any specific emergency-deployment figure (5%, 10%, 25%) as unverified until you see it on your own quote, and know there is no promo code for an insurance policy.

The honest bottom line: the 15% is a real, apply-once-and-it-sticks premium reduction — but the winning number is a quote-vs-quote question. Claim GEICO’s up-to-15% military discount, then get at least one competing quote from a military-friendly carrier like USAA on the same coverage limits before you decide.
tillys-military-discount: Tillys is a no-official-discount, promo-driven mall apparel retailer. Its deals live in a near-constant public sale calendar — up to 40% off online, clearance up to 60%, and multi-buy tee/top and denim promos — rather than in any identity-gated military program.

The only verified identity discount runs through UNiDAYS, for students: verify once, get a single-use code, and apply it online to full-price eligible items. It won’t combine with sale items or excluded brands, so on already-discounted merch the sale usually wins.

Don’t confuse Tillys with Tilley, the Canadian hat brand whose GovX military discount shows up in searches — they’re different companies. And WeSalute/BenefitHub “military offers” for Tillys are just its public sales re-surfaced to paying members, not an exclusive military percentage.
staples-military-discount: The debunk first: aggregators currently advertise "25% Off Staples Military Discount 2026 — How to Claim Online" and "Staples military discount code: 50% Off." Both are false. There is no online Staples military discount and no code — the only verified military offer in Staples’ history is the ~25% in-store Veterans Day-week discount, redeemed by showing a military ID. ID.me Shop’s own Staples page shows no military offer, there’s no GovX storefront for the retailer, and Staples publishes nothing about the promo on staples.com — the terms exist only in each year’s coverage.

The Veterans Day history is real and dated: 25% off in-store ran November 6–12, 2022, through November 12, 2024 (active duty, reservists, retired or disabled veterans, and immediate family), and approximately November 5–11, 2025 ("veterans and active military" per that year’s coverage). Watch the eligibility drift — the older wording named "retired or disabled veterans" specifically, so whether every veteran qualifies is set fresh each year. Bring any military ID, VA card, or state veteran ID, mention the offer at checkout, and ask about exclusions (the list has never been published).

Outside that one week, a verified military shopper saves more elsewhere. Office Depot/OfficeMax runs a genuine everyday program: 20% off one qualifying regular- or sale-price purchase (verify with ID.me online or show military ID in store), plus a military/teacher 25%-back-in-Bonus-Rewards offer running December 28, 2025 – December 26, 2026 — though ink/toner and technology are excluded. And ShopMyExchange is tax-free on everything, open online to all honorably discharged veterans (Veterans Online Shopping Benefit, since November 11, 2017), with back-to-school events that have hit 40% off select supplies.

Staples’ own year-round levers are public, not military: Easy Rewards is free (1 point per $1, 2X on three self-picked categories, 200 points = $1, plus points for recycling ink/toner cartridges up to a dashboard-shown monthly limit); the price-match policy covers identical in-stock items including sold-and-shipped-by-Amazon; cashback portals paid ~4% on online orders as of July 4, 2026; and the July–September back-to-school season brings 25¢ doorbusters and weekly freebies — the category’s deepest public pricing. Coupon sites also report a $15-off-$60 email/text signup offer for new online subscribers, but it isn’t confirmed on any Staples-owned page — verify at signup before counting on it.
samsung-military-discount: Samsung verifies eligibility two ways. Automatic email approval: a .gov, .mil, .edu, or .company email is auto-approved when you create your Samsung Account, and you are signed straight into the Offer Program. ID.me: if you use a personal email, Samsung redirects you to ID.me to confirm your affiliation to a qualified group. For veterans, Guard/Reserve, retirees, and family, Samsung also points to WeSalute, which verifies your service when you create a free account and requires a paid WeSalute+ membership to access the Samsung store.

Samsung notes the discount available through the Offer Program (ID.me) and through WeSalute may differ — they are not guaranteed to be identical. Re-verification frequency is not stated in Samsung’s official source; ID.me and WeSalute apply their own periodic re-verification per their policies. For problems, Samsung’s order help center (order-help.us.samsung.com) and ID.me/WeSalute support are the paths.

One thing to watch: "up to 30%" is a ceiling, not a guaranteed rate. Samsung’s page repeatedly says "saving up to 30%"; actual savings vary by product and change over time, so do not expect a fixed percentage on any specific item. And while some aggregator and partner pages claim the discount stacks with public and seasonal offers, Samsung’s own Offer Program terms say the pricing "cannot be combined with any other offer" — where the brand’s primary terms and a third party disagree, treat it as non-combinable and verify at checkout.
scheels-military-veteran: How the SCHEELS 5% works: it is tied to a MySCHEELS account and unlocked by a one-time ID.me military verification. Once verified, 5% comes off your entire order, every day — online and in store — rather than as a single promo. Because it is a flat order-level discount, it generally cannot be combined with other promo codes, and clearance pricing may not stack.

How the Vortex 40% works: Vortex’s Vortex Discount Program is an application-based program for active and retired military and first responders. After approval you purchase eligible Vortex products through the program at 40% off MSRP. It is run by Vortex, not SCHEELS, so you cannot get the 40% by walking into a SCHEELS store — and the two discounts run on different channels, so they do not combine.

The practical rule: if you are buying Vortex optics and you qualify, the Vortex program (40% off MSRP) dwarfs everything else — on a $300 MSRP optic that is $120 off versus $15 from the SCHEELS 5%. For everything else at SCHEELS, the everyday 5% via ID.me is your baseline, though a seasonal sale can occasionally beat it (and usually will not stack with the 5%).

A note on rates: where a row depends on a moving figure — a seasonal sale, a cashback portal that may or may not list SCHEELS, or loyalty rewards — it is stamped "rates as of June 16, 2026," because those move over time. The 5% and the 40% are program rates set by SCHEELS and Vortex respectively; confirm both on the official pages before you buy.
fashion-nova-military-discount: Fashion Nova uses VerifyPass, a merchant-integrated verification service, rather than ID.me, SheerID, or GovX. You confirm your military status once through VerifyPass and receive a single-use code; you re-verify for another. The 30% is the only brand-run military figure that verifies — coupon sites throwing out “40/50/80% off military” are either quoting public sitewide codes or fabricating the number.

The structural quirk that makes Fashion Nova different from most brands is its perpetual public-code firehose. Because a large sitewide code is live almost continuously and the checkout accepts one discount code per order, the military 30% is frequently not the best available price. TikTok “military discount” tutorials often just apply a public code, which anyone can use — that’s a different thing from the verified VerifyPass code.

The reliable optimization: before verifying, check whether a live sitewide code already meets or beats 30%. If it does, use it and skip verification. If it doesn’t (or there’s none), verify for the military 30%. Either way, a cashback portal pays on the post-code total, so it’s the one add-on that stacks on top.
gunscom-military-discount: The discount is delivered as an auto-applied coupon once ID.me confirms your eligibility at checkout — you do not hand-enter a code. It does not stack onto sale or clearance products, and it never applies to auction listings, which are two of the most common ways Guns.com prices are already cut.

Verification runs through ID.me, the same third-party identity service used across many military-discount programs. You verify once and confirm your information at checkout; ID.me may require periodic re-verification under its own policy. Support for the discount itself runs through Guns.com customer service, while identity issues route to ID.me support.

During special promotions, Guns.com has let verified ID.me members "nearly double" the discount. That boost is a replacement promotional rate for verified members rather than a second coupon stacked on the standard 5% — treat it as one enhanced rate during the window, and watch Guns.com email and news for when it runs.
bear-creek-arsenal-military-discount: Verification is manual and email-based, not through ID.me, GovX, or SheerID. You submit proof of service to BCA’s service-member address; BCA reviews it and returns an approval. Re-verification cadence and code expiration are not specified on the page, so treat the discount as subject to BCA confirmation each time.

The bigger lever for most buyers is BCA’s own pricing. Public sitewide sales (often 10–20% off) and clearance or "blem"/overstock pricing routinely beat the 5% and are open to everyone — but you can’t stack the military discount onto them. On a $199.99 full-price upper, the 5% saves about $10, while a live 15% sale saves about $30. Use the 5% on full-price parts during no-sale windows, and take the public sale otherwise.

One thing to watch: coupon-aggregator pages advertise "50%/65%/70% off" codes and even a "15%/20% military" figure. Those are inflated claims — the only verified military figure on BCA’s own site is 5%, and BCA’s big percentage-off deals are public sales, not a military code.
disneyland-military-discount: Eligibility is verified either in person at a participating U.S. military base ticket office or online through GovX, which checks military status during account setup. A valid military ID is required both to purchase and to use the 3-Day/4-Day tickets. Disney does not state how often GovX re-verifies status, so treat verification as per GovX’s own policy rather than permanent.

Disney never publishes a percentage off versus standard gate prices. The 2026 promotional prices are: 1-Day 1-Park $104 adult / $98 child; 3-Day Park Hopper $314 ($416 with Lightning Lane Multi Pass); and 4-Day Park Hopper $369 ($505 with LL Multi Pass). Buy 3-Day/4-Day tickets through Dec 27, 2026 (valid Jan 1–Dec 31, 2026); buy 1-Day tickets through Dec 30, 2027.

A separate 2026 offer gives eligible members discounted rates on select Disneyland Resort hotel rooms (travel Jan 1–Dec 31, 2026; book by Dec 27, 2026). Disney does not publish a percentage; book by calling (866) 309-9737, and bring a valid military ID at check-in. The "no combining" rule applies within ticket discounts, not between the separate ticket and hotel offers.
realtruck-military-discount: RealTruck runs a Minimum Advertised Price (MAP) policy on the brands it manufactures, and it does not price-match. That is why "shopping around for a lower advertised price" rarely moves the number on premium covers — the same product sells for the same price on realtruck.com, on Amazon, and at third-party retailers. The reliable lever on a full-price MAP item is therefore a cashback portal, not a coupon code.

Cashback portals have rules that matter: TopCashback (4% as of July 10, 2026) and Rakuten (2%) both exclude gift cards and require starting from an empty cart, and TopCashback does not surface RealTruck coupons on-portal. Using an outside coupon code alongside a portal purchase commonly voids the cashback tracking — and on a full-price MAP cover you are not using a code anyway, so the portal route is clean.

RealTruck also supports the veteran community, but as a donation, not a discount: it has donated 5% of Veterans Day (and, in 2023, July 4) sales to Building Homes for Heroes, more than $1 million over 5+ years. Buying that day directs 5% to veteran housing, but it is not a personal discount to you. Re-check RealTruck’s own pages for the current program before relying on any figure here.
victoria-secret-military-discount: The debunk, with receipts: HotDeals advertises a "Victoria’s Secret military discount 50%," Coupert claims "military discount — up to 40% off," WorthEPenny runs a VS "Military & Veteran Discounts" page, and posts circulate claiming code "NENA20" gives military members 40% off. None of this is confirmed by any Victoria’s Secret or verification-provider source — and ID.me, the provider that would run such a program, explicitly states no VS offer exists for military or first responders. No credible community reports of an in-store discretionary discount surfaced either; this isn’t a your-mileage-may-vary situation. The program simply doesn’t exist.

The honest maximum is a timing play. The Semi-Annual Sale runs twice a year — June and December — at up to 60% off select bras, panties, sleep, beauty, lingerie, clothing, swim, and accessories (the summer 2026 window opened around June 3 and typically runs into early July; VS doesn’t pre-announce dates). Sale pricing stacks reliably with a cashback portal, because the portal tracks whatever price you pay — just use only codes the portal itself surfaces, or none, since scraped codes can reduce or void the payout. Free Rewards membership adds free shipping at $50+.

For fragrance and body care, the Exchange is the quiet win: shopmyexchange.com carries VS Bombshell and other fragrance, mists, body care, and VS gift cards, all tax-free — worth roughly 6–10% depending on your state — with MILITARY STAR cardholders getting free standard shipping and periodic extra promos. Know the access rules: all honorably discharged veterans can shop the Exchange online, while in-store privileges are narrower. VS.com codes and portals don’t apply at the Exchange; it’s a separate, closed channel.

Two more layers for regulars: the free VS & PINK Rewards program earns points toward reward dollars, and the Victoria’s Secret Credit Card (Comenity) pays 10 points per $1 — 30 points per $1 on bras — with a $10 reward per 2,000 points, a birthday reward, and a 15% anniversary benefit at $0 annual fee. Store-card math only works if you pay in full monthly. And skip the WeSalute route: its "discounted VS gift cards" listing publishes no rate and sits behind a $9.99+/month membership — don’t join for this alone.
brandy-melville-military-discount: There is no verification because there is no military discount. Brandy Melville is not an ID.me or SheerID partner, and no Brandy Melville GovX storefront exists. Ignore any site claiming a “military code” or an “ID.me/SheerID unlock” — the words “military,” “veteran,” “loyalty,” “rewards,” and “student” appear nowhere on the brand’s official customer-service page. Even if a generic public code ever works, it is not a military benefit, and any order using it becomes final sale.

Because there is no first-party discount, loyalty program, or cashback layer, the savings are narrow and public. Brandy Melville has no standing sale section and issues essentially no public codes (SimplyCodes has tracked zero working codes in roughly two years), and it is not listed on Rakuten (the store page 404s). Its one reliable public sale is the occasional Black Friday / Cyber Monday flash deal, historically up to about 30% off in 2023 — open to everyone, not a military tier.

Two fine-print points matter more here than usual. First, all discounted orders are final sale, and whole categories — intimates, swimwear, jewelry, belts, hats, hair accessories, backpacks, eyewear, scarves, handbags, and keychains — are non-returnable regardless of discount. Second, most Brandy Melville is one-size, so be certain on fit before buying anything discounted. Returns otherwise run 30 days on unworn, unwashed items with original tags, and the buyer pays return shipping.
nissan-military-discount: The verified, standalone Military Program value is $500. Some dealer pages advertise “$500 to $1,000 off MSRP,” but that larger number is the $500 bonus plus other stacked incentives or VPP pricing — not a higher military amount. There is also no online promo code; the program is redeemed at the dealership via a generated certificate, so any coupon-site “Nissan military code” is fabricated.

The stacking is the program’s defining feature. Nissan states the $500 “can be combined with all current national and regional incentives” — customer cash, APR/lease cash, and seasonal offers — so it’s pure additive savings on top of whatever public deal is live. It cannot, however, combine with the Nissan College Grad Program or other VPP-family offers; a buyer eligible for both must compare and choose the larger.

Because the $500 is constant while the public incentive layer swings monthly and by region, timing is the real lever. Shop when national/regional cash or APR is deepest — typically model-year sell-down, May (Military Appreciation Month), July 4, and Black Friday/year-end — so the $500 stacks on the biggest public deal. Retail savings channels like GovX, cashback portals, the military Exchange, and ExpertVoice don’t apply to a new-vehicle purchase from a dealer.

The Military Program is separate from the general Nissan VPP (Vehicle Purchase Program / supplier-employee pricing) and the College Grad Program — they can’t be combined with each other. Dealers reproduce the terms but aren’t the primary source; confirm the standalone $500, the excluded-models list, and any offer window directly with Nissan VPP.
lacoste-military-discount: Verification is handled by ID.me. You confirm your military status once through ID.me (an account is required), and it returns a single-use promo code for a single online purchase. Because the code is one-per-week and single-use, you re-request it from ID.me for each qualifying order — this is not a permanent account-level discount. Support for verification issues goes through ID.me’s help flow, not Lacoste.

Ignore coupon-site claims of a "15% military discount" or "up to 25% off." The verified first-party offer is 10% via ID.me. The 15% figure is almost certainly a conflation with Lacoste’s public Le Club welcome and text-signup offers, which anyone can get without military status. Claims that the military discount works in stores or in the app are also not confirmed by ID.me’s own redemption page, which describes an online benefit.

The best total-savings path depends on your situation. New customers do better with the 15% Le Club welcome or the 15% text/app signup than with the 10% military code. Repeat full-price buyers with no code live get the most from the 10% ID.me discount. And when a semi-annual or holiday sale (up to ~50%) is running, the sale price is the deepest deal — the non-combinable military code can’t stack on top of it, so don’t waste it.
beautyrest-military-discount: The math below uses one baseline: a queen Beautyrest mattress (≈$1,299 at typical online prices; Beautyrest Black lines run higher). Beautyrest Black is the pivotal case, because Mattress Firm’s military discount excludes it.

Beautyrest itself verifies nothing — it has no program. For the retailer path, Mattress Firm uses ID.me: you create or sign into an ID.me account, it confirms your service record, and it issues a discount code worth 10–20% off eligible Beautyrest models (Beautyrest Black excluded). For the Exchange, eligibility is your existing military/veteran shopping authorization; veterans verify once via the Exchange’s veteran verification.

The decision comes down to one question: is it a Beautyrest Black? If yes and you’re Exchange-eligible, the tax-free Exchange usually wins because Black is excluded from Mattress Firm’s discount. If it’s a non-Black Beautyrest (BR800, Harmony, etc.), Mattress Firm’s 10–20% ID.me discount usually beats a tax-free Exchange sale — compare the two final, tax-included numbers. If neither works, buy direct during a Beautyrest holiday event and request a price adjustment if a better sale lands within 100 nights.

Beautyrest’s own holiday events (Presidents Day, Memorial Day, July 4, Labor Day, Black Friday, Cyber Monday) are public sales open to everyone — none are military-appreciation offers, and they cannot be combined with other promotions.
