tsa-precheck-military-discount: The serving-member benefit is not a code or a card — it’s the 10-digit DoD ID number from the back of your CAC, entered as the Known Traveler Number in DTS, your frequent-flyer profiles, and every booking. It covers active duty, Reserves, Army and Air National Guard, the Coast Guard and its Reserve, service-academy cadets and midshipmen, and USPHS and NOAA commissioned officers, for official and personal travel alike. USMMA and state maritime academy students use their TWIC CIN instead, and DoD civilians (including NAF employees) must opt in once at the ID Card Office Online (milConnect) before their DoD ID works as a KTN.

The VETS Safe Travel Act (Public Law 118-238, signed January 4, 2025) made enrollment and renewals permanently free for a specific group: veterans enrolled in VA healthcare whose service-connected disability is permanent blindness, or who require a VA-issued wheelchair or prosthetic limb. The VA issues a TSA PreCheck Application Fee Waiver Letter through VA.gov; you email it to IDEMIA with "VETS Safe" in the subject line for an offer code. The waiver is IDEMIA-only — TSA will not reimburse CLEAR or Telos enrollments — and it covers the veteran, not family members.

Two more paths are worth knowing. Military spouses of currently serving members get $25 off enrollment or renewal at all three providers by showing a USID card with a "Spouse" relationship. And military survivor families — anyone eligible for the Gold Star lapel or Next of Kin Lapel Button, plus families of members who died of a service-connected injury or illness after separation — enroll free using a TAPS verification letter or TSA acknowledgement form, with each family member needing their own letter.

One misconception to correct: veterans do not "automatically keep" PreCheck after separation — the DoD ID number stops working as a KTN once you’re out, and TSA’s own FAQ says benefits do not continue after leaving DoD. There is also no "military promo code," and aggregator pages claiming a blanket veteran discount are wrong in both directions: most veterans get nothing, while the VETS Safe subset now gets PreCheck completely free. Fees never go on sale — they’re set by federal rule.
advance-auto-parts-military-discount: Advance verifies military status in person, at the register, with a physical ID — a U.S. Uniformed Services ID card, a Common Access Card (CAC), or a Veteran Identification Card (VIC). There is no online verification for this discount: Advance does not use ID.me, SheerID, or GovX for the military offer, despite what some coupon sites claim. If you don’t have one of the accepted IDs, the discount can’t be applied.

Eligibility runs to active-duty, reserve, and retired members (retired counts only with 20+ years of service), all veterans receiving VA benefits, and immediate family — spouses and dependent children up to age 18. Commercial and professional-account purchases are excluded; the discount is for personal, in-store DIY shopping only.

Watch out for a common myth: several aggregators and even some military-listing sites claim the Advance Auto Parts military discount works both online and in-store and that you verify via ID.me or SheerID. That is false per Advance’s own help-desk article, which plainly states the discount cannot be used for Advanceautoparts.com purchases and describes in-store, physical-ID verification only. Around Veterans Day, Advance has historically amplified its military messaging and, in some past years, run a larger temporary military promo through a partner — treat any expanded figure as a limited-time promo to verify each November, not the standing 10% offer.
ugg-military-discount: UGG verifies Community Heroes eligibility through SheerID — military, first responders, medical professionals, and educators all confirm their status there. College students verify separately through UNiDAYS. You select your group, submit your information, and may be asked to upload documentation; UGG states registration "should be confirmed within 24 hours." Once verified, you redeem the 10% on UGG’s Promotions & Discounts page.

The single most important caveat: the everyday 10% applies to full-priced styles only, so sale and clearance items are excluded. The exception is Veterans Day, when military get 10% off all orders including sale items — a broader benefit worth timing a larger or sale-item purchase around.

One thing to watch: an older UGG help-center article reportedly states UGG offers no military or professional discount. That page is outdated and contradicted by UGG’s current story page and the live SheerID Community Heroes offer, both of which confirm the active 10% discount. Aggregator claims of "up to 25%" or an ID.me route are unconfirmed — UGG’s official verification is SheerID (and UNiDAYS for students).
legoland-military-discount: For online purchases, LEGOLAND verifies military status through ID.me, a third-party verification service. You sign in or create an ID.me account and confirm your affiliation; once verified, you can access the discounted pricing. For in-person redemption and at hotel check-in, you must present a current, valid Military/Department of Defense ID or a government-issued ID indicating veteran status — inability to provide it can result in being charged the higher (non-discounted) rate. LEGOLAND does not publish how long ID.me verification lasts, so do not assume it is permanent.

The discount structure differs by park. California publishes the clearest number ("up to 35% off," from $72.54 vs. $129 full price) plus up to 10% off hotels. New York gives a 1-Day ticket with a free second day plus up to 10% off the hotel. Florida advertises "special" / "heavily discounted" ticket pricing — no exact ticket percentage is published, so the price appears only after ID.me verification — plus a limited-time 20% off hotel rooms for stays now through September 3, 2026.

On-base ITT/military ticket offices sometimes carry deeper bundles than the website, and LEGOLAND Florida explicitly points veterans and families there for "deeply discounted" tickets. In recent years LEGOLAND Florida and New York have also run limited-time free-admission events around Veterans Day for military and first responders — those are announced each year, so verify current-year terms before planning.
paramount-plus-military-discount: The SheerID page title is "Military Discount: 50% Off Any Plan For Life," and the asterisk clarifies "Until cancellation. T&Cs apply." So "for life" means for the life of the subscription — until you cancel — not a one-time lifetime grant independent of keeping the plan. The verbatim eligibility line is "Offer available to active military, veterans & their spouses."

Paramount+ uses SheerID, not ID.me, to confirm military eligibility. You submit a few details on the SheerID verify page; in many cases verification is instant, and if SheerID needs more it will request documentation such as a military ID, DD-214, or a .mil email. After verification you proceed to Paramount+ signup, and the discount applies for the life of the subscription. Some third-party pages mention a 12-month re-verification step, but that is not stated on Paramount+’s official offer — keep the subscription active and watch your account for any re-verification request.

The 50% is applied to the then-current base price. Paramount+ raised base prices in January 2026, so the post-discount dollar figure is not fixed — with the discount the Essential plan has run around $4/month and Premium around $6.50/month, but treat those figures as illustrative and time-stamped, not guaranteed. If you are already a subscriber, editorial sources report you must cancel and re-subscribe through the offer link so the discount attaches to the new subscription; confirm the exact steps in your account, since this is not spelled out on the official offer page.
peloton-military-discount: Per Peloton’s offer page, you enter qualifying information that is "checked by our verification partner" before the discount unlocks; once verified, pricing applies automatically in your cart. Peloton’s page does not name the partner in the copy we reviewed. ID.me’s own Peloton page states that Peloton does not use ID.me for Military verification and that military members "verify their status directly with Peloton," while some editorial coverage reports Peloton moved special-pricing verification from SheerID to ID.me. Because the primary sources conflict, treat the specific provider, account requirements, and re-verification frequency as unconfirmed and verify on Peloton’s offer page.

The clearest published savings are on the App: App One and App+ have stated military monthly and annual prices. Equipment savings are not published per product, so the safest approach is to verify, then compare the price you’re shown against Peloton’s current public sales — since the military discount cannot be combined with other offers.

Peloton runs separate special-pricing groups for healthcare workers, first responders, educators, veterinarians, government workers, and students (students for the App offer only); each has its own offer page and is not part of the military offer documented here.
belk-military-discount: Belk’s online discount is powered by ID.me, the same identity-verification service used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of major retailers. You verify once on Belk’s service-discount page, then click the ID.me button in your cart to apply the 10% — and on future visits you simply sign in rather than re-proving your status.

The make-or-break fact is stacking: Belk’s own press release says the online 10% is "stackable with most other eligible promotions." Belk runs frequent extra-25%–50%-off coupon events, so for a regular-price online order the everyday best play is a public promo code plus the ID.me 10% (and a cashback portal on top) — not the 10% alone.

The in-store Tuesday event is a different program with different rules: it is in-store-only, non-stacking, and applies even to sale and clearance items (where online coupons and the 10% are typically excluded). That makes the ~20% Tuesday rate the winner for clearance bought in a store, while the online stack wins on regular-price online orders.
purple-mattress-military-discount: Purple routes its discount through SheerID. You verify your eligibility (military, first responder, healthcare, education, or trucker) once; SheerID confirms status — most instantly, otherwise by email within about 20 minutes — and issues a single-use code. SheerID states it does not store uploaded documents. There is no confirmed ID.me, GovX, or WeSalute route for Purple.

Because the 10% is non-combinable and full-price only, it competes directly with Purple’s frequent public sales rather than stacking on them. A public, auto-applied sale is also portal-safe, so routing an on-sale order through a cashback portal like Rakuten (about 2% as of July 10, 2026 — verify the live rate) is the combinable play a SheerID code cannot match.

Purple and SheerID can re-verify eligibility and can change or end the program at any time, so treat the numbers here as a starting point and confirm the current offer on Purple’s official Military Discount page before you buy.
autozone/military-veteran: AutoZone runs a published corporate Military Discount Program — not store-manager discretion. Its official page states a flat 10% off in-store purchases for active or retired members of every U.S. branch, including the Space Force, the Army and Air National Guard, and the Coast Guard, and it explicitly extends eligibility to their dependents.

There is no third-party verifier and no account to create. In store, you state that you qualify and present a military ID or one of AutoZone’s accepted documents to an AutoZoner, who applies the discount at the point of sale. Accepted documents include a valid DoD ID, Uniformed Services ID, Veteran ID Card, Veteran Health ID Card, a state ID or driver’s license designating veteran status, a DD214, or a DoD dependent ID (DD form 1173 or 1173-1) — and the list is "not limited to" these.

Because the discount can’t be used online, online shoppers should lean on AutoZone Rewards (free) and AutoZone’s standard, open-to-everyone promo codes instead — the military rate simply doesn’t apply on AutoZone.com or in the app.
manscaped-military-discount: Verification is handled by ID.me — the same third-party identity service used across hundreds of brands. Create a free ID.me account once, confirm your military affiliation (which may require documents), and you can reuse it at checkout. ID.me may require periodic re-verification, and the discount is issued as a code that is no more permanent than Manscaped’s current program.

Because the military code does not stack, the public sale is the real competitor to the military discount, not an add-on to it. Manscaped’s recurring ~20% sitewide events often beat the 15% military code and require no verification, bundle kits deliver the best total value on a full grooming setup, and marketplaces periodically cut the flagship trimmer well below MSRP (Amazon reached about $77 on the Lawn Mower 5.0 Ultra in November 2025). Compare all four and take the lowest single price.

Manscaped also has a separate GovX marketplace store as a secondary channel; its live rate was not displayed on our access date, so verify it against ID.me if you are already a GovX member. Support for verification problems goes through ID.me’s help center, not Manscaped.
rack-room-shoes-military-discount: The mechanic is simple and manual: you present a valid military ID at the register on a Tuesday for 10%, or on Memorial Day, July 4, or Veterans Day for 20%. A servicemember or their spouse may present the ID for a family member’s purchase. Rack Room does not use ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or any online verifier for this offer, and there is no unique online code.

The headline feature is stacking. Rack Room states verbatim that the 10% and 20% military discounts “can be combined with the BOGO 50% OFF offer & applied to all sale prices.” That makes a two-pair trip the deepest realistic path: two $80 pairs list at $160, BOGO takes the second pair half off to $120, and a Veterans-Day 20% brings it to roughly $96 — about a 40% effective discount that no single coupon matches. Just note BOGO excludes accessories and many top brands (Nike, adidas, Crocs, Timberland, Vans), so confirm eligible brands at the register.

On the debunk: coupon and military-listicle pages claim you can “verify through ID.me and receive a unique Rack Room 10%-off code for online checkout.” This is not supported. Rack Room’s own page says the offer is in-store only with a military ID at the register and names no online verifier, and the ID.me store page for Rack Room shows no Rack Room-specific offer. Treat any “Rack Room online military code” as unverified.

For online buyers there’s no military discount, but the free Rewards program carries the everyday value: 1 point per $1, 200 points for a $15 reward, plus free shipping on every order. Non-members get free shipping on orders over $65 after discounts, and a cashback portal (Rakuten listed 2% as of July 10, 2026) can add a little online — though it doesn’t touch the in-store military discount.
carnival-military-discount: Carnival’s direct military rate is verified after you book, not at checkout. You reserve the military rate on your sailing, then submit an eligibility document to Carnival’s Interline Desk (Interline@carnival.com or fax 305-406-6478) within 72 hours — or 24 hours if the cruise sails within a week. Accepted documents include a military LES with the SSN blacked out, retirement papers (DD214/DD256), or an honorable-discharge DD214. There is no ID.me, SheerID, or GovX gate; a Veterans Administration card is explicitly not accepted.

Because the military rate competes with Carnival’s public promotional fares rather than stacking on them, Carnival prices each sailing at the single lowest applicable fare. That is why the honest advice is to price-compare: sometimes a live public sale beats the military rate, in which case you simply take the lower fare. Coupon and cruise-agency sites circulate specific figures — "$50-$250 per cabin," "up to 50% off," a "PME / Exclusive Military Early Saver" rate code, and extra-cabin claims — but none of these appear on Carnival’s official military page, so we do not publish them as fact.

The one verified, dated deeper discount on record is the separate WeSalute+ Carnival offer: "up to 40% off cruise rates and up to $100 onboard credit" per room. It is an alternative route, not a stack on the plain military rate — you register on WeSalute.com (by July 31, 2026), then book through a private link into Carnival’s VIFP Club for sailings through April 2027. It requires a paid WeSalute+ membership, and the "up to" figures are ceilings, so weigh the membership cost against your sailing’s actual savings.

Onboard credit is separate from the fare and can layer on. A military travel agency (such as Military Cruise Deals, iCruise, or Vacations To Go) can add group onboard credit or a reduced deposit on top of the fare, and the Carnival Corp shareholder benefit gives holders of 100+ CCL shares $50/$100/$250 in onboard credit by cruise length — though its terms exclude reduced-rate or interline bookings, so confirm it can pair with the military rate first. VIFP loyalty points and Carnival World Mastercard FunPoints accrue on any fare.
callaway-golf-military-discount: Verification is handled by ID.me (Callaway also refers to it as "ID.me/TroopID") on the Secure Checkout page. You log into or create an ID.me account and verify your military status; once the credential is verified, the 15% is applied immediately. Callaway’s pages do not state how often ID.me re-verification is required, so re-verification frequency is governed by ID.me, not Callaway. For verification problems, ID.me support is the path for credential issues; Callaway customer service handles order/discount-application questions.

Two limits to plan around: the discount cannot be combined with other promotional codes, and total discounts are capped at $1,000 per person per year. Gift cards are excluded, and Callaway notes "some exclusions may apply" without listing specific SKUs — so confirm at checkout whether a particular new release or custom order qualifies.

Callaway also runs a separate 15% First Responder program (also via ID.me). If you’re comparing golf OEMs, TaylorMade offers a 15% military discount via ID.me, while PING runs a "Thank You Troops" rebate on select clubs rather than a percentage — confirm current terms on each brand’s site.
fleet-farm-military-discount: Multiple coupon aggregators state Fleet Farm gives a "10% year-round military discount, verified through SheerID, valid on fleetfarm.com, the app, and in stores." This appears to be recycled template copy: there is no Fleet Farm SheerID verification landing page in search results, and Fleet Farm’s own posts describe the benefit as a limited-window, in-store, show-your-ID event, not a persistent online code. We do not publish the SheerID/online-code claim as fact.

Fleet Farm’s military events verify at the register with a military ID — there is no online identity-verification step and no confirmed SheerID, ID.me, or GovX integration. If Fleet Farm ever launches an online verified program, it would appear on an official fleetfarm.com page; as of July 12, 2026 none exists.

Because the military event can’t be combined with other coupons, ad-stack promos, price-matches, or the Fleet Rewards member 10%, compare it against the plain weekly-ad price and take whichever is lower — a real clearance markdown routinely beats a 10% event. For the premium brands Fleet Farm excludes (Carhartt, YETI, Traeger, Weber, Under Armour), the AAFES/NEX Exchange sells them tax-free and is often the cheaper path.
samsonite-military-discount: All the math below uses one baseline: a $300 hardside checked spinner (a Freeform-class 28-inch case) at shop.samsonite.com list price. Because a tax-free channel competes here, tax matters: at a ~7% sales-tax rate, a non-exchange purchase adds about $21 — which is why the exchange route can flip close comparisons even without any discount.

Rule 1 — there is no military discount to stack, so the game is sale price + cashback. Samsonite sale prices aren’t codes, which makes sale + Rakuten the portal-safe stack; what voids cashback is adding a scraped coupon code the portal doesn’t list. Use only codes Rakuten itself surfaces. On the baseline case, an event-priced spinner plus 2.5% cash back lands roughly $187–$278 all-in — saving $43–$134 versus paying full freight.

Rule 2 — the exchanges are their own channel. AAFES (shopmyexchange.com) and the Navy Exchange (mynavyexchange.com) both stock Samsonite — Freeform, Outline Pro, Evolve SE, and Alliance SE lines among them — with no sales tax. Samsonite promo codes don’t apply there, but MILITARY STAR cardholders get the exchange’s own financing and promo perks. Since the 2017 Veterans Online Shopping Benefit, every honorably discharged veteran can shop both exchanges online; in-store access is limited to narrower groups. Compare the exchange sticker against Samsonite’s taxed sale price before buying.

Rule 3 — GovX and WeSalute are worth a look, not a detour. GovX’s Samsonite storefront ("Samsonite – Discounts for Military & Gov’t") gates member pricing behind free verification; it’s a closed marketplace, so nothing stacks on top, and its pricing is unpublished — spot-check your exact model and expect it to compete with, not beat, a deep public sale. WeSalute runs an unpublished Samsonite cash-back offer through BenefitHub, but it requires a paid WeSalute+ membership (from $9.99/mo), can’t be combined with Rakuten, and rarely clears the fee unless you already subscribe.
best-buy-military-discount: The honest core fact: Best Buy’s official answer is that it does not offer a military discount. Its Memberships Expert Team points shoppers to the Price Match Guarantee instead, calling it the way "to help you save even more." That makes Price Match — not a military code — the starting point for any service member shopping Best Buy.

Why the "10%" claims keep circulating. Coupon aggregators and military-discount listicles widely advertise a "10% Best Buy military discount," but no official Best Buy source confirms it. The only "10%" Best Buy actually publishes is the new-cardmember credit-card bonus (10% back in rewards on first-day purchases upon approval), which is open to every approved applicant, not just military. A separate "up to 10%" store-manager line exists only in a user-generated Q&A answer and is not Best Buy policy.

Where the real savings are. Best Buy’s genuine levers are the Price Match Guarantee, My Best Buy rewards and membership tiers, the credit-card bonus, and Best Buy Outlet/Open-Box. All of these are open to everyone — none is a military benefit, but each is a real way to lower your price.

The most reliable "military" route is often elsewhere. Many manufacturers Best Buy carries — Samsung, LG, Apple, and Dell among them — run their own verified military discounts. For a service member buying electronics, going direct to the manufacturer with a true military rate frequently beats buying the same product at Best Buy, where there is no military discount at all.
ralph-lauren-military-discount: The only brand-run military offer is in person: at a Polo Ralph Lauren Factory (outlet) Store, you show a valid military ID at the register and the associate applies 10% off eligible items. The offer’s own terms state it is not valid at Ralph Lauren stores, on RalphLauren.com, or at Polo Ralph Lauren Clearance Factory Stores, and it excludes categories such as watches, MLB product, Ralph’s Coffee, and gift cards.

Online, the substitute channel is GovX, which runs a “LAUREN Ralph Lauren” marketplace storefront. GovX verifies current and former military, first responders, law enforcement, healthcare workers, and government employees, but its pricing is gated behind login and nothing stacks on top of it. Ralph Lauren’s old ID.me “Ralph Lauren Fragrances” page now returns “Page not found,” so there is no active ID.me military offer.

Two things to correct: coupon aggregators fabricate a Ralph Lauren online military program (for example an “60% off Ralph Lauren military code”) — none of it exists on any Ralph Lauren property. And the widely cited “20% military discount” belongs to U.S. Polo Assn., a completely separate company; it must not be attributed to Ralph Lauren.

The honest math: on a $200 cart, a public sitewide sale code at 25–30% off lands you around $140–$150 and needs no verification, while the outlet 10% only applies in person on top of already-reduced outlet pricing. Wait for a sale code, shop the outlet in person for the 10% bonus, or compare the GovX storefront — in that order.
ross-military-discount: Ross is an off-price retailer: it buys overstock, closeouts, irregulars, and packaway merchandise and pre-marks it below original retail, typically 20–60% below department-store and specialty prices. That means the "discount" at Ross is baked into the tag rather than applied at the register — there is no code, no membership, and no military tier layered on top. The low sticker is the deal.

Be cautious of coupon and aggregator pages (and AI-summary snippets) that claim Ross gives "10% off year-round to active-duty, veterans, and immediate family." This is not accurate. Ross’s own FAQ lists no military discount, and ID.me explicitly says it is not aware of one. The only 10% Ross runs is the age-55+ Tuesday senior discount; writers appear to have copied that number onto a "military" label. We omit the circulating figure on purpose because repeating it would imply an offer Ross does not run.

The 55+ "Every Tuesday" senior discount is real and reliable: customers age 55 or older enroll at the Customer Service Desk, shop on Tuesdays, notify the cashier before paying, and show ID verifying their age if asked. Ten percent comes off eligible in-store items. Some brands and items are excluded, and Ross does not publish the exact excluded list, so ask in store.

If what you specifically want is a guaranteed military discount, it lives elsewhere. Many apparel, footwear, and gear brands offer verified 10–20% military discounts through ID.me, and the military exchanges (AAFES, Navy Exchange, MCX) sell comparable apparel and home goods tax-free. Off-price peers like T.J.Maxx, Marshalls, and Burlington also lack military discounts but offer similar treasure-hunt value — compare the item, not the label.
norwegian-cruise-line-military-discount: NCL verifies eligibility through ID.me, its named third-party partner. You create/log in to My NCL, complete a one-time ID.me check (~5 minutes; documents like a .mil email or DD214), and your account is flagged — the 10% then applies automatically whenever you’re logged in. There is no ID.me code to paste, and no GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute path for NCL.

The military rate combines with More at Sea™ (formerly Free at Sea), which is unusual among cruise-line military discounts. A travel advisor can also layer their own group onboard credit and reduced deposit on top by booking under your My NCL/Latitudes number — that agency perk isn’t an NCL discount, so it doesn’t conflict.

The year-round floor is 10% off cruise fare; the "up to 20%" figure some listings quote reflects the select-sailing bump, not a guaranteed everyday rate. No path waives the taxes, port fees, or gratuities — every percentage applies to the cruise fare portion alone.
yard-house-military-discount: Yard House is a Darden Restaurants brand (alongside Olive Garden, LongHorn Steakhouse, and The Capital Grille), and Darden runs no unified everyday military program across its brands. That is why there is no percentage off to enter at a Yard House checkout and no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute gate for a Yard House military offer.

The Veterans Day free appetizer is verified informally in person: tell your server and show a military ID or proof of service if requested. Because it is server-checked rather than gated by an online provider, the experience can vary by location and staff. Yard House has run the same structure — one appetizer per person, dine-in, November 11 only, no purchase necessary — in 2023, 2024, and 2025, so re-verify the terms each late October.

For everyday savings, two non-military levers beat the fictional "military percentage." Happy Hour (50% off select apps and all pizzas, dine-in, typically ~3–6pm) needs no ID at all, and discounted Darden gift cards bought below face value shave roughly 10–15% off the whole check — and because a gift card is just the payment method, it layers on top of Happy Hour pricing or a Veterans Day comp.
west-elm-military-discount: All the math below uses one baseline: a $1,299 upholstered sofa, a representative West Elm big-ticket order. Sales tax applies on every path (there’s no tax-free channel and no cashback portal), and rewards are issued as certificates for future Williams-Sonoma-brand purchases, not cash back on this order — factor that into "effective cost."

The record-correction matters here because the legacy figure is sticky. Older editorial pages (e.g., a 2022 Bob Cut Magazine piece, some veteran.com copy) describe West Elm’s former SheerID mechanic — a verified email code for ~15% off — but no primary West Elm page confirms it live today. Three independent checks say it’s lapsed: ID.me is "not aware" of a West Elm military discount, West Elm is absent from SheerID’s 2026 Community Heroes roster (which does name dozens of active brands), and sibling Pottery Barn’s identical 15% is documented as discontinued. Don’t assert a current 15%.

The real savings engine is the loyalty wallet plus sale timing. The Key Rewards is free (Silver 2%), the West Elm Key Rewards Visa adds Gold 5% (10% the first 30 days), and rewards accrue even on sale-priced items — but they convert to certificates, not cash. On the $1,299 sofa that’s roughly $26 back at Silver 2%, ~$65 at Gold 5%, or ~$130 at the 10% intro rate. The biggest lever, though, is timing a sitewide sale or clearance event, whose markdowns dwarf a 2–10% rewards rate.

If a verified military percentage is what you actually want, the honest move is to cross-shop. Home brands that do publish a verified military discount via SheerID — OXO (20%) and Hydro Flask (20%) for kitchen and home, Ashley Furniture (5%) for furniture (as of July 8, 2026) — can beat West Elm outright on comparable items, and those offers apply to that brand rather than West Elm.
johnnie-o-military-discount: johnnie-O routes eligibility through GovX. You verify once; GovX confirms your military, first-responder, healthcare, government, or teacher status and unlocks the 15% discount. There is no confirmed SheerID, ID.me, or WeSalute military path for johnnie-O — GovX is the named partner, and ID.me explicitly states it is not aware of a johnnie-O military discount.

The 15% is issued as a single-use GovX code. johnnie-O publishes no stacking terms, but GovX-issued codes are generally non-combinable with other promos, so treat the discount as an either/or against a live sale rather than something you stack on top of it.

On the brand’s signature Original 4-Button Polo ($98), the 15% GovX discount works out to about $83.30. During an End of Season Sale (up to roughly 50% off select styles), the marked-down price can drop well below that — and since the two generally won’t combine, the sale price is the better buy when it’s deeper than 15%.
nfl-sunday-ticket-military-discount: The military and community offer is verified through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. You verify once for your group and are routed to YouTube checkout. Existing subscribers who verified through ID.me auto-renew at the $198 eligible price unless they cancel before the renewal date.

A separate Student Plan is available at $119 for the season (add NFL RedZone for $10), verified through SheerID. It is a one-time purchase that does not auto-renew, includes a single signed-in device with one concurrent stream, and is not part of the ID.me military/community program.

Because YouTube sets NFL Sunday Ticket pricing seasonally, treat the figures here as the verified 2026 numbers and confirm the current price and the exact redemption deadline at checkout — ID.me’s terms reference December 31, 2026, while YouTube Help references availability until January 10, 2027.
ram-military-discount: Ram verifies eligibility through SheerID, a third-party verification service, using two separate entry points on the military-incentive page: one for active/retired military and one for disabled military. Either path issues an authorization number that you bring to the dealer.

The $500 is additive, not exclusive — Ram’s own FAQ states buyers "may also qualify for other offers," meaning the bonus cash layers on top of national incentives, regional offers, financing deals, and dealer discounts rather than replacing them.

One thing to watch: some dealer landing pages and aggregator sites imply this is a store-wide or percentage-based military deal, or that it applies to any Ram model. In reality it’s a fixed $500 bonus-cash allowance limited to a specific list of 2026 models, redeemed only at the dealer via a SheerID authorization number — never a percentage and never an online promo code. The eligible-vehicle list changes by model year, so re-verify against Ram’s official page at purchase time.

Because the $500 is a flat amount on what is typically a $45,000-$60,000+ vehicle, it is a small piece of the total deal. The bigger lever for savings is timing your purchase or lease to Ram’s largest live public incentive, APR offer, or lease event, then adding the $500 on top.
whirlpool-military-discount: SheerID verifies your status inside your Whirlpool account: in My Account you select Military and authenticate — instant for most, document review otherwise. The discount then applies to new whirlpool.com orders while you’re verified. Note that ID.me is not the partner here: ID.me’s own Whirlpool page says it isn’t aware of a military discount, which is true only of ID.me’s network — the program exists and runs on SheerID. SheerID’s shopper hub also lists Whirlpool offers for students, teachers, first responders, healthcare workers, and seniors alongside the military program.

The scope is major appliances — washers, dryers, refrigerators, ranges, cooktops, wall ovens, microwaves, beverage and wine centers, dishwashers, hoods, ice makers, and compactors — on new whirlpool.com orders. Coupon sites headline "25% off Whirlpool military," and no source confirms that; even the widely-repeated 15% is only a secondary-source figure that Whirlpool’s page never states. The same gated-percentage pattern runs at Whirlpool’s sibling brands KitchenAid and Maytag, so cross-shop equivalent models. At the time of verification, whirlpool.com also showed a public free-delivery promo on orders $399+ (ends July 22, 2026), and military-benefits reporting describes additional verified-account perks — free 60-day returns and free delivery, installation, and haul-away on $1,000+ orders — that we haven’t confirmed on Whirlpool’s own terms.

Stacking is where big-ticket math gets decided. The SheerID discount is an account-level price, not a code, and per Whirlpool’s standard promotion terms it can’t be combined with other offers — so when a holiday appliance event is live (those events commonly run 25–35% off select majors), the public sale price usually wins. The genuine stack in this category is the exchange route: AAFES’s Home Depot storefront on shopmyexchange.com prices major appliances, Whirlpool included, at 1% below Home Depot’s current price — sale prices included — with no sales tax, plus MILITARY STAR 0%-interest 12-month financing on $399+. Eligibility includes active duty, retirees, dependents, DoD civilians, and honorably discharged veterans (confirm at shopmyexchange.com).

Two traps and two extra paths. Trap one: Lowe’s and Home Depot’s own 10% military discounts explicitly exclude major appliances — their value on a Whirlpool washer is zero. Trap two: no cashback-portal rate was verified for whirlpool.com’s account-gated checkout, so don’t count on that layer. Extra paths: the Whirlpool Outlet sells new-in-box discontinued units at some of the deepest prices of the year (limited warranty, 15-day full-refund window, inventory by zip code), and Whirlpool Corporation’s VIPLink / Inside Pass portal offers affiliate pricing through partner employers — an employee program, not a military one, but worth checking your benefits portal.
ag1-military-discount: AG1’s discount is powered by ID.me, the same identity-verification service used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of major retailers. You verify your group status — military, first responder, nurse, teacher, or medical — through an ID.me account at checkout, and the 25% applies automatically to eligible subscription products.

The discount applies only to subscription forms of AG1 Pouch, AG1 30-count Travel Packs, AG1 Pro Travel Packs, AGZ 30-count, and AG Omega-3 (up to 3 of each per shipment). It cannot be combined with any other offer, so the 25% and AG1’s first-order welcome kit are mutually exclusive — you pick one. Keep the subscription active to keep the discount; if it lapses you may need to re-subscribe and re-verify.

One thing to ignore: coupon aggregators advertising "50% off" or "35% off" AG1 promo codes. AG1 does not publish public percentage coupon codes — those are fabricated or dead. Its real deals are the ID.me 25% discount and the standard first-order welcome kit.
24-hour-fitness-military-discount: The "15% off memberships and 10% off personal training" figure that coupon sites repeat as a nationwide 24 Hour Fitness military discount appears to describe the login-gated GovX offer — and 24 Hour Fitness publishes no such percentage anywhere on its own site. Until you see the terms inside a GovX account, treat those numbers as unverified. The same goes for claims that the chain verifies military status via ID.me or SheerID (no such integration exists) and the "$0 initiation + $5 off monthly dues" claim (club-level, no official source). The WeSalute "24 Hour Fitness benefit" circulating in search results is a 2009-era GlobalFit announcement — stale.

The standout official military benefit is contractual, not a price cut: the Active Duty Military Transfer freeze. With a copy of your transfer or deployment orders, your membership freezes with no minimum or maximum period and no dues while frozen — though the $69.99 Annual Fee still bills, and freezes longer than 6 months don’t auto-reactivate, so unfreeze when you’re back. Veterans Day is the other real tradition: the company has historically opened its clubs free to active and retired military with photo ID on November 11.

On price, the substitutes win. Against an illustrative first year at $49.99/month plus the $69.99 Annual Fee (about $670), Costco’s 2-year All-Club Sport eCertificate at $429.99 works out to roughly $215/year — if your club confirms it’s accepting Costco certificates again (shoppers report acceptance was suspended in August 2023, and the certificates remain on sale at Costco, so the safe sequence is: call the club, then buy). Active&Fit Direct — offered through BCBS Blue365, AAA, and many employers and insurers — runs $28/month plus a $28 enrollment fee with no annual fee, month to month after a 2-month minimum, with 24 Hour Fitness explicitly in network.

Nothing here stacks: Costco certificate, Active&Fit Direct, the GovX route, public promos, and in-club military pricing are mutually exclusive enrollment paths, and no cashback portal carried 24 Hour Fitness as of July 7, 2026. Public sale windows (a July 4 sale was live at verification; New Year specials recur) are open to everyone and often beat unpublished military pricing — price them against your GovX or in-club quote and pick one. Active-duty members should remember the honest benchmark every paid path must beat: DoD base fitness centers are free.
nuna-military-discount: The honest core fact: Nuna’s own site publishes no military discount. Its USA support/contact pages describe consumer service and concierge routes, and its US Proud Partners page describes community and military sponsorships — brand philanthropy, not a consumer offer. There is no discount program to point service members to, and no verification gate because there is nothing to unlock.

Why the "codes" keep circulating. Coupon aggregators advertise "Nuna 15% off sitewide," "30% off," or a "Nuna military discount," but Nuna publishes no such offer. As a MAP-enforced brand, Nuna’s flagship car seats and strollers hold fixed retail pricing, so these codes are expected to fail at checkout on exactly the products shoppers most want them for. Treat any "Nuna military discount code" as unverified aggregator noise.

Where the real savings are. Because Nuna is MAP-enforced, the genuine levers are almost all retailer-side: authorized-retailer loyalty and rewards (e.g., Bloomingdale’s Loyallist), registry-completion discounts (often around 10–15%, retailer-specific), cashback portals, and sales-tax strategy on big-ticket gear. All of these are open to everyone — none is a military benefit, but each is a real way to lower your effective cost.

A note on holiday claims. Some third-party sites mention rare "military-only" gestures around Veterans Day or Thanksgiving. These are not confirmed on Nuna’s own site and are inconsistent with its MAP posture, so we report them only as unverified signal, never as a standing offer. If you want certainty, ask Nuna’s concierge directly whether anything is currently running before you buy.
oakley-military-discount: Oakley Standard Issue is a catalog, not a code. Oakley states that “membership into Oakley Standard Issue is free and entitles its members access to exclusive Oakley products and direct pricing.” Because the savings are built into SI prices, you never see a percentage applied at checkout — the price you see is already the member price.

The official OSI registration flow is three steps: verify your credentials with Oakley SI’s trusted verification service (ID.me is used for OSI verification, typically via a valid ID or a .mil/.gov email), create an oakleysi.com password, and you’re a member. Membership is non-transferable, lifetime for U.S. military (active/retired/veteran), and renews every 12 months for all other members under “My Account.” For help, Oakley SI Customer Care is 1-800-525-4334 (Mon–Fri, 8:30am–5:30pm EST).

Watch the accuracy trap: many aggregator and even Military.com pages headline “Oakley offers up to 50% military discount.” That figure traces to OSI member pricing, not a coupon code, and “up to 50%” applies to select styles only — it is not a flat, sitewide, automatically-applied percentage. And the Oakley.com 15% ID.me offer is a separate, non-military program for nurses, teachers, medical providers, and hospital employees.
pelican-military-discount: Pelican routes its own-site discount through ID.me. You verify once (military or first responder); ID.me confirms your status and unlocks the 15% in your pelican.com cart. There is no confirmed SheerID or WeSalute path — and note that GovX is a separate Pelican "Pro Deal" marketplace (govx.com/m/116/pelican), while the licensed Pelican Hydration drinkware site is the one that uses GovX. Don’t conflate the three.

Government employees and nurses are not offered a discount on pelican.com itself — those categories run through the separate GovX channel. There is no verified teacher or student discount on pelican.com.

On big-ticket coolers, the military exchange (NEX/AAFES) tax-free path frequently beats 15% off MSRP once you count sales tax; a genuine Pelican seasonal sale deeper than 15% also wins, since it won’t combine with the ID.me discount.
momcozy-military-discount: Momcozy’s only identity discount is occupation-gated, not service-gated. The 15% community offer is verified through ID.me for nurses, medical providers, hospital employees, teachers, and students (Canadian nurses, doctors, and students are also listed). A service member qualifies only via a separate healthcare, education, or student credential — never via a DD-214 or military ID. That distinction is the whole story: many military spouses and dependents already hold a nursing, medical, teaching, or student credential, and that is the real route to the 15%.

Be cautious of coupon and deal sites that advertise a specific "Momcozy military discount" of "up to 10-25%." No such offer exists. That figure is boilerplate template copy, not a verified Momcozy term. The only verified Momcozy identity discount is the 15% ID.me community offer for healthcare and education workers and students, and military service is explicitly not a qualifying group. We omit the circulating number because repeating it would imply an offer Momcozy does not run.

For a military family, the cheapest path is usually not an identity discount at all. Momcozy runs frequent sitewide sales — often 20-40% — and during those events the public sale price almost always beats the 15% community rate, because identity discounts generally do not stack with sale items. When no sale is live, grab the newsletter/welcome code (open to everyone) and compare Momcozy’s Amazon store, where clipping the on-page coupon can match or beat the site price with fast Prime shipping and returns.

How verification works: Momcozy uses ID.me for its community discount only. You verify your occupation or student status once, ID.me stores it in your Wallet for reuse, and the 15% applies at checkout automatically with no code. There is no military verification path because Momcozy publishes no military discount. Terms and eligible groups can change, so re-check at signup.
dreamcloud-military-discount: DreamCloud’s military benefit is a verified add-on, not the headline sale. The "up to 60–73% off" you see promoted is DreamCloud’s standard sitewide sale, available to everyone. The military-specific offer is an extra 5% off "our best onsite offer" — worded to apply on top of whatever sale price is live. On a Queen DreamCloud Classic Hybrid priced at $699 during the Summer Spectacular sale, the verified 5% brings it to roughly $664.

Verification runs through SheerID’s on-site "Get Verified" step rather than ID.me. You confirm your status once, receive a one-time-use code on-site and by email, and one code can cover your and your family’s orders. First responders (law enforcement, EMTs, paramedics, firefighters) and healthcare professionals each verify on their own DreamCloud page and receive the same extra 5%.

The stacking rules matter. The 5% "cannot be combined with any other offer," so you use either the verified code or a public promo code — not both. It covers merchandise only (not shipping, taxes, or packaging), and using it likely voids Rakuten cashback (about 3% as of July 14, 2026), so treat those as either/or. DreamCloud’s military page also carries legacy "valid on full-price merchandise only" language that conflicts with the "extra 5% off best onsite offer" wording; because DreamCloud runs a near-permanent sale, the practical reading is that the 5% comes off the sale price — but confirm at a live checkout before ordering.

Because DreamCloud controls the terms and can change them at any time, treat the figures here as a starting point. The single cheapest route for a service member is to buy during a deep seasonal window — Memorial Day, July 4, Labor Day, or Black Friday — where sale depth drives the price far more than the 5% ever will, and add the verified 5% on top.
goodyear-military-discount: Verification depends on the channel. Online, it’s handled by ID.me — create or verify a free ID.me account, then shop through the linked Goodyear offer, and the cash back posts to your ID.me account after purchase. In store on Veterans Day, a store associate simply checks your military or first-responder ID at the counter. There is no SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute military program with Goodyear, and the ID.me store also lists communities such as nurses and teachers for its online offers.

The stacking rules are what make the smart path. Goodyear’s public rebates are open to everyone and are the base layer, so a service member’s real "discount" is usually a rebate plus a combinable retailer discount, not a special Goodyear military percentage. The Veterans Day 10% is explicitly combinable with current tire and service offers — the rare stack that genuinely works, but only in the promo window at company-owned stores. ID.me online cash back does not stack with a partner exclusive promo code and is not paid on installation labor.

That’s why the retailer-substitute path often wins. Discount Tire carries Goodyear tires, and its verified 5% ID.me military discount is explicitly combinable with manufacturer rebates and instant savings — so buying Goodyear tires through Discount Tire, applying the 5%, and stacking the current Goodyear rebate typically nets more than Goodyear’s own discretionary in-store discount. Ignore aggregator pages promising a flat "Goodyear military discount code"; no such standing percentage exists.

total-wine-and-more-military-discount: The debunk first, because it dominates the search results: aggregator pages claim Total Wine gives "up to 10%–25% off for military, active duty, veterans and immediate families." No such discount exists in any official source — Total Wine’s own Military Benefit page, the very page those sites link to, describes only the 2x points multiplier on three categories. Alcohol retail pricing is heavily state-regulated (Total Wine’s own price-match policy lists 14 states where it can’t even match below cost or state minimums), which is part of why a flat national percentage was never plausible.

Here’s the dollar math nobody else does. &MORE Rewards pays 10 points per $1, and 5,000 points converts to a $5 Reward — about 1% back. The military 2x doubles that to roughly 2% back, but only on Winery Direct, Spirits Direct, and beer singles. On a $100 mixed cart that’s about $1.50–$2.00 in future store rewards. Worth enrolling — it’s free, verified once via ID.me inside your account, and it stacks on any price because it’s a multiplier, not a code — but it is not the reason your cart gets cheaper.

The paths that actually move the total: TopCashback paid 5% on online orders as of July 4, 2026 (no outside coupon codes, or the cashback voids; site-priced sales like Yellow Tag and mix-and-save pricing aren’t codes). Total Wine’s recurring public deals — "15% off 8+ select wines," "up to 25% off select wines," "$5 off $50 spirits" — dwarf the points benefit on qualifying carts. In-store, the Lowest Price Guarantee matches a local competitor’s currently advertised price on an identical in-stock item. And historically, Total Wine has boosted the military benefit to 5x points through Veterans Day (an undated official store post — a points boost, not a percentage, and never guaranteed to repeat).

For spirits-heavy shopping with base access, the honest alternative is off-site entirely: Class Six package stores at the exchanges sell spirits with no state or local sales tax — roughly a 6–10% swing depending on your state, which beats everything above on that cart. Note the access rule: alcohol is in-store only, so it requires in-store exchange privileges (active duty, retirees, and the 2021-expanded veteran groups) — the veterans’ online shopping benefit doesn’t cover it. One more flag: WeSalute lists a discounted-gift-card-style Total Wine offer, but the rate is membership-gated and unverified, and gift cards kill portal cashback — we don’t recommend it until the rate is verifiable.
brownells-military-discount: The Valor Program is account-level pricing, not a coupon. After you verify — through ID.me as a "Valor Individual," or by emailing documents to orderdesk@brownells.com (agency accounts upload employer ID; allow 1–2 days) — eligible products show a discounted price near the Add to Cart button with the everyday price crossed out. Brownells’ own help page describes the depth only as "Discounts vary by brand and product, but prices are generally lower than our everyday prices." Community chatter pegs many items at small, manufacturer-dependent percentages, but no official number exists and this page won’t invent one.

Verification duration is the standout term: verifications run 18 months, but Brownells states plainly that military customers are not required to re-verify — the military discount does not expire. First responders see a re-verify button one month before their 18-month mark. Verification is free either way.

Brownells is also a high-frequency promo retailer, which shapes the honest best-path advice. On July 7, 2026 a public "Freedom To Boom" sale offered 12% off almost everything with code FREEDOM12 (or free shipping over $99 with 99FREESHIP) — codes like these are limited-time and change constantly. Public codes carry long exclusion lists (ammunition, firearms, reloading components, flash-sale items, and 30+ brands), take one code per order, and Brownells doesn’t say whether they apply on top of Valor pricing — so treat the two as either/or and compare per item. On the categories codes can’t touch, Valor pricing is one of the only levers.

Round out the stack with a cashback portal (best listed rate was ~5% on July 7, 2026 per CashbackMonitor; Rakuten doesn’t carry Brownells) and Brownells’ manufacturer-rebates page — rebates are post-purchase and stack with everything. New subscribers can also take 10% off a first order over $100 when no bigger code is live.
espn-plus-military-discount: The rebrand trips people up. The old ESPN+ content tier was folded into ESPN Select at ESPN’s August 2025 direct-to-consumer launch; existing ESPN+ subscriptions were auto-converted. Sources put ESPN Select at roughly $11.99/mo or $119.99/yr (some 2026 summaries cite $12.99/mo), with ESPN Unlimited at $29.99/mo. None of these tiers has a military discount.

The one genuine offer is on a different product. MLB.TV — the out-of-market baseball package — moved its distribution to ESPN in 2026, so new subscribers now register through the ESPN app. MLB.TV carries an official military discount of up to 35% off (about $49 off the ~$149.99 all-teams annual pass), verified through GovX with a military ID, DD-214, or VA letter. The exact percentage varies by package, so check the live price in the GovX flow.

A note on the ID.me "ESPN cash back" you may see (up to $5 on Select, up to $15 on Unlimited): that is a general perk for all ID.me members, not a military discount, and it isn’t a stack on any (nonexistent) military rate. For MLB.TV, the verified military discount does not stack with promo codes — compare it against any public in-season price drop MLB runs and take whichever is lower.
bass-pro-military-discount: Online verification runs through your Bass Pro / Cabela’s store account: sign in, verify your status on the Legendary Salute page, and the discount applies to your orders. SheerID’s own shopper catalog lists the Bass Pro offer, indicating SheerID powers the check (Bass Pro’s page shows the three-step account flow without naming the vendor). Bass Pro publishes no re-verification schedule — shoppers on boat forums report military status persists while first responders re-verify monthly, but that’s unofficial. Phone orders work too: verify online first, then call 1-800-227-7776 (Bass Pro) or 1-800-237-4444 (Cabela’s).

The stacking rule is what separates this program: officially, the Legendary Salute "can be used on top of other promotions or on select sale items." On a $150 cart with a 30% seasonal markdown, sale price plus the stacked 10% lands around $94.50 — roughly 37% off — versus $135 with the everyday 10% alone. Watch the word "select": some sale items won’t take the extra 10%, and community reports suggest big-ticket electronics are sometimes refused in store. The exclusion list is now published: boats/trailers/motors (canoes and kayaks are fine), ATVs/UTVs, tractors, related services, alcohol, gift cards, and licenses/services like Gear Guard.

Since September 2024, there’s also a tax-free route: AAFES’s ShopMyExchange.com carries hundreds of Bass Pro house-brand items (Bass Pro Shops, Cabela’s, RedHead, World Wide Sportsman, Ascend and more) with the 10% Legendary Salute already baked into the price — "the Exchange’s price includes the 10-percent Legendary Salute Discount" — and no sales tax. You can’t apply the discount again there; the win is the tax delta, which grows with cart size. Exchange online shopping covers active duty, retirees, dependents, DoD civilians, and honorably discharged veterans (Veterans Online Shopping Benefit).

A few debunks: WeSalute still lists Bass Pro as a "5% military discount in stores" — stale; the everyday rate has been 10% (5% firearms/ammo) per Bass Pro’s own pages. Coupon sites advertising "15%–50% off Bass Pro military codes" are recycling public-sale noise — no public military promo code exists; the discount is account-level. And aggregator claims that the discount "cannot be combined with promotions" say the opposite of Bass Pro’s own FAQ. There is no Bass Pro storefront on GovX, and the ExpertVoice listing is an employee program, not a military route.
jbl-military-discount: There is no JBL military verification — jbl.com has no ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute military button. JBL’s only real verified consumer offer is a student 20% discount via UNiDAYS, a different audience. The military-verified paths live at retailers: Sonic Electronix uses VerifyPass, World Wide Stereo uses ID.me, and GovX runs a JBL marketplace behind free GovX verification for military, first responders, government, and teachers.

Because there’s no first-party route, the honest best path is almost never a "military" one. JBL’s Factory Refurbished store (30% off, full 1-year warranty) is usually the cheapest way to buy, and its frequent public sales push the Charge series to roughly $159.95 — both beat every military-verified route on a new unit, for everyone.

When you do want a verified military price on a new unit and no deeper public sale is live, Sonic Electronix’s 10% is the strongest route (JBL is a listed eligible brand; car-stereo models are excluded). If you’re exchange-eligible, buying tax-free at NEX or AAFES is a small win on a Charge 6 but a meaningful one on a big-ticket PartyBox or soundbar.
starbucks-military-discount: How verification works: it mostly doesn’t — and that’s the point. Starbucks has no verification partner (no ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute) because there is no standing discount to verify. On Veterans Day the offer is honor-system-plus-discretion: coverage has varied between "let your barista know" and "proof of service," so bring ID and don’t expect a formal scan.

The everyday math on a typical ~$9–10 two-drink order: Starbucks Rewards returns roughly 4–8% of spend in Star value over time, an in-café refill turns the second brewed coffee into $0, and the on-base AAFES Starbucks skips sales tax entirely — about a 6–10% edge in most states. That tax-free licensed store is the only recurring military-specific advantage that exists.

Watch the calendar: the free Veterans Day tall coffee (November 11) and the public Red Cup Day freebie (November 13 in 2025) landed the same week, and Starbucks ran free coffee for first responders on National First Responders Day (October 28, 2025). All are announced each year — history, not promises.

One smart Veterans Day move from the fine print: the freebie can’t be ordered in the app, but Stars still accrue on paid items — so get the free tall coffee at the register or drive-thru and run everything you’re paying for through Rewards as usual.
u-haul-military-veteran: U-Haul’s military benefit is a free month of storage tied to a qualifying move, not a rate discount, and there are two ways to get it. With orders for a personally procured move, you complete DD Form 2278 (the Do-It-Yourself Move and Counseling Checklist) with your transportation office and present it at a participating U-Haul to receive your first month of self-storage or a U-Box container free, at your origin or your destination. Alternatively, a qualifying one-way PPM truck or trailer rental applies a free first month of storage automatically — no DD Form 2278 required.

U-Haul was founded in 1945 by L.S. "Sam" Shoen, a U.S. Navy veteran of World War II, and the company leans on that heritage rather than a discount code. Read the fine print before you rely on a benefit: the free month is a first-month perk on a qualifying military/PPM move, not unlimited free storage; it does not apply to a post-service civilian move; there is no rate discount to stack on truck or trailer rentals; and the occasional price adjustment some customers report from calling is anecdotal, not a guaranteed policy. Always confirm participation and current terms with your specific U-Haul location.

Even without a percentage discount, military movers have several legitimate ways to save with U-Haul: the one free month of storage (via DD Form 2278 or a one-way PPM rental), free standard shipping on moving supplies ordered from U-Haul, moving-supply buy-back on unused and undamaged boxes, the one-way rental promotions U-Haul runs for PPM moves, and U-Box refunds for containers you reserve but do not use. The biggest saving is not a U-Haul perk at all: your transportation office reimburses qualifying PPM move costs, so keep every receipt and weight ticket. Shoppers who want a flat percentage rather than the storage perk should also cross-quote Penske and Budget, which have at times advertised explicit military discounts on truck rentals.
comfort-inn-military-discount: Comfort Inn and Comfort Suites are Choice Hotels brands, so the military benefit is the umbrella Choice Privileges military program that runs across all Choice brands (Quality Inn, Sleep Inn, Clarion, Cambria, Econo Lodge, and more). There is no brand-specific Comfort Inn military rate — you select the Choice "Military/Veterans" rate at booking, and it varies by property and date because hotels price by availability rather than a fixed percentage.

The most reliable win is the free limited-time Gold Elite status. Because it is status and not a rate, it stacks on top of whatever rate you book — adding bonus points, late checkout, and a welcome gift on every stay while active. The rate discounts, by contrast, are mutually exclusive: the military leisure rate, WeSalute’s up-to-15% offer, Pay Now & Save, and the public member rate cannot be combined, so the smart move is to price-check all of them and book the single lowest.

Two facts trip travelers up. First, you must be a Choice Privileges member and book direct on choicehotels.com or the Choice app — booking through an OTA like Expedia or Booking.com forfeits the rate, your status, and your points, and it is the single most common way people lose the benefit. Second, the old "Lifetime" Gold status was downgraded to a limited-time benefit in early 2025 and the former 2,500-point sign-up bonus appears to have been removed, so ignore any page still promising Lifetime Gold or guaranteed bonus points and confirm the current terms on Choice’s live page.
barnes-and-noble-military-discount: The debunk, with receipts: WorthEPenny and Knoji claim "10% off for active duty/veterans, in-store and online with military ID," Goodshop pages imply up to "75% off" military coupons, and AI-content blogs describe a "verify through the Barnes & Noble website" flow. None of it exists — no B&N source confirms any military discount, ID.me explicitly disclaims one (for first responders too), and there’s no GovX storefront. The stale listings trace back to a single Veterans Day 2015 promotion on NOOK devices that expired over a decade ago. No credible shopper reports of a discretionary register discount surfaced either.

The loyalty math is what actually saves. Free Rewards: 1 stamp per $10, 10 stamps = a $5 reward — roughly 5% back, with stamps earned on the post-discount total. Premium ($39.99/year): an everyday 10% in stores and online plus free standard shipping with no minimum — since 10% of $400 is $40, it beats the fee only if you spend about $400+ a year at B&N. And the stacking rules matter: the member 10% cannot be combined with coupons (a code like PREORDER25 applies to list price instead — either/or), but $5 reward certificates stack on top of everything, applied after all other discounts.

The strongest percentage B&N runs isn’t military — it’s the recurring members-only codes. PREORDER25 gave 25% off list price on eligible pre-order books, eBooks, and audiobooks in its June 23–27, 2026 window, open even to free-tier Rewards members (not valid on titles already discounted more than 25%). Pair everyday orders with Rakuten’s 2% (as of July 4, 2026) — the account-based loyalty program won’t trip cashback, but treat code orders as cashback-forfeited, since neither B&N nor Rakuten states whether tracking survives a coupon checkout.

Ruled-out paths: the military exchange isn’t a real substitute — AAFES itself says hardbound book sales are "extremely limited" in exchanges, so check shopmyexchange.com for a specific title but don’t count on it. Amazon offers no military book discount either; it competes on list-price markdowns, so a per-title price check is always worth it. The one genuinely military-flavored gesture on record: some B&N cafés have offered veterans a free tall coffee or tea on Veterans Day (2021 and 2024 store-level announcements) — ask at your local café on November 11.
smith-optics-military-discount: The Pro Program is a closed channel: up to 50% off does not combine with sales, promo codes, or other discounts; a flat $15 shipping applies (it is not eligible for free-shipping offers) and pro orders cannot be returned. Its eligible groups are outdoor-industry pros, athletes, gear-company and retailer employees, first responders, and active military personnel — veterans are not on that list, so veterans should use GovX or the Exchange instead. Because of the flat $15 shipping and the $1,200 MSRP/year cap, the Pro Program pays off most when you batch a larger full-price order rather than buy one item.

GovX is a closed verification marketplace, not a Smith checkout code. You create a free GovX ID, verify once, and shop the Smith storefront at member prices. GovX verifies a wide net — active/reserve/veteran/retired military, military family, law enforcement, fire, EMS/medical (including nurses), government employees and teachers — which is why it is the route for everyone the Pro Program excludes. You cannot add a Smith promo code on GovX, and cashback portals generally do not track GovX orders, so judge GovX purely on its net member price versus the public sale.

Be cautious of aggregators that advertise "20% off via ID.me," "up to 60% military," or "10–25% military" for Smith. None of these appear on Smith’s own site. The "20% ID.me" figure is a conflation of Smith’s student offer (up to 40% via Student Beans, for full-time students age 16+) with an invented military tier. Smith operates no first-party ID.me military discount as of July 14, 2026.

Even without a brand-run military discount, there are honest ways to lower your cost: watch the End-of-Season sale (up to 40% off) and Black Friday/Cyber Monday public sales — no verification, free shipping over $50; stack a plain, no-code sale purchase with a cashback portal (TopCashback was 5.05% as of July 14, 2026) so tracking stays valid; use the 15% newsletter code on a first order when the item is not already on sale; and, if you have Exchange access, buy big-ticket goggles or helmets tax-free at AAFES or the Navy Exchange, where the tax saving is largest.

starlink-military-discount: There is no Starlink military-verification flow because there is no program. Starlink doesn’t partner with ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute for any consumer military discount, so there’s no status to verify and no military account tier to unlock. The only price variation is "regional savings," which Starlink sets by local network capacity and geography — it’s open to everyone in qualifying areas and has nothing to do with military status.

Be skeptical of "Starlink military discount" results. The two most common ones aren’t Starlink offers: an independent installer (ProSat Networks) advertises $50 off its own installation labor for veterans, active-duty members, and spouses, and GovX lists third-party Starlink accessories (like mounts and flagpole adapters) at military pricing — both governed by those third parties, not SpaceX. And coupon-aggregator "Starlink military codes" aren’t reliable; Starlink issues no military promo code.

Two things often confused with a discount: shipping and Starshield. Starlink can ship to some military/APO-type addresses for personal use, but at standard pricing — that’s logistics, not a discount. And Starshield is a separate SpaceX product built for government and defense customers, sold through government contracts (U.S. Space Force CSCO PLEO, DoD, NATO); it’s not a consumer discount and isn’t available to individuals. The legitimate ways anyone can lower Starlink cost are open to all: check for regional savings by address, watch for periodic hardware price drops, and pick the plan tier that fits your use. Veterans who qualify for the federal Lifeline benefit may be able to apply it to a participating provider — confirm Starlink’s participation with USAC/Lifeline directly, not aggregators.
rogers-sporting-goods-military-discount: The “Rogers Sporting Goods military discount” circulating online is fabricated. Aggregators like Valuecom and WorthEPenny advertise “up to 80% off military,” and TheGunZone asserts a “30% military code OUTDOORLIMITS” or “show your military ID in store” — none of which is supported by any Rogers source. Rogers publishes no military discount, no such code appears on its site, and it’s primarily an online retailer with no published in-store military-ID policy. The “up to 80%/95% off” figures are recycled clearance/coupon-site inflation, not a military offer.

The genuine best-savings path for a service member is the same one available to everyone, because Rogers has no military program. Join the free Rogers Rewards loyalty program (earn 1 point per $1; 50 points = $1, roughly 2% back; redeem from 250 points in set increments), stack it on Clearance Corner and seasonal-sale prices, and clear the free-shipping-over-$99 threshold. Codes are typically one per order, and a legitimate live sitewide code can layer with Rewards earning on non-regulated goods.

Two caveats matter. First, firearms and regulated ammunition are commonly carved out of promo codes (the standard FFL-category pattern, and ammunition carries age/shipping rules), so on guns and ammo the lever is price comparison and clearance, not a discount code. Second, if you specifically want a verified member discount, Rogers itself isn’t on GovX or the military exchanges — but many brands Rogers carries have their own military programs or appear on GovX, so buy those directly if a member discount is what you’re after.
lids-military-discount: Lids verifies eligibility through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. You create a free ID.me account, confirm your military or first-responder status, and receive a unique promo code tied to that verification. Treat it like a personal coupon: you paste it in the promo box at lids.com checkout, and it can’t be shared or combined with another code.

Because the discount is a single code, it collides with everything else. It won’t stack with a public sale code, with another Lids coupon, or with Access Pass Premium’s 20%. The honest move is to compare three numbers for your order — the 15% military code, Access Pass Premium (20% online), and any clearance price — and take the biggest.

That comparison often doesn’t favor the military code. Lids’ paid Access Pass Premium tier (about $10/year) advertises 20% off online, so if you shop Lids more than once or twice a year the fee pays for itself and the 20% beats 15% on full-price gear. We frame the 20%/$10 figures as "confirm live" because they come from editorial coverage — check lids.com/accesspass before relying on them.

A note on the noise: aggregators headline "35% off," "30% off," or imply a stackable "military code." The only verified military and first-responder discount is 15% via ID.me, delivered as a unique code — which behaves like any coupon and won’t stack with another Lids offer.
adorama-military-discount: The math below uses one baseline: a ~$1,999 camera or lens order in an ~8.5% sales-tax state, because that’s where Adorama’s real levers actually move the needle. Because a store card is the main lever and tax is the second-biggest line, effective prices here include tax.

The Edge card’s 5% is applied after other applicable discounts at the point of sale and excludes taxes and shipping — so it layers on a sale price but never touches tax. Crucially, the 5% and the card’s special financing cannot be used together: you choose one benefit per purchase. If you need to spread the cost of an $800+ item, take the 0% financing instead of the 5%.

VIP Rewards points accrue on purchases and redeem independently, so they’re the one perk that stacks with anything — always enroll. Adorama is not on GovX, ID.me (for military), ExpertVoice, SheerID-military, or the military exchanges, so don’t expect any military-gated path; the honest maximum-savings play is the Edge card plus Rewards, price protection, and Adorama Used.

One thing to watch: coupon and Q&A pages occasionally claim a “10% Adorama military discount.” No primary source confirms it, and ID.me states Adorama offers no military discount — treat any such claim as unverified and disregard it.
spotify-military-discount: Spotify’s US Premium plans page lists four paid tiers — Individual ($12.99/mo), Duo ($18.99/mo), Family ($21.99/mo), and Student ($6.99/mo) — plus a free ad-supported tier. There is no military, veteran, or first-responder plan anywhere on the page or in plan navigation, and no military eligibility path for any tier.

The only identity-verified discount is Premium Student. Spotify uses SheerID, a third-party service, to confirm you’re enrolled at an eligible US Title IV accredited college or university and are 18 or older. Student access runs up to 12 months per verification, and students can re-verify once every 12 months for a maximum of 3 additional 12-month periods (about four years total). There is no equivalent path that accepts a military ID, DD-214, or ID.me / GovX / WeSalute military verification — Spotify does not use those for any service-based discount.

Spotify’s community forum has closed multiple military, veteran, and first-responder discount requests, citing Idea Exchange guidelines that bar pricing and subscription requests. That indicates no military discount is in development through that channel. Treat any "Spotify military promo code" from a coupon site as invalid, and note that ID.me’s "Does Spotify Have Military Discounts?" page is a marketing landing page, not evidence of a Spotify partnership.

For the cheapest real route: Spotify Free costs $0 if you can tolerate ads. New customers can run Premium Individual free for 3 months (then $12.99/mo; ends July 6, 2026). Splitting Premium Family across a 6-account household is the best per-person value (~$3.67/person), Premium Duo is about $9.50/person for two, and enrolled students pay $6.99/mo with Hulu bundled.
chubbies-military-discount: Chubbies verifies military status through GovX ID, a free real-time identity service. Each verification issues a single-use code capped at one per day; re-verification is not described as annual — you simply log back in with GovX ID to generate a new code for a future order. Support for verification failures runs through the GovX ID help center. Note that GovX ID (a discount code for the brand’s own site) is different from the GovX marketplace: Chubbies does not sell discounted inventory through a separate GovX storefront.

The value of verifying is genuinely undercut by Chubbies’ own free email-signup offer, which also gives 15% off. Because Chubbies allows only one offer per purchase and the two discounts are equal, GovX verification is useful mainly if you would rather not join the email list. A standard newsletter code is usually cashback-portal-safe, whereas a GovX-gated single-use code is the kind that can void portal tracking — so treat "15% + cashback" as only sometimes valid, with the email code rather than the GovX code.

For the lowest real price, watch the calendar and the channel. Chubbies runs deep sitewide sales (Memorial Day, July 4, Labor Day, Black Friday) roughly a week each, with clearance up to ~50% off — public prices that routinely beat any 15% and cannot be stacked with it anyway. And if you are exchange-eligible, the Navy Exchange (and AAFES) stock select Chubbies styles tax-free, which becomes the quiet winner as sales-tax rates rise. Chubbies’ older promo-hub page still shows a stale "10%" for military; the dedicated verification page and GovX both show 15%, so treat 15% as current.
yeti-military-veteran: YETI’s discount is powered by ID.me, the same identity-verification service used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of major retailers. Verifying once links your eligibility to your ID.me account, so future YETI purchases — and discounts at other ID.me partners — go faster.

The military and veteran tier sits alongside parallel ID.me communities for first responders, medical providers, teachers, and government employees. The discount is typically the same across these groups, though YETI occasionally runs higher promotional rates during limited windows.
Because YETI controls the terms and can change them at any time, treat the numbers here as a starting point and confirm the current offer on YETI’s official ID.me deals page before you buy.
herman-miller-military-discount: The only military-relevant offer Herman Miller ever ran was the April–May 2020 "Heroes" promotion — 25% off task chairs for healthcare workers, military, and first responders during the early COVID period. It was a one-time, time-limited promotion, not a standing program, and it was not reinstated. Today the /herman-miller-heroes URL redirects to a general Home Office Sale, the customer-service FAQ lists no service-member offer, and ID.me states it is "not aware that Herman Miller offers First Responders discounts." Coupon and deal sites that still present a live "Herman Miller military discount" are simply wrong.

The genuine savings levers are Herman Miller’s own channels, and none of them is military-gated. The Outlet / Open Box store carries certified returns and overstock — full or near-full warranty retained — typically 15–40% off, though stock and colorways are limited. Recurring seasonal sitewide sales (Home Office, Memorial Day, Black Friday) mark items down up to about 25%, with Black Friday usually the deepest of the year. Business and practice owners can register for Herman Miller Professional for exclusive trade pricing.
