WeSalute+ members may present their WeSalute+ ID card as in-store proof, but the discount itself is Finish Line’s own in-store program, not a WeSalute-gated online deal.

The discount is 10% off and applies only to in-store purchases. It cannot be stacked with other coupons or offers, is capped at one discount per eligible customer per day, and is not valid on gift cards. The only allowed combination is a single valid Finish Line STATUS Reward.

If you want to shop online, Finish Line’s general sales, promo codes, and the free STATUS rewards program are available to everyone — they are simply not combinable with the in-store military discount. Finish Line’s official military FAQ is the source of truth for current terms.
penfed-military-discount: Honors Advantage has two routes. The military route is automatic and covers anyone "in an active military service status, a member of the Reserves or National Guard, an honorably discharged U.S. Military Veteran or retired from such service" — no checking account needed, no maintenance condition, ever. The civilian route requires being primary owner of both the credit card and a qualifying PenFed checking account: Access America Checking, or Free Checking with a $500 minimum daily balance or $500 or more in monthly direct deposits (PenCheck Limited doesn’t count). Timing matters: qualify at application and the Pathfinder’s $95 fee is waived immediately; qualify later and it’s waived at your next anniversary; stop qualifying (checking route) and the waiver ends with advance notice. On our baseline — one Pathfinder plus $20,000 a year of everyday spend on Power Cash — the program is worth roughly $195 a year ($95 fee waived plus $100 in extra cash back from the 2%-vs-1.5% bump), before counting the richer 4X/3X travel earning.

The card lineup, for context: the Pathfinder Rewards Visa Signature ($95, waived with Honors Advantage) earns 4X travel/3X dining for Honors Advantage members and 1.5X on everything else, with a 50,000-point welcome bonus for $3,000 spend in the first 90 days (PenFed values it at up to $500; points redeem at a minimum of $0.0085 and up to $0.01), a $100-a-year domestic air ancillary credit, a $120 Global Entry or $85 TSA PreCheck credit every 4 years, and complimentary Priority Pass Select membership plus a guest (a $99 value — lounge visit fees apply). Power Cash is the $0-fee flat-rate card: 2% for Honors Advantage members, 1.5% otherwise, no caps, with a $100 statement-credit welcome bonus (check PenFed’s current terms for the exact spend requirement). The other two cards — Platinum Rewards (5X gas at the pump and EV charging, 3X supermarkets, 15,000-point bonus for $1,500 in 90 days) and the Gold Visa (no rewards; 0% intro purchase APR for 15 months, then 17.99% variable) — get no Honors Advantage benefit at all. All four cards carry the same 17.99% variable purchase APR (as of July 2026) and no foreign transaction fees.

SCRA is a separate, statutory benefit and it’s worth being precise about: for PenFed accounts opened before you went on active duty, PenFed caps interest at 6% and charges no late or over-limit fees, effective from your active-duty start date. You must request it — upload activation orders to PenFed.org/secureupload during active duty or within 180 days after your last day of active service. Note the comparison: Navy Federal voluntarily caps SCRA-eligible balances at 4%; PenFed publishes the statutory 6%. PenFed publishes no MLA fee policy for accounts opened during active duty — largely moot here, since active-duty members already get the lineup’s only annual fee waived through Honors Advantage. If you’re currently serving, the highest-value play is to hold both ecosystems: Honors Advantage at PenFed for the 2%/4X boosts that survive your separation, and MLA $0-annual-fee premium cards (like an $895 Amex Platinum) at issuers where federal law waives far bigger fees while you serve.

Three myths to close out. First, there is no PenFed promo code or percent-off military discount — coupon-site "PenFed military codes" are fabricated, because there’s no code field anywhere in PenFed’s card products. Second, "PenFed is military-only" is false — membership has been open to everyone since January 1, 2019; the military angle is the Honors Advantage rate and fee treatment, not the membership door. Third, don’t credit PenFed with the 4% SCRA cap some pages attribute to military issuers generally — PenFed’s published SCRA benefit is the statutory 6% plus waived late and over-limit fees; it’s Navy Federal that voluntarily goes to 4%.
venture-x-military: Why is an unwaived fee legal? The Military Lending Act caps during-service credit at a 36% MAPR, but its own rules — 32 CFR 232.4(d) — exclude bona fide, reasonable credit-card fees, including annual fees, from that calculation. Amex and Chase zero their premium-card fees for covered borrowers voluntarily; Capital One chooses not to, and its published SCRA decline criteria reject any account "opened after the active duty start date." Fee-waiver listicles that lump the Venture X in with the Amex Platinum and Sapphire Reserve without that condition cost readers $395 a year.

On the SCRA side, the program is genuinely strong. The law requires a 6% interest cap on pre-service obligations; Capital One caps at 4% and assesses no fees except bona-fide insurance. Relief is retroactive to your active-duty start date ("order to" date for reservists), runs until one year after active duty ends, and can be requested up to one year post-service — online at capitalone.com/military, at 1-855-CAP1-MIL (1-855-227-1645) 24/7, by mail, or in a branch, with your orders or a commanding-officer letter. One request sweeps every Capital One and Discover account you hold, the decision letter arrives within 2 monthly billing cycles, and none of it touches rewards: the $300 travel credit, 10,000 anniversary miles, earning rates, and lounge access all work normally on a covered account.

If you can’t pass the pre-service test, run the honest math. Unwaived, the Venture X roughly pays for itself if you use its credits: the $300 annual Capital One Travel credit plus 10,000 anniversary miles (about $100 toward travel) come to roughly $400 a year against the $395 fee — a conditional break-even, not a discount, and it collapses to $0 in value if you wouldn’t book through Capital One Travel. Longtime cardholders also report product-changing an old pre-service no-fee Capital One card into a Venture X and keeping the SCRA fee waiver, since it stays the same account with the same open date — Capital One doesn’t document that path, it usually forfeits the welcome offer, and you should confirm at 1-855-227-1645 before relying on it. And if the actual goal is a $0-fee premium travel card while on active duty, that card exists at other issuers: the Amex Platinum ($895 list) is $0 automatically under MLA, and the Chase Sapphire Reserve ($795 list) is letter-confirmed at $0 for covered borrowers — see our guides to both.
petco-military-discount: How verification works: Petco itself verifies nothing — there is no military checkout on petco.com. The GovX gift-card route uses GovX ID (one-time free verification for military, veterans, retirees, Guard/Reserve, first responders, police, medical, government, and education groups; then log in per purchase). The Pet Supermarket alternative uses ID.me linked to its free VIP Rewards account.

The origin of the myth, since every aggregator repeats it: in October 2019, AAFES announced Petco would open at Joint Base Lewis-McChord with "the company’s 10% military discount… on all purchases, including services, at the Lewis Main Exchange" — an on-base store benefit, never a chain-wide program. Employees on r/petco confirm the chain has no active military discount; the POS button and "thank you for your service" signage are leftovers.

The honest math on a $100 cart: GovX gift cards make it $90 anywhere, any time. A first Repeat Delivery order at 35% through TopCashback (4%) nets about $62.40 — and roughly $58.50 if gift-card payment works on Repeat Delivery (unverified — test first). The layers that do combine: sale price → live promo (like the current BOPUS 10% off $50+) → gift-card payment → Petco Perks points (10 per $1) on top.

Cross-shopping note: Pet Supermarket (SE US footprint) runs the discount Petco doesn’t — 10% off every day for active duty, veterans, and reserves (plus seniors 55+ and teachers) via ID.me and its free VIP Rewards account, online and in-store, with sale items excluded. And exchange-eligible shoppers can buy pet supplies tax-free on base.
camelbak-military-discount: The GovX CamelBak brand store is the most broadly-available verified route. Create a free GovX account, verify your status once, and shop member pricing — it’s particularly strong on mil-spec hydration (Crux and Antidote reservoirs, ArmorBak) that’s hard to find at ordinary retail. Because GovX is a closed marketplace, you check out there at the member price; there’s no stacking a brand code or cashback portal on top.

CamelBak’s Pro Purchase program via ExpertVoice is the deepest path for those who qualify. For outdoor and tactical brands, pro pricing often runs 30-50% off, but it comes with strict personal-use and no-resale terms and purchase caps. The exact depth and CamelBak’s eligible-group list aren’t published on-page, so confirm both when you verify.

A third angle: CamelBak (especially tactical and mil-spec gear) is stocked tax-free by the military exchanges (AAFES/NEX/MCX), which also price-match. On a small item the tax saving is modest, but it compounds on larger tactical orders. What we won’t assert is the flat "ID.me 20%" some aggregators cite — sources disagree on whether the mechanism is ID.me, GovX, or ExpertVoice, and no CamelBak page confirms it.
uag-military-discount: UAG uses VerifyPass to confirm eligibility. You verify your community (military/veteran, first responder, government, healthcare, or teacher), and VerifyPass issues a one-time discount code. It is not a permanent account discount — you re-verify to get a fresh single-use code for each order. UAG does not use ID.me for this program, despite what some aggregators claim.

Also worth debunking: coupon sites advertising "60% off," "80% off," "$150 off," or a stackable "military code" for UAG are unverified aggregator copy. The only confirmed service offer is the 20% VerifyPass discount on full-price items — non-combinable, one code per order.

The honest math on a $59.95 Monarch Pro case: the 20% code lands at $47.96, but a 25–30% public sale (Black Friday/Cyber Monday, Memorial Day, Labor Day — typically about a week) lands at $41.97–$44.96 and clearance markdowns on discontinued models often exceed 30%. Since the 20% can’t stack on any of those, skip your code whenever a 20%+ public markdown is live. GovX separately runs a UAG marketplace storefront (a closed channel — price-check specific items against the brand site minus 20%), and UAG’s Explorer Perks rewards earn 1 point per $1 with 100 points worth $10 off — a rewards redemption counts as your one code.
msc-military-discount: The offer itself is straightforward once you know it’s a booking-time fare rate, not a coupon. MSC’s terms name active and retired US and Canadian military — Army, Air Force, Marine Corps, Navy, Coast Guard, National Guard, and Army Reserve — plus Department of Defense personnel. Immediate family members get the same rate, but only when the member or employee cruises with them. Verification happens at booking: there is no ID.me, SheerID, or GovX portal — qualifying guests present an ID badge from their respective organization, over the phone or through their travel agent. Aggregator pages implying a typed-in "MSC military discount code" are wrong; no such code exists.

The make-or-break fact is stacking: the military rate combines with nothing. MSC’s terms say the offer "cannot be combined with any other discount or promotion" and explicitly rule out combining it with the MSC Voyagers Club discount. That makes it an alternative fare, not a bonus — when MSC’s recurring public sales (up to 30% off plus up to $500 onboard credit at this review) apply to your sailing, the public fare can beat the military fare outright, and choosing the military fare means forfeiting that promo’s onboard credit too. Kids Sail Free is the one adjacent offer MSC lists alongside the military rate, and even that is select-sailings-only.

The booking channel creates a second honest trade-off: because the military rate is requested by phone or agent, portal cashback never applies to it. Rakuten’s MSC terms (1.5% as of July 13, 2026) pay only on bookings completed online at msccruisesusa.com — not by phone — and cover the cruise fare only. So the choice is binary each time: the phone-booked military fare, or the online public fare with cashback. Price both, every time. Whether the 5%/10% is quoted off the same base fare as a live public promo is not published, which is one more reason to compare the final totals rather than the percentages.

If you fall outside the stated terms — most notably veterans who separated without retiring — the verified fallback is the free MSC Voyagers Club: members get a 5% discount on all cruises, plus up to 15% off Voyagers Selection sailings, and MSC’s Status Match program can match status from other travel loyalty programs into a Voyagers tier. That path books online, so cashback stays intact. Non-retired veterans comparing cruise lines should also cross-shop lines that publish veteran-inclusive military rates, such as Carnival and Norwegian.
allstate-military-discount: Allstate’s own auto-insurance discounts page lists bundling, Drivewise (safe driver), responsible-payer, anti-theft, anti-lock-brake, and good-student discounts. A service member can use any of these general discounts, which combine with each other on a single policy, but none is a military, veteran, or deployment benefit — so there is nothing military-specific to "verify" or "claim" with Allstate outside Louisiana.

Louisiana is the sole place a "25% Allstate military discount" is real, and it exists because the state mandates it for every insurer, not because Allstate created a program. Under R.S. 22:1482 (administered through Louisiana Department of Insurance Regulation 81), qualifying military drivers garaged in Louisiana get a 25% premium discount; the statute also bars an insurer from using a deployment of more than six months to reclassify risk. Eligible categories are active duty, reservists, Louisiana Air/Army National Guard, retired military, and veterans with a 50%+ VA disability rating.

To claim the Louisiana discount, confirm the vehicle is garaged/registered in Louisiana and you meet an eligible category, complete the Louisiana Application Form for Military Discount, and attach proof — a copy of military orders (active/Guard/Reserve/retired) or, for 50%+ disabled veterans, an LDVA Form A25/A17, VA card/CAC, or VA benefits/award letter — then submit it to your agent so the 25% is applied to the qualifying vehicle’s premium. There is no online national identity check because there is no national discount.

Because insurance is individually rated, the real question is not "which code do I enter" but "which single carrier’s total, after all discounts, is lowest for me." Compare net premiums rather than trying to combine carriers. Check USAA first if you are eligible — it is usually the lowest reliable military premium and has the strongest deployment vehicle-storage break; if not, get a GEICO military quote for its up-to-15% discount plus emergency-deployment/storage savings. Louisiana residents should claim the mandated 25% at whichever carrier is cheapest after the discount.
brooks-brothers-military-discount: The Brooks Brothers military discount is verified through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of major retailers. You verify once, then the 10% applies at checkout on future visits with no manual code. Brooks Brothers does not publish a separate eligibility list beyond the ID.me categories, so ID.me governs which groups qualify and how often you re-verify.

The catch is stacking: Brooks Brothers promo terms state offers "cannot be combined with any other discounts, offers, or promotions," and the ID.me discount is full-price only. That means the 10% cannot touch a sale price, a 15% signup code, or clearance — you pick one path. Since the brand marks down 30–50% seasonally, the public sale price frequently beats the 10% outright.

A common myth is worth debunking: Brooks Brothers is not on GovX (that storefront is Brooks Running, a different company), the verified ID.me tier is 10% and not 40%, and there is no confirmed WeSalute / Veterans Advantage or VerifyPass partnership. The only verified year-round military route is the 10% ID.me offer.
knotts-berry-farm-military-discount: s routes verification through ID.me: you create a free ID.me account, verify once, and get the login prompt at checkout. There is no confirmed SheerID or WeSalute route on the Knott

valvoline-military-discount: Valvoline’s military page keeps the mechanic simple: show your military ID at the register and the 15% comes off your eligible invoice. There’s no account to create and no ID.me, SheerID, or GovX verification required for the discount — it’s an in-person, point-of-sale benefit.

One point worth separating: ID.me lists Valvoline Instant Oil Change for cash back, but that is a distinct ID.me Shop affiliate program with its own terms — not the in-store 15% discount. Don’t conflate the two. Similarly, while third-party sites assert that active duty, veterans, and retirees all qualify, Valvoline’s own page does not publish a subgroup breakdown; it states only "show your military ID." We reflect that honestly: the offer is keyed to the ID, and whether separated veterans, spouses, or dependents are covered is not specified by Valvoline — confirm locally.

Because the discount is good only at participating locations, and VIOC operates a mix of company-owned and franchise stores, the safest move is a quick call to your nearest location to confirm participation and any local terms before your visit. If a nearby competitor (for example, Take 5 or Jiffy Lube) runs a deeper military offer, it’s worth comparing — but those also vary by location.
nfl-redzone-military-discount: The ID.me discount attaches to NFL Sunday Ticket, not to RedZone itself — RedZone is a paid add-on (+$42 one-time / +$3.50/mo) on top of the discounted Sunday Ticket. You do not need to be a YouTube TV subscriber to buy the discounted Sunday Ticket via Primetime Channels.

NFL+ Premium already includes RedZone, so you do not add it separately there; but there is no verified military percentage on NFL+ Premium’s price. NFL documents a Military/First Responder discount activation via ID.me for NFL subscriptions, but the exact NFL+ percentage is not published on an accessible page, and ID.me’s catalog notes it is not aware of an NFL+ community discount.

Returning ID.me subscribers renew at $198 (or $240 bundled with RedZone), and the offer auto-renews at the eligible price. If you already have YouTube TV or cable carrying RedZone, add it through your existing provider instead of paying twice.
converse-military-discount: Converse verifies military status through SheerID, an identity-verification service used by many major retailers. You start at converse.com/military-verification, enter your name exactly as it appears on your military document, and confirm your branch of service and current status. If you are not instantly verified, SheerID compares your form entries against uploaded documents, so match your name and status to your paperwork. Documents are reviewed in the order received, and you receive an email result — usually within about 20 minutes.

Eligibility is generous on the military side — reservists, veterans, and retirees are all named explicitly — and it extends to the spouses and dependents of active-duty members. Dependents of a deceased sponsor may still qualify if they are currently registered and SheerID offers a Family Member/Spouse/Dependent status; otherwise Converse directs shoppers to contact the retailer. Converse does not use ID.me or GovX for this discount, and re-verification may be required on future visits.

One thing to watch: aggregator and coupon sites advertise Converse "military discounts" of "up to 30%" or "40% off." Those figures are general Converse sale or coupon claims, not the military benefit — Converse’s own page states the military discount as 15%. Because Converse runs frequent, often-deeper public sales, treat the 15% as a floor, not a ceiling: verify once through SheerID, then compare the 15% against whatever sale is live and take the lower single price. A cashback portal such as Rakuten can layer a few extra percent on top of a public sale, since that is outside Converse’s own stacking rules.
cedar-point-military-discount: Cedar Point’s online discount is powered by ID.me, the same identity-verification service used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of major retailers. Set up a free ID.me account, and after you choose your tickets you’ll get an ID.me login prompt to confirm your status. Verifying once links your eligibility to your ID.me account, so future purchases — and discounts at other ID.me partners — go faster. The $49 ticket is online only; there is no walk-up register price for it.

The everyday $49 price and the free Memorial Day admission are two different offers with different rules. The $49 single-day ticket is year-round, verified through ID.me, and cannot be combined with any other offer, including sales. The free Memorial Day admission is redeemed in person at the gate with a valid U.S. Military ID, is stated for active and retired military, and covers the member only — guests buy their tickets online in advance. Because Cedar Point operates seasonally, there is no Veterans Day promotion; the brand’s military moment is Memorial Day weekend.

Because the public online advance price (around $52 on the verification date) sits so close to the $49 military price, the discount’s real edge is the ability to lock $49 in for up to six people in one order and the free Memorial Day window — not a dramatic single-ticket saving. Public ticket prices and sale windows move often, so compare the current public price before you buy; during a deep public flash sale, the open-to-everyone price can rival the military price. If you have base access, price-check your ITT/MWR/ITR office, which can sometimes undercut online pricing.

A few separate marketplaces also list Cedar Point tickets for verified members — GOVX (via a GovX ID) and WeSalute+ (a paid membership, through Working Advantage, quoting "up to 45%" across admission, meals, and parking, with tickets mailed and all sales final). These are separate storefronts with their own prices and terms, not a discount you stack on the Cedar Point site, and their exact net prices were not confirmed on the research date — verify before choosing one over the direct $49 ID.me ticket. Nurses have a separate offer via WeSalute rather than through Cedar Point directly.
babbel-military-discount: Babbel’s discount is verified through ID.me, the same identity-verification service used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of major retailers. One free ID.me account covers Babbel’s military, veteran, first-responder, teacher, nurse, and student rates — verify once and the discount unlocks at checkout and in the app.

Babbel does not use a GovX-exclusive price or a paid WeSalute membership for this offer. GovX lists Babbel but routes back to the same ID.me military program, so there is no deeper price to find there. The offer is first-party — Babbel’s own page plus ID.me.

Because Babbel’s biggest discounts are its ever-present public seasonal sales (open to everyone) and its periodic Lifetime deal (~$170–200 for all languages on sale), the smartest move for a full year is to compare the military 12-month rate against the live public promo in the same session. For a short commitment, the 6-month/$36 military rate is the strongest number.
costa-del-mar-military-discount: Costa uses ID.me as the primary verifier on its own site, while GovX and WeSalute are separate verified marketplaces and memberships that also offer the 15%. You create a free account, confirm your status once, and the discount unlocks. Re-verification frequency is set by the provider, not Costa, and support for verification issues runs through the provider’s help center rather than Costa directly.

The 15% is applied through a verified account, not a public code, so it does not stack with public promo codes or clearance — Costa allows only one promo code per order. Coupon aggregators advertise codes like "COSTAFF10" and "50% off" Costa promo codes; treat these as unverified. The genuine "up to 50%" number is Costa’s clearance, not a stacked military code.

For in-person buying, eligible patrons can shop Costa sunglasses at Navy Exchange (NEX) and other exchanges tax-free. Exchange prices are generally MSRP but carry no sales tax, and the exchange occasionally runs its own sales — a separate channel from the online ID.me 15%.
john-deere-military-discount: John Deere’s “military discount” is not a percentage. Through the Military Service Program, qualifying service members receive a free two-unit affiliation credit that lifts them straight to Platinum 1 in John Deere Rewards — the tier a normal customer only reaches after two qualifying purchases in twelve months. Platinum then unlocks the equipment discounts, applied at deere.com, in the John Deere app, or at participating dealers when you provide your Rewards number.

The stacking is the whole game. John Deere states these Platinum discounts can be combined with its national/affiliate offers, and dealer program pages confirm they also combine with current dealer sales and special financing. That combinability matters far more on a Gator, a 1–5 Series tractor, or a commercial mower — where the Platinum discount runs to $1,700 — than on a $2,600 residential mower where it caps around $150.

Two corrections worth making: aggregators claim a “10%” or “10–25% John Deere military discount” — that percentage does not exist. And some listicles say to verify through GovX; the confirmed on-site partner is ID.me, and no John Deere equipment-Rewards GovX storefront was verified. Because deere.com returned an access error to our automated fetch on the verify date, treat the per-category dollar ranges as a starting point and confirm the current figure for your machine with the dealer.

If you don’t qualify for the military program or Everyday Heroes, a national affiliate such as a Farm Bureau membership (roughly $25–$60/year) buys the same Platinum 1 tier — worth it above about $1,000 of equipment.
dickies-military-discount: Dickies routes its hero discount through SheerID. You verify your status (military, student, or first responder) once through SheerID’s Dickies landing page; SheerID confirms eligibility and unlocks the 10%. There is no confirmed ID.me, GovX, or WeSalute military-discount path for Dickies — SheerID is the named partner.

Because the 10% is a single order-level discount, it does not stack with clearance, promo codes, or the 15% "Join Our Crew" email signup. On sale styles the public price usually wins, and a new subscriber is better off with the larger 15% first-order offer. For eligible trades, the separate ExpertVoice Pro Deal is a gated, personal-use-only channel — not a military benefit.

Dickies and SheerID can re-verify and can change or pause the program at any time (the First Responder tier is being restructured now), so confirm the current terms at the SheerID landing page before you buy.
tractor-supply-military-veteran: All the math below uses one baseline: a $200 mixed Tractor Supply cart — feed, pet, workwear, and tools — the kind of order most rural shoppers actually ring up. Shipping is excluded from the ranking because it applies roughly equally and many orders are in-store pickup; tax varies by state and applies to every path about equally.

Rule 1 — there is no flat everyday military %. This is the page’s core correction. “10% every day” is the dominant aggregator myth; the real everyday benefit is the Neighbor’s Club Hometown Heroes wallet of targeted brand offers, not a store-wide discount.

Rule 2 — the holiday 10% is in-store and time-boxed. It lives in the late-October → Veterans Day (Nov 11) Hometown Heroes window — National First Responders Day (Oct 28), National Hometown Heroes Day (~Nov 1), and Veterans Day — and historically July 4. Plan big purchases around it. The figure is 10% in the latest announcements; it was 15% on Veterans Day and July 4 in prior years.

Rule 3 — wallet offers can out-save the 10%. Because they’re manufacturer/category deals on high-frequency rural purchases (feed, pet food), a verified shopper buying Purina, Victor, Nutrena, or Standlee may save more year-round through the wallet than from the once-a-year 10%.

Rule 4 — sale/clearance generally won’t stack with the 10%. So it’s pick-the-lower, not stack: compare the sale price against 10% off the regular price and take whichever is cheaper. Gift cards and live animals are also typically excluded. And ID.me verification (with a free Neighbor’s Club account) is the single gate for both the wallet and the seasonal reward bonuses — verify once.
warby-parker-military-discount: Warby Parker’s pricing model explains why there’s no discount to find: prescription glasses start at $95 including lenses ($145 is the most common frame tier), shipping is free on every order, and the brand famously does not run sitewide sales or public promo codes. Its only evergreen offer is Add a Pair and Save — buy two or more prescription pairs (prescription sunglasses count) and 20% comes off the lesser-priced pair(s) automatically, no code needed. The offer’s own terms state that vision benefits can’t be combined with promo discounts, so on a two-pair order your insurance applies to the full-price pair while the 20% applies to the cheaper one.

The biggest lever is vision insurance. Warby Parker is reported in-network with several carriers — including UnitedHealthcare/Spectera, Davis Vision, MetLife Vision, Guardian, and BCBS FEP Vision — and supports out-of-network reimbursement through warbyparker.com/reimbursement. A typical $130–$150 frame allowance takes a $145 pair down to $0–$50. The brand’s insurance page blocks crawlers, so confirm your specific plan’s network status at checkout or with support before relying on it.

The genuinely military-specific play is FEDVIP — and it’s precise, so don’t overread it. Uniformed-service retirees entitled to retired pay who are enrolled in a TRICARE health plan, plus active-duty family members, can enroll in a FEDVIP vision plan through BENEFEDS during open season (second Monday of November through the second Monday of December) or within 91 days of retirement. Several FEDVIP carriers’ plans are reported in-network at Warby Parker. Veterans without retired pay are not FEDVIP-eligible, and active-duty members themselves get exams and glasses through military health care. It’s enrollment-gated — you can’t invoke it at checkout; you plan for it in November.

Without insurance, stack what stacks: pay with FSA/HSA dollars (prescription glasses, prescription sunglasses, contacts, and eye exams all qualify — an effective ~20–30% savings at typical marginal tax rates), take the second-pair 20% if you can use two pairs, and click through a cashback portal (~2% at Rakuten as of July 14, 2026; ~2.5% at the best-paying portals). Be skeptical of aggregator claims of "occasional military-only holiday offers" — we found no brand confirmation of any military-holiday promo, ever. And if you want an actual military discount on eyewear, cross-shop retailers that run one via ID.me or GovX, or the on-base military exchange optical shops, which are tax-free for eligible shoppers.
uworld-military-discount: UWorld verifies manually by email. Accepted proof is a DMDC SCRA Status Report, VIC card, or a .mil email address. UWorld explicitly warns not to send your CAC or other military IDs, because doing so violates military regulation and federal law. Allow 1–2 business days, and the issued code works on uworld.com, the UWorld app, and participating retail locations.

The military discount is new purchases only — renewals and past orders are excluded — and it is one code per order, so it cannot combine with a public promo code. Because UWorld’s public seasonal codes routinely exceed 10%, the military code wins mainly when no live public code beats it.

Aggregators advertise "UWorld military discount 85%," "50% off," and "36% verified" codes. Those are fabricated or recycled public-sale claims — the only verified military rate is 10% off new packages, email-verified.
brumate-military-discount: Verification runs through GovX via the "Get Offer" button on BrüMate’s Frontline page. GovX confirms your eligibility online and issues a single-use code; a new code is issued each time you re-verify. No permanent account discount is implied beyond re-verification.

The important correction: multiple aggregators (WorthEPenny, UCMJ.us, SemperSave) claim "15% off via ID.me" for BrüMate. That is outdated and incorrect — BrüMate’s own Frontline page states 10% off via GovX, single-use and non-combinable, with the exclusion list above. Do not rely on a 15% or ID.me figure.

Because nothing stacks and the exclusion list is meaningful, the best path depends on the item. On full-price, non-excluded drinkware, the GovX 10% is the clean win. If your item is a cooler, Collab, Paragon pack, bundle, or already on sale, the code won’t apply — take the sale price or a public code. And when a seasonal or Black Friday sitewide code exceeds 10%, use it instead, since the two can’t be combined.
dixie-stampede-military-discount: There is no online verification for the Stampede military rate — no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute. Because booking is done by phone, staff handle eligibility at the point of sale; expect to present valid military identification. Ask on the call exactly what ID is required and whether veterans, dependents, or National Guard/Reserve members qualify, since the official source does not spell this out.

Coupon aggregators state the military discount is "$10 off adult tickets and $4 off child tickets" and advertise "30% off Dixie Stampede" codes. None of that is confirmed by Dolly Parton’s Stampede. The only official fact is that a special military rate exists and must be booked by phone; the exact amount and eligible groups are not published, so treat any specific figure as unverified until the box office quotes it.

On a baseline of two adult plus two child tickets (Pigeon Forge Regular Experience, about $209.96 before tax), the honest play is to call for the military rate, then compare it against the standard online advance price and third-party reseller packages (Tripster, Tiqets, and similar). If you’re traveling with 20 or more guests, ask about the group rate, which may beat the per-ticket military rate.
vera-bradley-military-discount: Vera Bradley verifies eligibility through ID.me. You create or sign in to a free ID.me account and verify your community — military, teacher, student, first responder, medical professional, or nurse — and once verified, the 10% is taken at checkout. Vera Bradley’s terms warn the program is personal: ID.me can detect and revoke shared or fraudulent use.

The discount is channel-limited. You get the full 10% at participating Vera Bradley Stores and on verabradley.com; at Vera Bradley Factory Outlet stores it applies to one qualifying in-stock item only; and it is not valid at all at the Vera Bradley Online Outlet. Vera Bradley’s terms name "Military Personnel" without enumerating veterans, retirees, or family members — ID.me’s military-community verification governs who passes, so confirm your status when you verify.

One thing to watch: several coupon round-ups claim Vera Bradley gives 15% off for military. That figure is wrong — the brand’s own Appreciation Discount terms say 10%, full stop. The same pages also tend to omit that the discount is not valid at the Online Outlet.

Because nothing stacks with the 10%, the smart move is to check the price first. Seasonal and end-of-season sales (ID.me Shop itself listed "up to 50% off select items" at verification time) routinely beat the 10% outright, and the Online Outlet runs the deepest past-season markdowns. Exchange-eligible shoppers have one more path: AAFES and the Navy Exchange stock Vera Bradley tax-free.
dennys-military-discount: The one company-confirmed military offer comes from Denny’s own Veterans Day releases: on November 11, active-duty and retired military who dine in at participating restaurants get a free Original Grand Slam (2 buttermilk pancakes, 2 bacon strips, 2 sausage links, 2 eggs), with a valid military ID or DD 214, historically from 5 a.m. to noon local. It "cannot be combined with any other offers," and there is no online code and no ID.me, GovX, or SheerID flow — proof of service is shown in person.

The everyday "10–20% off" figure that circulates on coupon and listicle sites is not published anywhere by Denny’s. It’s franchisee discretion — some locations grant it if you show a military ID, many grant nothing, and the amount is never guaranteed. WeSalute, the aggregator most often cited, explicitly says the offer is not in its partner coalition and "cannot be guaranteed, varies by location." So the honest read is "possible but unofficial; call ahead."

A note on timing: the Veterans Day program is a recurring annual tradition, but the meal name and date have shifted (2023 "Build Your Own Grand Slam" on Nov 10; 2024–2025 "Original Grand Slam" on Nov 11), and participation is by location. Re-check Denny’s newsroom about two weeks before November 11 for the current year’s details, and confirm your local restaurant participates before you go.
state-farm-military-discount: Insurance "savings" here means premium discounts and programs, not a cart price, and all of them are individually rated — so the numbers below are directional. The honest maximum-savings move for a service member is comparison shopping across insurers plus stacking State Farm’s telematics and bundle discounts, not hunting a State Farm military code that doesn’t exist.

The Louisiana exception is real but narrow. State Farm’s Louisiana discounts page lists a "Military Personnel Discount" because Louisiana law requires insurers to offer one. It applies to the named insured / registered owner who is on active duty or an active reservist in the Louisiana Air or Army National Guard and completes the state’s military-discount application. State Farm’s page states the discount exists but doesn’t publish the percentage; third-party trackers put the reduction at about 25%, which we flag as a secondary estimate rather than a State Farm figure.

Outside Louisiana, the real State Farm savings stack is Drive Safe & Save (up to 30% for safe, low-mileage driving) plus multi-policy bundling plus good-driver and vehicle-safety discounts — most of which combine on one policy. Drive Safe & Save is not available in California, Massachusetts, or Rhode Island and is capped at 30% in New York.

Because State Farm has no nationwide military discount, the biggest lever for many military households is switching, not adding: get a USAA quote (military and family) and a GEICO military quote and compare. Many service members find a military-focused insurer is cheaper than State Farm regardless of discounts.
stanley-military-discount: Stanley 1913 verifies eligibility through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. You create a free ID.me account and confirm your community — Military, Nurse, First Responder, Medical Provider, Hospital Employee, Teacher, Government Employee, or Student. On Stanley’s ID.me page you click “Verify with ID.me”; once verified, a one-time discount code auto-applies at checkout. For future orders, you sign in to ID.me at checkout, so the benefit is reusable, though ID.me may re-confirm identity or status per its own policies.

The 20% rate comes from the ID.me Shop store page for Stanley 1913, which lists 20% off for every eligible community. Stanley’s own ID.me page lists the eligible groups but does not print the percentage — it sits behind the ID.me verification flow — so the ID.me store page is the authoritative source for the figure.

One thing to watch: some coupon and aggregator pages, and even some news write-ups, advertise a “30%” or “up to 40%” Stanley military discount. Those figures are not supported by the primary sources as of June 23, 2026 — the confirmed rate is 20%. A separate GOVX channel also exists at 20%, but it excludes Quenchers and accessories; the offer on Stanley’s own site is the ID.me route.
cybex-military-discount: There is no CYBEX military verification because there is no CYBEX military discount. No CYBEX primary source names a military discount or a verification provider, and coupon-site claims that "military members can grab 25% off with code LUCKY" describe a public code anyone can use — where it’s valid at all — not a military benefit. CYBEX’s seasonal sales are likewise open to every customer.

The reliable stack is a seasonal sale plus CYBEX Club. Time your purchase to a live sale (up to 25% off select SKUs), join the free CYBEX Club for points and free shipping, and confirm the specific stroller or car seat you want is included in the sale. On a roughly $500 stroller, up to 25% off brings the effective price to about $375 before tax.

Two more paths can beat that. Some authorized baby-specialty retailers run their own military discounts on CYBEX products — that’s real, but retailer-specific and verified at that retailer (often via ID.me or SheerID at the retailer level). And if you have base access, the tax-free Exchange (AAFES/NEX) can be cheaper on stocked SKUs, since it avoids sales tax.
aquatica-orlando-military-discount: United Parks uses ID.me to verify eligibility. You create a free ID.me account, verify once (which may require a document upload), and eligible pricing unlocks on aquatica.com. The two offers serve different situations: the 50% single ticket is for a one-and-done active-duty visit, while the $139 Silver Pass — open to both active-duty and veterans — is the better value for families or anyone visiting more than once.

The math almost always favors the pass. A single active-duty adult visiting once pays about $40 with the 50% ticket, but two single-day visits already exceed the $139 pass price, and the pass adds free general parking (~$30+ a visit), roughly 20% in-park discounts, and 3 free guest tickets on a rolling calendar. For veterans, the pass is effectively the only military channel, since the 50% single ticket is active-duty only.

A note on channels: Aquatica is also listed on GovX, but the authoritative pricing lives on aquatica.com behind ID.me — confirm any GovX price against the park’s own page, and ignore aggregator "up to XX% off" banners. The pass benefits (parking, in-park discounts, guest tickets) are built into the pass rather than separate codes.

enterprise-military-discount: The difference between the two programs matters. Government Leisure Travel is off-duty travel and/or for personal needs, and Enterprise offers a 5% discount off base rates for it — note "off base rates," not off the total. Official Government Travel is for official government business or temporary duty, and instead of a flat percentage Enterprise provides specific contracted rates, which is why this page does not encode a fixed official-travel figure (it varies).

For the leisure discount, Enterprise states you are not required to have a membership to any military-related association, and that a military or government identification may be asked for at the time of pickup. For Official Government Travel, eligibility is confirmed at the counter by showing official orders or a government-issued credit card; renters must hold a valid driver’s license or military ID and be 18+. Enterprise is a participating vendor under the U.S. Government Car Rental Agreement, which governs the official rates.

One thing to watch: several aggregator pages claim the Enterprise military discount runs "through ID.me," via a "Veterans Advantage 5% off" code, or with a specific "USAA member program" corporate number. None of these mechanics is stated on Enterprise’s own military/government discount pages as the route for the general military/veteran leisure discount. Enterprise separately notes that USAA members receive added benefits, but that is a distinct partner program. Because the exact online redemption mechanic is not published, confirm the correct rate with Enterprise or your branch before booking.
medieval-times-military-discount: U.S. military verification is handled by ID.me through Troop ID, a digital ID card ID.me issues to military and veterans, spouses, and family members. You sign in to or create an ID.me account and verify your affiliation, then the discounted rate is available online. The official page does not state a re-verification frequency for this offer; that cadence is governed by ID.me. If the page won’t load, Medieval Times advises clearing your browser cache and retrying.

Buying on base is the only path that adds the free Royalty upgrade (an upgraded ticket tier). Availability varies by base ITT/MWR office, and you present a valid military ID as required by that office.

Because Medieval Times does not publish a figure, be skeptical of coupon sites: the percentages they cite (ranges of 10–25% and "up to 35%" both appear) are unverified and conflict with each other. The only reliable number is the one shown to you at checkout after verification.
walmart-plus-military-discount: Walmart+ Assist is a needs-based subsidy, not a military program. It cuts the membership 50% for shoppers who receive a qualifying government-assistance program — the full list Walmart publishes includes SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, SSI, TANF, the National School Lunch Program, LIHEAP, Federal Public Housing Assistance, the Federal Pell Grant, and the VA "Veterans and Survivors Pension Benefit," among others. The only reason a veteran or survivor can reach the $49 price through the VA is that the Veterans and Survivors Pension is itself a low-income pension. Standard veteran status is not enough.

Verification runs through SheerID, which confirms Walmart+ Assist eligibility — not military service. You enter your details at walmart.com/plus/assist, SheerID checks that you are in a qualifying program and may ask for documentation, and there is no credit check and no impact to your existing government benefits. Verification lasts one year, and Walmart re-checks eligibility annually to renew the discounted membership. There is no ID.me, GovX, or WeSalute path for a Walmart+ membership discount, because no military-specific membership discount exists.

One honest caveat worth knowing: Walmart’s own help article lists the Veterans and Survivors Pension Benefit among qualifying programs, but SheerID’s public offer page and the /plus/assist landing page summarize eligibility as "SNAP, WIC, Medicaid & more" and do not name the veterans pension. We treat the Walmart help article as authoritative, but SheerID’s live screen determines the final answer at signup — so if you receive the VA Pension and SheerID declines you, that outcome governs.

If you do not receive a qualifying program, the best "discount" is the same one open to everyone: Walmart’s free 30-day trial lets you test free delivery, member fuel savings, and streaming before paying, and Walmart periodically runs public $1-for-first-month trial promos that are not military-gated. Enrolled college students can get the same $49/year membership through Walmart+ Student, an education-based gate. And if you rarely order delivery, you can skip the membership entirely — Walmart’s everyday low prices and in-store pickup are free without Walmart+.
kay-jewelers-military-discount: Kay verifies military eligibility through ID.me, the same identity service used across many major retailers; SheerID appears on some of Kay’s "Get Offer" flows as well. Once verified, ID.me issues a one-time code — reported valid for about 30 days — that you apply at kay.com checkout to eligible, full-price items.

One thing to watch: aggregator pages sometimes present the 10% military discount as broadly stackable or applicable to engagement solitaires. It is not. The everyday 10% specifically excludes Now & Forever®, Adore®, and Lab-Created Diamonds by KAY solitaire rings, along with certain designer brands, watches, and loose diamonds/gemstones — and it cannot be combined with other offers, codes, or Kay’s public sales.

If you’re shopping for an engagement solitaire in one of the excluded lines, the general military 10% won’t apply — but Kay/ID.me runs a separate "10% off solitaire rings" offer that does cover Now & Forever, Lab-Grown Diamond, and Adore solitaires. Treat it as a distinct promo, not an extension of the military discount.

Because Kay’s public sales (up to 35–50% off during events like July 4th or the Big Summer Sale) are open to everyone and don’t require verification, they frequently beat the 10% outright on the same item. The honest move is to check whether a storewide sale is live on your piece before defaulting to the military code.
enhauto-military-discount: ENH Auto is the storefront of Enhance Ltd., a small EU company describing itself as a "small team of car enthusiasts" that makes products to "enhance already great vehicles." Its line is aftermarket Tesla accessories — the S3XY Buttons, S3XY Dash, S3XY Strip, S3XY Stalks, S3XY Knob, and the "Commander" OBD automation dongle. A footer disclaimer confirms enhauto.com has no affiliation with Tesla Motors, Inc.

Because the company is EU-domiciled and prices in EUR (with free shipping over EUR 250), a US-style verified military discount is simply not part of its model. There is no discount or perks page, no military mention in the FAQ or terms, and no verification integration — so there is nothing service-gated to unlock or stack. Any group you belong to pays the same public price.

The only genuine levers are public ones: the newsletter (which may carry a welcome or first-order offer, though no fixed percentage is stated on-page), an occasional public promo code, and the 14-day money-back guarantee. Be cautious with coupon aggregators that list "10% off" ENH Auto codes or cite a one-off "frozentesla 30%" code — none is a military benefit, none is a verified brand term, and they are frequently expired.

For US buyers, the dominant cost variable is import tax, not the absence of a coupon: EU orders include VAT, but non-EU orders pay VAT and duties separately, collected by the carrier on delivery. Factor that landed cost in before comparing enhauto to alternatives. Because Enhance Ltd. controls its own pricing and can change it at any time, confirm the current terms at enhauto.com before you buy.
lego-military-discount: For a military discount there is nothing to verify: LEGO publishes no military offer, and ID.me confirms it lists none — the same "not aware" language appears across ID.me’s LEGO community pages (military, nurse, responder, teacher, government). Separately, ID.me offers cash back to all members at LEGO (not a military discount), with restrictions on gift cards, LEGOLAND tickets, the BrickMaster subscription, and non-ID.me coupons.

LEGO does operate a verified-community offer gateway through Beans iD / Student Beans, linked from LEGO.com’s footer as "Student & exclusive offers." That platform exposes verification tabs including student, graduate, parent, first-responder, and military — but the offers it surfaces appear to be LEGO’s general promotions (a free gift over a spend threshold, free shipping over $35) rather than a military-specific percentage. We could not confirm a military-specific value from a primary source, so we don’t assert one; treat any specific figure as unverified until you see it in the LEGO checkout after verifying.

The ways to save are the same for everyone, including service members: the free LEGO Insiders program (points, members-only rewards and gifts), free standard shipping over $35, frequent themed promotions (Star Wars Day, Insiders Weekend) with gifts-with-purchase and bonus points, and the Sale / "Last chance to buy" sections. And keep the boundary clear: much "LEGO military discount" search intent is really about LEGOLAND — those Merlin-run attractions do offer military ticket discounts, entirely separate from the LEGO toy brand.
crunchyroll-military-discount: There is nothing to verify — Crunchyroll has no military program and no military verification partner. Any percentage you see attached to “military” on a coupon site is unverified, and the CRNEW-style codes people circulate are simply the general new-subscriber promo, available to anyone regardless of service.

The reliable saving is billing cadence. Crunchyroll’s Fan tier lists at $9.99/mo after the February 2026 price increase, while the Fan Annual plan runs about $99.99/year (≈ $8.33/mo) — roughly $20 cheaper across a year. Higher tiers (Mega Fan $13.99/mo, Ultimate Fan $17.99/mo) add offline viewing, more concurrent streams, and swag, but the annual-vs-monthly gap is the same everyday lever.

The best public deals cluster around New Year, Black Friday, and Cyber Monday, when Crunchyroll discounts the first annual term (a recent promo hit ~$66.99 for year one). For light watchers, the free ad-supported tier or the 14-day premium trial costs nothing. A student’s cheapest route is the same as everyone’s — annual billing beats an unverifiable student percentage.
at-home-military-discount: There is no digital verification. At Home judges eligibility visually at the register from your Military card — there is no ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute account to create and no online gate. That also means the discount is only as reliable as the individual store’s practice, and shoppers report which ID counts (retiree ID, dependent ID, VA card) can be cashier-dependent.

The single verified rule set is narrow: 10%, in-store, active and retired service members and their families, shown by a Military card before paying, and not applied after payment. Aggregator pages embroider that with terms At Home does not publish — an anti-stacking clause and exclusions on clearance, gift cards, or special orders. At Home’s own Help Center article states none of that, so we do not assert those exclusions; confirm at the register.

For online carts, the math flips. Since the 10% doesn’t exist online, the levers are Rakuten cash back (4% as of July 8, 2026, rates rotate) and the public Sale/clearance section. On an item already marked down 30–70%, the public price frequently beats a 10% discount on full price. For repeat shoppers, the Insider Perks card’s 15%-off-first-purchase welcome offer beats the one-time 10% on the opening cart, and its ~5% ongoing rewards ($5 certificate per $100) become the engine after that.
avis-military-discount: Verification is handled by WeSalute, not by ID.me, GovX, or SheerID. You enroll in the paid WeSalute+ tier and verify your military status; WeSalute issues a secure WeSalute+ ID so you don’t share your military ID directly with each merchant, and assigns the personal Avis AWD number used to apply the rate. Treat WeSalute+ as an ongoing paid membership and confirm its current cost before relying on it.

The headline rate is a maximum. Avis publishes only "up to 35%" (with a stated minimum of 5% in Canada and up to 20% in other international regions), and the actual savings vary by location, dates, and car group. WeSalute itself advises comparing the member rate against current public "Pay Now" rates on avis.com before applying the AWD.

A separate WeSalute enhancement — a complimentary Avis Preferred Plus upgrade and $15 off when you spend $175+ on a 3-or-more-day rental — is listed by WeSalute as valid until June 30, 2026; re-verify that promotion and the headline percentage after that date. There is no free public Avis military AWD code: the AWD is assigned to your membership, and codes circulated on coupon sites (such as "T765700") are not confirmed on Avis’s or WeSalute’s own pages.
osprey-military-discount: Osprey uses SheerID — not ID.me — to confirm eligibility. You submit your status once through SheerID’s secure flow; on approval, the 20% unlocks for your Osprey order. Re-verification may be required periodically or per offer window. Because SheerID (not Osprey) runs the identity check, keep documentation such as service records ready if asked.

The verified consumer rate is 20%, and it applies to eligible full-priced gear. Sale and clearance items are generally excluded and are treated as the competing path rather than a stack: because the seasonal sale can exceed 20% on select models, the smart move is to compare your model’s sale price against the 20% before buying. Shoppers also consistently report the discount will not combine with other promo codes or free-shipping offers.

Be cautious of coupon and aggregator pages claiming military members get "up to 40% off through the Osprey Pro Deal, verified with the ID.me widget." That conflates two different things and is not accurate as stated. Osprey’s verified consumer discount is 20%, not 40%, and it is verified through SheerID — ID.me’s own site says it has no Osprey military offer. The deeper Pro Deal / Program Sales pricing is gated to outdoor professionals by profession, which military status alone does not satisfy.

Reserve and National Guard members, retirees, spouses, and dependents are not explicitly named on Osprey’s military offer, so this guide does not promise them the discount. If you fall into one of those groups, start the SheerID flow and see whether your status can be verified rather than assuming it qualifies. Osprey controls the terms, so always confirm the current offer on Osprey’s official page before you buy.
angel-studios-military-discount: The honest core fact: Angel Studios has no military or veteran discount. Its support page states it "does not offer specific senior or military discounts," and there is no verification partner — no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, WeSalute, or VerifyPass — anywhere on angel.com. There is nothing to verify because there is no military offer.

Why the "15% off via ID.me" claim keeps circulating. Coupon aggregators advertise fabricated Angel Studios "military discount" codes and an invented "15% off via ID.me." None is verified, and the specific ID.me claim is contradicted by Angel’s own documentation. Where real, the "20–70% off" codes trace to public promotional membership pricing that anyone gets — not a military rate.

Where the real savings are. Most of Angel’s catalog streams free with ads on a free account. Pay It Forward lets anyone claim one free theater ticket per email to a current release (subject to a waitlist). And Angel’s frequent public promos — including a historical Veterans Day "4 months free" on annual Premium — are the cheapest route onto a paid membership, which itself bundles 2 free theater tickets per Angel release and 20% off merch. None of these is a military benefit, but each is a real, honest way to save.
express-military-discount: The only percentage Express itself clearly states in rendered page text is the Express Credit Card’s extra 5% off every purchase, which is a cardholder tender benefit — not a military discount. The ~5% military figure rests on Military.com and SemperSave plus convergent trackers (medium confidence), and the honest in-store terms are quoted from SemperSave: "This discount is only offered in stores. Be prepared to present some form of identification (Military ID, Veteran ID, DD214, etc.)."

Because the appreciation 5% applies to full-price items only and does not combine with anything, while the Express Credit Card’s 5% and cashback portals DO stack on top of the public sale, the military discount and the maximum-savings stack are mutually exclusive. On essentially every real cart you want the sale stack, not the 5%.

Express, Inc. filed Chapter 11 in April 2024 and its operations were acquired by Phoenix Retail, LLC (a WHP Global / Simon / Brookfield / Centennial venture) in June 2024. The brand still operates express.com and roughly 450 stores, but discount programs are more volatile than usual after a bankruptcy — re-verify terms before relying on them.
gap-military-discount: Verification is in person: you show a valid military ID to a Gap store associate at the register. Gap Inc. explicitly ties the in-store-only rule to needing to physically verify that ID. Unlike sibling brand Old Navy (which has used online verification services), Gap-branded online orders have no SheerID/ID.me military flow — so there is no online code to enter at gap.com checkout.

One thing to watch: many coupon and aggregator pages headline a "Gap 10% online military discount, verify with SheerID," and some describe a "10–15%" range. Neither is accurate for Gap-branded shopping. The verified figure is 10%, in-store only; the SheerID "military verification" pages some results surface belong to Old Navy and to Foot Locker, not Gap.

Old Navy, Banana Republic, and Athleta are sibling brands under Gap Inc., each with its own policy — don’t assume Gap’s in-store rule applies to them or vice versa. If Gap ever adds online verification the way Old Navy has, the "in-store only" headline would change; until then, treat any "online Gap military code" as unverified.
subaru-military-discount: Subaru uses ID.me to confirm military status during the online request at subarunet.com/vip/customer/military. Once verified, you proceed to a participating Subaru retailer to complete the purchase or lease. Eligibility questions go to VIP Program Headquarters at vipprogram@subaru.com.

The reason to always claim it: the $500 is additive. Subaru states it applies "plus any current zone or regional cash incentives," and the dealer restatement of SOA terms confirms it "may be combined with any other retailer or customer incentives when purchasing." The one hard wall is that it cannot be combined with another Subaru VIP program offer.

Where the real money is won is timing and negotiation, not the badge. The $500 is fixed, but zone/regional cash and APR incentives move by thousands month to month, so buy in a strong-incentive month and stack the $500 on top. If you belong to Costco Auto Program or USAA Car Buying, treat those as substitutes, not stacks — get their prearranged price and compare it to (negotiated price − incentives − $500), then take the lower total.
popeyes-military-discount: Popeyes is a franchised quick-service chain with no national military program. Register courtesies, when they happen at all, are set by individual owner/operators and are consistently framed on Q&A and coupon boards as "call your local store first." Shoppers report that some locations have honored an informal military courtesy while others decline — that is anecdotal and location-specific, not a corporate policy, so do not present it to yourself as a guaranteed discount.

Popeyes is also absent from the major curated Veterans Day free-meal lists (Military.com and BrandEating for 2025), which is a strong signal there is no reliable corporate military promo. A "spend $20, get a free chicken sandwich" line appears in one general roundup but is not a military-verified offer — treat it as a general app promo. No Military Appreciation Month, Memorial Day, July 4, or Armed Forces Day military-specific promo is documented either.

The genuine everyday value is Popeyes Rewards: a free loyalty program that earns 10 points per $1 on app/online orders, gives a sign-up offer (historically a free apple pie, regular side, or small drink), runs $1 regular sides during happy hour, and surfaces frequent member-only and limited-time free-item deals such as the National Chicken Sandwich Day free sandwich. These beat chasing an unadvertised, location-dependent "military discount" that no primary source confirms.

If you have installation access, the on-base Popeyes inside an AAFES Exchange food court is worth knowing about: Exchange sales are tax-free for authorized patrons, so a ~$12 combo saves roughly $0.70–$1.10 in sales tax automatically. It is not a discount on the menu price and needs no verification — the tax is simply never charged. Exact Popeyes Rewards point values and the current sign-up offer can shift, so confirm them in-app before quoting specifics.
peak-design-military-discount: Peak Design verifies eligibility through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA and many major retailers. You click "Verify With ID.ME" on Peak Design’s discount page, sign in or create a free account, and the 10% applies to qualifying full-price purchases at checkout. Peak Design doesn’t state a re-verification frequency, so don’t assume the verification is permanent; eligibility questions route to ID.me’s help center.

The stacking rules are the whole game here. Peak Design’s own page says additional discounts "may not be valid during a site-wide sale, bundles or on already discounted (Sale) items" — so the 10% is effectively a full-price-only discount. During Black Friday 2025, everything on the site was discounted up to 30% off (including the new Pro Tripod line, with a free gift over $300), which beat the military rate decisively. In a sale window, the smarter stack is the public sale price plus a cashback portal (Rakuten listed 3%, with up to ~8% at other portals, as of July 14, 2026) — no code is entered, so standard portal terms are satisfied, whereas an ID.me-gated checkout frequently breaks portal tracking.

One thing to watch: coupon aggregators advertise Peak Design codes like "60% off" or a generic 10% code — those recycle expired or invented codes. The real, verifiable offers are the ID.me-verified 10% on the brand site and Peak Design’s public sales, including its "Last Call" clearance collection. There is no Peak Design GovX storefront; the third-party channels that do exist are ExpertVoice (an active Peak Design brand store — pricing and eligibility sit behind the ExpertVoice login, so verify your profile qualifies before counting on it) and Provengo’s government/military shop, which lists Peak Design gear priced item-by-item.

Bottom line for a $300 camera-bag cart: no sale running, the ID.me 10% saves you $30. A sitewide sale at 2025’s depth plus cashback puts the same cart around $195–$204. ExpertVoice-eligible buyers should compare its store price too — it can beat both, but the depth isn’t publicly published.
ymca-military-discount: How verification works: the MOI has no ID.me or SheerID step — eligibility is verified by your service branch’s approving official (MCAO) against your Title 10 orders, and re-verified at each 6-month renewal with facility attendance records. Local Y discounts are verified in person with standard military/veteran documents. No national online verification exists; treat any site offering an "ID.me YMCA code" as fake.

The MOI’s value is real money: on an illustrative $80/month family membership, the free program is worth $960 a year — plus up to 16 hours a month of free respite child care (ages birth–12) at participating Ys. The DoD pays the facility directly (up to $80/month family / $57/month single per the August 2024 FAQ), and YMCAs absorb any difference, so there is nothing to pay and nothing to stack.

The catch most pages skip: the free membership has a usage price. Renewal requires 48 visit-days per 6 months — about 8 days a month — activation takes 30–45 days after MCAO approval, and the whole program rides an annual August-to-July funding cycle (stated intent as of July 7, 2026: extended through July 31, 2027).

For everyone the MOI excludes, the honest comparison at your local Y is between two numbers: the military/veteran rate (documented 5–20% where offered — Toledo runs 15%, Cincinnati posted a $76/month military family rate in November 2025) and income-based financial assistance. They don’t combine — take whichever prices lower, and watch for November free weeks to try before joining. Active duty near an installation: your MWR base gym is free; the Y’s paid discount only makes sense for family amenities like pools, classes, and Child Watch.
san-antonio-zoo-military-discount: Verification is entirely in person at the front gate with a valid Military ID — there is no ID.me, GovX, or online military code to apply. For the Month of the Military Child program and the November Zoo Salutes window, the same Military ID is shown on the date of visit.

One thing to keep straight: some aggregators round the benefit up or imply "military free admission" year-round. That’s not accurate. The verified everyday benefit is $5 off admission — free admission is limited to the seasonal events (military children in April and members/veterans during the November Zoo Salutes window). Don’t expect year-round free entry.

The family benefit is also often overstated. It is not free family admission; it is a 50%-off upgrade on Standard/Any Day admission that is tied to the April Military Child program. The zoo’s own wording puts the family cap at three (Military Child page) to four (a social post) members, so confirm at the gate.

For the best value, time your visit: April (military kids free plus family 50% off) or a November Zoo Salutes window (members/veterans free) both beat the everyday $5. If you’ll return often, price an annual membership, which amortizes below per-visit admission. On any other day, just bring your Military ID for the easy $5 off.
beretta-military-discount: The website discount runs through ID.me. You add eligible non-firearm items to your cart, click "Verify with ID.me" at checkout, verify your military or first-responder affiliation once, and Beretta auto-applies an exclusive promo code to eligible items. The exact percentage rotates — the 2022 official announcements state 15%, while current sources and ID.me’s marketplace show 20% off eligible items — so confirm the figure in your cart. Expect the code not to stack with other coupons, and clearance items may be ineligible.

The American Defender Program is a different animal: discounted firearm pricing delivered through Beretta’s LE dealer network, not the website, and with no public number. You register on Beretta’s site, find your closest LE dealer, and contact them for pricing on covered models (APX A1, M9A4 and 92X RDO pistol families, TIKKA TACT A1 rifle, 1301 Tactical shotgun, and more). Eligibility is heavily law-enforcement and first-responder weighted but also includes active and retired U.S. military of all branches.

Honest verdict: for apparel and gear, the ID.me discount is a straightforward, genuine win. For firearms, do not trust any "X% off guns" claim — the real value is a quoted dealer price you must compare against ordinary street prices, because GunBroker, PSA, and local FFL sales frequently beat MSRP with no verification. A current Beretta factory rebate ("Beretta Bucks") can also attach to a firearm purchase. Coupon aggregators advertising "40% off" or generic Beretta promo codes are not the military program and are not verified.
six-flags-military-discount: Six Flags uses ID.me to verify eligibility. After you select your Military & First Responder product(s) online, you receive an ID.me login prompt to confirm your status before completing the purchase — you must be registered with ID.me. The official pages don’t state how often re-verification is required or which documents ID.me will request; ID.me manages its own verification and renewal. For free in-person appreciation days, verification is by presenting a valid U.S. Military ID at Guest Services. If automatic verification fails, follow ID.me’s support process — Six Flags doesn’t publish a separate path.

The key thing about pricing: there is no single nationwide percentage, because each park sets its own discounted price and those change periodically. As of June 24, 2026, Six Flags Magic Mountain listed a Military & First Responder single-day from $50 (gate $110) and Six Flags Great Adventure from $39 (gate $90), with discounted Hurricane Harbor waterpark tiers too. Always check your specific park’s page for its current price rather than assuming one park’s deal applies elsewhere.

Two ways to get more value. Some parks sell a discounted Military season pass (e.g., Magic Mountain’s Gold pass online at $105 vs. $135) that bundles park + waterpark access, free general parking, and in-park discounts — often a better deal than per-visit tickets for repeat visitors. And a few parks run free-admission Military Appreciation days: California’s Great America gave active and retired military free single-day admission over Memorial Day Weekend (May 22–25, 2026), redeemed in person with a military ID. Those dates are park-specific and change each year, so confirm your local park’s current offer.
marshalls-military-discount: There is no military verification partner for Marshalls — no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, WeSalute, or VerifyPass military offer. Any site telling you to "verify your military status for a Marshalls discount" is describing a program that does not exist.

Coupon and affiliate sites push several false or misleading Marshalls "military" claims. Headlines like "Marshalls Military Discount: Ways to Save 60% Off" misuse Marshalls’ ordinary off-price markdown vs. department stores — that 20%–60% is available to every shopper, not a military offer. WeSalute’s "T.J. Maxx" offer is free shipping on $89+ only (the same as public SHIP89), lists no percentage, and doesn’t cover Marshalls. A ~10% senior (55+) discount reported at some stores is store-by-store discretionary, not company-wide, and not a military discount.
Because Marshalls controls its policies and could change them, we re-check this quarterly; confirm the current terms on Marshalls’ own pages before relying on any figure here.
san-diego-zoo-military-discount: Verification is in person and ID-based — there is no third-party verification provider (no ID.me, GovX, or SheerID) and no online account requirement for the military benefit. Active Duty present a CAC or Uniformed Services ID at the gate; spouses and eligible dependents present a valid dependent ID card at a ticket window. Verification happens at the point of entry or purchase each visit.

The free Active-Duty admission is unusually generous for a major attraction — it is valid every day of the year ("Visit as often as you wish!"), except it is not valid for special ticketed events or programs. Its lack of any retiree or veteran park discount, however, is more restrictive than some peer zoos and aquariums.

For retirees and veterans, the support path is the MWR / ITT ticket office on a local military installation, which partners with the Zoo on discounted package deals. Separate, non-military promotions such as "Kids Free" in October and "Seniors Free February" at the Safari Park can also lower the cost of a family visit.
northern-tool-military-discount: Verification is a physical military ID shown in-store — there’s no ID.me, SheerID, or online account. Because the discount is in-store only, there’s no online verification path at all. ID.me’s own shop page states it is "not aware that Northern Tool offers Military discounts," and Military.com lists redemption as in-store only with a valid military ID presented at the time of purchase.

Aggregators embellish the real 10% in-store discount with claims primary sources don’t support: an online "unique discount code," ID.me or SheerID verification, and blanket family-member eligibility. We don’t assert any of those. The verified rule set is narrow — 10% in-store, physical military ID, $500 maximum discount, no Stihl or gift cards, and non-combinable.

The 10% reaches full value only up to a ~$5,000 cart (the $500 cap), so it pays to batch major purchases — a generator, welder, or pressure washer — into one in-store trip. Online, where the military discount doesn’t exist, the levers are public promo codes (e.g. $20 off $100) and clearance, which are open to everyone; on an already-reduced item the public price frequently beats 10%.
cvs-military-discount: The make-or-break fact is cost. Verification runs through WeSalute (a third-party service, formerly Veterans Advantage): you verify your service once, then subscribe to the paid WeSalute+ tier and activate the CVS offer via a link in your account. The discount is only active while your paid membership is current, and the free WeSalute basic tier does not unlock it. On the baseline of a $40 full-price CVS.com cart, 20% is $8 off — real money, but you have to clear the roughly $300/year of full-price, non-excluded CVS.com spend it takes to out-earn the membership fee.

CVS does say the 20% “can be combined with rewards” through ExtraCare, so your 2% ExtraBucks and eligible digital coupons can layer on a full-price order. But the items where a drugstore run really saves — sale prices and BOGO deals — are exactly the ones the 20% excludes, and those are usually cheapest with the free ExtraCare + coupon stack instead.

Do not confuse the two “20% off” figures CVS uses. The military benefit is WeSalute+ (military-gated, full-price CVS.com). Separately, ExtraCare Plus ($5/month or $48/year) gives 20% off CVS Health brand products plus a $10 monthly reward and free delivery — it is open to anyone, not military-specific, and for a frequent CVS shopper it can out-save WeSalute+ for less money.

If you have base access, over-the-counter and health-and-beauty items are tax-free at the commissary or exchange — a clean substitute for a CVS front-store run. And there is no confirmed CVS in-store Veterans Day military discount; the WeSalute+ 20% is a year-round, membership-gated benefit, while CVS’s public weekly deals run all year for everyone.
pirates-voyage-military-discount: There is no online verification partner. Eligibility is checked the old-fashioned way — a person at the box office reviews your military ID when you book by phone and/or pick up tickets. Nothing about the rate is tied to an ID.me or SheerID account, so there’s no re-verification cycle; you simply show ID each time.

Because the rate is phone-only, it inherently cannot be combined with any online checkout coupon code or reseller cart. Third-party reseller deals (Tripster, Groupon, Westgate/Reserve Direct) are alternatives, not add-ons — you pick the reseller price or the phone military rate, not both. The first-responder pricing reported at Pigeon Forge appears to be a separate rate, not stackable with the military rate.

On a baseline of two adult plus one child standard-seating tickets to the Myrtle Beach show (roughly $150 before tax), the single best move for an eligible service member is a phone call to the box office; the military rate almost always beats the small "$2 off adult" public coupons floating around. If you’re not eligible or want to bundle multiple attractions, compare a third-party reseller package against the base site price for your show time.
lowes-military-veteran: Lowe’s discount is built into its free MyLowe’s Rewards program and verified through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers.
