You enroll in a personal MyLowe’s Rewards account, verify your military status once, and the 10% discount is tied to that account for online and in-store purchases.

Unlike one-time holiday promotions, the Lowe’s military discount applies year-round with no annual cap, so it can add up on larger projects. Verified members also receive free MyLowe’s Rewards Silver Key status, which adds free standard shipping on eligible orders.

First responders are not eligible for the everyday 10% discount — that standing program is for the military and veteran community only. Lowe’s does, separately, run a first-responder program that is not a percentage discount: verifying at Lowes.com/firstresponders through ID.me unlocks a free upgrade to MyLowe’s Rewards Silver Key status (which adds free standard shipping on eligible orders), with occasional added perks around National First Responders Day in October.

Because Lowe’s controls the terms and can change them at any time, treat the numbers here as a starting point and confirm the current offer and exclusion list on Lowe’s official military discount page before you buy.
sonos-military-discount: The honest core fact: Sonos does not publish a U.S. military or veteran discount. Its Frontline Workers page names only first responders and healthcare workers as eligible for the 15% ID.me offer — it does not list active-duty military or veterans. So there is no military code, no military ID.me or SheerID gate, and nothing military to verify on the U.S. site.

Why the "15% military" claims keep circulating. Coupon aggregators and military-discount listicles widely advertise a "Sonos military discount 15% via ID.me," and some claim "25% via SheerID." Against Sonos’s own pages, the ID.me relationship is the Frontline Workers program for first responders and healthcare workers; the only 15% genuinely tied to military status is the UK Defence Discount Scheme on sonos.co.uk, not a U.S. offer; and no SheerID military term is documented on any Sonos-owned page. Treat any "U.S. Sonos military discount" figure as unverified.

Where the real savings are. Certified Refurbished is the deepest standing saving — an Era 100 recently at $134 vs $219 new (about 39% off), with the same one-year warranty as new. That beats every percentage-off code Sonos offers, so for a service member wanting the lowest price, refurbished is usually the answer. Add the price-match guarantee (new units at named resellers), seasonal set/bundle sales, and Black Friday, and you have several real levers — none of them a military benefit, but each a genuine way to lower your price.

Pick one path, don’t stack. Sonos allows one discount code per order, and codes do not apply to Certified Refurbished, speaker sets, or limited editions. A veteran who is also a first responder or healthcare worker can use the 15% frontline code on a new unit — but should still compare it against the refurbished price and any live sale, because the refurb price often wins. In the UK, military status is verified through the Defence Discount Scheme (Defence Privilege Card) for a single-use code on sonos.co.uk.
ancestry-military-discount: Ancestry verifies eligibility through SheerID, which checks your details against DoD records and is usually instant. The military discount cannot be combined with other promotions, is not applied retroactively, and is valid online only. Existing members typically must cancel and rejoin under the military offer at the end of their current term, since you can’t toggle it mid-subscription.

Aggregators advertise "30% on DNA kits," "$60 off + cashback," and "50% off" Ancestry codes. The official military offer is 20% off All Access via SheerID — the DNA-kit and dollar-off figures are aggregator or seasonal-sale claims, not the verified military term. All Access already includes Fold3, the military-records hub, so there’s no separate purchase needed for military records.

The smartest routing depends on your need. For one-off record lookups, use Ancestry’s free military-records windows around Memorial Day and Veterans Day — they cost nothing. For ongoing research, verify with SheerID for 20% off All Access. And if you’re a brand-new member during a big intro sale, compare the public first-term sale price to the 20% — the sale sometimes wins term one, after which the military rate can apply (terms permitting).
wss-military-discount: WSS verifies eligibility through Beans iD, the identity-verification service tied to Student Beans (WSS’s hosted "connect" partner). You create or sign into a Student Beans / Beans iD account, verify your military status, and unlock the 15% discount. Re-verification cadence and document requirements are set by Beans iD, not published by WSS, so don’t assume verification is permanent. WSS does not use ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute for this offer — and ID.me’s own WSS page states it isn’t aware of any ShopWSS military discount, so aggregator listings pointing military shoppers to ID.me for WSS are wrong.

The 15% is a solo discount. WSS’s offer terms state it is "not valid in combination with other discounts, promotions, programs, or offers" and "cannot be combined with Buy One, Get One (B.O.G.O.) or ‘2 for’ promotions." It never applies to the enumerated hype styles or gift cards, and clearance is excluded entirely and final. The one thing that layers is WSS Rewards ("sneaker bucks"), a free loyalty mechanic separate from a percentage-off promo — the realistic way to add a little value on top, though the 15% itself doesn’t stack.

On a $120 full-price, non-excluded sneaker, the 15% drops the price to $102 — the best single path for an eligible member. For an excluded hype style or a clearance shoe the 15% can’t touch, take the sale/clearance price and earn WSS Rewards instead. And because WSS is a Foot Locker banner, it’s worth comparing: sibling stores Foot Locker and Champs Sports run SheerID-verified 10% military discounts, so if the exact shoe is cheaper there, compare — but at an equal sticker, WSS’s own 15% beats their 10%.
asus-military-discount: ASUS uses ID.me — not GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute. Verification happens on the product buy page, and the program covers the Military and Educational communities (military, students, teachers). The one trap is the email match: if your ASUS membership email and your ID.me email differ, verification fails with an on-site error until you align them.

The honest math on a $999.99 laptop: the ID.me pricing (5% per ID.me Shop) saves about $53 with tax; the tax-free Exchange saves about $70 at a 7% rate if AAFES matches the sticker; and a routine 20% sale saves $214 — the program discount can’t combine with sales, so during a real sale the sale simply wins.

ASUS’s FAQ is unusually explicit on the rules: "You can’t combine the program discount with other discounts. However, some coupons can be used in addition to the program discount," and "You can use the discount as many times as you like. There is no limit." It doesn’t say which coupons stack — test at checkout rather than assuming.

Watch out for aggregator spin: Groupon’s "50% off" and WorthEPenny’s "25% off" military-code headlines are inventions (the program is auto-applied member pricing, not a code), and a circulating "APCSUMMER23 = 25% military" claim is a stale 2023-era public promo. In 2025 ASUS did run an "Exclusive Veterans Day Savings" window through ID.me, valid through November 12, 2025 — percentage unpublished, and past promos don’t guarantee future ones.
xtool-military-discount: xTool verifies eligibility through VerifyPass. You confirm your group online — military, first responder, government, healthcare, teacher, or student — and receive a unique, one-time discount code. Each purchase requires fresh verification, and there’s no minimum spend. Verification problems route through VerifyPass; order issues go through xTool customer service.

Coupon aggregators advertise "xTool 20–50% off military" and "$80/$100 off" codes. The only verified discount tied to military status is 5% via VerifyPass — the big percentages are xTool’s public bundle and flash promos, open to everyone, not a military benefit. Since the 5% code can’t combine with those public promos, treat them as an either/or and pick the larger.

The most under-appreciated lever for machine owners is the Trade Up program, which gives a $50–$800 credit toward a new xTool machine when you trade in an old laser — this can dwarf the 5%. Reported credit values vary widely by model and condition, and whether a promo code can co-apply on a Trade Up order should be confirmed at checkout. For the deepest public pricing, Black Friday and prime-season bundle events are typically the year’s best.
foot-locker-military-discount: Foot Locker uses SheerID — not ID.me, not GovX. Online, you select "military discount" in the Payment field at checkout and complete the SheerID form; if prompted, you upload a government-issued document showing your full name, branch of service, and current status, and verification takes up to about 20 minutes. In store, Foot Locker recommends simply showing a valid photo/military ID at the register. Claims on some coupon sites that you can "verify through GovX" are wrong — Foot Locker’s own page reads "Verification Powered By SheerID," and no Foot Locker GovX storefront exists.

The offer is rate-limited, and the caps are per verification, not per year: each verification caps the discount at $100 (about $1,000 of eligible spend at 10%), and you can complete up to four SheerID verifications on a rolling 30-day basis. That means a big kit-out can capture up to $400 per month in military savings by splitting orders across verifications.

Two sister banners run their own identical programs: Kids Foot Locker and Champs Sports each document the same 10% SheerID military discount — with the same groups and the same $100 / four-per-30-days caps — in their own help centers, and FLX Rewards points and free-shipping perks work across the Foot Locker family. Eastbay no longer exists: Foot Locker shut eastbay.com on January 13, 2023, so any "Eastbay military discount" page you find is stale.

Know when 10% isn’t the play. Foot Locker’s public welcome offer — 20% off $99+ for first-time email + SMS subscribers (one-time use, online only, discount-eligible items; select Nike/adidas/ASICS styles and all New Balance excluded) — beats the military rate outright on a first order. FLX Rewards is free and layers on everything: free standard shipping with no minimum while logged in, plus 100 XPoints per $1 toward FLX Cash. Rakuten paid 2% cashback as of July 4, 2026, but only reliably on no-code orders, and its terms exclude marquee styles like Jordan Retro and Nike LeBron/Kobe. And in late November, Black Friday / Cyber Monday markdowns have historically run up to ~50–60% — the military discount is irrelevant during those windows.
xbox-military-discount: Microsoft's military discount is narrower than most listings admit. The published terms grant up to 10% off "select consumer Surface devices and accessories" to active, former, and retired military members and their immediate families — and then list what's ineligible: Xbox consoles, games, and accessories; digital games, apps, and in-app content; subscriptions including Game Pass, Microsoft 365, and Skype; Windows; Office; gift cards; Surface for Business; and personalized products. Every Xbox product a service member might want is carved out.

Verification is also different from what aggregator sites claim. Microsoft uses its own eligibility check, tied to the email on your personal Microsoft account — not ID.me, GovX, or SheerID. You're approved immediately if eligible, and the discount then shows on eligible Surface items. Because Xbox is excluded, there is no verification path of any kind that unlocks an Xbox discount, and shoppers on Microsoft's own Q&A boards who try are declined — exactly as the terms say.

The real savings on an Xbox console are channel and timing plays. The Exchange (AAFES/NEX) sells consoles tax-free, which is worth roughly the 6–10% sales tax you'd otherwise pay — the closest thing to a military price on an Xbox. Public holiday bundles at Best Buy, Amazon, Costco, and Walmart often deliver the best absolute prices, and certified refurbished consoles with warranty typically run 10–20% below new. None of these is military-gated except the Exchange itself.

For Game Pass, the one lever that touches Xbox spend is discounted Microsoft gift cards: buying cards below face value (Costco, Sam's Club, or resellers — vet resellers carefully) and redeeming them toward Game Pass effectively cuts roughly 5–15% off the subscription. New and returning subscribers can also catch Microsoft's intro pricing. Also note the Surface 10% is non-combinable even where it does apply — Microsoft gives you the better of the discount or the sale price, never both.
callaway-preowned-military-discount: The two storefronts are separate. The 15% military discount is verified through ID.me/TroopID at CallawayGolf.com checkout — the new-gear site — and CPO has no verification step because it has no military discount. Any site prompting you to “verify for a Callaway Pre-Owned military discount” is not offering a real CPO program.

Which path wins depends on what you’re buying. Open to certified used? CPO’s condition-graded pre-owned pricing (deep clearance can run up to ~45–49% off) typically beats 15% off a new club, and CPO’s Trade-In credit plus free shipping over $199 lower the net further. Must have a specific new club? Use the 15% military discount on CallawayGolf.com, mindful of the $1,000-per-year discount cap and that it can’t be combined with other codes.

Ignore “Callaway Pre-Owned military discount 40% off” aggregator pages — there is no verified CPO military discount. That “40%” conflates ID.me cash-back marketing with CPO’s public clearance. The only verified Callaway military discount is 15% on CallawayGolf.com (new gear), ID.me-verified, with a $1,000/year cap.
grunt-style-military-discount: Grunt Style’s discount is verified through GovX ID, a third-party service for military, veteran, and first-responder status. You verify your eligibility once; if you already have a GovX ID account you just log in. On success, GovX issues a single-use code to paste at checkout. Note the migration: Grunt Style previously used ID.me, and that page now redirects to the GovX page, so GovX is the current provider. ID.me still lists Grunt Style on its separate shopping marketplace, which is not the same as the brand’s current discount program.

The eligible groups are listed verbatim on the GovX page: U.S. Military (active duty and veterans), military families (spouses and dependents), and first responders (Fire, Law Enforcement, EMS, and healthcare workers/nurses). Retired, reserve, and National Guard members fall under "U.S. Military," so confirm your specific status in GovX at verification. There is no dedicated teacher, student, or general government tier on the brand’s GovX page.

The verified official discount is 10% — full stop. Coupon aggregators advertise "up to 25%," "40%," even "50% military discount," but those figures conflate the 10% GovX code with unrelated public promo codes and the Rewards store-credit tiers. The single confirmed benefit on the brand’s own page is 10% via GovX.

Because Grunt Style discounts hard and often, the smart money is situational. On a full-price cart, use the 10% GovX code. When a sitewide sale, BOGO 50% event, or clearance is live, the public price usually beats 10% — and the single-use code likely won’t stack anyway (checkout takes one code field). Layer the free Grunt Style Rewards program for 5% back in store credit (redeem within 90 days), and route a plain no-code sale order through a cashback portal for a few extra percent. Grunt Style controls the terms and can change them at any time, so confirm the current offer before you buy.
priceline-military-discount: The honest starting point is that priceline.com has no on-site military rate and no military verification — the question is which channel wins, not how to layer a military code. Coupon pages that advertise a "Priceline military discount up to 60%" are misattributing a figure that actually comes from American Forces Travel or from Priceline’s ordinary Express Deals; the "10–25% military" number is invented.

American Forces Travel is the deepest genuine military value. The DoD created it and manages eligibility through MWR; Priceline powers the booking platform and negotiates the exclusive military rates. Since July 16, 2021 eligibility expanded to include all veterans with an honorable or general-under-honorable-conditions discharge, bringing the eligible population to roughly 22 million, and the MILITARY STAR card was added as a payment option. First-time users verify through a DoD record check — last name, last 4 of SSN, and date of birth — not ID.me or SheerID; Priceline does not retain the data.

Because AFT is a separate, closed DoD site, you cannot add a Priceline coupon, VIP tier perk, or (typically) a cashback portal on top — its price is its price, and the MILITARY STAR card is a payment perk, not a discount stack. Note too that Priceline’s Best Price Guarantee explicitly excludes military, student, group, coupon, and loyalty fares from price matching, so an AFT or military-rate booking cannot be BPG-matched.

For everyone, or as a comparison, sign into the free Priceline VIP program before pricing a hotel or car — it unlocks member rates and Express Deal coupons of 5–10% by tier. Express Deals offer the deepest public rates but are opaque and usually non-refundable, so weigh them against booking the hotel’s own government/military/per-diem rate direct, which stays refundable and earns loyalty points and elite nights. Renting a car and hold a paid WeSalute+ membership? WeSalute runs a separate private Priceline car engine (up to 40% off). And it’s worth cross-shopping other OTAs and the hotel’s own site before committing.
dairy-queen-military-discount: There is no digital verification for any DQ military discount. Any discount is applied at the counter at the cashier or manager’s discretion when you show a physical military or veteran ID. DQ Rewards is a separate free loyalty account (the Dairy Queen app) and is not a military-verification program.

The everyday reality is franchise-by-franchise. One Georgia location publicly states "every single veteran receives 10% off any item that hasn’t already been marked down"; a Hampton Roads operator advertises 50% off first responders in uniform every day; another location reportedly runs "Veterans Eat Free every third Tuesday of the month." These are real but single-location signals — prompts to ask your own store, never chain policy.

Ignore the aggregator noise. The widely-scraped "military10 — 10% off with case-sensitive code military10 online" claim is the discount for DQ Events, an unrelated race-timing/triathlon company at dqevents.com, and has nothing to do with the ice-cream chain. There is no official Dairy Queen online military promo code, and DQ runs no GovX, exchange (AAFES/NEX), or cashback channel.
zara-military-discount: Zara is a classic “no military route” brand: neither Zara’s site nor any verification partner lists a military, veteran, or first-responder offer, and the GovX marketplace shows only third-party reseller listings of Zara-labeled items — not an official Zara military storefront.

The one verification Zara honors is student status via Student Beans. That makes the real max-savings play about timing and channel: shop the year-round Special Prices section, catch the twice-yearly seasonal sales, and add a Student Beans code if you qualify.

The military exchanges (AAFES/NEX/MCX) don’t stock Zara, so there’s no tax-free path, and Zara isn’t an ExpertVoice pro-deal brand — the aggregator claims of a flat “25% military” discount or a working “FHLO” code are fabricated.
kendra-scott-military-discount: Kendra Scott’s military discount is a first-party brand offer, not a limited event. It applies year-round; the brand simply promotes it harder around Veterans Day. Online, the discount is verified by ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers — you verify once, then choose "Verify with ID.me" at checkout to receive and apply a coupon code. In store, no ID.me account is needed: an associate checks a valid photo ID and applies the 15%. The discount is non-transferable, and Kendra Scott can cancel accounts for misuse.

In practice the 15% is a fashion-jewelry discount. Fine jewelry, sterling silver, vermeil pieces, watches, fragrance, apparel, accessories, and rotating brand collaborations are excluded, and the discount cannot be combined with any other offer, promo code, or Kendra Gives Back charity event — it is one code per order.

Because Kendra Scott behaves like a promo- and loyalty-driven fashion brand, the 15% is frequently not the cheapest single purchase. The new-subscriber 15% email code matches it with no verification; the "Share the Love" 20% referral for new customers beats it once; and Kendra Scott Insiders get 50% off one fashion-jewelry item during their birthday month. Public sales and Black Friday markdowns can also run deeper than 15%. None of these are military benefits and none stack with the ID.me discount, so compare and pick the single biggest offer for each order. For repeat buying, the standing 15% ID.me discount is the reliable everyday path because it works both online and in store and covers the widest eligible selection.

Two clarifications worth knowing: ID.me’s auto-generated aggregator subpage has at times claimed Kendra Scott offers no military discount — that is stale and wrong, since Kendra Scott’s own ID.me page names Military as an eligible group at 15%. And a separate GOVX marketplace storefront ("Kendra Scott — Military & Gov’t") exists, but that is a different retailer with its own pricing and selection; the brand’s own discount is the ID.me 15%.
target-military-discount: Many aggregator pages frame Target’s military benefit as a standing "10% off." That is misleading. The discount is only live during Target’s twice-yearly Military Appreciation windows, and the amount has varied — historically about 10%, but 20% for the June 21–July 4, 2026 window per Target’s own June 2, 2026 announcement. Treat the rate as set per campaign, and always check the live offer.

Target verifies military eligibility through SheerID. You submit a one-time verification form — name, branch, current affiliation, and discharge date if applicable — plus an accepted government document through your Target Circle account in the Target app or on Target.com. Once SheerID approves you, your status is stored to your Circle account and the Military Appreciation discount auto-loads as a Circle Bonus whenever a live campaign is running. If verification fails (often a name mismatch or typo), correct your details to match your documents exactly and resubmit.

The discount appears as a Target Circle Bonus in the verified member’s account when a campaign is live; allow up to 1 hour after successful verification for it to appear. Because verification is stored to your Circle account, you generally verify once and the offer reloads in future campaigns, though Target or SheerID may ask you to re-confirm. The summer 2026 offer is framed as one qualifying storewide purchase; confirm per-event limits in your account.
hogworkz-military-discount: Verification never happens at HogWorkz because there is nothing to verify — no military program and no third-party verifier integration was found. A HogWorkz Facebook group post literally titled "Does HOGWORKZ offer a military/veteran discount?" exists with no authoritative company answer, which shows the question is open, not that a program exists.

The uniform "contact us for a code" phrasing across coupon sites is the classic pattern of an aggregator-invented offer. Treat any specific percentage or code as unverified until HogWorkz publishes an official offer.
For actual savings, sign up for the newsletter before a first order, buy during a seasonal sale, and bundle purchases during a sale to justify shipping on heavy parts like saddlebags and tour packs.
ariat-military-discount: Verification is handled by SheerID through your free Ariat Insider account. You select "Military Discount 10% — Get Verified" on your account page and complete the SheerID flow. Many applicants are verified instantly; if not, Ariat says it will email your eligibility status, typically in under 20 minutes (though it notes verification "may take a few hours"). In some cases additional documentation is required. Ariat states it uses your information only to confirm eligibility, does not sell it, and that SheerID does not store uploaded documents. Ariat’s official source does not state how often re-verification is required, so don’t assume it is one-time.

The most important practical caveat is that the 10% cannot stack with sales, clearance, or coupon codes. Ariat runs frequent site-wide sales and a large Sale section, so a sale price may beat 10% off full price — check both before buying. The discount also can’t be used on gift cards and is US-only (APO/FPO shipping, but no territories or international).

Two eligibility notes worth repeating: National Guard isn’t named separately (Reserve is), and spouse/dependent eligibility isn’t officially confirmed despite "for you and your family" marketing — SheerID verifies the member’s own status. If you also qualify as a first responder, Ariat runs a parallel 10% First Responders Discount. To save more overall, Ariat Insider itself adds free shipping and free returns, and Ariat’s Reboot Resale program (reboot.ariat.com) sells discounted pre-owned gear.
annie-selke-military-discount: The math below uses one baseline: a $400 area rug, a realistic single-item Annie Selke / Dash & Albert order. Prices exclude tax; no tax-free channel competes here, so tax is neutral across the paths.

Annie Selke’s archetype is a home-decor brand with no military discount but deep public sales. The reliable saving is the brand’s own clearance: the “Shop by Discount” 30% / 70% / Last Chance Clearance sections routinely reach up to 70% off, which for most shoppers beats any percentage-off code by a wide margin.

The stacking reality is simple: codes generally do not apply to Sale / Last Chance / clearance items — Annie Selke maintains a Promotion Exclusions page precisely because markdowns and select items are carved out. So treat a deep sale and a promo code as mutually exclusive, not additive. A cashback portal (Annie Selke lists on United MileagePlus Shopping, and likely others) can layer on a brand-site purchase, but a non-portal coupon code commonly voids cashback — a plain sale order is the portal-safe move.

If you’re a verified design professional, the Trade Program (tiered ~20–58% off MSRP) is the only large credentialed discount — but it’s a wholesale/designer account, gated by business credentials, and has nothing to do with military service.
red-robin-military-discount: The one brand-confirmed military benefit is the Veterans Day free burger. Red Robin’s own 2025 terms say the offer is valid exclusively on Tuesday, November 11, 2025, dine-in only, with proof of service required (a valid military ID), for veterans and active-duty. It’s a single Red’s Big Tavern Burger with a bottomless side, with no modifications or alternative Tavern Burger styles, and it is explicitly not valid with other offers, including Red Robin Royalty rewards. The burger name has shifted over the years — a Red’s Tavern Double (two patties) in 2021–2022, and the single Red’s Big Tavern Burger from about 2023 on.

The July 15% figure is real in the sense that reputable military-editorial sites (Military.com, MyMilitaryBenefits) report it consistently as an in-store discount for Red Robin Royalty members during July — but it is not published on Red Robin’s own site or newsroom, so we present it as editorial-reported, not brand-official. Coupon aggregators separately advertise generic public promo codes near the word "military"; those are ordinary coupons, not a military discount.

For everyday value, the free Red Robin Royalty program is the real play: 1 point per $1 (roughly 10% back as rewards, since 100 points = a $10 reward on $100 spent), a free welcome appetizer, a birthday treat, and member-only deals. There is no everyday military rate, so the loyalty program plus current public app or email deals is how service members and civilians alike save the rest of the year.
ihop-military-discount: There is no online verification provider — no ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute for IHOP. Verification for the Veterans Day meal happens in person: you show proof of military service to restaurant staff. IHOP’s promotion has historically listed acceptable proof as a U.S. Uniformed Services ID card, a Retired ID card, a current Leave and Earnings Statement (LES), a veterans organization card (American Legion, VFW), a photo of yourself in uniform, a DD-214, military dog tags, or a citation/commendation. Acceptable proof can vary by year and location, so confirm with your restaurant.

Be skeptical of any "IHOP everyday 10–20% military discount" you see on coupon sites — no IHOP primary source confirms it, and IHOP’s own FAQ says special offers are available "on a per-restaurant basis," which means a standing discount depends entirely on the franchise. If your local IHOP does offer one, it sets the amount and terms, so ask before you order and show your military ID.

The everyday ways to save are open to everyone: join IHOP Rewards (the International Bank of Pancakes) for member offers and a sign-up bonus, sign up for the MyHOP eClub for local offers, watch for coupons (often in Sunday newspaper inserts), and check the value menu and specials. Many restaurant chains run their own Veterans Day free-meal promotions worth comparing around November 11.
kia-military-discount: Kia does not use ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute for this program. Verification is in-person and document-based at the dealer: you present a current Earning Statement (LES), honorable discharge papers (DD-214), a bank statement showing Armed Forces pension or disability earnings, or an official future-pension document. A military ID card alone is explicitly not sufficient, and spouses must additionally provide a marriage certificate. Because it’s per-transaction at the dealer, the two-specialty-per-year cap limits repeat use.

The dollar amount and the excluded-vehicle list reset roughly monthly — Kia runs the incentive in rolling program windows (for example, a July 2026 window ran 7/7–7/31/2026). That’s why no honest page can promise you an exact figure: it’s currently $500, was $400 in some periods, and certain models have been carved out in past windows. Aggregator pages that imply a fixed lifetime “Kia military discount” oversimplify a program that changes every period.

The real savings come from stacking. Kia states the Military Bonus “may be combined with KMF Special Low APR or KMA Cash Back offers, if eligible,” so it is additive to your model’s current national incentive rather than a substitute. A recent college grad who is also military may be able to add the separate College Grad/Student incentive (~$400), and current Kia owners or owners of a qualifying competitor vehicle may add an Owner Loyalty or Competitive/Conquest bonus — all subject to the two-specialty-per-year cap. There is no GovX new-car channel, no AAFES/NEX exchange path, and no cashback portal for a new-vehicle purchase, so those routes are ruled out.
road-runner-sports-military-discount: Verification runs through ID.me. Online, you create a free ID.me account, verify your military or first-responder status once, and get a code; in store, an associate checks your military ID. Because Road Runner Sports doesn’t publish a detailed standalone terms page, the exact percentage and eligible groups are confirmed via the ID.me listing and editorial reporting rather than a brand terms page — so confirm the current amount at checkout.

The reason the military discount usually loses is structural: it’s full-price only and non-combinable, so it can’t touch marked-down items or stack with a code. VIP’s 10%, by contrast, applies on top of sale prices and earns Rewards Cash rebates — which is why regular buyers come out ahead with VIP even after the membership fee. During a deep public sale (30–60% off), the public price simply beats a 10% that can’t apply to sale items anyway.

Ignore coupon-aggregator pages advertising a "Road Runner Sports 50% off military/first responder" code — those figures are fabricated. The verified military figure is about 10%, full-price only. Treat the ID.me cash-back offer (reported up to ~3%) as a moving rate to re-check, and don’t assume it stacks on an ID.me-gated or coupon order.
helly-hansen-military-discount: The verified everyday offer is 20% off, confirmed on SheerID’s own Helly Hansen offer page (last modified May 22, 2026) and echoed in Helly Hansen’s military landing-page metadata. Verification is instant through SheerID; the discount applies online only, to personal purchases.

Separately, Helly Hansen runs an application-based "Pro/Member" military program. Approval requires uploading accepted documentation (LES, DD214, VHIC/VIC, VA disability letter, etc. — never a photo of a military ID) and typically takes about 48 business hours. Helly Hansen does not publish a fixed discount for this tier: its own FAQ says the rate "varies between individuals and professional groups" and only appears once you’re signed in to My Account. Approved members get a one-year membership, reviewed annually, that can be revoked or changed at Helly Hansen’s discretion.

Debunking the "35% off" claim: several coupon and directory sites (and a VA-focused roundup) advertise Helly Hansen military discounts of up to 35%. No primary Helly Hansen or SheerID source confirms that number. The verified figure is 20% via SheerID; the application membership’s unpublished, variable discount is the likely source of the confusion. Treat 35% as an unverified claim, not a fact.

A separate reported healthcare discount (aggregators cite 25%) could not be confirmed on a reachable Helly Hansen primary page as of this review, so it is not asserted here as fact — treat it as reported and unconfirmed until Helly Hansen publishes it directly.
amex-gold-military: The Gold-specific math is unusually good. The card’s annual fee is $325 — raised from $250 effective July 25, 2024 for new applicants and at renewals on or after October 1, 2024 for existing cardholders — yet an MLA-covered servicemember or military spouse holds it for $0 while keeping everything: up to $424 a year in statement credits ($120 Uber Cash at $10/month, $120 in dining credits at $10/month at partners like Grubhub and Five Guys, $100 in Resy credits split $50 per half-year, and $84 in Dunkin’ credits at $7/month), plus the earn engine — 4x points at restaurants worldwide (up to $50,000 per calendar year), 4x at U.S. supermarkets (up to $25,000 per calendar year), 3x on flights booked direct or through Amex Travel, and 5x on prepaid hotels via AmexTravel.com, added in the April 2026 refresh. Every credit is "up to," every credit requires enrollment, and monthly amounts don’t roll over — the fee is waived, but the credits still take management to collect.

Which law applies comes down to one variable: the account-open date. Open the Gold while you’re a covered borrower — active duty, Guard/Reserve on orders over 30 days, or a DEERS-listed spouse or dependent — and the MLA zeroes the fee automatically; there is no military application form, no ID.me or SheerID step, and nothing to enroll in for the waiver itself. Held the card before you activated? File an SCRA request (online is fastest, or 1-866-391-1460) with your orders, a DD-214, or a commanding-officer letter; Amex counts annual, late, and returned-payment fees as "interest" under its 6% SCRA cap, advises your status within about two billing cycles, and servicemembers have reported meaningful refunds of previously paid fees on long-held accounts — amounts depend entirely on account history. The claim window closes 180 days after leaving active duty.

Two more things shape the smart play. First, the community’s favorite Gold angle — commissaries earning 4x as "U.S. supermarkets" — is real as a pattern of member-reported datapoints, including many overseas locations in Japan, Korea, Germany, and Spain, but it is not an Amex-published rule and it varies by base: Incirlik and Aviano, for example, have been reported not to code as U.S. supermarkets for Amex. Treat 4x at the commissary as a bonus when it happens, never a promise. Second, MLA coverage is per person, per personal card — military-finance communities widely report couples each holding their own fee-waived Gold, and one covered member holding Gold and Platinum together at $0 apiece (versus $325 + $895 list). The card also charges no foreign transaction fees, which makes it a solid companion on OCONUS orders, PCS moves, and deployments. Coverage ends with your covered-borrower status per DoD records, so plan for the full $325 at the renewal after you leave service.
factor-military-discount: Factor verifies eligibility through ID.me or GovX — you pick one provider, verify your status, and the discount applies automatically at checkout for new or reactivated accounts. The offer is structured in two phases: 55% off the first box plus free shipping, then 15% off each of the next 51 boxes, all within a 380-day window from purchase.

One thing to correct: some sources, including a Military.com discount listing, still quote an older "50% off first box + 10% off next 12 boxes" figure. That figure is out of date. Factor’s own Hero Discounts page states 55% off the first box plus free shipping, then 15% off the next 51 boxes — use the 55/15/51 figures, not 50/10.

Watch the cliff: the entire Hero offer expires 380 days after purchase, and then pricing reverts to standard rates. The discount also does not stack with gift cards or any other promotion, including Factor’s own public first-box welcome codes — it’s an either/or choice, not an add-on.
If you’re not verified, or only want to try one box, Factor’s public "50% off first box + free shipping" welcome code (open to everyone) is the fallback to compare against the Hero discount.
southwest-military-discount: The clearest, verifiable value is the active-duty baggage-fee exemption. Southwest changed its general checked-bag policy in 2025 — free bags are no longer universal for all customers — which makes the active-duty exemption a meaningful, distinct benefit. Active-duty members pay no fee for additional, excess, oversize, or overweight bags, provided no piece exceeds 100 lb or 80 linear inches, up to 20 pieces per flight, with a valid Uniformed Services ID at check-in. Dependents traveling without the active-duty member pay normal fees.

The Military fare itself is unpublished. Southwest lists no percentage or dollar amount, and the fare is not bookable on Southwest.com or with Rapid Rewards points — you call 1-800-435-9792 or use a ticket counter. Because it is unpublished, the smart move is to call for a quote and compare it against the best published Southwest fare and any current sale before booking. Any "10%" or "10–25%" figure you see on coupon sites is not confirmed by Southwest.

Verification is manual — there is no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute on Southwest’s military page. Eligibility is established when you book by phone or at a ticket counter, and a valid Uniformed Services ID is presented at check-in. Because there is no online account flow, there is no "verify once" convenience — each trip requires the ID. Separately, federal/state Government fares exist through agency channels or the Government Reservation Desk (1-888-871-8167), and Southwest refunds a customer and traveling companions when military or government orders conflict with a non-refundable trip.
delta-military-discount: The real, quantifiable value here is the free bag allowance, not a fare percentage. With Delta charging $45 for a first checked bag and $55 for a second (domestic, no card or status), an active-duty member checking two bags on leisure travel saves roughly $100 each way versus a civilian — often more than a small fare discount would deliver.

On military orders, Delta gives more free bags than civilians and a larger size limit (up to 80 linear inches). The exact on-orders count and per-bag weight — widely cited as 5 bags at 100 lb — did not render on the official table we fetched, so confirm those numbers at the ticket counter. For personal/leisure travel the published allowance is 2 free bags in Delta Main/Comfort, 3 in Delta Premium Select, and 3 in Delta First/Delta One, up to 62 linear inches.

Verification is in person, not online. Delta does not route military verification through ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute on its own pages — you confirm eligibility with your military ID (plus a copy of your orders when on orders) at the ticket counter. Because fares are unpublished, a Delta agent confirms fare eligibility when you book by phone or message.

Two things to watch. First, the “10%” and “20%” fare figures on coupon sites are not on delta.com — the “20%” actually belongs to an unrelated “Delta Extrax” brand. Second, free Sky Club access in uniform and a “Military & Government Desk” phone number are not stated on Delta’s own pages; do not rely on them until Delta confirms.
lifelock-military-discount: The confusion comes from coupon and “promo code” sites advertising a specific “LifeLock military discount” of 15/25/30% plus stackable “extra % off” codes. Those are largely conflated with the public first-year promo (available to everyone) or are affiliate-coupon inventions. There is no verified standalone everyday LifeLock military percentage — the one legitimate military-gated channel is GovX, and even its exact discount needs live verification.

The gated channel uses GovX ID, a one-time military/government status check tied to your GovX account, and covers active duty, retirees, veterans, Guard/Reserve, government employees, first responders, and dependents. The public promo requires no verification. Because subscription discounts don’t stack, GovX pricing and a public promo are mutually exclusive — compare the same tier across both.

The decisive long-run variable is the renewal rate, which is higher for every path. The public first-year promo (and often the GovX price) applies to year 1 only; year 2 renews at full price. So the honest plan is to buy the lower year-1 price, then re-shop both channels — or switch tiers or providers — at renewal, when the real cost lands.
j-crew-military-discount: J.Crew’s discount is verified through SheerID — not ID.me and not GovX. You verify once for your group (military, medical, first responder, student, or teacher); once approved, the discount is tied to your free J.Crew Passport account and appears in your wallet roughly a day later. Re-verification may be required periodically under SheerID/J.Crew terms, and if verification fails you can use SheerID’s document-upload fallback or contact J.Crew support.

Because J.Crew allows only one promo code per order, the verified 15% competes with — it does not combine with — a sitewide public sale code. The smart move is to take the larger single discount: during a 40%+ public event (Memorial Day, July 4th, Black Friday, end-of-season) the sale typically wins, while with no meaningful sale live the verified 15% is your best route. J.Crew Passport (free) layers free shipping and rewards on top of whichever path you choose.

Coupon sites circulate "J.Crew military codes" and sometimes a flat 20% military figure. The verified durable brand rate is 15% via SheerID, and there is no manual code to paste — the discount is bound to your verified J.Crew Passport account. A 20% figure is a periodic, limited-time first-responder/healthcare promo, not a standing military rate, so confirm the on-site banner before relying on it.

J.Crew is not carried at AAFES/Navy Exchange, on the GovX marketplace, or on ExpertVoice, so those military channels do not apply here — J.Crew routes all eligibility to its own SheerID flow. Students and teachers who do not qualify on the military or first-responder side have their own identical 15% SheerID program.
fox-one-military-discount: FOX One and Fox Nation are different subscriptions, and the confusion drives most "fox one military discount" searches. FOX One (launched August 2025) is the live news and sports app — FOX News, FOX Business, FOX Weather, FOX Sports, FS1/FS2, and FOX local and network — at $19.99/month or $199.99/year. Fox Nation is the older opinion/documentary/entertainment app. Only Fox Nation runs a military offer: a free first year, then 50% off annual renewals, verified through SheerID. FOX One has no equivalent — no military percentage, no promo code, and no identity gate at checkout.

Because FOX One has no military discount, the cheapest routes are non-military and open to everyone. If you already pay for cable, satellite, or a live-TV service that carries FOX, you can authenticate and watch FOX One free — "pay TV subscribers receive access for free." That is the single best deal when it applies.

Verizon customers have a strong second option: the FOX One perk, added in My Verizon, gives 3 months free on new 5G Home Internet, a $10/month credit when bundling mobile plus home internet, or $15/month on a single eligible plan. If neither pay-TV auth nor Verizon applies, the $199.99 annual plan is the only real direct discount — about $16.67/month, saving roughly $40 a year versus monthly. These paths are either/or: a Verizon perk or a fox.com plan, an authentication or a paid sub — they do not stack, and the public "buy 1 month, get 1 free" promo (ends 7/19/2026) is "not combinable with other offers."

If it is genuinely Fox Nation you want, claim the military/veteran free first year at foxnation.com/military (or the separate first-responder path at foxnation.com/first-responders) through SheerID — but know it unlocks Fox Nation, not FOX One’s live news and sports. FOX One itself verifies no military status because it has no military offer to verify.
ihg-military-discount: The number one mistake is conflating IHG’s two first-party programs. The Military Leisure Rate is the one veterans can use for a vacation — a minimum of 5% off Best Flexible Rate, open to US and Canadian active duty, veterans, retired military, and family members, verified with a military or veteran ID at check-in. The Government Rate is an official-travel rate for government employees, military on orders, and defense/CRC contractors that requires official ID or work orders; some hotels align it toward the GSA per-diem cap, though IHG’s own page describes it as a percentage off Best Flex.

Both are rates, not stackable coupons. IHG’s terms state the Military Leisure Rate "cannot be used in conjunction with any other offer, discount or promotion" — including promo codes and reward (points) nights — and the Government Rate is "not applicable with other discounted-rate promotions" or group bookings. What does still apply is loyalty: IHG One Rewards points accrue on qualifying military/government cash rates and elite benefits still apply. That’s the classic hotel-loyalty pattern — status layers on, but the rates themselves are mutually exclusive.

Because the military minimum is only ~5%, the honest best-value play is to compare rates for your exact dates. IHG’s member advance-purchase (non-refundable) rate routinely runs 10-20% under Best Flex and often beats the military rate outright — while public flash/"Cyber" member sales can beat it too. If your dates might change, the refundable Military Leisure Rate is the safer pick; if they’re locked, price the member advance rate and book the lower one. Coupon aggregators present the military benefit as a stackable sitewide code — it is not; it’s a rate you book by selecting the Government/Military option.

If you have US Army base access, IHG Army Hotels — on-base lodging (Candlewood Suites, Staybridge Suites, Holiday Inn Express) at roughly 39 installations — is usually the cheapest option of all, but it’s a separate program requiring base access and military ID, and the public leisure rate does not apply there. IHG and its individual hotels control these rates and can change them at any time, so confirm the current terms and the exact percentage for your stay before booking.
expedia-military-discount: Verification is handled by ID.me. You create or sign in to an ID.me account, prove your eligible status (military, veteran, first responder, nurse, medical, government, teacher, or student), and ID.me issues a coupon code for use on Expedia.com. Account creation with ID.me is required, and the transaction should go through the ID.me link for the code to be valid. Re-verification frequency, document requirements, and the support path are governed by ID.me’s standard process and are not stated on Expedia’s offer pages — direct verification issues to ID.me’s help center, and do not assume one-time verification is permanent.

Two honest caveats. First, value: Expedia’s marketing pages say "10% off select hotels," but the only terms page we found states 8% — so we present the discount as "up to 10%" and urge you to confirm the live number in the ID.me flow. Second, validity: that terms page carried a redemption window that ended December 31, 2025 (travel through March 31, 2026), and we could not locate a current 2026 replacement terms page, even though the marketing pages still promote the offer. Expedia’s "Limited Time Military Travel Deals" page separately states there are no military-only package deals currently available, so the ID.me hotel coupon is the active offer.

To stretch the value further, join One Key (free) for Member Prices on select hotels and OneKeyCash, and note Expedia advertises "up to 20% on select hotels" when you book in the app — though the ID.me coupon is not combinable with other offers, so these generally won’t stack. For comparison, Hotels.com and Booking.com, plus hotel chains’ own military rates (Marriott, Hilton, Choice), are worth checking against the Expedia coupon.
dixxon-military-discount: VerifyPass confirms your military/veteran or first-responder/government status and issues a unique, single-use code — it’s not a permanent account discount, so you reverify each time you want a new code (reportedly limited to about one per 24-hour window). Eligibility is tied to the verifying individual; spouses and dependents are not confirmed on the offer page.

One accuracy caveat: the brand’s public VerifyPass tile states only that you "receive a discount" without printing the number, so treat the rate as the consistently reported ~10% and confirm the exact figure shown after a live verification. Coupon aggregators dangling "up to 25%" or "50% OFF Dixxon" codes are not the verified program.

The practical decision is the ~10% code versus whatever public sale is live, because the code applies to full-price items only and won’t combine with drop or sale pricing. On a $79.95 flannel the ~10% code lands around $71.96, but Dixxon’s frequent drops and Black Friday sales often beat that — so take whichever single discount is larger, and layer a cashback card or portal on top of the final price. If you specifically want the collab pieces, the DIXXON x James flannel is sold separately on GovX.
adt-military-discount: Eligibility is confirmed through WeSalute (a paid membership/verification service, formerly Veterans Advantage) or GOVX (a free military/first-responder verification marketplace). You create an account, verify your service, then redeem the ADT dealer offer. The redemption is completed by calling the dealer’s toll-free number in the WeSalute/GOVX steps — not by checking out on ADT.com, which forfeits the offer terms.

Be careful with the headline numbers. The "$914.90" figure is a best-case marketing aggregate, not a guaranteed quote — the concrete, consistent wins are the $99 install and the free starter equipment kit (roughly $125 of door sensors, a motion detector, keypad, battery backup, keychain remote, and a window decal). The "$100 Visa reward gift card" is also a standard public promo on systems of $349+, so it is not a unique military perk and you get it once, not twice.

The offer is either/or: it cannot be combined with other ADT offers or promotions. If you want cameras or a smaller/DIY setup, ADT’s public deals — such as two Google Nest Cams with $250 off (on $349+ systems, 36-month plan), or 40% off ADT Blu DIY kits — can out-value the free sensor kit. If you’re age 50+, ask the dealer whether the AARP 5% monitoring discount (recurring) beats a one-time setup break, though its combinability with a dealer new-customer offer is not verified.

If you’re a renter, don’t want a multi-year contract, or mainly want cameras, this offer may not be your best route — many DIY home-security brands offer their own military discount with no long contract. There is no AAFES/NEX exchange path and no ExpertVoice/pro-deal channel for a monitored home-security subscription, so those routes are ruled out.
geissele-military-discount: Geissele runs verification itself — there is no third-party identity provider. Active-duty military and law enforcement can self-verify simply by registering with an official .mil or department email; otherwise (and for veterans and first responders) you upload an allowable ID card or document — veterans specifically can use a DD-214. A human reviews it within 1–2 business days, then attaches the group discount to your account so eligible-product prices drop automatically at login. Because it’s account-based rather than a code, you don’t re-verify per order.

The non-stacking rule is the make-or-break detail. Per Geissele’s FAQ, an account carrying a Veteran/Military/LEO/First-Responder group discount “will be unable to use any additional discount codes at checkout, as discounts do not stack.” And Geissele states that during sale events “the prices displayed already reflect the best available discount and no additional promotional codes or group discounts will be applicable” — so during a sale, verified and non-verified buyers pay the same price.

Because nothing stacks, the correct move is always to buy whichever is cheaper: compare the current sale/retailer price to (MSRP − 10%). Geissele parts often sell below MSRP everyday at major retailers, and the deep cuts cluster around Black Friday/Cyber Monday. Ignore aggregator “Geissele 30–35% off” coupon codes — those are fabricated, and the group discount blocks checkout codes anyway.
wrangler-military-discount: Wrangler uses ID.me as its verification provider. You verify once with your ID.me account — military status confirmed via a .mil email or an uploaded service document — and the 10% applies to your wrangler.com order. ID.me may periodically require re-verification per its own policies; support for verification issues goes through ID.me’s Help Center, not Wrangler.

The military tier sits alongside parallel ID.me communities for first responders, nurses, medical providers, and hospital employees, each at the same 10%. Widely repeated claims of a "25% off" Wrangler military discount are unverified and appear to be an aggregator or AI-summary error — every primary source we could read states 10%.

Because the 10% is not confirmed to combine with promo codes or sale prices, the smartest play is often to skip it: buy on a public sale (frequently 30–50% off), grab core basics like Cowboy Cut, Authentics, and Rugged Wear at Walmart or Amazon, or buy tax-free at the AAFES/NEX exchange if you have access. Reserve the 10% for current full-price styles you cannot find cheaper.
rock-auto-military-discount: RockAuto’s whole pricing model explains why no discount program exists. Its stated philosophy: "We think it makes more sense to set part prices low and allow you to see the actual cost of the shipping decisions that you make." Shipping is never free — it’s charged at real cost per warehouse — so a cart pulling parts from three warehouses pays three shipping charges, which can add $20–$40+ and erase RockAuto’s price advantage over a 10%-off local store. The single biggest RockAuto "discount" is building your cart from one warehouse.

The only official price cuts are on the Current Promotions & Rebates page: rotating manufacturer instant-savings promos (typically 10% on specific brands — recent examples include Bosch spark plugs, Nissens A/C, Power Stop brake kits, and WJB hubs/bearings, with expirations July 15–31, 2026) that apply automatically, plus Wholesaler Closeouts — clearance inventory you surface with the "Show Closeouts Only" filter, often the cheapest per-part price anywhere. Neither requires a code or any identity verification.

About those codes: RockAuto’s help page confirms discount codes go in the "How did you hear about us" box at checkout, one code per order, "without any other numbers or characters" — and the codes are targeted, not public. Shoppers on forums like BobIsTheOilGuy and Grassroots Motorsports report a single-use ~5% code emailed to past customers months after an order (with several 2024–2026 threads saying the codes arrive less often than they used to), and club-sponsorship codes distributed through car-club newsletters. RockAuto publishes nothing about either program — treat both as YMMV, never as a plan. There’s no cashback layer either: Rakuten listed no active RockAuto rate as of July 14, 2026, and no GovX storefront exists.

The honest military math is a two-way comparison. If you can wait 2–7 days for shipping and your cart ships from one warehouse, RockAuto’s base price (plus any auto-applied promo or closeout) usually wins outright — no discount needed. If you need the part today, or it’s heavy and ships expensive, take the real 10% military discount at the counter: O’Reilly gives 10% off most retail-priced items in-store to active duty, reserve, retired, veterans, and eligible family with ID at each visit (excludes oil, antifreeze, sale items, special orders, and online), and Advance Auto Parts gives 10% off regular-price items in-store to verified military and veterans (excludes online orders, sale items, and gift cards). Then compare that discounted total against RockAuto’s delivered price — heavy parts like rotors and batteries swing toward local.
dollar-car-rental-military-discount: The VetRewards lane uses Veterans Advantage, a paid membership program, to issue a CDP code you enter in Dollar’s booking flow for 5% off the pay-later base rate (taxes and fees excluded). It also carries perks like no fees for additional or underage drivers and travel/accident insurance, per the program’s terms — so for frequent renters the 5% plus perks can justify the membership fee, while an occasional renter may not recoup it.

The online military rate uses ID.me/SheerID — a free, one-time status check tied to your account — and surfaces on ID.me Shop as “up to 25% off.” That “up to” matters: the real number varies by date and location and is frequently beaten by Dollar’s own prepaid “Pay Now” rate, so always price both. At the counter, a physical military or government ID is required, and official-travel rates require orders or a government card.

The honest optimization here is channel comparison, not a single percentage. Run the VetRewards/ID.me rate, a prepaid “Pay Now” rate, and your Costco/USAA/AAA rate side by side; decline the counter LDW/CDW if your credit card provides rental collision coverage; and check airport versus off-airport pickup, since off-airport can dodge airport concession fees.
burton-military-discount: Burton routes its discount through SheerID, an identity-verification service. You submit basic personal information and, if prompted, upload proof of service; SheerID confirms eligibility and issues a single-use code. There is no confirmed ID.me, GovX, or WeSalute path for Burton — SheerID is the named partner.

The military tier sits alongside parallel SheerID offers for first responders, healthcare workers, teachers, and students, each at 20% (healthcare "up to 20%"), with the same online-only, non-combinable terms. You use one offer, not several stacked.

Because the code is full-price-only and non-combinable, a live public sale of 20% or more beats it and won’t stack with it — so during a real Burton sale, buy the public price instead of using your code.
kennywood-military-discount: Kennywood’s military ticket is a fixed discounted price, not a loose percentage: $36.99 for single-day admission against a $74.99 gate price — a saving of about $38, or roughly 50%. Uniquely, that one ticket covers the service member plus up to four guests, which makes it the strongest group value for a qualifying family or party.

The online ticket is gated by an affiliation-verification step at purchase. Kennywood’s own page states only that "affiliation verification is required"; discount-tracker sites report the check runs through SheerID, but the provider name is not confirmed on Kennywood’s page, so treat it as reported rather than certain. The ticket page names "Active Duty and Retired Military," so veterans should confirm their status is accepted during that verification step.

On top of the everyday ticket, Kennywood runs free "Military Days" each summer — July 1–5, 2026 this year — for active, retired, veteran, and reservist military. Verification here is simply a valid military ID shown at the gate, with no online account needed, and the free-admission member can add up to four companion passes at $34.99 each. The exact July window shifts year to year, so re-verify the dates each spring before planning a visit.

The military ticket does not stack: no public promo code, coupon, or online sale layers on top of the $36.99 price, and the free Military Days admission is member-only and separate from the online ticket. Because Kennywood controls pricing, the Military Days window, and verification and can change them at any time, treat the numbers here as a starting point and confirm the current offer at kennywood.com/buy-tickets before you buy.
booking-com-military-discount: Coupon aggregators invent a "Booking.com military discount" you supposedly unlock by verifying through a phone line and redeeming at "participating retail locations." That is copied boilerplate: Booking.com is an online travel agency with no retail locations and no military verification line. ID.me, the verification service used by dozens of retailers, states plainly it is not aware of any Booking.com military discount. Treat any "Booking.com military promo code" as a generic public coupon, not a verified military rate.

The Genius program is the real everyday lever, and it is open to everyone. Level 1 gives 10% off participating stays instantly on account creation; Level 2 (after 5 bookings in 2 years) and Level 3 (after 15) reach 10-20% off and add perks like free breakfast, room upgrades, and priority support. The discount applies to the room price before taxes and fees, on "select" properties, and the Level 2/3 percentage is set by each property — many land at the low end, so verify the actual rate shown for your stay.

For anyone with a DoD ID, American Forces Travel is usually the deepest cut. It is the DoD’s official Morale, Welfare and Recreation leisure-travel site, operated by Priceline, and it advertises up to 50% off hotels (plus cars, flights, packages, and cruises). Eligibility is broad — active duty, Guard/Reserve, retirees, honorably or general-discharged veterans, disabled veterans, Purple Heart recipients, former POWs, dependents, caregivers, and DoD/Coast Guard civilians — and is verified through AAFES using the last four digits of your SSN and your date of birth. It is a closed channel: you cannot stack a Genius rate, a Booking.com promo code, or reliably a cashback portal on top.

The smart routing is simple: if you hold a DoD ID, price-check American Forces Travel first. If not (or for a quick one-off booking), create a free Genius account and route a plain booking through a cashback portal like Rakuten (4% on accommodations as of July 12, 2026). And whenever the hotel is a major brand, price-check its own direct military or government rate — it often beats the OTA and earns loyalty points. Booking.com controls the Genius terms and can change them at any time, so confirm the current offer before you book.
aquarium-of-the-pacific-military-discoun: The Aquarium’s own Discounts page lists exactly one military line: "Discounted tickets may be purchased in advance at any MWR/ITT office on base." It names no verification partner — no ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute — and there is no online military checkout. That is the standing everyday military route, and its price varies by base office (for example, LA AFB’s Force Support Squadron has run group trips at roughly $5 per person), so it is worth calling your local ITT before you buy anywhere else.

The standout offer is Veterans Day. Veterans and active military are admitted free on November 11 with a valid service ID, but you must make an advance online reservation — capacity is limited and there are no walk-ups. The free admission covers the ID holder, not automatically the whole family: guests pay general admission or can be bought discounted guest tickets at an MWR/ITT office. Re-check the terms about two weeks before Nov 11 each year, as capacity and rules change.

Be cautious of coupon and AI-snippet sites that repeat a flat "10%–25% military discount" and a "SheerID unique code at checkout." None of that appears on the Aquarium’s own pages — the figures are aggregator template copy, not Aquarium terms. An older "10% at the ticket window" line comes from MilitaryBridge, which itself flags "check to make sure this is still offered," so treat it as historical and unverified.

For companions without base access, the public routes usually beat full price on the family cart. General admission online is $49.95 adult (12–61), $34.95 child (3–11), $46.95 senior (62+), and free under 3 — and California charges no sales tax on admissions, so every path is directly comparable. AAA offers up to 10% any day and a limited-time up-to-30% off on Wednesdays booked online; authorized resellers (GreatWorkPerks, Tripster, Groupon) and Go City Los Angeles bundles often land below the gate price; and combo tickets with the LA Zoo or Queen Mary make sense if you will do both. A membership pays off at about two visits a year.
zales-military-discount: Zales uses ID.me to confirm military status — the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. You verify once through ID.me as active duty, Guard/Reserve, veteran, retiree, spouse, or eligible dependent, typically with a military ID, Veterans ID, or DD214. Zales notes that ID.me is a third-party site with its own privacy policy and terms. After you’re verified, you receive a one-time code to redeem online, or you can show your ID.me verification to redeem in-store.

Watch the fine print, because it decides the winner. The 10% is a single-use code that can’t be combined with Buy More Save More or any other offer, and it excludes clearance, all watches, pre-owned, custom, loose stones, and several designer lines. Zales runs frequent deep sales — up to 50% seasonal "Summer Steals" events, up to 60% off select clearance, and tiered "spend more save more" offers — and those are exactly where the 10% doesn’t apply or is beaten. Since the discount and the sale don’t stack, compare them and take whichever is bigger.

One correction to watch for: some coupon and aggregator sites frame the offer as "up to 10%," imply it stacks with sales, or quote a 4% Rakuten cash-back rate. As of July 6, 2026, the rate is a flat 10% (not "up to"), it is explicitly non-stackable, and live Rakuten shows 2% at zales.com, not 4%. No credible source shows Zales carrying its discount through GovX — the mechanic is ID.me.
shutterfly-military-discount: There is nothing to verify, because Shutterfly has no military program and no verification partner for one. ID.me works with Shutterfly only as a general cash-back/shopping layer for ID.me members, not a military discount — so if a site tells you to “verify military status for a Shutterfly discount,” it’s describing an offer that doesn’t exist. The medical, first-responder, teacher, government, and student ID.me pages for Shutterfly all show the same: ordinary member cash back, no profession discount.

The make-or-break fact for a shopper is Shutterfly’s stacking rule. Its terms state an offer “cannot be combined with other code-based %-off or $-off offers,” a code “can only be entered once,” and “free product offers cannot be combined with free shipping.” So there is no “military code + sale code” stack to chase; you pick the single best public code for your cart, and a free-book or free-print offer still means you pay shipping.

The real levers are the public sitewide code (30–50% off tiered by cart size), the app’s unlimited free 4x4/4x6 prints (best value at roughly 25+ prints per order), and the new-customer free-gift bundle (a free 8x8 hardcover photo book, pay only shipping). You can layer a small cashback portal such as Rakuten (~2% as of July 2026) under the code, but treat it as a bonus and verify it tracks — and time big orders to Black Friday/Cyber Monday, Shutterfly’s deepest public sales.
jersey-mikes-military-discount: There is no national verification partner — no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute program with Jersey Mike’s. At participating franchises, verification is simply a cashier checking your military ID or proof of service in person. For the Veterans Day free sub, you present an email-club code plus proof of service in store. Nothing is verified online, and no everyday discount carries between locations.

The real everyday winner is open to everyone: Shore Points. It’s free to join, you earn 6 points per Regular sub, 72 points earns a free Regular sub, and points never expire. Stack any live public app or email deal (rotating dollar-off and BOGO offers) on top of ordinary purchases, and over time that typically beats a small counter discount — which, remember, can’t be combined with other offers anyway.

On the baseline of a roughly $11 Regular sub: a participating franchise’s ~15% brings it to about $9.35; the Veterans Day promo makes a Regular sub free (about $11 saved) on Nov 11; and Shore Points quietly earns a free Regular sub about every twelve paid Regular subs. Take whichever total is lowest on any given visit.
ogio-military-discount: OGIO uses ID.me. You create or sign in to a free ID.me account and confirm your military (or nurse/first-responder/teacher) status once; ID.me handles the document and records check, and on future OGIO orders you sign in rather than re-verifying from scratch. Support runs through ID.me’s help center for verification problems and OGIO customer service (1-800-975-6358) for order questions. OGIO has been part of Topgolf Callaway Brands since 2017, and Callaway Golf also sells OGIO bags — worth a price comparison if you shop the golf line.

Know the fine print before you verify: the 15% carries a $1,000 annual discount cap per person (the discount amount, not your spend, is capped), excludes gift cards, and explicitly does not combine with other promo codes. That non-stacking rule is why the public 20% welcome code wins on a first order — you have to choose one, and 20% beats 15%. Cashback portals are also unreliable through an ID.me-gated checkout, so don’t count on layering Rakuten on top of the military discount; a plain code-free sale order is more likely to track.

A debunk worth knowing: aggregator pages claim OGIO gives "up to 10%–25%" to military "and their immediate families." Neither is confirmed by OGIO — its own page states a flat 15% and lists only active-duty, veteran, reserve, and retired. Coupon sites advertising "50% off" or "20% off" OGIO codes are generic clearance or newsletter offers, not a military rate. OGIO also runs OGIO and OGIO Powersports storefronts on GovX — a separate verified-military marketplace, not a stack on the OGIO.com discount.
chrysler-military-discount: Chrysler verifies eligibility through SheerID, a third-party verification service, using two separate entry points on the military-incentive page: one for active/retired military and one for disabled military. Either path issues an authorization number that you bring to the dealer.

The $500 is additive, not exclusive — Chrysler’s own FAQ states buyers "may also qualify for other offers," meaning the bonus cash layers on top of national incentives, regional offers, financing deals, and dealer discounts rather than replacing them.

One thing to watch: some dealer landing pages and aggregator sites imply this is a store-wide or percentage-based military deal, or that it applies to any Chrysler model, and some bundle it with a separate first-responder offer. In reality it’s a fixed $500 bonus-cash allowance limited to a specific list of Pacifica and Voyager models, redeemed only at the dealer via a SheerID authorization number — never a percentage and never an online promo code. The eligible-vehicle list changes silently by model year, so re-verify against Chrysler’s official page at purchase time.

Because the $500 is a flat amount on what is typically a $40,000-$60,000 minivan, it is a small piece of the total deal. The bigger lever for savings is timing your purchase or lease to Chrysler’s largest live public incentive, APR offer, or lease event, then adding the $500 on top.
newegg-military-discount: The honest core fact: Newegg has no current military discount. Its own historical military-offer page now shows "Offers expire 11/11/2018" and a "Promotion Has Expired" notice, and its ID.me store page lists only email-signup deals with no military percentage. There is nothing to verify because there is no discount to unlock.

Why the "10%" claims keep circulating. Coupon aggregators and military-discount listicles widely advertise a "Newegg military discount," but no official Newegg source confirms one today. The claim traces back to a real Veterans-Day 10% code — but that code expired in 2018. Treat any current "military promo code" as a dead code or a public coupon relabeled as military.

Where the real savings are. Newegg’s genuine levers are the Shell Shocker and Daily Deals flash sales, combo bundles with mail-in rebates, open-box/refurbished listings, and cashback portals that stack on the public price. All of these are open to everyone — none is a military benefit, but each is a real way to lower your price. Because Newegg pricing is dynamic and promo-driven, verify the live price and any rebate or cashback rate before you buy.

The maximum-savings play. For a bigger purchase, catch the exact SKU on a Shell Shocker or Daily Deal, add any combo bundle and mail-in rebate, and route the order through a cashback portal — those stack. Consider open-box or refurbished when condition allows for extra savings. Black Friday and Cyber Monday in November bring Newegg’s deepest public component drops; a nonexistent military rate does not.
gamestop-military-discount: The scope change is the story most pages miss. When GameStop launched the program on Veterans Day 2019, it covered 10% off new video game software and accessories plus all pre-owned products and collectibles, for "all active and former military." The current official page is dramatically narrower: toys, collectibles, and pre-owned only, with new games, new accessories, new consoles, tablets, PC hardware, TVs, gift cards, DLC, and all sale/clearance items excluded — and the body copy now names only "active members of the military and Law Enforcement." Most third-party listings (and even WeSalute’s) still describe the 2019 terms.

Verification is refreshingly simple but strictly physical: at the register, show a military ID, Form DD214, or your ID.me verification (in practice, the ID.me wallet on your phone shown in-store). There’s no pre-enrollment, no account gate, and no online field — aggregator claims that the 10% works "via gamestop.com, the GameStop mobile app," or an ID.me checkout button are false. The veteran question is genuinely unresolved: the page accepts veteran documentation and is titled "Video Game Discount for Veterans," while its body copy says active-only. Bring your DD214 and expect the register to decide.

Run the math before relying on the discount. On a $69.99 new release with 7% tax ($74.89 all-in), the military discount is worth $0 — new games are excluded. The exchange gets that game to $69.99 tax-free, and AAFES has occasionally priced consoles below MSRP (a PS5 disc console at $429 in August 2023). GameStop Pro’s $5 monthly reward does work on new physical games ($69.54 net on the baseline), and the $25 annual fee repays itself in five months of used rewards. Where the military 10% genuinely wins: full-price pre-owned, toys, and collectibles in-store — a $54.99 pre-owned copy drops to about $52.95 with tax, beating Pro’s 5% on the same item.

The stacking rules are mostly moot but worth stating: the 10% never applies to sale/clearance/promotional pricing (sale prices replace it), it can’t meet cashback portals (those track online orders only, and the discount is in-store only), and whether it combines with Pro member pricing is not stated — on pre-owned, just take the bigger, free 10%. Gift cards are excluded from every discount as purchased items. Trade-in credit layers under everything as tender, and Pros get 10% extra credit. One watch item: media reports say Pro’s 2% points program ends for memberships starting or renewing on/after July 15, 2026, with existing points expiring August 15, 2026 — that’s reported, not yet in GameStop’s official terms as accessed, so verify before counting on points.
hp-military-discount: The headline figures are an "up to" range, not a flat percentage applied to every item. HP’s own Frontline Heroes page advertises "up to 40% everyday savings," while HP’s store listing on ID.me Shop advertises "up to 60% off plus free shipping for Military." Both are HP-attributed but inconsistent, and member pricing is only visible after you verify and log in — so treat the percentages as ceilings that vary by product and over time, and check the actual price on each item.

Verification runs through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many retailers. You verify once from the Frontline Heroes Store, then complete HP store registration to link the status to your hp.com account; returning members can skip the ID.me step and just sign in. HP’s page does not state how often ID.me re-verification is required, so don’t assume it’s permanent — ID.me governs that on its own terms.

Watch the fine print: ink and toner have been excluded from program discounts since March 1, 2023; the offer can’t be combined with other HP discounts unless stated; and there are per-calendar-year purchase caps (2 PCs, 2 tablets, 10 accessories, 2 printers, 12 supplies). HP’s ID.me listing also shows rotating, time-sensitive offers (for example a "25% off select full-MSRP PCs") without published dates — treat those as promotions, not evergreen pricing.
