Exchange-eligible shoppers can also find many Western/work brands tax-free at AAFES/Navy Exchange (all honorably discharged veterans can shop the exchanges online). Neither is a Cavender’s offer, but each can lower what you actually pay.
footjoy-military-discount: The savings math is easy to see on a baseline pair of FootJoy Pro/SL golf shoes at the $175 list price. A military discount would save you $0, because it does not exist. The Semi-Annual Sale/outlet, by contrast, often brings prior-season colorways to roughly $110–$150 — a saving of about $25–$65 and the deepest FootJoy-direct value. A working public code can knock off another ~10–15% on eligible items, and routing a full-price order through the ID.me Shop returns up to ~2.5% (about $4.38 on $175). FootJoy gives free standard shipping over $150, and free FJ Insider membership adds free shipping and perks on top.

Be cautious of coupon and deal sites advertising a FootJoy "20%", "25%", or even "94% military discount, in-store only," or a stackable "GOLF25FIRST 25% off" military code. All of these are false or misleading. FootJoy publishes no military discount; codes like "GOLF25FIRST" (where they work at all) are ordinary first-purchase or newsletter offers open to anyone, not a military benefit; and there is no FootJoy retail-store military program. ID.me’s own FootJoy page confirms the brand does not offer a military discount.

Don’t confuse the ID.me Shop cashback with a military discount. FootJoy appears on the ID.me Shop for a general rebate of up to ~2.5% back that is open to all shoppers — it is a cashback rebate, not a verified military rate, and it may not track on orders that also use a coupon code. There is no ID.me military verification or discount for FootJoy at all.

If it does not have to be FootJoy, the cheapest route is often a competing golf-shoe brand that runs a real military discount — PUMA, Callaway, and others verify service members through ID.me, and that discount frequently beats every FootJoy path. And if you are eligible to shop the base exchange (AAFES’s shopmyexchange.com or NEX’s mynavyexchange.com), tax-free pricing plus a price match can beat list when the exchange stocks the model.
gold-bjj-military-discount: Gold BJJ uses GovX ID for real-time verification of military and first-responder status. You verify once and receive a single-use code; for each subsequent purchase you log back into GovX ID to generate a new code (one per day). Codes are for personal use only, and verification permanence follows GovX ID’s own rules.

The 35% code applies to all gear but does not combine with any other promotion or discount code — it is a single applied discount. Because Gold BJJ states it "doesn’t do many sales or much discounting," the 35% military and first-responder rate is almost always the best price available, so there is no holiday sale worth waiting for.

Ignore the "40–75% off," PACIFIC25, and SHADES codes advertised on coupon aggregators — none is a verified standing Gold BJJ offer. The only verified standing discount is 35% off via GovX ID for military and first responders; everyone else should expect to pay full price outside of the occasional email-list promotion.
surefire-military-discount: Verification happens on the phone call itself: SureFire doesn’t publish which documents are required, and community threads describe the validation as case-by-case — so treat the requirements as unpublished until you’re on the line, and have proof of service ready. SureFire also doesn’t enumerate which groups count as "military" for the 20%; if you’re a veteran, retiree, or spouse, ask when you call rather than assuming.

The math on the benchmark: on a ~$300 SureFire light, the phone-order 20% brings you to $240 — a $60 saving, and the only published number for this brand. GovX member pricing and ExpertVoice pro-deal depth for SureFire are both unpublished, but ExpertVoice deals run up to about 60% off MSRP platform-wide, so on some SKUs a gated price can beat the phone discount. Price-check first; the channels cannot be combined.

One thing to watch: aggregator pages like WorthEPenny advertise "20% off SureFire military" in a way that implies an online coupon code. The number happens to match, but the mechanic doesn’t — there is no SureFire military promo code, and no ID.me or SheerID gate exists on surefire.com. The 20% is granted on a phone order after you request it.

Two more things that are easy to confuse: unit and agency purchases are a separate program (use the request form on SureFire’s Military Sales page — law enforcement has its own channel), and there’s no cashback layer to weigh, because surefire.com is not on Rakuten. Public dealer sales (OpticsPlanet and other authorized SureFire dealers) are the other route worth comparing against your $240-per-$300 benchmark; some tactical dealers have also historically offered SureFire qualified-professional pricing for mil/LE, so it can be worth asking your local dealer.
cookunity-military-discount: The military route here is GovX, not ID.me. ID.me’s shop page lists CookUnity, but that is a general shopping-portal offer for everyone — not a separate ID.me military verification path. CookUnity verifies military and other eligible status through GovX only; it does not use ID.me, SheerID, or WeSalute for this program.

The catch that drives the whole savings decision: the GovX rate is not combinable with CookUnity’s public first-order or welcome offers. A first-timer has to choose. Ordering for months? The GovX $9.99-per-meal rate, held for 17 straight weeks, is the only path that sustains a discount that long — roughly $245 saved on a typical 8-meals-a-week plan. Just want one trial week? The public 50%-off-first-week offer (add a friend’s $50 referral credit and Rakuten cashback) beats GovX’s week-one price, because it’s a deep one-time discount rather than a modest per-meal cut.

Treat aggregator figures like "$8.50 per meal," "75% off," or scraped "military promo codes" as unverified — CookUnity’s own pages state $9.99 per meal for 17 weeks and frame it as up to 35% off. The exact percentage depends on which standard per-meal price ($10.39–$12.69) you compare against.
fubo-military-discount: Fubo’s own discount is powered by ID.me, the same identity-verification service used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of major retailers. You verify your group once, and the “Heroes” credit unlocks at Fubo checkout. Importantly, this is a broad Heroes program — it covers first responders, teachers, nurses, government workers, hospital workers, and medical providers on the same terms as military, so it is not a military-only offer.

A separate route is WeSalute, an independent military-and-family membership platform that runs its own Fubo Pro offer: 25% off your first month (about $21 off Fubo Pro). WeSalute’s eligibility covers active duty, retirees, veterans, current and former Guard and Reserve, and immediate family. It is a different provider from ID.me, with its own verification, and — like the ID.me offer — it is a one-time intro discount, not a standing rate.

Be cautious of coupon and roundup sites that advertise a “$10 off every month forever via GovX” Fubo military discount. That claim could not be confirmed against a GovX primary offer page, and it conflicts with Fubo’s own statement that it does not guarantee an ongoing military discount. We deliberately do not publish that figure as fact; if you see a GovX Fubo storefront at signup, verify any value there directly before relying on it.

Even for verified shoppers, the intro-only nature matters: after the discounted month or two, Fubo bills at the regular plan price, which changed in 2026 and remains volatile. Start the free trial to test channels before committing, compare the ID.me Heroes credit against Fubo’s public first-month promo (often within a few dollars and needing no verification), and price the plan at its full rate for your real long-term budget rather than the intro figure.
chene-military-discount: Verification is Chêne’s own in-house document review — there is no ID.me, SheerID, or GovX anywhere in the flow. Military applicants (active or retired) upload a DD Form 214 (Report of Separation) or an LES (Leave and Earnings Statement); first responders upload a paystub from the last 60 days or a tax document. Black out sensitive details like your SSN before uploading. Chêne’s team reviews the application — some auto-approve, others get manual review — and the page doesn’t state a re-verification cadence for military members.

Nothing stacks. Pro pricing is account-based at chenegear.com only, and Chêne runs no visible public coupon channel to layer on top of it. The pricing is also personal and confidential by the program terms: sharing your pricing, buying for friends or family, or reselling gear violates the terms and gets the account permanently revoked. Staying subscribed to Chêne’s emails is a membership requirement.

One thing to watch: coupon aggregators advertise "Chêne Gear 20% OFF promo code," "30% OFF," even "60% OFF." None of these is confirmed by anything on chenegear.com, which publishes no public promo codes and keeps even its Pro pricing confidential. There is also no "Chêne military discount code" — the only military route is the Pro Program application. We found no public military-holiday sale history (Veterans Day, Memorial Day, July 4) either; for this brand, discounts flow through the Pro Program, not holiday promos.

A few honest ways to keep the bill down regardless: apply before you buy, because there’s no retroactive discount path; free shipping kicks in at $150+ for everyone in the contiguous US; and youth waders run $850 (vs. $1,150 adult), with Chêne’s Youth Wader Program offering upgrade support for growing kids.
mlb-shop-military-discount: MLB Shop is a Fanatics-operated licensed-merchandise store. Its 15% military and first-responder discount is evergreen and verified through ID.me, the same identity network used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of major retailers. Verifying once links your eligibility to your ID.me account, so future checkouts — and discounts at other ID.me partners — go faster.

The important nuance is stacking. MLB Shop’s own FAQ states the discount "cannot be combined with any other promotional codes," and its public sales routinely reach 20–30% off — deeper than the 15% military rate. Because the two can’t be layered, the honest best-savings answer is situational: take the 15% ID.me discount only when no better public code is live; otherwise the public sale wins. A cashback portal such as Rakuten (about 2% as of July 12, 2026) is a rebate, not a checkout code, so it can layer on top of either path.

Coupon aggregators sometimes headline "20% off MLB military discount." That conflates two different things: the verified military discount is 15%, while the 20–30% figures are ordinary public sale codes anyone can use. Note too that "MLB military discount" is a mixed search — MLB.TV streaming and MLB game tickets have their own military pricing (often via GovX or mlb.com), separate from the MLBShop.com merchandise covered here.
walgreens-military-discount: The discount amount is 20% off regular-price eligible items. Several aggregators imply military shoppers get "30% off Walgreens-branded items" during the event, but Walgreens’ official promo page and corporate press releases state 20% off eligible regular-price items — full stop. The "30%" appears to conflate the everyday myWalgreens 5%-back-on-Walgreens-brand rewards accrual with the event discount; treat 30% as unverified.

Verification is manual at the register: a cashier checks your physical military ID or proof of service against your myWalgreens account. There is no third-party digital verifier and no online pre-verification, so there is nothing to "re-verify" between events — but the offer is only live during the roughly three annual windows.

Historically the windows have been Memorial Day weekend (Fri–Mon), the Fourth of July long weekend (~July 4–7), and Veterans Day (Nov 8–11 in both 2024 and 2025). These are a labeled historical record, not a promise of future dates — verify the exact dates about two weeks before each holiday at walgreens.com/offerdetails.

Separately, myWalgreens is a free year-round loyalty program that earns 1% Walgreens Cash storewide and 5% on Walgreens-branded products, plus weekly sale prices and digital coupons. Whether that Walgreens Cash is earned on top of the 20% military discount is not explicitly stated in the terms, so we do not promise it as fact.
vevor-military-discount: VEVOR is a budget-equipment e-commerce brand whose whole pricing model is permanent coupons and tiered member pricing — which is exactly why it runs no identity-based discounts. Its Coupon Center is the discount mechanism: claim-on-site coupons currently tiered at $20 off $249+, $30 off $379+, $40 off $499+, plus a 5%-off-per-item coupon, in limited-quantity batches (the current batch is valid April 21 to August 14, 2026 UTC). On a $300 equipment order, the $20-off-$249 code plus a ~3% portal click-through lands around $272–$280 effective — roughly 7–9% off, the best default path for any $249+ cart.

Be cautious of coupon aggregators that advertise a specific VEVOR "military discount." valuecom promotes "50% OFF with Vevor Military Discount," and other coupon sites claim "military members can grab 20% off with code FBOFF" or a "10% military discount." None of this is confirmed by VEVOR or any verification provider — VEVOR’s own site has no military page, and ID.me Shop explicitly says it’s not aware of any VEVOR military discount. Those pages recast VEVOR’s public seasonal sales and coupons as "military deals"; we deliberately publish no military percentage for VEVOR because none exists.

Cashback portals are the quiet second layer: TopCashback listed ~3% and Rakuten 2% on VEVOR orders as of July 14, 2026 (rates move weekly). One caveat from the portals’ own terms — applying a coupon the portal doesn’t list can void or reduce cashback, and VEVOR’s coupon-center coupons are claimed on-site, not portal-listed. Treat the combo as coupon-guaranteed, cashback-at-risk: worst case you still keep the $20–$40 coupon. Portal-only (no code) is the safest way to make sure the cashback tracks.

Repeat and shop buyers should build VEVOR’s free Pro/Personal Member tier instead of chasing one-off codes: member pricing scales from 2% to 15% off based on your trailing-365-day spend, with priority service above $1,500 — at 5%+ it beats the coupon tiers on every order. (The program’s tax-exemption registration is business-only and requires a business tax ID — it is not a military benefit.) New app users can also take $5 off $99+ on their first three VEVOR app orders, and Black Friday / seasonal sales bring VEVOR’s deepest public prices of the year — open to everyone, not military-gated.
hm-military-discount: We checked the places a real offer would appear: ID.me’s H&M page says it isn’t aware of an H&M military discount, and H&M is absent from the military marketplaces (WeSalute lists only third-party discounted gift cards, not an H&M military offer). H&M’s own help content documents membership and returns, not a military program.

The free H&M Member loyalty program is the real everyday saver — member prices, points toward rewards, a birthday offer, and free-shipping perks. On top of it you can apply one public promo code per order and route the purchase through a cashback portal.

The practical plan: join H&M Member (free), shop the sale/clearance, add the best current public code, and start at a cashback portal. Students can separately use H&M’s student verification where it’s offered — but that’s a student benefit, not a military one.
mt-high-military-discount: The honest math turns on Mountain High’s dynamic pricing. On a peak Saturday or holiday, a walk-up adult ticket can run around $169, so the flat $99 military rate saves roughly $60–$70. On a low-demand early- or late-season day, the public online "Anytime Flex" rate can already sit near $99 — meaning the military rate saves little or nothing that day. Buy the right channel for the day: peak day, take the VIP-window rate; quiet day, compare the public online rate first.

Verification is in person for the resort’s own rate — a staff member checks your Department ID or Military ID at the VIP Window, with no account and no re-verification schedule. GovX is the separate online channel: a one-time digital verification tied to your GovX account (military, veteran, first responder, healthcare, or government). GovX and the VIP-window rate are separate — you buy through one or the other, not both — and GovX pricing is set by GovX.

A few honest caveats: the discount is one ticket per valid ID, so it is not a way to price a whole non-military group; the $59 night rate runs only "when available," so confirm night operations before you drive up; and although coupon aggregators advertise "20%–30% off" Mountain High promo codes, those are generic scraped codes, not a military offer — the resort publishes no online military code.
blenders-military-discount: On-site verification uses ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. You create a free ID.me account, verify your eligibility group, and the 20% applies at cart. First responders, nurses, and teachers verify through the same gateway. GovX uses its own separate verification on its storefront.

The stacking rule is the key trade-off. The ID.me 20% is one-per-order and cannot be combined with other promo codes or with sitewide sale pricing. Because Blenders runs frequent public sales that often exceed 20% (Black Friday and Cyber Monday are typically the deepest), the winning path shifts to the public sale during those windows — you choose the larger single discount, then pay with a rewards card on top.

One thing to watch: some aggregator pages still list a "15% off" figure. That is out of date — the currently verified official rate is 20% via ID.me, and the military discount does not stack on top of a public promo code.
choice-hotels-military-veteran: All the math below uses one baseline: a $120/night standard room for a 3-night leisure stay = $360 before tax, at a participating Choice brand (Comfort Inn, Quality Inn, Sleep Inn, Clarion, Cambria, and others). Hotel rates move constantly, so every figure is illustrative and stamped “as of June 16, 2026” — treat them as a way to compare paths, not as quotes.

Rule 1 — status stacks; rates don’t. Limited-time Gold Elite is the one status that layers on top of every booking while it’s active, because it’s status rather than a rate. The discounted rates — the military leisure rate, WeSalute 15%, and Pay Now & Save — are mutually exclusive, so you’re choosing one, not adding them up. This single distinction is the most important thing to understand about saving at Choice.

Rule 2 — the military rate still earns points. Many “discount” rates strip your loyalty earning; Choice’s military/veteran leisure rate does not. You keep earning Choice Privileges points and airline rewards on top of the lower rate — a real, under-reported advantage that makes the military rate more valuable than its sticker price alone, especially once you’ve claimed Gold (which boosts your points earning).

Rule 3 — you must be a Choice Privileges member and book direct. The leisure rate requires a (free) Choice Privileges membership, and both the rate and your status only attach when you book on choicehotels.com or the Choice app. Book through an OTA like Expedia and you forfeit the military rate and the points/status — this is the most common way travelers accidentally lose the benefit.

Rule 4 — WeSalute 15% is a paid path with one catch. WeSalute (formerly Veterans Advantage) gives a flat 15% off at Choice and still earns points, which on the $360 baseline is about $306. But it needs a paid WeSalute+ membership (~$10/mo) and it can’t combine with the non-refundable Pay Now & Save advance rate, so it pays off mainly for current members or frequent travelers — do the math against the military rate for your stay.

Rule 5 — leisure vs. official are different rates. The military/veteran leisure rate is for personal travel; if you’re a government or military employee or contractor on official business, use the separate government/military official rate (often at or near the federal per-diem). They live on the same Government & Military Rates page — pick the one that matches your trip, and bring proof of service for check-in either way.
ikon-pass-military-discount: For online purchases, Ikon uses SheerID during checkout to confirm the name, branch of service, and current military status you enter against government-issued documentation (which you may be asked to upload if not instantly verified). If your last name changed since your military document was issued, SheerID asks for an additional government ID showing your current name; SheerID states it does not sell, rent, or store uploaded documents. There’s no phone verification path for the online offer — if automatic verification fails, use SheerID’s feedback form. Re-verification frequency isn’t stated, so don’t assume it’s one-time. And critically: don’t run verification until you’re ready to buy, because multiple attempts lock your Ikon account (call 888-365-IKON to unlock).

On amounts, Ikon publishes flat military prices rather than a percentage. That’s deliberate: standard 26/27 pass prices are tiered and rise as the season progresses, so the dollar savings versus retail depends on when you’d otherwise buy — the earlier in the season, the smaller the gap, and later, the larger. We state the flat military prices ($899 / $589 / $389) and don’t claim a fixed percent off.

Two eligibility notes. First, the program is framed around active, retired (20+ years for the on-base route), reserve/guard, and dependents — general separated veterans without one of those statuses or a base ID aren’t clearly addressed, so the SheerID status dropdown is the real gate; verify your own case. Second, a one-pass cap and a no-stacking rule show up on aggregator pages but not on Ikon’s own pages, so treat those as unconfirmed. If a family member is a nurse or enrolled college student, Ikon runs separate Nurse and College discounts (also via SheerID). For comparison, Vail Resorts’ Epic Pass has its own Epic Military Pass, also SheerID-verified — worth checking if your home resorts span both networks.
bowflex-military-discount: The reason the old advice is everywhere is that it used to be true. Before 2024, Nautilus (BowFlex’s former owner) ran a phone-verified military program — reported at 10–30% off by model, redeemed by calling 1-800-618-8853 and confirming with a DD-214, military ID, or .mil email. That program is no longer verifiable: after Johnson Health Tech Retail bought the assets out of bankruptcy in 2024, the legacy /military.html redemption page began returning HTTP 410 Gone, the customer-service FAQ and footer make no mention of a military discount, and the old phone number is dead (current BowFlex support numbers are different). Treat every stated BowFlex "military %," the 800-618-8853 line, and the "SheerID at checkout" claim as stale pre-2024 information, not a current offer.

The exchanges are the strongest structural route. AAFES (shopmyexchange.com) and the Navy Exchange (mynavyexchange.com) carry BowFlex home gyms, treadmills, and SelectTech dumbbells, and sell them with no sales tax. On a big-ticket machine, that ~8% tax saving alone can beat a small percentage discount, and you can layer MILITARY STAR card financing/rewards and exchange price-matching on top. Veterans who verified once for the Veterans Online Shopping Benefit can use the exchanges online even without base access.

Johnson Fitness & Wellness is the verified GovX route. It is BowFlex’s parent-company retail arm and carries the BowFlex line, and it honors a GovX ID discount of about 7% off the whole order (in-store or on johnsonfitness.com). The discount covers the equipment price only (not shipping), excludes Peloton and Tonal, and is not combinable with other offers — and because GovX checkout is identity-gated, do not expect a cashback portal to also track. Note there is no BowFlex storefront hosted directly on GovX; the GovX route to BowFlex gear is through Johnson Fitness.

Often the best deal skips the military angle. BowFlex discounts heavily and often — recurring seasonal markdowns of $500–$900+ on machines, sometimes with stackable-looking promo codes and 0% APR financing. Those sales are public (no verification), and they don’t require giving anything up, so on this brand the sale price plus a cashback portal (no code, so tracking survives) is frequently cheaper than any military-specific route. The two military routes — the tax-free exchange and Johnson Fitness GovX 7% — matter most when no sale is live.
tesla-military-discount: Verification is handled by ID.me. You must verify your eligible status before placing the order; once verified, the adjustment appears before you order, and an ID.me account is required with the purchaser matching the account holder. Tesla does not publish a re-verification frequency for this discount; ID.me’s own status verification governs how and when your status is confirmed. If automatic verification fails, ID.me’s support path is the route to resolve it.

The discount stacks with Tesla’s current finance offers and Refer & Earn, but not between hero groups (one affiliation per order). Because Tesla rarely discounts new vehicles directly, this $500 — plus a stackable referral or finance offer — is one of the few official ways to reduce a new-Tesla price. Check Tesla’s Current Offers page for any active incentives.

Older sources citing a $1,000 Tesla discount are out of date: that was the launch amount, reduced to $500 around October 2025. Tesla’s current pages (American Heroes; Honoring Our Country, last updated November 2025) state $500 and list the Cybertruck among eligible new models alongside Model S, 3, X, and Y.
free-people-military-discount: The military Exchange (AAFES / NEX) is the genuine best military value for Free People. The Exchange carries Free People and runs military-exclusive markdown events — Exchange social posts have advertised "30% less than MSRP," and a past Hawaii Exchange event took "up to 40% off MSRP" — and every Exchange purchase is sales-tax-free. That combination of a military-exclusive price plus no sales tax typically beats any price on freepeople.com. The assortment and the specific "% off MSRP" rotate, so verify the exact item and price live before you count on it.

Exchange access is broad: active-duty, retirees, reserve, and National Guard members and authorized dependents shop under standard eligibility, and all honorably discharged veterans can shop the Exchange online tax-free for life through the Veterans Online Shopping Benefit. Eligibility is verified by the Exchange, not by Free People.

For everyone — military or not — Free People’s own public sales are usually the deepest single price. FP Mart (clearance and vintage) and seasonal sale events run up to roughly 70% off, open to all shoppers with no code required. New email/SMS subscribers get 10% off a first order, but that code excludes sale and FP Mart items and is online/app only, so it does not stack on a sale price.

The only on-brand identity discount is a student discount, verified through UNiDAYS or Student Beans — not ID.me and not military. Its percentage is login-gated and not published, so confirm it at the provider. And ignore the "20% military code" and "INSTAGRAM 30% off" figures on coupon sites: those are ordinary public promos, not a verified military program.
disney-military-discount: There is no online ID.me or SheerID flow for the parks Salute offer. Verification is done in person with a physical, valid U.S. military ID — first at the point of purchase, and again at activation or first use. Tickets are sold only through authorized military channels: base ticket offices, the Shades of Green Resort, Disney park ticket windows, and — for Disneyland — GOVX.com, which verifies military status online. The eligible member or spouse must be the purchaser, and at least one of the tickets must be used by that member or spouse.

Each eligible member or spouse may buy up to 6 Salute tickets (5 if they hold a valid Annual Pass or Magic Key). At Walt Disney World, tickets are not valid until activated in person at a park ticket window; at Disneyland, the member or spouse must present current military ID at a Main Entrance turnstile on first use. Park reservations are required in addition to a valid ticket and are limited.

Room savings at Walt Disney World are tiered by resort and date for 2026: Deluxe and Villa resorts save 25% on most dates and 30% in summer (June 1 – August 31); Moderates save 20% (25% summer); Values and campsites save 15% (20% summer). Disneyland offers special military rates with a 2-room-per-reservation limit. A valid military ID is required at check-in or the non-discounted rate is charged, and the member or spouse must stay in the room.

Two money-saving notes: buying at a base ticket office or Shades of Green adds no sales tax (tax applies at Disney park ticket windows), and individual base offices may charge less than Disney’s published prices. And every dollar figure here is 2026-specific — Disney resets ticket prices, room percentages, blockout dates, and validity windows each calendar year, so always re-check the official 2026 pages (or the current year’s) before booking.
rural-king-military-discount: Rural King uses no third-party verification for a military discount — no GovX, ID.me, SheerID, or WeSalute — because there is no standing program to gate. The only "verification" is showing a Military ID at the register during an announced in-store holiday promotion. There is no online account, code, or re-verification cycle to manage.

The verified 10% figures come straight from Rural King’s own posts: a 10% in-store discount on Veterans Day 2024 (present your Military ID at checkout) and an extra 10% off for active military and veterans during the Memorial Day 2024 sale (ran 5/23–5/27, in-store only, "some exclusions apply"). Rural King has repeated this Veterans Day / Memorial Day pattern, but it does not promise the offer will recur, so treat any in-store 10% outside a holiday window as manager discretion, not policy.

Because the holiday 10% is not guaranteed, the genuine best everyday path is the Rural King Rewards Visa (~5% back in rewards; 5 pts/$1, $5 per 500 pts), with the free Rural King Rewards program (~1% back) as the no-strings floor. Reward earning is not a competing discount, so it stacks with the holiday 10% — you take 10% off at the register and still earn points on what you actually pay, roughly 14–15% of combined value in the best case.

One more lever, open to everyone: Rural King’s price match beats a nearby competitor’s advertised price on an identical item within 30 miles. But the price-match policy explicitly excludes group/military and loyalty discounts, so you pick price-match or the holiday military discount, never both. Rural King’s ordinary weekly-ad and clearance sales are also open to all and often beat a nominal group discount.
garmin-military-veteran: All the math below uses one baseline: a single Garmin Fenix 8 47mm AMOLED at about $1,000 full price, the kind of flagship most shoppers are comparing. Garmin ships free over $49, so shipping is $0 on every path and doesn’t change the ranking; tax varies by state and applies to all paths roughly equally, so it’s excluded to keep the comparison clean. Refurb rows reference a comparable certified-refurbished model because a refurb is a different unit.

Rule 1 — there’s no code, so this is “pick the winning path,” not “stack codes.” Unlike a brand whose military discount combines with other deals, Garmin gives you several independent routes — GovX, an on-site sale, and certified-refurb — that you cannot use together. Price each for your model and buy the single lowest one. Don’t treat any of them as a layer on top of another.

Rule 2 — the most common winner is a live on-site sale + ~2% Rakuten. When Garmin runs a public sale on your model (often $200–$300 off a flagship), that sale plus ~2% Rakuten on the sale subtotal (garmin.com only, as of June 16, 2026) usually beats the GovX price — and it needs no verification. Activate Rakuten first and use only portal-listed codes so a non-portal code doesn’t void the cashback.

Rule 3 — the highest-value, least-known lever is certified refurbished, and warranty length is part of the value. A certified refurb runs 30–50% less than new. Garmin’s own refurb outlet carries a 1-year warranty; an eBay Garmin-authorized refurb often carries a 2-year warranty — longer than a new unit. So a refurb can be both cheaper and better-covered; just remember cashback doesn’t apply to eBay, and the refurb may be a prior generation.

Rule 4 — GovX is the real military-specific route, but it’s a marketplace price, not a Garmin discount. Verify once at GovX, then compare the standard Garmin storefront and the GovX “Garmin Open Box” storefront, where open-box premium models are often the lowest GovX price. Cashback portals don’t apply to GovX, so don’t expect to add Rakuten on top.

Keep students separate from military — this is where the internet gets it wrong. Garmin’s Student Beans 20% is for verified students only, isn’t combinable, and excludes the Instinct 2, Fenix 7, and Epix. Coupon aggregators copy that 20% onto a “military discount” headline; it doesn’t exist. If you’re a military student, you’d use the student route as a student — not as a service member.
duluth-military-discount: Duluth uses ID.me as its verification partner. Create a free ID.me account (or sign in), submit your service information and proof of identity once, and your status is stored for future logins; ID.me periodically requires re-verification per its own policy. Online, click the ID.me button at checkout; in-store, scan the ID.me QR code or show your eligibility card. Verification issues go through ID.me’s help center, while order questions go to Duluth customer service.

The stacking angle is the real edge here. Duluth’s terms explicitly allow combining the 5% with other offers, so there is no "sale vs. 5%" choice — you get both. Percentages apply sequentially rather than summing (20% then 5% is about 24% off, not 25%). The discount does not apply to gift cards, "select items," or a long list of third-party brands (Benchmade, Birkenstock, Blundstone, Big Agnes, BioLite, and more) that set their own pricing, and it is not valid on phone orders.

A cashback portal can add a little more, but with a caveat. Rakuten showed 4% for Duluth Trading as of July 15, 2026 — a post-purchase rebate paid on the final amount. The technical risk is that invoking ID.me’s checkout redirect can break Rakuten’s click-through tracking, so if cashback matters, start from the portal link and confirm the session tracked. Duluth Heroes covers military and first responders only; we found no separate nurse, teacher, or student tier as of the verified date.
nike-military-discount: Nike verifies military eligibility through SheerID. You complete a short SheerID form (status, branch, name, date of birth, email); SheerID checks it against authoritative records and, when it can’t auto-verify, may ask you to upload documentation. After verification you receive a promo code tied to your Nike Member account. This is a per-code model rather than a permanent account flag, so online you generally request a fresh code for each purchase window — reported as every ~7 days, with codes expiring ~2 weeks after issue — rather than getting a one-and-done lifetime discount.

The 10% rate is confirmed straight from Nike’s own page: its Military Discount help page states a "10% discount off most items—online and in stores—to all active, reservist, veteran, and retired US military personnel, and to the spouses and dependents of active personnel." The provider is SheerID (the verification flow lives at offers.sheerid.com/nike/military), not ID.me, GovX, or WeSalute. The exact code-timing and the itemized exclusion list, however, come from secondary military-focused guides because Nike’s page body is JavaScript-rendered — we present those as reported and link to the official page to confirm.

Nike runs a full family of parallel 10% audience discounts — Student, Teacher, First Responder & Medical Professional, and a Nike Member birthday offer — each at 10% and each verified separately through SheerID on its own help page. If you qualify for more than one, you pick the single offer that applies rather than stacking them. For verification problems, SheerID provides a shopper help center; Nike directs discount questions through its standard Help/Contact Us channels.
pga-superstore-military-discount: The military discount is verified the old-fashioned way: manually, at the register, with a valid Military/Armed Forces identification card. There is no ID.me, SheerID, or GovX flow, and no online military checkout — the ID.me store page for PGA TOUR Superstore lists only public sales, which corroborates that no online military tier exists.

The brand exclusions are the whole story. PING and Babolat get no discount at all, and Mizuno, Callaway, TaylorMade, Cleveland, Srixon, XXIO, Wilson, Head, and Titleist are excluded from the 10% as well. Between them that’s most of the drivers, irons, and premium equipment a serious golfer actually shops for — so on a $499 excluded-brand driver, the military discount saves $0. The 10% is meaningful mainly on apparel, accessories, non-excluded balls, and gear.

For the equipment the discount excludes, the real levers are different. PGA TOUR Superstore runs an in-store price match against named local competitors (Dick’s, Carl’s Golfland, Edwin Watts, Golf Galaxy, Tennis Warehouse, TGW, and Worldwide Golf Shops) on identical in-stock items, subject to manufacturer pricing (MAP) rules. Trade-in and certified pre-owned are usually the biggest savings on premium clubs. And when an item is on sale online, the public markdown plus Rakuten cashback (2%, as of July 8, 2026) often beats 10% without a store trip.

A note on the noise: coupon aggregators overstate this badly, floating "up to 50% off" military claims and stackable "veteran codes." The verified offer is 10% in-store only, for active and retired military with a valid ID, with the exclusions above. Any "PGA Superstore military promo code" for the website is fabricated — there is no online military discount.
whoop-military-discount: Verification runs through ID.me. You verify once through WHOOP’s hosted ID.me offer page and receive a single-use code for a new membership purchase; WHOOP doesn’t publish a re-verification schedule or whether a code can be re-issued, so assume one code, one new membership. WHOOP’s public wording covers "Military, Nurses & First Responders" without breaking down military sub-groups — ID.me makes that call at verification, so veterans and Guard/Reserve members should simply attempt the flow. If verification fails, ID.me support handles document review.

Know the honest either/or math before you verify. The 10% takes Peak Annual from $239 to $215.10 — but WHOOP’s public Black Friday/Cyber window (November 20 – December 2, 2025) priced Peak Annual at $199, beating the military price outright, and WHOOP doesn’t state whether the ID.me code applies to sale pricing. The deepest verified always-on path is the 24-month Peak plan plus the 10% (~$359 for two years, pending checkout confirmation of the reported $399 base — roughly $180 a year). And whatever price you pay, WHOOP memberships are HSA/FSA-eligible via Truemed at checkout — paying pre-tax is worth more than the 10% for most buyers, though WHOOP doesn’t state whether Truemed can combine with a code order.

The ruled-out paths save you the search: no GovX storefront exists (GovX search hits are unrelated apparel), Rakuten delisted WHOOP and no cashback portal listed it as of July 4, 2026, and neither AAFES nor the Navy Exchange stocks WHOOP. Used devices are a trap, not a hack — a secondhand WHOOP still needs a paid membership, and new memberships already include the hardware free. The Chase Sapphire credits (up to $359 on a Life Annual plan for Reserve cardholders) expired May 12, 2026 — any site still promoting them is stale, though Sapphire holders should check Chase Offers for a repeat before buying.

One more correction worth making: coupon aggregators advertise "30% off WHOOP promo codes" — no such public sitewide code is confirmed by any WHOOP source, and WHOOP publishes a Minimum Advertised Pricing policy. Existing members hoping to apply the 10%: WHOOP’s official forum answer is that the discount is for new membership purchases only, and WHOOP hasn’t said whether a rejoining member counts as "new" — we don’t recommend cancel/rejoin gymnastics on that basis. WHOOP does run a separate tactical/government & defense program, but that’s for unit deployments, not an individual discount.
rawlings-military-discount: Rawlings publishes no military, veteran, or first-responder discount and uses no verification provider — there is nothing to verify and no code field to unlock. ID.me’s own Rawlings Gear listing says it plainly: "We’re not aware that Rawlings Gear offers Military discounts." The only ID.me connection is ID.me Shop cashback, a portal rebate open to all shoppers — a rebate on a brand-site order, not a military discount, and one that generally requires an un-coded order to track.

Be cautious of coupon sites advertising "Rawlings military discount" codes such as RSGHIP2SAVE ("35% off for military") or "10% for military and employees." These are not official military offers — Rawlings publishes no military discount, and such codes are generic or scraped public codes miscategorized as "military." Treat any "Rawlings military code" as an ordinary public promo, if it works at all, never a service-member benefit.

The real levers on a Rawlings order are public. The newsletter signup offer can trim roughly $20 off a $200 glove when a percentage offer is live, seasonal and outlet sales often cut 20–40% off select gear (deepest around Black Friday and the offseason), and ID.me Shop cashback returns a few percent on an un-coded order. Exchange-eligible shoppers have one genuinely military-only path: where AAFES, NEX, or MCX stocks Rawlings, buying at the exchange is tax-free — roughly $12–$18 saved on a $200 glove — with MILITARY STAR perks on top.

One competitor note matters: Wilson, Rawlings’ chief rival, runs a verified 15% military discount for active, reserve, and retired military. A service member choosing between comparable gloves can effectively "get a military discount" by buying the Wilson equivalent — about $170 on a comparable $200-class glove. That 15% applies to Wilson gear only and never to Rawlings, but it is the built-in service-member deal Rawlings lacks.
chevy-military-discount: GM uses ID.me to confirm eligibility — via a USAA account, a .mil email, military service records, or uploaded documents such as an LES within 30 days, a DD214, or a retiree statement. A CAC/military ID card is not accepted due to Title 18 restrictions. Once verified, you no longer show proof at the dealer, but you must still bring the authorization number and a redacted driver’s license.

The program’s edge is stacking. GM’s FAQs say you can combine the program price with most current GM offers and incentives, and it can also be combined with GM Mobility reimbursements. The hard walls: it cannot be combined with GM’s First Responder, Educator, College, Family First, Supplier, Dealership Employee, Supplier-for-Friends, or Executive Referral/Employee Purchase programs — those are strictly either/or, so if you also qualify for one, compute each and take the single lowest total.

The mechanics reward planning: up to two vehicles per calendar year (two authorization numbers, each valid 90 days), a 6-month retention requirement, and new/unused vehicles only (demo units under 7,500 miles may qualify). National cash and APR incentives swing monthly, so the whole strategy is to buy in a deep-incentive window and stack the program price on top. If you’re overseas, you can arrange the offer online and take delivery in the U.S.
rivian-military-discount: Verification is not applicable here: Rivian uses no military verification provider because it has no military discount to verify against. If any site claims you can "verify with ID.me or GovX for a Rivian military discount," it’s inaccurate — a widely repeated answer on owner forums is that Rivian has not announced any military-specific incentive.

Rivian is the fixed-price direct-to-consumer archetype: everyone pays the posted price, and savings come from published offers rather than negotiation. As of the July 18, 2026 check, those offers included 1.99% APR (60-month) on a new 2026 R1 Tri or Dual with Performance Upgrade, 2.99% APR on the Dual Standard/Dual, $3,000 off qualifying 24/36-month leases, and package discounts of up to $7,000 (Forest Edge), $2,500 (Road Trip), and $2,200 (Stealth). All are config- and term-limited and rotate often — treat the live Offers page as the authority.

Two more real levers: the referral code stacks with any published offer (it grants Rewards points plus roughly three months of complimentary Adventure Network charging without touching the price), and demo vehicles at demovehicles.rivian.com sell below new-build pricing with a factory warranty. One lever that’s gone: the federal $7,500 EV tax credit expired for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, so don’t count it in 2026 math — though state and utility EV incentives may still apply where you live.
summit-one-vanderbilt-military-discount: SUMMIT handles military verification manually: you request the ticket through the Contact Us form and show valid military ID at the venue. It does not use an instant ID.me, SheerID, or GovX code for the free ticket — the ID.me Shop listing (~11% off for military, first responders, nurses, teachers, government, medical, and students) and the GovX offer are separate, weaker paths that forgo the comp entirely.

The offer is evergreen, not a holiday promo — SUMMIT publishes it year-round, and NYC Veterans Day deal roundups have simply pointed at this standing offer. Visitors on Tripadvisor report the military discount being honored on-site, which is consistent with the published terms (anecdotal, not a term of the offer).

One thing to watch: coupon aggregators advertise "SUMMIT Vanderbilt promo codes" up to 60% off. Those codes are not published or confirmed by SUMMIT and are not a military offer. The only military-specific offer SUMMIT publishes is the free Experience ticket plus the 25% guest discount, arranged through the Contact Us form.
owlet-military-discount: Owlet’s savings engine is its public promo cycle, not an identity discount. Its welcome codes are valid on select products (Dream Duo and others), are time-boxed and not retroactive, and its terms state that "Other discounts or promotions cannot be combined with this promo code" — one offer per order. The 2025 calendar shows the pattern: spring ran up to 25% off the Dream Sock and Dream Duo, Mother’s Day took 20% off bundles and select items, Memorial Day reached up to 30% sitewide with bundles deepest, and Black Friday (November 20 – December 2, 2025) took $100 off the Dream Sock — the yearly price floor. That history is a guide to timing, not a promised future promo.

The exchange route is the genuinely military angle. mynavyexchange.com lists the Owlet Dream Sock Monitor — the listing showed a $299.00 retail-price field on July 14, 2026, though you should verify the live sell price — and exchange purchases carry no sales tax. On a $299.00 Dream Sock at an illustrative 7% sales tax, skipping tax saves about $20.93 versus paying full price with tax at owletcare.com. Active duty and retirees qualify, and since the 2017 Veterans Online Shopping Benefit, honorably discharged veterans can shop the exchange online too; in-store base privileges are narrower. NEX pricing doesn’t take owletcare.com codes — its win is tax-free checkout, plus the usual MILITARY STAR cardholder perks where applicable.

The HSA/FSA angle can be the biggest lever of all. After the FDA cleared the Dream Sock, retailer listings — Walmart’s, for example — mark it HSA/FSA-eligible, and paying with pre-tax dollars effectively saves roughly your marginal tax rate, often 22–30%. It isn’t a coupon: it layers conceptually on any purchase price. But eligibility is confirmed by your plan administrator, not Owlet, and whether owletcare.com itself accepts HSA/FSA cards at checkout wasn’t confirmed in our research — so verify with your plan and your chosen retailer, and keep documentation.

Put together, the verdict logic is simple. If a sitewide sale or code is live — very common for Owlet — take the public deal: click through a cashback portal first on automatic markdowns (Rakuten paid 2% and top portals ~4–5% as of July 14, 2026), but expect a coupon code to void cashback, and pay with HSA/FSA funds if your plan covers it. No sale live and exchange-eligible? Buy tax-free at the Navy Exchange. Able to wait until November? Black Friday has been the yearly floor, taking $100 off in 2025. What never works is hunting for a "military code" — Owlet’s real discounts are public and time-boxed, and every offer is one-per-order.
hibbett-military-discount: The "no military discount" finding is not a "we couldn’t find the page" gap. ID.me publishes dedicated Hibbett pages for military, first responders, nurses, and government, and each says ID.me is not aware of a Hibbett offer. Independent discount directories reach the same conclusion. If a coupon site tells you to "verify with ID.me for 10% at Hibbett," that flow does not exist.

The widely copied "10% Hibbett military discount verified through ID.me — online only, for active duty, veterans, reservists, National Guard, and family" line is fabricated. Ignore the separate "67% off military in-store, show your military ID" claim too: the 67% is a maximum coupon-stacking figure some sites headline, not a military discount, and Hibbett’s savings are code/rewards-based online, not a flash-your-ID register discount.

Because there’s no identity discount to compete with, a service member gets the same everyday value any shopper gets. The free Hibbett Rewards welcome offer (15% off your first order plus free shipping) is the single best standing route; a live holiday sale is often deeper but won’t combine with the welcome code; and if you’re exchange-eligible, pricing the same shoe tax-free at ShopMyExchange or the Navy Exchange is the only genuinely military-specific edge that exists.
old-navy-military-discount: Verification is done in person at checkout — you simply present a valid, current military ID and the associate applies the discount. There is no third-party verification provider (no ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute) and no account to create. This means there is no re-verification cycle: eligibility is confirmed at each visit by your ID.

Several aggregator pages imply you can "verify online through ID.me" for an Old Navy military discount. That is incorrect. ID.me’s own Old Navy page states it is "not aware that Old Navy offers Military discounts," and there is no online military discount channel. Coupon sites advertising "30% off military" or "online military codes" are not supported by Old Navy or any verification provider and should be treated as false.

Because the program isn’t published on Old Navy’s website, the figure and all terms rest on secondary military-discount directories (military.com and Veteran.com) — treat the existence and exact terms as medium confidence and confirm at your store. Veteran.com notes the discount is "generally brand wide, but some Gap brand stores may not participate," so it is best to ask when you visit.
netgear-military-discount: NETGEAR verifies eligibility through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA and the IRS. You verify once through your free ID.me account by confirming your status; ID.me may require re-verification periodically under its own policies. Support runs through ID.me for verification issues and NETGEAR customer service for order issues. All seven eligible audiences receive the same 10%/$100 offer — there is no larger military-only tier.

Do the math before you verify. The 10% is capped at $100, so on expensive Orbi-class mesh systems the discount stops growing right when the price gets serious. NETGEAR’s own public promos, retailer sales at Amazon and Best Buy, and the NETGEAR refurbished / Amazon Renewed channel frequently beat a capped 10% — and if you have base access, an Exchange purchase (AAFES/NEX/MCX) is tax-free, which can beat 10% on its own once sales tax is counted.

One thing to watch: coupon and aggregator sites variously claim a "15% military discount," a "single-item only" restriction, and stackable "promo codes." None of these are confirmed on NETGEAR’s or ID.me’s primary pages. The only figure both primary sources support is 10% off, up to $100, via ID.me — treat any 15% or "single-item" claim as unverified.
shedd-aquarium-military-discount: Shedd verifies on site with a valid military ID — there's no third-party online provider (no ID.me or SheerID) for this benefit. Active-duty members show proper ID for free year-round admission; Blue Star guests present a CAC, DD Form 1173/1173-1, or a Next-Generation Uniformed Services (Real) ID. Gold Star families show an Illinois driver's license or state ID with the Gold Star designation. Reserve a timed ticket in advance (online or at 312-939-2438) — free slots are in high demand.

Blue Star Museums is a national summer program: at Shedd it runs May 16 through September 7, 2026, and covers currently serving members of the Army, Marine Corps, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, and Coast Guard, plus the Reserve, National Guard, and the U.S. PHS and NOAA Commissioned Corps — each with up to 5 family members. It is not a year-round family benefit, and it excludes veterans and retirees by design. Dates reset annually, so confirm each spring at arts.gov.

Coupon sites imply a broad "Shedd Aquarium military discount" or a percentage off for veterans. What Shedd actually publishes is free admission for active duty — self year-round, plus 5 guests during Blue Star — not a veteran or retiree discount. A veteran's real levers are Illinois Resident Free Hours (free general admission on select dates for any Illinois resident), Museums for All (discounted admission with an EBT card, up to 4 tickets), or a CityPASS/Go City bundle worth up to roughly 50% off versus buying attractions separately.

For context on what the free ticket is worth: non-resident adult general admission runs roughly $40.95 with date-based plan-ahead pricing, while Chicago residents pay a flat $19.95. Admission isn't sales-taxed here, and the free routes are alternatives rather than stackable discounts — pick the one route that fits your status for each visit.
bambu-lab-military-discount: Bambu Lab is a direct-to-consumer manufacturer that discounts through sitewide sale events and a rewards ecosystem — not through audience-gated codes. That is why there is no military-verification flow: the deepest, most reliable savings are the seasonal sale prices, which apply automatically to every shopper. If you can time your purchase to the Anniversary Sale or Black Friday, that price beats any military percentage a coupon site claims.

Be cautious of aggregators advertising a specific Bambu Lab "military discount" — you’ll find the same brand listed at 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, even 50% across different sites. Those contradictory figures are the tell of fabricated coupon-affiliate content. Bambu Lab publishes no brand-run military rate, so entering any "military code" at checkout will simply fail. We omit the circulating numbers here on purpose, because repeating them would imply an offer Bambu does not run.

The real stack, if you’re buying now and no sale is live, is: pick the printer+AMS Combo bundle (its own SKU, roughly $50–$150 cheaper than buying the AMS separately), apply any MakerWorld gift-card credit you’ve earned (points redeem for Bambu store gift cards, commonly in $40 tiers, that act as store credit on top of a sale price), and check the permanent /collections/sale page. MakerWorld and gift-card mechanics are community-reported, so confirm they apply on your cart.

Bambu Lab does run a student/education track — an education store collection and Student Kits, with SheerID student verification referenced by third parties — but the exact discount percentage is not confirmed from a Bambu primary source, and it is an academic program, not a military benefit. There is also a tax-exempt account, but that is for education, non-profit, and business organizations by application, not for individual service members.
halloween-horror-nights-military-discoun: The eligibility list is broadest at Universal Orlando, which names active duty, Reserve, National Guard, retirees, 100% Disabled Veterans, DoD Civilians, and spouses of active/retired members. Universal Studios Hollywood’s listing includes veterans more broadly and gives "two easy ways to purchase: online once identity is verified or at your local military base." For HHN event tickets specifically, confirm dependent coverage at the point of sale, since the daytime Freedom Pass terms (up to 6 tickets per member, blockout dates) do not automatically carry over to the separate HHN ticket.

The genuine channels are base ITT offices and GovX. GovX runs dedicated HHN venue pages — Orlando venue 35737 and Hollywood venue 35738 — verified through GovX ID for military, first-responder, and government communities, and ID.me also lists a Universal Studios Hollywood military offer. The military price is a channel-specific price, not a stackable code, so you buy through one channel or the other rather than layering it on a Universal cart.

Because Universal fixes no public HHN military percentage, the smartest move is to compare. Standard single-night gate prices run about $89.99 (value nights) to $129.99 (peak Saturdays) pre-tax, and authorized resellers such as Undercover Tourist list single nights from around $78 — which frequently beats the undocumented military price with no verification. If you’re attending two or more nights, a public multi-night or Frequent Fear pass usually beats any single-night discount, military or not.
north-face-military-discount: The North Face uses SheerID as its verification partner. Online, you click "Verify Military Status," then submit details such as your name, branch of service, current affiliation, and discharge date if applicable. A successful online verification produces a single-use promo code; for in-store purchases, verification is done at the register by showing a valid military ID.

The discount works at both full-price stores and outlets and is United States only. The single most important caveat is that it is not a permanent saved discount — each code is single-use, and you may verify once every 30 days to get a new code, so plan one qualifying order per code.

Some aggregator and editorial pages say verification runs through "SheerID or ID.me." The North Face’s own military discount page names SheerID only, and the "Verify Military Status" button points to a SheerID URL — so SheerID is the confirmed provider, and we do not assert ID.me. For verification problems, The North Face points to SheerID support.
aulani-military-discount: Verification is manual and in-person: a valid military ID (CAC, retiree ID, or eligible dependent/spouse ID) shown at the front desk. There is no ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute account involved, and no code to enter online. Because the check happens at check-in, an ineligible booking can be re-priced to rack rate on arrival — so only book it if you can present a qualifying ID, and the eligible member or spouse must be staying in a room on the reservation.

The discount is seasonal and tiered. For 2026 the windows ran up to 25% off in winter (stays Jan 4 – Apr 9), up to 30% off in spring (Apr 10 – Jun 12) and late summer (Aug 9 – Oct 18), and up to 35% off in the fall/holiday window (Oct 19 – Dec 23). The peak-summer gap (roughly mid-June to early August) typically has no military window. Stays must be 2+ consecutive nights, are capped at two rooms/villas per reservation, and cannot be combined with any other room or villa discount — the resort fee, Hawaii taxes, and parking are charged on top of every rate and are not discounted.

On value, the military rate is usually the best easy win for a standard hotel room (30% in the current late-summer window). For a Deluxe Studio or 1-bedroom villa, though, renting DVC points through a broker (David’s Vacation Club Rentals, DVC Shop) frequently beats even a 35% Disney discount — a ~$700/night rack studio can rent for roughly $425–$500/night via points. Disney Visa cardholder offers (up to 30–35%) can rival the military rate on longer stays, but mind their 4–5 night minimums. Book early in each seasonal window, because the military allocation is limited and sells out.
home-chef-military-discount: ID.me confirms your group during signup — or, for existing customers, from the payment page of your account. Home Chef doesn’t state a re-verification cadence; the discount is described as applying to future orders once verified ("lifetime"), and verification support runs through ID.me. Note that some listings mention SheerID, but Home Chef’s official Heroes page names ID.me only.

Here’s the fork that matters: Heroes vs. the public "18 Free Meals" intro, and they’re either/or — Home Chef applies one signup promotion. On a standard 4-meal, 2-serving weekly box (≈$80), both paths land your first box around $40. But the public intro exhausts after roughly your first four boxes, while Heroes keeps paying 10% plus a free item on every box. Over a year of weekly boxes (~$4,160 list), Heroes works out to roughly $3,784 versus about $3,950–$4,000 on the public intro. Any verified hero who subscribes more than a couple of months comes out ahead with Heroes; a strict trial-and-cancel shopper who’ll quit by about week five should compare both signup screens first.

One thing to watch: coupon sites headline "75% off Home Chef promo codes." The verified official offers are the Heroes 50%-first-box/10%-lifetime deal and the public 18-Free-Meals intro (≈50% off early boxes) — inflated stacked percentages are marketing math on multi-box totals, not a real code.

Two more routes exist, and neither beats Heroes. WeSalute runs a parallel Home Chef offer (50% off the first box + 10% recurring), but it’s for paid WeSalute+ members only and is explicitly non-combinable — never pay for WeSalute+ just for this, because Heroes gives the same thing free. USAA members can also check the member-gated Home Chef offer at usaa.com/perks and compare. And Home Chef is Kroger-owned, so you’ll see its kits on Kroger-family shelves — but that retail channel carries no verification and no Heroes pricing.
simms-military-discount: Simms uses ID.me at checkout for the consumer military/first-responder discount, applied by selecting the military/first-responder option and verifying — it is a per-order verification, not a reusable public code. ExpertVoice independently verifies pros, military, and first responders for a separate (often deeper) pricing tier.

Verified discounts generally will not stack on already-discounted closeout/sale items, so on this brand the public sale can be the better deal — compare the ID.me price against the current sale price on the same SKU before committing. ExpertVoice pricing is separate from the ID.me consumer discount — you buy through one channel or the other, not both.

Aggregator claims of "up to 50% off sitewide" or "10–25% military" are unverified — the ID.me discount value is not publicly stated and is unlocked only after verification. Simms gear also appears in GovX’s fishing category as an alternative.
georgia-aquarium-military-discount: Georgia Aquarium verifies eligibility two ways: in person with a valid government-issued Military ID, or online through ID.me. The Aquarium notes that setting up an ID.me account takes about 5–10 minutes and can be reused for future visits and at other ID.me businesses. For Military Memberships, you will still be asked to show your Military ID when you arrive to redeem.

The Aquarium’s official Military Appreciation Days page names ID.me as its online verification platform. Georgia Aquarium also appears on GovX, but the Aquarium’s own pages direct online verification to ID.me; treat GovX listings as secondary.

Military Appreciation Days fall on select dates each year. The dates published for 2026 were May 16 and May 25 (both now past as of June 23, 2026), so check the official page for newly announced dates before planning a free-admission visit.
pit-boss-military-discount: The 25% applies only to non-discounted items on pitboss-grills.com; it is direct-to-consumer only, so the code cannot be used at Walmart, Lowe’s, Academy, Costco, or other retailers that also sell Pit Boss.

Pit Boss uses both ID.me and GovX as verification partners. You create a free account, confirm your military/veteran/first-responder status, and receive a single-use code. Re-verification cadence follows the provider’s rules; support runs through ID.me/GovX and Pit Boss customer service. You do not need both providers — either yields the same 25%.

If a grill is already discounted on the DTC site (Heroes blocked) or on a deeper clearance elsewhere, price-check the same model at a big-box retailer — a steeper closeout can occasionally beat 25%. Otherwise, the Heroes 25% on a full-price grill is the ceiling for most buyers.
breeze-military-discount: The fare discount is verified through WeSalute, not ID.me, GovX, or SheerID. You create a WeSalute account (the free tier qualifies), confirm your status, and receive a unique WeSalute code to use each time you book Breeze. Book a new round-trip reservation on flybreeze.com or in the Breeze app at least 7 days before travel and apply the code — it takes 15% off the base fare and is not retroactive. WeSalute sets the eligible groups: active duty, veterans, National Guard/Reserve, and immediate family.

The active-duty baggage benefit is a separate, self-serve program with no code. Active-duty U.S. military traveling for leisure get one carry-on plus two checked bags free; active duty traveling on orders get one carry-on plus up to five checked bags free — each military checked bag allowed up to 99 lbs and 80 linear inches with no oversize or overweight charge. The allowance is claimed at the ticket counter with a valid military ID (re-checked at the gate for the free carry-on and courtesy preboarding), and it is explicitly not available to veterans, retirees, ROTC, spouses, or dependents.

Because the two benefits are independent, an active-duty member can stack them: book the fare with a WeSalute code for 15% off and still claim free bags at the counter. On an orders move with multiple heavy bags, the bag waiver alone can be worth more than the fare discount. For everyone else, the 15% is the only military-specific lever — but compare it against a live public Breeze seat sale first, since Breeze runs frequent sales, the 15% is off base fare only, and its combinability with sale fares is not published.

Treat the numbers here as a starting point. The WeSalute offer has carried a limited booking window that renews over time, and Breeze controls the bag allowance and its counts. Confirm the current WeSalute booking window and the live Breeze support-page terms before you buy.
top-of-the-rock-military-discount: The only discounts Rockefeller Center itself publishes for Top of the Rock are open to everyone: group sales for parties of 10 or more, a seasonal weekday kids 50%-off promo (code SPRINGKIDS50, paired with an adult or senior ticket), and bundle products — the All-In Pass and Express Pass, plus third-party city passes that include the observation deck. None of these is military-gated, and there is no ID.me, GovX, or SheerID verification anywhere in the ticket flow.

About that widely-quoted "$17 military ticket": multiple coupon and military-discount sites state a firm box-office price, but none of it appears on Rockefeller Center’s own site, the figures disagree ($17 vs. $20 + tax), and the most-cited source — JustForMilitary.com — is now a parked, for-sale domain. There may well be a discretionary military rate at the physical box office, and a Tripadvisor review reports one, but the honest treatment is: reported, unverified, call ahead. If it’s honored, reports also say it’s in-person only and not combinable with passes or promo codes.

For a service member buying online, the real levers are timing and bundling. Timed admission uses "from" pricing that varies by date and time, so an off-peak slot is the cheapest single-ticket path. For a multi-attraction NYC trip, a city pass drops the per-attraction cost sharply — usually further than any single-ticket saving. All bookings carry Rockefeller Center’s sitewide terms: reschedule up to 24 hours ahead, no hidden fees.
volvo-military-discount: Verification is handled by ID.me — the same identity provider Volvo uses across its affinity tiers (healthcare, first responder, teacher). After you verify, Volvo issues a PIN tied to your address, and the dealer redeems it. The PIN is time-boxed to a 90-day delivery window, so generate it close to when you’ll actually buy, and note the limit of one PIN per vehicle and two PINs per participant per year.

The $500 is a flat affinity bonus, not a percentage off MSRP. Unlike a "can’t combine" retail coupon, it’s designed to combine with most publicly advertised Volvo national offers, and the dealer applies it at signing. If you also qualify for another affinity group — healthcare, first responder, or teacher — compare which bonus is larger, because you generally use only one affinity PIN per deal.

On a roughly $46,000 vehicle, the $500 is meaningful but small next to the real levers: negotiating the vehicle price and timing your purchase to strong national APR, lease, or cash offers (model-year closeout in summer and fall is often best). Do that first, then add the $500 military bonus on top. Some directory pages imply a percentage-based "Volvo military discount" — that is unverified; the confirmed benefit is the flat $500.
new-era-military-discount: The most authoritative provider signal confirms there is no New Era offer: ID.me’s New Era page states, verbatim, that it is "not aware of New Era offering Military community discounts," and invites shoppers to request that New Era join. New Era is not enrolled with ID.me or SheerID for a military offer, and there is no New Era-branded storefront on GOVX. In other words, there is no New Era military code to enter or stack anywhere — the question is moot at neweracap.com.

Because New Era does not run a discount, the real move is to buy the same New Era cap from a retailer that does. Lids sells New Era 59FIFTY MLB and NFL caps and gives verified military members and first responders 15% off, confirmed through its checkout verification (ID.me/GovX). On a typical ~$44.99 59FIFTY fitted cap, that 15% brings the price to roughly $38.24 — usually the best military-priced route to a New Era cap. Other New Era retailers such as Hat Club also advertise a military/first-responder discount; compare before paying full price.

Direct from New Era, the honest levers are open to everyone, not just the military community: a 10% email/SMS welcome offer on a full-price style (roughly $40.49 on the baseline cap), the free VIP Club (1 point per $1, 200 points = $10, plus free shipping on all tiers), and the 59FIFTY Sale and seasonal events like the Memorial Day and Black Friday sales. On a marked-down style, those public sale prices — often 20–50%+ off — frequently beat any 15% military discount, and none of them require verification.

GOVX rounds out the picture as a check-it-last option. It is a closed verification marketplace that occasionally lists New Era caps through third-party brand storefronts (for example, an ASRV 59FIFTY listing) rather than a dedicated New Era store. The selection rotates and is limited, so treat GOVX as worth a look only when the specific New Era cap you want happens to be listed for verified members, and compare its member price against Lids-minus-15%.
adidas-military-discount: adidas verifies eligibility through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. You create a free ID.me account and confirm your community — Military, First Responder, Teacher, Nurse, Medical Provider, Hospital Employee, or Senior 65+. Online, you click "Verify with ID.me" at checkout and the discount applies automatically; for stores and factory outlets, you verify through adidas’s ID.me hosted pages and receive a unique code to use at the register.

adidas does not publish a re-verification cadence; under ID.me’s own policies, some community statuses may expire over time and require re-verification. For verification problems, adidas directs shoppers to ID.me support. The redemption caps are monthly — online max 2/month, in store max 1/month, and factory outlet max 1/month — not a per-customer or lifetime limit.

A few claims circulating on aggregator and coupon sites are not on adidas’s official page: that the offer is verified by SheerID, that there is a $250 savings cap or "one use per customer," that it expires 12/31/2026, or that you show a military ID at the register. adidas’s page specifies ID.me, monthly caps, an ID.me in-store verification link (not a physical ID), and no dollar/expiry cap. The factory-outlet percentage is also not published by adidas, so we don’t state one.
nintendo-military-discount: There is no Nintendo military verification because there is no program to verify. Eligibility only comes up at the Exchange (verified once at shopmyexchange.com or mynavyexchange.com against DoD/veteran status) or, for GameStop’s separate in-store 10%, at the register with a military ID or DD-214. Console MSRP is uniform across Best Buy, Amazon, Walmart, Target, Costco, and GameStop, so the only real differentiator on hardware is the Exchange’s tax exemption.

On digital software, My Nintendo Gold Points are the everyday edge: you earn 5% back on digital eShop purchases and 1% on registered physical games, redeemable at 1 point = 1¢ toward future digital games. Points expire 12 months after you earn them and can’t be used to renew an active Switch Online membership, so treat them as a running rebate on your next game rather than a way to zero out a purchase.

Two stale claims to ignore: the flat “Nintendo 30% / 50% off military” codes and “SCORBUNNY” on coupon sites are fabricated (SCORBUNNY was a Pokémon promo, not a military code), and a “GovX Nintendo” storefront is third-party marketplace inventory, not a Nintendo-authorized military price. The steady, verifiable savings are the tax-free Exchange on hardware and Gold Points plus eShop sales on digital.
marc-jacobs-military-discount: The honest picture: ID.me expressly reports no Marc Jacobs military program, and no Marc Jacobs-controlled page confirms one. So the coupon-site claims of a “Marc Jacobs military discount 70% OFF,” a “HALFOFF” code, or a “20% veteran code” are fabricated — we don’t repeat them. The only verified military-linked savings are the three partner channels.

Each channel works differently. WeSalute+’s My Bag offer is about 15% off full-price Marc Jacobs but excludes sale items, gift vouchers, and certain brands, and it routes to a UK/EU designer retailer, so shipping, currency, and stock differ from marcjacobs.com. GovX is a verified military/government marketplace with member pricing that varies by item. The Veterans Canteen Service (ShopVCS) sells select items to veterans, VA employees, and families — and is the one channel with a potential sales-tax advantage.

Because these are closed marketplaces or partner offers, none stacks with a marcjacobs.com public code, and there’s no Marc Jacobs military code anywhere. The smart move: for a current full-price item, WeSalute My Bag’s 15% (if you’re a member and it’s stocked); if you’re VA-eligible, check ShopVCS first for price plus tax; and for anything on sale or past-season, a Marc Jacobs or off-price retailer markdown usually wins.
little-caesars-military-discount: The one verified, brand-official military benefit is the annual Veterans Day free HOT-N-READY Lunch Combo — four slices of Detroit-style Deep Dish plus a 20-oz Pepsi — served on November 11 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. at participating U.S. stores to veterans and active-duty military only. It needs no coupon; you simply show proof of service. Little Caesars has run this offer annually since 2006 (19 straight years through 2025), inspired by founder Mike Ilitch’s Marine Corps service. Family members are not covered, and stores can sell out, so arrive early in the window.

Because Little Caesars is a franchise brand, pricing is set store-by-store. Some individual operators may honor a small everyday military courtesy discount (community-reported around 10%) with a military ID, but many will not — it is entirely operator discretion and not corporate policy. Ask before ordering and treat any "yes" as a bonus, not a plan.

Be cautious of coupon aggregators that claim Little Caesars gives "10%," "up to 10%–25%," or an online military discount you "verify with SheerID/ID.me at littlecaesars.com." All of that is fabricated boilerplate: Little Caesars publishes no percentage, SheerID does not list Little Caesars, the ID.me "Caesars" pages are the casino company (Caesars Entertainment), and GovX "Little Caesars" results are Little Caesars Arena event tickets in Detroit. None is a pizza military discount.

The genuine year-round best-savings path is open to everyone: the Little Caesars mobile app. Its in-app "Challenges" rewards and coupon codes (like free Crazy Bread with a pizza) beat any of the phantom "military" percentages. On base, some AAFES/MWR food-court Little Caesars locations exist, but pricing there is set by the on-base operator and is not a military discount.
spirit-halloween-military-discount: The online flow, as shoppers and aggregators consistently describe it, is: select "Military and First Responder Discount" at checkout, verify, and receive a one-time 10% code; in-store you simply show a valid ID at the register. The reported percentage is consistently 10% across community and editorial write-ups — the outlier 15% and 25% claims trace to coupon sites, not to Spirit’s own FAQ.

On the verification provider: aggregators name "SheerID or ID.me," but ID.me’s own Spirit Halloween page states it is "not aware" of a Spirit military discount, which points to SheerID as the live provider. Because that isn’t confirmed from a first-party read, this guide does not assert a specific verifier — confirm the exact provider on the live checkout when the season opens. In-store verification needs no third-party account: you present a valid ID at the register.

The maximum-savings reality is that 10% is small for this brand.
