In-season public sitewide codes (often 20%+) and post-Halloween clearance (up to roughly 50%+ off) usually beat the identity discount and are open to everyone, and a cashback portal like Rakuten (~2%) only tracks reliably on a plain, no-code order. Spirit Halloween isn’t carried at the military Exchange and has no GovX storefront, so those money-savers don’t apply here.
panera-military-discount: Panera’s own help center addresses whether it offers discounts to veterans or seniors and points to no standing national offer, and Panera is not listed as a partner on any military verification marketplace. Multiple news reports (2022–2025) document its recurring Veterans Day freebie, but even that is franchisee-driven and location-dependent — largely a Covelli Enterprises program in regions such as Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Florida — so it is best described as "participating locations only."

The Veterans Day offer is a free bagel or bakery item plus one regular hot or iced coffee on November 11, redeemed in-café by wearing a uniform or showing a Military ID or discharge papers. It excludes loaves of bread, cannot be combined with any other offer, and is not valid on Rapid Pick-Up, delivery, or online ordering. It is a once-a-year bonus worth roughly the price of a bagel and a coffee, not a savings strategy.

For everyday savings, the biggest lever is the Unlimited Sip Club: unlimited drip coffee, iced coffee, hot tea, fountain soda, and select Charged Sips (once every 2 hours) for $14.99/month or $119.99/year, with promotional rates seen at $5/month for the first 3 months or about $89/year with code USC2025. Espresso drinks, smoothies, Energy Refreshers, and customizations carry upcharges. Pair it with free MyPanera Rewards — the two stack, since the Sip Club runs on your MyPanera account and you still earn and redeem personalized food rewards.

Be cautious of a five-year-old community Q&A claiming Panera gives "10%… 15%" around November. That is a single unverified anecdote and does not reflect any national Panera policy; a Tripadvisor report even describes a café declining a military discount, consistent with there being no national program. We deliberately omit any percentage figure because repeating it would imply an everyday offer Panera does not run. If a local café extends a discretionary courtesy, treat it as a lucky bonus, not something you can count on.
jay-peak-military-discount: The military season pass and Canadian 50% day ticket are standalone rates — treat them as the final price, not a code stacked on a public ticket. The season pass pays for itself in roughly two days against a single weekend window ticket ($139).

Verification is in person, not through ID.me, GovX, or SheerID. Jay Peak checks physical documents at Tramside Guest Services (US) or at each location (Canada). US applicants need orders showing a Vermont base assignment plus military and Vermont ID.

On top of the pass, US active-duty can add 50% off rentals and the Pump House waterpark and 10% off lodging packages. Jay Peak also participates in Ski Vermont’s Mission Affordable low-cost access program (an affordability program, not military-only).
vineyard-vines-military-discount: Vineyard Vines routes online eligibility through SheerID. You submit your credentials once; SheerID confirms your military (or first-responder, healthcare, teacher, or student) status and emails you a one-time 15% code, limited to one code per eligible person every 30 days. There is no confirmed GovX, ID.me, or WeSalute path for Vineyard Vines — SheerID is the named partner.

In full-line stores, a military ID at the register substitutes for online verification. Outlet stores are excluded from the discount entirely — the code works only on vineyardvines.com, at full-line retail stores, and by phone.

Because the 15% is full-price merchandise only, a live sale (up to 70% off sale styles) usually beats it and won’t stack with it — so during a real Vineyard Vines sale, buy the marked-down price instead of using your code.
lifetime-fitness-military-discount: The benefit is documented from Life Time’s May 2019 press release, which announced a standing, preferred military rate: 50% off standard initiation fees for all active and retired military and all veterans, including Reserve and National Guard, extended to military personnel and family members in their immediate household, and to Life Time’s Canadian clubs and the Canadian armed forces. It is a discount on the initiation/enrollment fee — not monthly dues — so the real dollar value depends entirely on your club’s current enrollment fee.

Verification is in person at the club. A membership advisor checks your military ID or DD-214; there is no ID.me, SheerID, or GovX verification for Life Time. This is the key debunk: aggregators claim you can "authenticate through ID.me" to claim the discount, but ID.me’s own Life Time page states it is not aware of a Life Time military discount through ID.me. Verify at the club instead.

Two practical cautions. Life Time no longer maintains a live military web page — the old /military-discount.html URL 404s — so confirm the offer is still current with the club before joining. And because Life Time periodically runs public "join" promotions that reduce or even waive initiation for everyone, compare the military rate against any live public promo and take whichever removes more of the fee; don’t assume they stack.
chewy-military-discount: Coupon and aggregator pages advertise a "Chewy military discount — 30–40% off your first Autoship, 5% recurring, free shipping over $49." That is not a military discount: it is Chewy’s ordinary public new-customer Autoship offer that anyone gets without verifying service. Chewy’s own FAQ and ID.me both confirm there is no military, veteran, or senior program, and older sitewide codes like 20OFF, SAVE30, and FREESHIP are dead.

Because there is no identity discount, there is nothing to verify — no ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute path beats the public deal. If a third-party portal ever surfaces a "Chewy military offer" (often around military holidays), expect it to gate the same public first-Autoship offer behind a verification step; verify only if you would want that public deal anyway, because it will not beat it.

The real max-savings play for a service member is the public first-Autoship discount (up to 40%, commonly ~$20-capped), ideally started through Rakuten for about 2% cashback, plus the $20 WELCOME eGift on a first $49+ order. Chewy is online-only, so for a physical, tax-free option on staples like food and litter, the base commissary or exchange pet aisle is worth a price-check against Chewy’s delivered price.
arlo-military-discount: Arlo verifies eligibility through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. You sign in or create a free ID.me account, verify your military status, and the discount applies at Arlo.com checkout. Re-verification follows ID.me’s standard cadence.

The standout feature is that Arlo’s ID.me storefront states the 15% applies to "all full priced and sale items" — so it can stack on Arlo’s own sale prices, a genuine advantage most brand military discounts don’t offer. It won’t stack with a separate promo code, so you can’t layer an extra coupon, but buying during a hardware sale is the best-value move. WorthEPenny and other aggregators advertise "25% Off Arlo Military," but the verified figure on Arlo’s own ID.me storefront is 15% — the 25% claim is unverified inflation.

The consistent community complaint is the subscription. Arlo Community threads repeatedly note there is no military discount on Arlo Secure ("MILITARY DISCOUNT YEARLY SUBSCRIPTIONS," "no military discount"), which corroborates the hardware-only scope. Budget the subscription separately at full price, and compare Arlo’s sale-plus-15% against Amazon or Best Buy pricing — a deep third-party sale can sometimes beat it.
huckberry-military-discount: Huckberry uses ID.me’s Troop ID to confirm your US military status. You verify once, and the discount then attaches to your account for future orders. The critical requirement is that your Huckberry account email and ID.me email are identical — the system can’t match you otherwise. ID.me may periodically ask you to re-verify per its own policies, and support runs through Huckberry’s help center and ID.me’s 24/7 support.

Because the 10% doesn’t stack, the honest best-savings question is when it wins. On full-price goods — Huckberry’s in-house Proof and Flint & Tinder lines and new arrivals that rarely discount — the military 10% is the top lever. When your size and style are in the rotating "Last Call" clearance, the sale price routinely beats 10%, and you can’t add the military discount anyway, so buy the clearance price instead.

Public seasonal sales (Memorial Day editor’s picks, Black Friday / Cyber Monday) run alongside the evergreen 10% but never combine with it — pick the larger discount for a given item. New customers can also compare a first-order newsletter code against the 10%, but those don’t stack either.
ll-bean-military-discount: Verification is handled by SheerID, not L.L.Bean directly. You submit basic personal info and, if not instantly verified, upload official government-issued documentation showing your first name, last name, branch of service, and current military status. SheerID matches the document against your form entry, so enter your name exactly as it appears on the document. If your last name changed since the document was issued, upload an additional government ID showing your current name.

Once verified, you get a code valid for five uses; re-verify after five uses or if you lose the code, and eligible individuals may receive up to 3 verification codes every 30 days. The offer terms currently state it is valid until August 24, 2026 — historically L.L.Bean renews these windows, but treat it as a dated/renewable promotion and re-verify after that date.

Because the discount excludes so many name brands, it functionally applies to L.L.Bean’s own-label products; for excluded gear, L.L.Bean’s frequent sales and Outlet pricing often beat the 10%. L.L.Bean also runs separate 10% SheerID offers for first responders, medical professionals, and students/teachers.
wayfair-military-discount: There is no military verification step at Wayfair because there is no military discount. ID.me powers community discounts for many retailers, but its Wayfair page explicitly says it is "not aware of Wayfair offering Military community discounts," and it invites shoppers to submit feedback asking Wayfair to partner. If Wayfair launches a verified offer in the future, expect it to run through a provider like ID.me with annual re-verification — but that does not exist today.

Be cautious of coupon sites advertising a "Wayfair 10% military discount" or "up to 50% off for first responders" — those are not supported by any Wayfair or ID.me primary source and typically don’t work. The legitimate levers are sitewide sale events (open to all) and Wayfair Rewards.

Wayfair does support the military community — but as charity, not a discount: it partners with Homes For Our Troops and reports contributing more than $1 million and partnering on the nonprofit’s 300th adapted home. Shoppers who specifically want a verified military discount may find one at a competing home/furniture brand; verify current terms on each brand’s official page.
nightforce-military-discount: Nightforce routes its individual discount through ExpertVoice. You create a free ExpertVoice account and verify your eligibility (military, law enforcement, fire/EMS, or government) once — a work or service email helps, or you upload an accepted document. Documents are encrypted and deleted after review; some applications take up to three business days. There is no confirmed ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute route for Nightforce — ExpertVoice is the named partner.

Because Nightforce enforces a minimum advertised price and publishes no percentage, the ExpertVoice member price is the only real "military" number — and it’s login-gated and modest. Verified shooters report single-to-low-double-digit savings off street price on many models, not the flat 30–60% aggregators claim, and ExpertVoice charges sales tax while an out-of-state authorized dealer may not.

For many buyers the smartest move is a dealer demo or like-new unit of the same model: it keeps the full transferable Limited Lifetime Warranty, carries no eligibility gate, and frequently comes in below the ExpertVoice price. Units and agencies, by contrast, buy direct from Nightforce via federal SAM registration (CAGE 1SLF0) for duty equipment — an institutional path, not a personal discount.
adventure-island-military-discount: Aggregator coupon sites list an "Adventure Island military discount" implying free or 50%-off water-park single-day tickets like Busch Gardens gets. That’s wrong — Waves of Honor’s free single-day admission and the 50%-off single-day tickets are for Busch Gardens Tampa Bay and SeaWorld parks, not Adventure Island. The water park is included only inside the Military Silver Annual Pass, which covers both parks for 12 months.

Verification runs through ID.me on buschgardens.com/tampa. Veterans upload a DD214, a driver’s license or state ID with a veteran endorsement, or an Honorable Discharge Certificate; active-duty members (including activated or drilling reservists and National Guard) verify their service status. The pass must be purchased online — it’s not sold at the park — and a photo ID is checked at entry. Adventure Island doesn’t run a separate verification for a standalone discount because none exists.

Eligibility is strict: the active-duty offers exclude inactive, standby, and retired reserve, military retirees, DoD civilians, and U.S. Merchant Marine, while the veteran pass covers active, retired, and honorably separated personnel. Each eligible buyer can purchase up to six passes, and spouses access guest tickets and family passes by logging in under the service member’s or veteran’s ID.me account.

Timing notes: Busch Gardens runs annual Waves of Honor enrollment windows (free single-day Busch Gardens/SeaWorld admission for active-duty, registered via ID.me each program year), and a 2026 limited-time veteran offer of up to 4 free Busch Gardens tickets — obtain by July 5, 2026, use by July 31, 2026 — with 4 more if unredeemed. Adventure Island’s inclusion in that veteran promo is not confirmed, and the park has only historically run occasional service-member promos, so treat anything beyond the annual pass as verify-live.
dish-network-military-discount: The offer is essentially free value stacked on a normal plan. DISH advertises it against America’s Top 120 at $89.99/mo on a 2-year agreement, and the bundle adds the Stars & Stripes Pack (American Heroes, Smithsonian, Crime & Investigation, Destination America, Get TV, The Cowboy Channel, Reelz, STARZ Encore), a free On Demand movie rental each billing month from 20,000+ titles, a Hopper DVR upgrade that streams local content to mobile via DISH Anywhere, and a 2-year price guarantee. DISH sums it up as "more than $500 in value over two years."

Coupon and retailer pages describe the discount as "$10 off for 25 months" or "up to 10%–25% off." DISH’s own military page states none of that — it presents the offer as a free value bundle, not a rate cut. Many "DISH military discount" pages are DISH Authorized Retailers (usdish.com, infinitydish.com, planetdish.com, allamericandish.com), not DISH corporate; they may add their own signup gift-card bonuses but can also restate terms loosely, so verify the live offer at dish.com or with the retailer before ordering.

Verification runs through SheerID or ID.me online, or a military ID in store. SheerID checks your name, branch, and status against authoritative data — usually instant — while ID.me authenticates an uploaded military or veteran ID. We found no evidence DISH uses GovX, WeSalute, or VerifyPass for this offer.

One deployment tip that isn’t part of the military offer: DISH’s Pause / seasonal hold suspends service for roughly one to nine months at about $5/mo while you keep your equipment and account — useful during a deployment or long absence. Call DISH to set it up. And skip premium or add-on channels you won’t watch: they’re excluded from the 2-year price guarantee and drive the bill up.
rockettes-military-discount: GovX and ID.me verify military/government status with a free account; Vet Tix independently verifies service members and veterans. Each provider governs re-verification and support, and the show itself does not verify at the box office for a discount.

Military marketplace pricing (GovX/ID.me) does not combine with public Broadway promo codes — you pick one channel per purchase. Vet Tix tickets carry only a delivery fee and cannot be combined with other discounts.

Verified pricing is inventory- and date-specific, so the same "discount" varies performance to performance. Aggregator claims of a "certkid" code for "50% off" are generic coupon claims, not an official military offer — the verified paths are ID.me Shop, GovX, and Vet Tix.
jackery-military-discount: Jackery uses ID.me as its primary verification partner (a parallel SheerID-based “Service Discount” page also exists). You create a free ID.me account, verify your military, first-responder, medical, or teacher status once, and receive a discount code to apply at checkout. Verification follows the provider’s process — nothing about it is more permanent than ID.me’s own re-verification rules — and the same 15% applies across all the eligible communities.

The catch that makes this page worth more than a coupon page is the stacking rule: Jackery’s promo page states the 15% “cannot be combined” with other promotions, and special collaborations are excluded entirely. Because the 15% is non-combinable and Jackery’s public sales run deep (30–50%), the public sale is frequently the better single path — you choose one, not both.

So the verdict is situational. If a 30%+ sitewide sale is live (Prime Day in July, Black Friday/Cyber Monday, or a seasonal event), take the public sale price — it usually beats your 15%. Between sales, on a full-price unit, use your ID.me 15%. And if you’re flexible on condition, check Jackery’s official refurbished/outlet stock against the 15%. Ignore any aggregator “Jackery military promo code” — the only verified military route is the ID.me 15% on Jackery’s own site.
quince-military-discount: Verification is handled by ID.me, a third-party identity/affiliation service. You create or sign in to a free ID.me account and prove your group affiliation (military status is checked against records or a .mil email; spouses/dependents upload documents). On success, you receive a one-time code for 10% off your first Quince purchase. ID.me, not Quince, controls your ID.me account. Because this is a one-time, first-purchase code, ongoing re-verification is not applicable.

Quince’s own page does not enumerate military sub-groups — it links ID.me’s eligibility criteria, so coverage for active duty, veterans, retirees, Guard/Reserve, spouses, and dependents is governed by ID.me’s military verification. Quince specifies "nurses" among healthcare workers; broader medical roles are not named.

Since the offer is new-customers-only and one-time, plan to use your single first-purchase code on a larger qualifying order, then rely on Quince’s standing markdowns ("Everyday Steals"), referrals, or seasonal sales afterward. Government employees and students are not listed as eligible for this offer.
ncl-military-discount: NCL uses ID.me, a third-party verification service. You must create a free My NCL account and verify your military status through ID.me before booking to receive the discount — verification is described by NCL as a one-time step ("You won’t ever need to verify again"). After verifying and while logged in, your 10% appears automatically in checkout pricing. If you have trouble enrolling, NCL provides a support path in its FAQ. (ID.me itself may have its own account and re-authentication requirements; this reflects only what NCL states about NCL-side verification.)

Two things to keep straight on value. First, the 10% applies to the cruise fare portion only, so taxes, fees, and onboard charges aren’t discounted. Second, be skeptical of the "20% off select cruises" figure that circulates on third-party sites — it isn’t in NCL’s own verified FAQ copy, so treat 10% as the confirmed number. On the plus side, NCL states the military discount is combinable with its Free at Sea promotion (open bar, specialty dining, Wi-Fi, and excursion credits — terms vary) and with other available promotions, though those can change.

A few specifics NCL addresses in dedicated FAQs rather than the main pages — whether the discount applies to your whole group, to multiple cabins, or to a spouse traveling without the member — so pull the exact answer before you count on it. To save more, cruisers can layer NCL’s Latitudes Rewards loyalty benefits or book through a travel advisor who may add group rates or onboard credit. Royal Caribbean, Carnival, and Princess also offer military rates worth comparing, with different terms per line.
dave-and-busters-military-discount:

benchmade-military-discount: Verification runs through GovX ID — not ID.me, despite what some aggregators claim. GovX handles the check in real time at checkout; you create a free GovX account once and log in for future purchases, with each order needing a freshly issued single-use code. Verification questions go to help@govx.com; discount-application problems to info@benchmade.com or 1-833-557-2526. Note one honest wrinkle: Benchmade’s brand page says "up to 15%" while its support KB says a flat 15% — we carry both phrasings rather than pick one.

The stacking rules are strict: only one promo code per order, so the GovX code never combines with anything. Benchmade also says it "doesn’t run traditional sales," but it does run limited-time select-product promos — in 2026 it ran free laser engraving through May and 20% off select blades through June 21 (both now ended). When a public promo covers your exact model at more than 15%, take the promo instead — they don’t combine, and whether the GovX code can be entered on top of auto-applied promo pricing is not stated.

The deeper programs are narrower than coupon sites imply. ExpertVoice runs 30–60% off, typically once or twice a year, but Benchmade’s eligibility list is outdoor-industry professionals, retail associates, LE/military instructors, and select creators/educators — professional status, not general military service. GovX.com also runs its own Benchmade marketplace storefront and periodic "Benchmade Day" events for members (member pricing varies — compare against the $170-net direct price on a $200 knife).

Two more angles worth knowing: AAFES’s shopmyexchange.com stocks Benchmade — including Bugout models — tax-free for exchange-eligible shoppers (all honorably discharged veterans can shop online under the 2017 Veterans Online Shopping Benefit); price-check the listing, since exchange pricing wasn’t verifiable in this pass. And every Benchmade includes LifeSharp — free lifetime factory re-sharpening, cleaning, and adjustment — which is real long-run value on any path. Benchmade.com itself is not a cashback-portal merchant, so there’s no code-voids-cashback trap; portal cashback only exists at third-party dealers (Cabela’s and Bass Pro paid 3% via Rakuten as of July 4, 2026), where the GovX code doesn’t apply either.
las-vegas-hotels-military-discount: There’s no single verification partner for "Las Vegas." Caesars uses ID.me — you create or sign into an ID.me account, verify as Military, and the rate unlocks online. MGM does not use ID.me: it verifies with a government/military ID, VA ID, DD-214, or a driver’s license with veteran designation, shown in person at an MGM Rewards desk or at check-in. Wynn and Venetian have no military verification because they publish no military rate.

One reconciliation worth knowing: Caesars’ own page states "up to 25% off the lowest available rate," while the older ID.me marketplace tile still shows "up to 15% + extra 10% off sale rates." Trust the brand page (25%) and treat the ID.me tile as possibly stale.

On a $300 pre-tax room subtotal (2 nights × ~$150), Caesars’ up-to-25% lands near $225 and MGM’s 10% near $270 (plus Pearl-status free parking), while a live public sale at Wynn/Venetian (30–33%) lands around $200–$210 — often the winner, and open to everyone. The resort fee (~$45–$55/night) and ~13.38% Clark County room tax are added on top of every path and are never discounted, so they don’t change the ranking. Figures are stamped as of July 18, 2026.
t-mobile-military-discount: T-Mobile runs military verification in-house — there is no third-party provider like ID.me on the military plan. You verify through the T-Life app (Profile > Military Verification) or on T-Mobile.com (Profile > Military Verification), or in store or by phone. If your credentials can’t be auto-verified, T-Mobile asks you to upload documentation appropriate to your status (Active Duty, Reservist, Veteran, Retiree, or Gold Star).

The military member must be the primary account holder, with an exception for a deployed active-duty member whose spouse or family may verify on their behalf with extra documentation. You have 45 days from activation to complete verification or the plan reverts to Magenta at up to +$20/line per month, and the account must maintain a valid military line. T-Mobile states submitted documents are used solely for verification and destroyed afterward.

One thing to watch: many aggregator and older news pages still advertise stale T-Mobile military terms — "$25/line for 4 lines," "40% off Go5G," or the "Go5G Military / Magenta Military" plan names. As of June 23, 2026 the official plans page sells Experience-tier plans (Experience More / Experience Beyond) "w/ Military Savings," so treat the plans-page per-line pricing as the durable figures to cite.
easton-military-discount: There is no verification path because there is no program. Easton’s own sites publish no military discount, and Easton’s ID.me presence is a cashback listing, not a military rate. An Easton Archery Facebook thread shows a customer asking, "Does Easton still offer a military discount? I no longer see them on ExpertVoice" — consistent with Easton having left ExpertVoice and having no direct military program. ExpertVoice, in any case, is a verified-pro/industry program, not a military discount.

Coupon aggregators claim an "Easton Archery Military Discount — 25% OFF" and blanket statements that "Easton is proud to support the military with special discounts on all products." No primary source supports this. Treat those percentages as fabricated, and route your savings through the real channels instead.

The practical split is by product. For archery gear, compare a retailer that honors military (Lancaster Archery Supply) against a current Easton rebate and a deep OpticsPlanet sale, and take the lowest — these usually don’t stack. For baseball or softball gear, check the Exchange (AAFES/NEX) first for tax-free pricing, then public retailer sales.
stubhub-military-discount: Verification is handled by GOVX, not StubHub. You register a GOVX account and provide documentation to prove eligibility (military, first responder, law enforcement, medical, education, or government). Once GOVX approves you, you can claim the StubHub code from the GOVX StubHub page. The code is single use and has an expiration date shown in the "About StubHub" section of the GOVX page. Re-verification frequency for the GOVX account itself is not stated on StubHub’s page.

The mechanics matter: the $20 is applied through the "Gift cards" field at checkout, not as an automatic promo, and it can’t be added after you submit — so confirm the discount appears before you pay. Because it’s a flat $20 on a $200 minimum, it’s a fixed-value offer, not a percentage that scales with your order.

Separately, ID.me Shop advertises "up to 5% cash back" on StubHub. That is an ID.me Shop affiliate rebate governed by ID.me Shop’s terms — a third-party benefit, not a StubHub-issued discount — so we document it as distinct from the GOVX $20 code.
burger-king-military-discount: Burger King is a franchise-discretion brand: the company runs no corporate military or veteran discount, so what you get depends entirely on the individual owner of your local restaurant. Military-discount aggregators report that roughly 10% off with a military ID is honored at some franchised locations but denied at others, which is exactly what you would expect from a store-by-store policy. Treat the widely copied flat "10%" figure as typical, not guaranteed — no corporate source states any percentage.

There is no digital verification for a Burger King military discount — no ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute coalition offer. Verification is simply a staff member checking a physical military ID at the register. WeSalute lists Burger King but explicitly notes that BK does not participate in its Partner Coalition, so a WeSalute card cannot be guaranteed to work, and there is no online path to verify against.

Be cautious of the "free Big Cheese burger on Veterans Day" claim that circulates on coupon aggregators. It is not corroborated by any major 2025 Veterans Day roundup — Military.com, Veteran.com, TODAY, and Food Network all leave Burger King off their lists — so do not count on a national Veterans Day free meal. Any Veterans Day freebie is participating-location only and should be confirmed with your local restaurant.

The genuine best everyday saver is the free BK app with Royal Perks: app-exclusive combo and BOGO coupons commonly bring a ~$11.99 Whopper combo down to roughly $6–9, usually beating a 10% counter discount, and they work everywhere with no ID. If you are stationed on or near an installation with a base Burger King, the on-base (AAFES) location is tax-free, saving the sales tax with nothing to ask for.
dorney-park-military-discount: Dorney Park’s military ticket is a fixed discounted price, not a loose percentage: about $39 for a single-day admission against a gate price near $80 — a saving of roughly $41. The offer is gated by ID.me, the same identity-verification service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers, so verifying once links your eligibility to your ID.me account for future visits.

Because the discount is online only and cannot be combined with any other offer or sale, treat it as a standalone ticket price. You can buy up to six tickets per qualifying order, which lets a verified member bring family or friends at the same discounted rate.

On top of the everyday ticket, Dorney Park has historically run "Military Days" with free admission during set windows — reported around late May (Memorial Day) and early July (Independence Day) — for active and retired military, veterans, and Guard and reserve members. Exact 2026 dates were not yet posted at last check (the events page said "Stay Tuned"), so confirm on the official Military Days page before planning a visit, and never assume a specific future date.

Since Dorney Park and Six Flags control pricing, eligibility, and Military Days dates and can change them at any time, treat the numbers here as a starting point and verify the current offer on the official military-discounts page before you buy.
google-military-discount: Google verifies eligibility through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of major retailers. You open the offer on the Google Store’s Special Offers page, verify once (automated record check, a .mil email, or document upload), and receive the one-time 10% code. Google doesn’t state a re-verification cadence — the current code offer itself expires December 31, 2026, and whether a new code is issued for future offer periods is not stated.

The math that matters: because the code is single-use and doesn’t combine with other offers, its realistic ceiling is one 10% saving on a full-price purchase — $99.90 on a $999 Pixel 10 Pro. Google discounts Pixels most months, and those public sales run far deeper (the current one is $300 off). So treat the code as a launch-window tool: use it when the device you want isn’t on sale — typically right after a new Pixel launches — and take the public sale price plus trade-in credit the rest of the time. Budget-first shoppers should also price Google’s Certified Refurbished program: previous-gen Pixels at up to roughly 40% off original retail with the same 1-year warranty as new. Outgoing-generation prices historically drop hardest around the annual August launch (the Pixel 11 event is reported for August 12, 2026).

Ignore the coupon-site version of this offer. Aggregators advertise "up to 15%" or "10%–25% off" for military families with sale-stacking — none of that is supported by Google’s own pages, which state exactly 10%, as a one-time-use code, that cannot be combined with other discount codes or offers, with no mention of spouse or dependent eligibility. "Google Play military discount" pages are equally false: the code explicitly excludes subscriptions, and Google’s own support forums confirm no military pricing exists for Google One, Photos storage, YouTube, or Google Play. For phone service, see our separate Google Fi guide — Fi has no military plan discount either.
camp-chef-military-discount: Camp Chef verifies eligibility through ID.me, the identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. You verify your military or first-responder status once through a free ID.me account, using a .mil email or an uploaded document. After validation the 20% is granted on campchef.com, the Camp Chef mobile app, or a participating retail location.

The 20% is described as sitewide, with no product-category exclusions surfaced on the terms page — a meaningful advantage over grill brands whose "up to 20%" applies only to select models. That said, absence of a stated exclusion isn’t a guarantee, so verify clearance and sale items in your cart. The resulting code is single-use and can’t be combined with any other promotion, so plan one consolidated order — pellets, covers, griddle add-ons, and cast iron all ride along under the same sitewide discount.

Two things circulate online that are not true. Aggregators list Camp Chef’s military discount as "up to 10–25%," "25%," or hand out "40–70% off codes" — the verified offer on Camp Chef’s own page is a flat 20% via ID.me, single-use and non-combinable. And the generic ID.me landing template that reads "We’re not aware that Camp Chef offers Military discounts" is stale and contradicts Camp Chef’s own live military page; the 20% discount exists.
silver-dollar-city-military-discount: Verification is handled by ID.me. Click "Verify with ID.me" in the offer and follow the prompts; if you already have an ID.me account, you log in to apply discounts to future orders. Silver Dollar City doesn’t state on these pages how often ID.me re-verifies military status — ID.me sets its own cadence, so don’t assume one-time-forever. For verification problems, ID.me support is reachable at help@id.me or via chat. Active-duty free-passport claimants additionally must present a valid Common Access Card (CAC) in person to activate.

Everything is online-only. The everyday discounted tickets (Silver Dollar City $69+tax, White Water $36+tax, Showboat from $49–$62+tax) are evergreen for eligible military and their spouse/dependent children ages 4–17. The 2026 passport deals are the standout: active-duty members get a free season passport (no Bring-A-Friend or added benefits; activate by 7/31/26 with a CAC), while veterans, retirees, spouses, and dependents get a discounted passport with add-ons from $12.90/month, limit 6. Military Appreciation Days ran May 1–29, 2026 with a $59+tax ticket for the member plus up to 5 guests — a dated window, so check whether the current-year event is live before counting on it.

A couple of separations worth keeping straight: prices are plus tax and subject to change, and blackout/refund/transfer terms aren’t spelled out on the offer pages, so read the full ticket terms. And first responders, healthcare workers, teachers, and public employees are covered under Silver Dollar City’s separate Community Heroes program (which also includes military veterans), reported around $59 for 2026 — confirm the exact figure and dates on the official Community Heroes page rather than assuming.
buffalo-wild-wings-military-discount: The debunk first: aggregators present a "10% Buffalo Wild Wings military discount" as a standard program, and coupon sites advertise "20% off" BWW codes. Neither is real as described. BWW’s corporate FAQ and site never mention a military discount, ID.me states it is "not aware that Buffalo Wild Wings offers Military discounts," and WeSalute itself labels the 10% a non-partner "community deal" that "varies by location" and can’t be guaranteed. There is no military promo code — and BWW’s own FAQ caps orders at one promo code regardless.

The Veterans Day meal is the real, corporate-promoted offer, and its shape has been consistent: in 2025 ("Wings for Heroes," November 11), veterans and active-duty service members got 10 free boneless wings and regular fries with valid proof of service — dine-in or a walk-in counter order at BWW GO, no delivery or third-party apps, no substitutions or add-ons, one per person. Accepted proof in 2024–2025 included a military ID, VA card, driver’s license with veteran designation, or a veterans-organization card. Franchisee participation can vary, so call ahead — and check back in late October for the 2026 terms.

The everyday math favors the public deals over the maybe-10%. On a ~$25 order, a granted franchise discount saves about $2.50; Boneless Thursday BOGO gets you a second boneless order free (roughly 50% off the wings line, ~$8.50 of free food), and Wing Tuesday takes 50% off a second traditional order. The BOGOs run through the BWW app/site or dine-in, exclude third-party delivery, and explicitly don’t combine with other discounts — so you couldn’t stack the 10% on them anyway. BWW Rewards is the only true layer: free to join, 10 points per $1 (12 after $250 a year), and points earn and redeem even on promo-code orders.

Two more levers: BWW runs gift-card bonus windows (most recently $10 in bonus coupons per $50 of gift cards bought April 27 – June 21, 2026, redeemable June 22 – July 31, 2026 on food and non-alcoholic drinks), and warehouse clubs rotate discounted BWW gift-card multipacks in and out of stock. There’s no GovX, cashback-portal, or exchange path for a restaurant chain — and no first responder, teacher, nurse, or student program in any official source. For Memorial Day and Military Appreciation Month, no corporate offer was found for 2024–2026; individual locations honoring 10% in May is franchise discretion, not a chain promotion.
alp-military-discount: ALP’s discount runs on GovX ID, embedded on its own site — you don’t leave alppouch.com. Create a free GovX account, prove eligibility (document upload or work email), and GovX issues a single-use discount code natively in ALP’s store. The button says "save up to 10%," but the offer is configured as a flat 10% off your order — there is no mystery range. Codes carry a GX prefix, can’t be shared, and a new one is typically limited to about one per day; an unused code is re-issued rather than duplicated. Separately, age verification (21+) applies to everyone at site access and purchase.

The eligible groups, per the offer itself: current & former U.S. military, military spouses & dependents, first responders including law enforcement, fire, and EMS, and federal, state, and local government employees. Reserve, National Guard, and retired members are covered by the "current & former U.S. military" wording rather than named separately. Teachers, nurses, and students are not listed in ALP’s offer. There is no ID.me, SheerID, or WeSalute path, no exchange (AAFES/NEX) listing, no ExpertVoice program, and ALP is not sold on the GovX marketplace itself — GovX’s role here is verification only.

Ignore the coupon-aggregator noise. Pages advertising "20% off ALP" codes and generic codes like "ALPSAVE10" are unverified — none checked out — and ALP’s own `NOTORIOUS` extra-10% cart promo expired June 21, 2026, though it still lingers on aggregator sites. Claims that the military discount "stacks with other promotions" are unsupported: checkout takes one discount code, ALP’s rewards FAQ allows only one rewards code at a time, and Swagbucks voids cashback on non-Swagbucks codes. Take the 10% GovX code over the 6% cashback — never plan on both.

Now the honest per-can math, on ALP’s $99.96 20-can pack (about $5.00/can at list). The GovX 10% lands it at $89.96 — $4.50/can. Subscribe & Save starts at 5% and grows to 15% off ($4.25/can at the ceiling) for monthly subscribers — the tier schedule isn’t published, and whether a GovX code applies on top of subscription pricing is not stated anywhere official, so confirm at checkout before counting on it. Meanwhile, Nicokick and Northerner sell the same cans on volume tiers from $4.99 down to $3.99, Nicokick advertises 20% off a first newsletter order ($3.75/can on 20 cans), and Northerner runs its own 10% GovX discount. One caveat on every channel: state nicotine excise taxes are added at checkout and can exceed the discount itself in high-tax states — always compare final checkout totals, not sticker prices.
cobb-tuning-military-discount: COBB uses SheerID to confirm military status. Verification issues a single-use coupon rather than a permanent account discount: each code covers one purchase, and you must regenerate every 30 days. If verification fails, SheerID typically offers a document-upload review step; contact COBB support or SheerID if a code doesn’t apply. The discount lives entirely on cobbtuning.com — it is not redeemable through authorized dealers, who set their own MAP-based pricing.

The stacking rule is simple and stated plainly by COBB: the 15% "cannot be stacked onto any existing promotional discounts offered and the greater discount will be applied." So there is no "military + sale" combo — the system uses whichever single discount is larger. In practice that means you’re never worse off using it, because if a public COBB event sale ever runs deeper than 15%, checkout just applies the bigger one automatically.

For almost every COBB cart the 15% military code is the best path, because — unlike COBB’s public promo codes and the coupon-site "deals" — it applies sitewide, including the Accessport (COBB’s flagship device that public codes routinely exclude). On the baseline ~$775 Accessport V3, 15% brings it to about $658.75. It only loses when COBB itself runs a public sale deeper than 15% (rare; typical COBB sales are ~10%), in which case the greater discount auto-applies instead.
sams-club-military-discount: There are two tiers and two links. Club: hosted-pages.id.me/sams-club-military — "Join Sam’s Club Membership for just $15 + $5 in Sam’s Cash." Plus: hosted-pages.id.me/sams-club-military-plus — "Join Sam’s Club Plus Membership for just $50 + $5 in Sam’s Cash," which the Plus page describes as an "Instant Savings offer for $60 off."

Sam’s Club uses ID.me to confirm military status for the online membership offer. You create a free ID.me account and verify in the Military community; ID.me may request service documentation. After verification you’re routed back to Sam’s Club to complete the new membership at the offer price. Verification follows ID.me’s own re-confirmation policies, so don’t assume one-time verification is permanent.

One thing to watch: many aggregators — and some of Sam’s Club’s own older help-center copy — still describe this as "60% off, join for $20" for Club and "$60" for Plus, with a "$5 in-club gift card." As of June 23, 2026 the current, live Sam’s Club–linked ID.me pages state $15 Club + $5 Sam’s Cash and $50 Plus + $5 Sam’s Cash. The dollar figures and the "Sam’s Cash vs. gift card" wording have changed over time, so confirm the current terms at signup.

If you’re not eligible as military, Sam’s Club runs separate discounted new-member offers for First Responders, Government Employees, Seniors (50+), and SNAP/EBT recipients through ID.me and its help center — these are distinct from the military offer, each with its own page and pricing.
crunch-fitness-military-discount: Verification is handled by ID.me. You can verify ahead of time online or on the spot at a club by scanning the front-desk QR code; ID.me confirms your eligible community status. Crunch’s page states each person can request a one-time code once a month via ID.me. ID.me may periodically require re-verification per its own policies, so don’t assume verification is permanent. If automatic verification fails, ID.me provides a support path, and the club front desk can help apply the discount manually — and remember the barcode must be entered by hand, it won’t scan.

Two honesty notes. First, there is no percentage: Crunch publishes only "$0 enrollment + $3 off dues" on the Peak Results Military Plan, so any "10%/25%/50% off" you see is from third-party sites and isn’t confirmed by Crunch. Second, Crunch’s own page is inconsistent about who qualifies — the body copy says military, veterans, and first responders, while the FAQ says "Military personnel, nurses, and healthcare providers," and ID.me lists Crunch under Military, Nurse, and First Responder categories. We reflect that (nurses/healthcare appear eligible via ID.me) but flag it; confirm your specific eligibility with the club.

A few things Crunch doesn’t spell out, so we don’t assert them: Reserve/National Guard (ID.me’s Military community typically covers them, but Crunch’s page doesn’t confirm), and spouse/dependent eligibility (marketing mentions "families" without a defined rule). To save other ways, Crunch runs a separate Student Special for enrolled students and participates in third-party fitness-benefit programs (e.g., Active&Fit Direct, Renew Active, One Pass) that depend on your health plan, not military status. Planet Fitness and Anytime Fitness run their own military deals worth comparing.
the-parking-spot-military-discount: The Parking Spot’s account-linked military discount is verified manually by its Guest Services team: you open a support ticket, upload proof of military affiliation, and the discount is tied to your Spot Club account, after which it auto-applies to future stays. No third-party verifier is named for this path, so allow time for the review before a near-term trip. The separate ID.me offer uses ID.me’s standard online verification.

Because the brand publishes no percentage for the military discount, the on-record figures to book against are the ID.me offer’s "save at least 15%" and the public seasonal promo codes, which routinely run 20–25% off. A first-booking email signup gives 10% off, and AAA members see seasonal "at least 20%" codes. Since only one discount applies per reservation, the winning move is simply the single largest discount live that week.

Be skeptical of any flat "25%" or "10%" military figure on coupon sites. The 25% traces to an older Parking Spot Facebook promo, not the current help article, which states no percentage at all. We deliberately omit a military percentage here because repeating an unverified figure would imply a rate the brand does not actually publish.

The one always-on layer is the free Spot Club loyalty program: 4 points per $1, a free anniversary parking day, and points redeemable for free parking. It is not a promo code and accrues regardless of which discount you booked with — so join it, get your military discount linked as a floor, and then book with whatever single discount is largest.
litter-robot-military-discount: Verification is handled by BeansiD, not ID.me or GovX. ID.me’s own store page says it is not aware that Litter-Robot offers a military discount, and no GovX storefront was found — so aggregator pages that frame this as an "ID.me discount" are wrong. The real gate is BeansiD, where you confirm eligibility and receive a single-use code.

The military tier sits alongside separate BeansiD/Student Beans gates for first responders (10%) and students (10%, up to five years post-graduation). Each is its own verification and none of them are additive to one another.

The 10% code is year-round, not a holiday event. Around Military Appreciation Month (May) Whisker has layered public bundle sales on top of the standing code, but those bundle sales are public deals the military code cannot stack onto. Because Whisker controls the terms and can change them at any time, confirm the current offer on Litter-Robot’s official page before you buy.
aeropostale-military-discount: Aeropostale’s discount is powered by ID.me, the same identity-verification service used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of major retailers. You create an ID.me account (or log into an existing one), verify your military status with an accepted document, and log in during Aeropostale’s checkout flow to receive a single-use promo code.

Aeropostale routes verification through ID.me’s military community but does not publish a segment list. Per ID.me’s standard military eligibility, that community covers active duty, National Guard and Reserve, veterans, retirees, military spouses (including surviving spouses), and immediate family 18+. Because Aeropostale’s page states no narrower restriction, the standard community applies — confirm your specific status during ID.me verification.

The military tier sits alongside parallel ID.me communities for first responders, nurses and other medical workers, teachers, government employees, seniors, and students, all of whom get the same 15% on the same terms. The code is per-issuance, so treat each one as one-time and re-request it for future orders as ID.me and Aeropostale require.

Because Aeropostale controls the terms and can change them at any time, treat the numbers here as a starting point and confirm the current offer on Aeropostale’s official ID.me page before you buy. The reliable, documented path is the online 15% ID.me code; Aeropostale publishes no in-store military policy.
gatorland-military-discount: The free-admission benefit is one of the most generous at any Orlando attraction: because entry is free for the qualifying member, there is nothing a cashback portal, coupon, or online code could beat. The member pays $0 (and avoids the Florida sales tax collected on paid admission), while family members save 20% at the same booth.

The key nuance is who qualifies and when. The year-round free benefit is documented for active and retired military. The extension of free entry to veterans without a current military ID is specifically the November Veterans Day promotion — historically running about November 11–30, though the park sets the dates each year. Do not assume year-round free entry for veterans who no longer carry a military ID; outside November, they can use the separate Florida Resident discount, an online coupon, or a base ITT office if they have access.

For families and add-ons, the on-base ITT/MWR ticket office is the other real lever: it sells discounted Gatorland and Screamin’ Gator Zip Line tickets, useful for accompanying family members who would otherwise pay and for add-on experiences the at-gate benefit does not cover. Prices are installation-set and change, so price them at your ITT office before you go.
mystery-ranch-military-discount: The headline offer works through ID.me: Mystery Ranch lists 30% off for military members — and the same 30% for nurses, first responders, teachers, and government employees — limited to its ID.me Eligible Items collection, which held 62 products at last check. ID.me verifies your status once per account and re-authorizes per merchant; ID.me's verification is the final say on which military statuses (active duty, veterans, retirees, Guard/Reserve, family) clear the gate for this offer.

The separate Pro Purchase program covers Military, Fire, Federal Law Enforcement, Search & Rescue, and POSSE members through third-party validation only — ExpertVoice, Guidefitter, GovX, IPA Collective, or ID.me. It spans the Hunting and Everyday Carry lines (except Harnessing and US-built packs), pricing is confidential, purchases are personal-use only with no resale, approval takes up to 5 business days, and membership expires every December 31. Shoppers report (dated 2022, pre-YETI) that pro-platform pricing has ranged roughly 25–42% depending on platform and status — with veteran rates far below active-duty rates on some platforms — so treat those figures as signal only and verify your own platform before counting on a number.

Watch out for aggregator claims: UCMJ.us headlines a "Mystery Ranch Military Discount: Save 20%" and coupon sites push a "TAKEAHIKE 35% off" military code — neither matches the brand's published program. The verified numbers are 30% via ID.me on the eligible-items list only, confidential Pro Purchase pricing, and zero discount on the Military/Fire product lines.

One more angle: the YETI transition is pushing clearance on remaining Mystery Ranch-branded consumer stock, and a deep public markdown — at mysteryranch.com or retailers like REI and Scheels — can beat 30% off list with no verification needed. There's also a Mystery Ranch storefront on the GovX marketplace worth price-checking against the ID.me net price, and roughly 4% cashback via Active Junky on public purchases (as of July 14, 2026; an ID.me code order will generally void portal tracking).
liberty-safe-military-discount: Verification is manual and mail-in: you submit proof of service (a service ID or documentation) plus your purchase receipt with the rebate form. There is no instant online ID.me or GovX gate for the rebate itself, though Liberty safes also appear separately in the GovX marketplace. Register the safe, mail the completed form by the postmark deadline, and allow roughly six to eight weeks for the check.

The rebate is a manufacturer mail-in rebate calculated from what you actually paid for the safe (excluding tax and delivery), and the value scales with the safe’s price — larger safes return larger rebates. On a roughly $1,500 mid-size safe, the reported tier lands somewhere around $25–$250; confirm the current-year tier chart on the official page.

Because the rebate is receipt-based, it generally stacks on top of a dealer’s sale price rather than requiring full MSRP — so the genuine maximum-savings path is a dealer sale plus the mail-in hero rebate, not the rebate alone. Coupon aggregators implying a flat "military discount" percentage at Liberty Safe checkout are wrong: there is no instant percentage code.
thrifty-military-discount: Thrifty’s military path runs entirely through Veterans Advantage (VetRewards). You verify your service when you enroll in that membership; Veterans Advantage issues a member ID, and the 5% applies to your Thrifty booking as a member rate. Thrifty itself does not run a military-ID counter check for this discount, which is why aggregator sites implying a simple "show your ID" Thrifty discount are misleading.

The real value on a short rental is often the perks, not the 5%. The Veterans Advantage rate bundles a free upgrade coupon and a waived additional-driver fee, which on a two- or three-day rental can beat the dollar value of 5% off the base rate. But the 5% is small and applies to the base rate only — not taxes, surcharges, or add-ons — so it frequently loses to a public prepay rate or an affinity code.

Cross-shopping matters because of the corporate family tree. Thrifty and Dollar are both Hertz-owned and run the identical 5% Veterans Advantage program with the same fee waivers, while Hertz offers its own, sometimes broader, military rate. For any given set of dates, the cheapest sibling wins — so price all three for the same car before you book, and compare against a public "pay now" rate or a USAA / AAA / Costco Travel code.
47-brand-military-discount: There is no on-site military verification because ’47 runs no brand-direct military program. ID.me explicitly states it is "not aware that ’47 offers Military discounts," and there’s no ID.me, SheerID, or VerifyPass integration on 47brand.com. The genuine military route is GovX, which uses GovX ID to confirm military or first-responder status before member pricing shows.

Be careful with third-party claims: a "MyMilitarySavings" social post advertises "15% off all ’47 headwear and apparel" as a military deal. That’s a military-shopping-club offer, not a ’47 brand-direct discount. The genuine military channel is GovX; the widely-cited on-site 15% is a first-order email code available to anyone.

For the lowest price, treat GovX and the on-site path as an either/or. GovX cap selection is team- and SKU-limited, so the exact hat you want may not be listed — if it is, compare its member price to a 47brand.com sale plus the 15% first-order code. Repeat buyers benefit from ’47 Family’s free shipping, and a cashback portal can stack on top of on-site sales.
oura-ring-military-discount: The GOVX path: you verify military or first-responder status once to obtain a GOVX ID, which then unlocks discounts across GOVX partner brands. GOVX states no document upload is required for most members. Oura does not publish the GOVX re-verification frequency, and because the storefront is login-gated, the current Oura percentage and covered models are confirmed only inside your GOVX account.

The ID.me path: on Oura’s Preferred Pricing page you complete a quick ID.me verification of your identity and student/educator/healthcare status; once verified, 10% applies automatically at checkout on Oura Ring 4 and Oura Ring 4 Ceramic. Help with verification goes through the ID.me Help Center. Oura does not state how long verification lasts.

Because discounts don’t stack and a strong site-wide sale can beat a partner rate, compare your verified price against Oura’s current public promotions before buying. The Oura Ring is also HSA/FSA-eligible, which effectively lowers the net cost with pre-tax dollars.
amex-platinum-military: The math is why this is the most talked-about card benefit in the military community. The Platinum’s annual fee rose from $695 to $895 — effective September 18, 2025 for new applicants, and at renewals on or after January 2, 2026 for existing cardholders — yet an MLA-covered servicemember or military spouse holds it for $0 while keeping every benefit: up to $600 a year in hotel credits, up to $200 in airline fee credits, $200 in Uber Cash plus an Uber One credit, up to $300 in digital entertainment credits, a Resy dining credit, CLEAR Plus and Walmart+ credits, access to 1,550+ airport lounges, and Marriott Bonvoy Gold plus Hilton Honors Gold status. Most credits require enrollment and carry monthly, quarterly, or semi-annual caps — the fee is waived, but the credits still take management to collect.

Which law applies comes down to one variable: the account-open date. Open the Platinum while you’re a covered borrower — active duty, Guard/Reserve on orders over 30 days, or a DEERS-listed spouse or dependent — and the MLA zeroes the fee automatically; there is no military application form, no ID.me or SheerID step, and nothing to enroll in. Held the card before you activated? File an SCRA request (online is fastest, or 1-866-391-1460) with your orders, a DD-214, or a commanding-officer letter; Amex applies the 6% cap and fee waiver within about two billing cycles, and servicemembers have reported meaningful refunds of previously paid fees on long-held accounts — amounts depend entirely on account history.

Two more facts shape the smart play. First, MLA coverage is per person, per personal card — so a married military couple can each open their own Platinum at $0 (military-finance communities widely report each spouse earning their own welcome offer this way), and one covered member can hold the Gold, Delta SkyMiles Reserve, or Hilton Aspire alongside the Platinum, all fee-free while covered. Second, coverage ends with your covered-borrower status: Amex applies relief while DoD records show you as covered, so plan for the full $895 at the renewal after you leave service — or claim SCRA within 180 days of separation for your active-duty period. Other issuers (Chase, USAA, Navy Federal, Citi) also honor SCRA/MLA, but Amex is notable for applying $0 to its most premium cards.
shokz-military-discount: How verification works: GovX verifies your service or first-responder status once, free, and membership then unlocks member pricing across its marketplace, including the Shokz storefront. There is no ID.me or SheerID flow on shokz.com itself — Shokz’s own help center answers the military-discount question by pointing to GovX. The Exchange verifies eligibility separately through its own patron system (VetVerify for the online veterans benefit).

The key stacking rule: GovX is a substitute, not a stack. It is a closed marketplace — no Shokz promo codes, no Shokz Rewards points, no cashback portals on GovX orders, and returns follow GovX’s policies. The workable stack lives on the public side: Shokz’s sale prices apply automatically at shokz.com, which keeps portal cashback (Rakuten paid 2.5% as of July 14, 2026) intact — it’s entering scraped coupon codes that voids portal payouts.

On our baseline — one OpenRun Pro 2 at $179.95 MSRP — the live 35% Prime Day price plus 2.5% cashback nets out around $114, and 2026 retailer deals as deep as 40% have taken it to roughly $108. Those public windows (Prime Day in July, spring, Black Friday) are the deepest prices of the year; Shokz ran no Veterans Day or Memorial Day military promo that we could find. Outside a sale, compare your GovX member price against the Exchange’s tax-free sticker — at MSRP, skipping ~7% sales tax on a ~$180 headset is worth about $13.

One thing to watch: aggregator sites claim a flat "15% Shokz military discount — submit military ID at checkout." Shokz publishes no such offer. There is no military field in shokz.com’s checkout, and the official route is GovX member pricing with no published percentage. Treat any flat "15%" claim as unverified unless Shokz itself states one.
pacsun-military-discount: How verification works: it doesn’t — PacSun runs no military verification with any provider (ID.me, GovX, SheerID, WeSalute, or VerifyPass). The only verification gate PacSun operates is UNiDAYS student verification for the 10% student discount. Any site telling you to "verify military status for your PacSun code" is describing a program that does not exist — the TikTok "how to apply military discount on the PacSun app" videos are engagement bait around the same myth.

The honest math on a $100 full-price cart (jeans + tee): a live 50% sitewide sale lands at ~$50–70, markdowns at ~$30–60, APP20 at ~$80 on eligible full-price items, and the UNiDAYS student 10% at $90 — while PacSun Rewards adds a $5 signup reward and ~4% back on top of all of them. There is no identity discount that would beat the sale.

One trap PacSun’s own fine print sets for this audience: free-shipping offers exclude shipments to military APO/FPO addresses (along with AK, HI, and PR) — so deployed and OCONUS readers should expect to pay shipping even during "free shipping sitewide" events.

The debunk, on the record: WorthEPenny’s PacSun military page claims "up to 10% – 25% off for military members… applied to purchases made at pacsun.com" two paragraphs after admitting "There is no official PacSun military program." ID.me confirms no offer exists. When a page contradicts itself, believe the half with a source.
onstar-military-discount: The most important distinction is between two separate products. The GM Military Appreciation discount applies to a new-vehicle purchase or lease price, verified through GM’s military discount portal (you present an authorization number at a GM dealer). It does not reduce OnStar subscription fees, and GM’s own note is that the OnStar Military Appreciation content historically does not apply to data plans.

That is why aggregator claims of "up to 20% off OnStar for the life of the subscription" for military should be treated with caution. The only verified ~20%-on-OnStar-plans program is the GM College Discount, a student program — the "life of subscription" phrasing is aggregator embellishment. We deliberately do not assert a standalone OnStar military percentage, because none is published.

For a service member managing an OnStar subscription, the practical moves are: activate the complimentary trial that came with an eligible new GM vehicle; downgrade to the lowest tier (for example Remote Access) if you don’t need in-vehicle data or navigation; and ask about promotional or retention pricing, or annual prepay, when you renew. If you are actually buying a new GM vehicle, the meaningful dollars are on the car through GM Military Appreciation, not on OnStar.
fandango-military-discount: Because Fandango only passes through each theater’s pricing, whether a "military" ticket even appears at checkout is decided theater by theater — and the three biggest chains (AMC, Regal, Cinemark) run their military discount at the box office with a physical ID, which cannot be applied to a ticket you bought in advance on Fandango.

The strongest online military path is GovX: after a free, one-time verification, GovX sells discounted AMC, Regal, and Cinemark e-tickets to military, veterans, first responders, government employees, nurses, and teachers. WeSalute+ offers deeper Regal savings if you go often enough to justify the paid membership.

If you buy on Fandango a lot, its audience-neutral programs can beat any military rate: free FanRewards earns $5 back per four tickets, and paid FanClub ($9.99/mo) waives all convenience fees and adds $10 off a month. And if you are flexible on the day, chain loyalty deals like Discount Tuesday routinely cost less than any military discount — for everyone.
texas-roadhouse-military-discount: The single company-confirmed fact comes from Texas Roadhouse’s Community Impact page, which states it has partnered with Homes For Our Troops for 17+ years and that "on Veterans Day, we’re honored to offer free meals to veterans and active military members across the country." That Veterans Day free meal is the only military offer the brand publishes on its site.

The detailed Veterans Day terms — the entrée choices, the ~11 a.m.–2 p.m. voucher distribution, and the voucher expiration commonly cited as ~May 30 of the following year — come from secondary reporting, not a fetchable official press release. The annual event is repeatedly called the "Texas-size Thank You for Serving Our Country" event in news coverage, but that name is not verified on an official page. Treat the specifics as Medium-confidence and re-check the annual press release each fall.

lmnt-military-discount: The headline question has a plain answer: no primary source — drinklmnt.com, GovX, ID.me, or SheerID — confirms any LMNT military percentage. Coupon aggregators variously advertise a "15%, 25%, 30%, 35%, or 50% military" figure and attach it to codes like MAXMEAD, SBGPORTLAND, PODFAM15, or BRIAN50, yet several of those same pages contradict themselves ("there is no official DrinkLMNT military program"). Because there is nothing to verify, there is no GovX, ID.me, SheerID, or WeSalute step for LMNT. hampton-inn-military-discount: Hilton does not use ID.me or GovX for these rates. Book direct and stay logged in as a Hilton Honors member to keep points and elite-night credit — the durable value here is loyalty status and points, not the one-night percentage.

On a two-night leisure stay at a ~$150/night Hampton, the ~10% Military Family Rate lands around $270 before tax — real, but a Hilton Honors member rate or advance-purchase deal sometimes undercuts it, so compare before you book. On official travel, the per-diem rate is usually the biggest saver in expensive markets; one Hilton example ran $97 versus a $179 rack rate, roughly 46% off. And if hotel status matters to you long-term, chase it through the Hilton Honors Amex cards (Aspire for Diamond, Platinum for Gold) rather than expecting free elite status for military service — it is a credit-card perk, not a military benefit.
loft-military-discount: There is no military verification at LOFT because there is no military program. The ID.me store directory lists LOFT, but no LOFT-specific military discount is confirmed there — coupon sites headlining "LOFT military discount up to 40%" are piggybacking on ID.me’s generic "up to 40% off" browser-extension banner, not a real LOFT offer. On a $150 full-price order, a "50% off everything" sale alone brings it to about $75, and a subscriber or card offer can push it lower.

StyleRewards loyalty points accrue on top of sale purchases, and LOFT Outlet carries lower base prices.

epcot-military-discount: Eligibility is narrow. celebrity-cruises-military-discount: Celebrity’s Military Savings is evergreen, not holiday-gated — it runs year-round on select 4-night and longer sailings. Because the discount is a fixed per-person amount rather than a percentage, its value is set by cabin category: $25 per person on the lowest cabins and $100 per person from Veranda up. Booking a Veranda or above unlocks the full $200-per-stateroom cap, so if the fare gap to a Veranda is small, moving up can be worth more than the cabin difference.

The real strategy is stacking. Public promo depth usually peaks during Wave Season (January through March), which is often the best time to book. The military offer does not combine with Exciting Deals, Interline, Loyalty, Net, Travel Agent, or Employee rates.

A travel-agency add-on is a separate calculation. Military-specialist agencies advertise their own onboard credit (often quoted at $200-$400 per person), but that comes from the agency, not from Celebrity, and the direct "MILITARY" code is not available when you book through an agent. Treat the two as an either/or: compare the agency’s verified net onboard credit against the direct code plus a live public promo, and book whichever nets more. Verification is by military ID or DD-214 at check-in — Celebrity does not use ID.me, GovX, or SheerID for this offer.
rack-room-military-discount: The standout fact is the stacking, verified verbatim on Rack Room’s military-discount page: "The 10% and 20% OFF military discounts can be combined with the BOGO 50% OFF offer & applied to all sale prices." That is unusually generous for retail. On an illustrative $120 two-pair cart, a Tuesday BOGO 50% plus the 10% military discount lands around $81, and on a military holiday the BOGO 50% plus 20% lands around $72 — assuming two equally priced, BOGO-eligible pairs. BOGO applies to select styles and discounts the cheaper pair, so confirm eligible styles in store.

Verification is manual and in person: you present a physical valid military ID to the associate at checkout. Rack Room does not use ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute for the military discount — ID.me’s own store page confirms Rack Room "does not use ID.me for Military verification." (ID.me Shop separately lists Rack Room for general cash back — that is not the military discount, and it wouldn’t stack with an in-store register discount.) There’s no account to create and no code to enter, so keep an eligible military ID with you.

Because the discount is in-store only, online shoppers get nothing military-specific. The best online play is the free Rewards program — a $15 coupon per $200 spent, a $10 birthday reward, and free shipping on every order — layered with a cashback portal like Rakuten (2% as of July 15, 2026) and timed to a sale. Rewards accrues independently of the military discount, so you can be a member and still use the in-store military percentage.
rockler-military-discount: We checked Rockler’s own Customer Service, Ordering FAQ, and Current Promotions pages: none reference a military discount, and no verification portal carries a Rockler military offer. Coupert’s “Rockler Military Discount — Up to 15% Off” and similar coupon-site claims cite no primary source, so we don’t repeat the number as fact.

Because there’s no military program, there’s nothing to verify — Rockler uses no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute flow. Woodworking forums show mixed reports: some shoppers say a local store extended a courtesy, others say there’s none. The consistent takeaway is manager’s discretion in store, not a company policy you can rely on.

The reliable path is Rockler’s public machinery. Join email or create an account for exclusive promo codes (which can’t be combined or applied retroactively), shop the Outlet/clearance section for the deepest single discounts, keep orders at $99+ for free shipping, and time larger purchases to public seasonal sales.
zagg-military-discount: Verification is straightforward here: there is no ZAGG military verification because there is no military offer. ZAGG appears on ID.me Shop, but that store page lists only general cashback available to every ID.me member — not a military group discount — and ID.me’s dedicated "Does ZAGG Have Military Discounts?" page answers that it isn’t aware of one. Do not expect an ID.me military gate at ZAGG checkout.

The aggregator claims are worth debunking specifically. Multiple coupon sites assert a "20% ZAGG military discount via ID.me" and a "30% first-responder discount." Neither appears on any ZAGG or ID.me primary source. The 20% figure conflates ZAGG’s public "buy 2, save 20%" bundle — available to everyone — with a ZAGG UK key-worker offer (run through gocertify) that is now expired and was never a U.S. program. One aggregator even concedes ZAGG "does not appear to offer any special discounts for students, senior citizens, or military personnel."

For the math, take a typical ~$60 two-item ZAGG.com order (screen protector + case). The buy-2 bundle drops it to roughly $48 (~20% off), or as low as ~$42 if the 30% tier is live. A cashback portal on a no-code order adds around 3% more (Swagbucks rate as of July 18, 2026 — verify before relying on it). GovX can undercut on older-model inventory it still stocks, and retailer substitutes (Best Buy, AT&T, Verizon, Amazon) sometimes bundle or price-cut the exact device-specific item under their own pricing and military policies — a retailer program, not a ZAGG one.
stockx-military-discount: StockX is a peer-to-peer resale marketplace: every price is a live bid (Ask) set by sellers and buyers, not a store-controlled retail price. Because there is no brand-run checkout, there is nothing for a military verification partner to plug into — StockX has no presence on ID.me, GovX, SheerID, WeSalute, or VerifyPass, and its Help Center lists only occasional public promo codes, never a group-based program. A veteran and a civilian pay exactly the same price.

Be cautious of coupon and deal sites that advertise a specific StockX "military discount" percentage or a code like "10OFFSALE" that supposedly gives military members 30% off. Those are fabricated. StockX publishes no military rate, so any code that is actually live is a public code anyone can use — not a service-member benefit. Student Beans’ "up to 60% off shoes" is likewise marketing language pointing at StockX’s ordinary marketplace listings (resale prices below original retail), not a verified student discount.

The only savings that genuinely exist are three: occasional public promo codes (email, influencer links, social) that trim the item price; a $10 "Give $10, Get $10" referral credit for a first-ever order; and third-party cashback portals (Rakuten ~1%, TopCashback ~2.02%, others 2–2.3% as of July 2026) that pay a small rebate separately. A code and the referral credit cannot both apply — one code per purchase — but a cashback portal is separate and generally stacks on top of a code.

Keep the fees in view: StockX charges a buyer processing fee, shipping, and sales tax on top of every purchase, and none of that is discountable. On the Listings Marketplace the processing fee is a flat 3% (minimum $3.95); on the Verified Marketplace it is dynamic, based on item price, location, and market conditions. So the smartest move is to compare total landed cost (item + fee + shipping + tax) against retail — a resale item below retail can beat any "discount" elsewhere, while one above retail is not a deal even with a code.
top-golf-military-discount: The Heroes Program is presented by GovX, which acts as the presenting sponsor and verifies eligibility. There is no confirmed ID.me, SheerID, or WeSalute path for Topgolf — GovX is the named partner.

Coupon aggregators often advertise a flat "up to 25%" military rate everywhere. Others imply a stackable "military 50% code" — the 50% is Topgolf’s public Half-Off Golf promo (open to any guest, Monday–Thursday), not a military code, and it cannot be combined with the Heroes 10%.

Because Topgolf controls the terms and pricing varies widely by venue, day, and time, treat the numbers here as a starting point and confirm the current offer on Topgolf’s official Heroes Program page before you book.
big-5-military-discount: Verification is refreshingly simple: a cashier checks your military ID, or the veteran designation on your state driver’s license, in person. There is no third-party service, no online account, and nothing to set up in advance — just bring your ID. That manual, in-store process is also why the discount can’t be applied to an online order.

The standing 10% is year-round, not a holiday event. The real decision on any given item is whether Big 5’s current weekly-ad sale or a live email/app coupon already beats 10% — during a strong sale, the public price often does. Since the military discount is "not valid with any other coupon offer," you can’t add it on top of a sale; you model each item at the lower of the two.

Big 5’s terms are stated plainly on its own page, so there are no inflated percentages to debunk here. The only common misconceptions worth correcting are that the discount works online (it doesn’t) and that it stacks with a coupon (it doesn’t). No separate first responder, nurse, teacher, student, or senior program was found — the military discount is the dedicated offer.
aquatica-military-discount: Aquatica uses ID.me (its military product is branded “Troop ID”) to confirm you’re a member of the military community. mavis-tire-military-discount: Mavis states the terms plainly on its Military Discount Tires page: 10% off, applied to the sale price before sales tax, honored in-store with a valid military ID. taylormade-military-discount: TaylorMade uses ID.me to verify eligibility, and verification happens during checkout — you click the ID.me button and confirm your status. TaylorMade occasionally runs elevated ID.me military promos (a 25% sitewide event ran in March 2026, now expired), so it’s worth checking for a higher rate around key dates — but 15% is the confirmed everyday figure. Reserve and National Guard members aren’t named separately but are generally covered within ID.me’s military verification.
coros-military-discount: COROS verifies eligibility through BeansiD (operated by Pion, the Student Beans company) and GovX.
