la-quinta-military-discount: Eligibility is broad: U.S. or Canadian military with active, reserve, veteran, or retired status — and their spouses. You verify at the hotel front desk with a valid military ID at check-in; there is no online verification provider for this rate. Wyndham Rewards membership is not an eligibility requirement, but you need a (free) account to earn points on the stay.

The rate applies across the Wyndham portfolio using the same SML code — La Quinta plus Baymont, Days Inn, Super 8, Ramada, Microtel, Wyndham Garden, and more — so the same mechanic works whichever Wyndham brand you book.

On a 2-night, $240 Standard-Rate baseline, the "at least 15%" floor is at least $36 off — about $204 before tax. Because SML doesn’t stack, the honest play is to compare it against the property’s advance-purchase ("Book Early & Save") rate and, if you hold it, AAA or AARP: book whichever single rate is cheapest for your dates. Illustrative figures are stamped as of July 18, 2026.
onx-military-discount: Verification runs through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA and the IRS. You verify your current or former military status once against your free ID.me account; then, at checkout on onX’s website, you open the Billing tab, click "Verify with ID.me," and the discount is applied to that purchase before you pay. Whether the discounted rate persists on auto-renewal is not stated — assume it’s purchase-time only and plan to re-run the ID.me flow (or repurchase) at each term until onX says otherwise.

The rule that costs people money: onX support states there is no way to apply a discount to an active membership. If you’re already a member, you can’t bolt the 50% onto your current term — cancel auto-renew, let the membership expire, then repurchase through the ID.me flow. Time the lapse for your off-season so you’re not without maps mid-hunt.

Buy on the web, and think about the tier. Redemption routes through onX’s website checkout, so subscribing inside the iOS or Android app can bypass the ID.me price. On tier choice: at 50% off, onX Hunt Elite (about $50/year against the $99.99 list price) costs roughly what the Premium Two-State tier lists for — and Hunt and Offroad Elite members also get "exclusive pricing on products and services" from onX’s pro-deal partner brands, which compounds the value of choosing Elite over Premium ($34.99/yr, single state).

One thing to watch: coupon aggregators advertise generic "60% off onX promo codes." On July 14, 2026, the verifiable ceiling was the ID.me 50% military rate plus time-boxed public sales — Backcountry’s PEAK70 at 70% (that app only) and Offroad’s July 4 sale at 50% — so treat scraped codes as expired until they prove out in cart. A GovX brand page for onX also exists, but its offer details sit behind GovX membership; the documented path is ID.me.
nespresso-military-discount: The absence is well documented: Nespresso’s full US FAQ — including its "Brand & Promotions" section — lists only registered-customer offers, with no military discount anywhere, and the ID.me store directory has no Nespresso listing. GovX carries Nespresso-compatible capsules from other brands (like Fire Dept. Coffee), but not Nespresso itself. So the aggregator claims — "30% off" (hotdeals), "verify with SheerID for a code," "up to 15%" (a stale UK page) — are fabricated or unsupported; no official Nespresso property backs any of them.

For machines, two real levers compete. Retail sales discount Nespresso machines roughly 20% routinely — a Vertuo Pop+ dipped under $100 in a March 2026 retailer deal. And the exchanges sell Nespresso by De’Longhi Vertuo machines tax-free to authorized patrons: AAFES and the Navy Exchange both list them, and honorably discharged veterans have been able to shop the exchanges online tax-free since 2017. Exchange product pages are login/JS-gated, so compare the live exchange price against the live retail sale price and buy the cheaper.

For capsules, Nespresso’s only standing discount is AutoReplenish: 10% off EasyOrders of $75 or more, a subscription mechanic rather than a coupon. The best realistic stack is a sale-priced (or tax-free exchange) machine plus AutoReplenish pods — different merchants and mechanics, so nothing conflicts.

OriginalLine owners have the largest genuine "military discount" in the Nespresso ecosystem — from third parties. Gourmesso sells Original-compatible pods from $0.39 and gives GovX-verified military, veterans, families, first responders, government, healthcare, and teachers 20% off every order (single-use code, one per day). Artizan’s organic Nespresso-machine capsules carry a 15% VerifyPass discount on consumables that explicitly stacks on sale items (but not with other codes; one code per 24 hours; no equipment or subscriptions). Both are those brands’ programs — check pod compatibility with your machine line before ordering, and note Gourmesso’s discount does not cover Vertuo.
two-men-and-a-truck-military-veteran: Two Men and a Truck is a full-service mover rather than a truck-rental brand, so its military support looks different from a flat rental-rate code. The company highlights a Movers for Military approach and a PCS Moving Priority Package with guaranteed dates and flexible rescheduling, and its franchises that specialize in military moving understand the needs of active-duty, reserve, National Guard, and veteran customers. The customer discount itself, though, is a franchise-level decision: participating locations offer discounted rates with a valid military ID or proof of veteran status, and the percentage is whatever that location sets.

That makes a phone call the most important step. Because two nearby franchises can price the same move differently and may or may not offer a military rate, get a quote from each location that could handle your move and ask specifically about the military discount, the PCS package, and guaranteed dates. Keep your orders and paperwork handy — a personally procured move (PPM/DITY) is reimbursable through your transportation office when you keep receipts, which can matter more than the discount itself.

One common point of confusion: Two Men and a Truck also advertises a 10% discount on its franchise fee for veterans buying a franchise, through its VetFran membership. That is a business-ownership benefit, not a discount on hiring movers — useful if you are transitioning into franchise ownership, irrelevant if you just need to move. For movers who want a guaranteed, published percentage instead of a location-by-location answer, the truck-rental brands (Penske, Budget Truck) and container brands (PODS) carry national codes worth comparing.
priority-tire-military-discount: Priority Tire uses ID.me to confirm eligibility. You verify your status online before checkout; once verification is complete, the 5% is applied to your cart automatically. Priority Tire doesn’t publish a re-verification frequency — ID.me manages its own affiliation checks and may require you to re-confirm periodically, so treat verification as ID.me-managed rather than a one-time permanent step. For verification problems, Priority Tire points to ID.me support; for order questions, Priority Tire support is 866-440-0177 or info@prioritytire.com.

The 5% is a flat rate that covers a broad set of communities at the same level: military (active, reserves, retired, veterans), first responders (police, firefighters, EMS), healthcare professionals (doctors, nurses, medical staff, hospital employees), and educational workers (teachers and school staff). Government employees and students are not part of the program — they’re absent from both Priority Tire’s discount pages and the ID.me verify scope — and military spouses/dependents aren’t addressed.

The key limit is no stacking: if the ID.me discount is on your order, you can’t add another coupon, and it generally won’t combine with sale/clearance prices or manufacturer rebates. So compare — sometimes a current deal, clearance price, or mail-in rebate (e.g., Continental, Pirelli, Milestar) beats 5% off on the same tire. Priority Tire also advertises free shipping on all orders and promotes a membership program worth checking. For a lower total delivered price, it’s worth comparing the 5%-applied price against other online tire retailers’ sales.
cabinets-to-go-military-discount: All the math below uses one baseline: a $6,000 in-store cabinet order (a typical mid-size kitchen), cabinets only, before tax. Tax is the same across every path since all of these are in-store at the same showroom, so it doesn’t change the ranking.

The 35% is the default winner for normal carts. On the $6,000 baseline it takes the order to $3,900 — $2,100 off. The current public "Buy More, Save More" tiers only reach 25% at that spend ($4,500), so the military discount is clearly better for a typical kitchen (roughly anything under ~$10,000).

The counterintuitive part is the big-order flip. The public sale is tiered by spend: recently 20% up to $5,000, 25% to $7,500, 30% to $10,000, 35% to $15,000, and 40% at $15,001+. So on a very large project the public 40% beats the non-combinable 35% — with no verification needed — and at $10,001–15,000 the two simply tie at 35%. Because they can’t be combined, the smart move on a large kitchen is to price the current sale tier against the 35% and take the lower one.

Two more levers. First, select featured collections (recently lines like Premiere, Gracious Home, Charleston Driftwood, and Kensington) run 45–60% off during sales — deeper than 35% on those specific cabinets, and again not combinable. Second, Cabinets To Go’s 30-Day Price Match / Best Price Guarantee is open to everyone and can protect your price if you find the identical item cheaper within 30 days.

Because Cabinets To Go controls the terms and can change them at any time — and the sale tiers rotate window to window — treat the numbers here as a starting point and confirm the current offer at the showroom or on Cabinets To Go’s official pages before you commit.
direct-energy-military-discount: The paper trail on Direct Energy’s military program is thin and contradictory. SheerID’s shopper site lists "Direct Energy: Military — Save on Home Services," an offer for "members of the US military and their registered dependents" promising "an exclusive rate on your home energy needs" — with no amount attached. But the landing page that listing points to, directenergy.com/military, returned a 404 on July 14, 2026 (we checked both www and the apex domain). The last confirmed program is a May 2017 press release announcing reduced Memorial Day military rates in 12 states plus D.C. and a year-round program at that now-dead URL. ChooseEnergy’s veteran-discounts guide, updated May 27, 2025, doesn’t list Direct Energy at all. Treat the offer as unverifiable until Direct Energy restores its page — and call before you count on it.

Even when an energy "military rate" exists, it works differently from a retail coupon: it’s a plan, not a code. You enroll in it instead of a public plan, so it never stacks with promotional new-customer rates — you compare the two totals and pick one. There are also no cashback portals, no GovX marketplace, and no code-stacking in energy supply; the category’s only real stack is a deposit waiver layered on whatever plan you choose. That’s why comparison-shopping the all-in ¢/kWh on your state’s official shopping site is the dominant lever: on a 1,000 kWh/month baseline (~$1,680/year at ~14¢/kWh all-in), each cent per kWh is worth about $120 a year.

Be cautious of coupon aggregators advertising a specific Direct Energy military percentage. WorthEPenny/Knoji-class pages claim "10%–25% off for military," redeemed by "selecting Military and First Responder Discount at checkout and verifying through SheerID or ID.me." No primary source states any percentage, no such checkout selector is documented anywhere, ID.me lists no Direct Energy partnership, and the brand’s own military URL is dead. The only verifiable artifacts are SheerID’s amount-less listing and a nine-year-old press release. Editorial reviewers at ElectricityPlans add useful context: "while there are some discounts available for veterans and active military, most of these programs have been cancelled," and they report that past Texas military "discounts" from major retailers ran as thin as a tenth of a penny off published rates — reported context, not a verified figure, but a signal that even a restored program may be marketing rather than money.

If you want a military energy program you can actually verify today, two Texas providers publish theirs. BKV Energy gives 5% off the energy charge every month to active military, veterans, police, fire, and medical first responders with proof of service — note the 5% applies to the energy charge only, not TDU delivery fees, so the real bill impact is closer to 3–4%. Reliant markets a Hero plan with up to $150 a year in bill credits for military and veterans, per ChooseEnergy’s May 27, 2025 guide — verify current terms at reliant.com, and remember bill credits on a padded base rate can be worth less than a cheaper public plan. Either way, only take a military plan if its all-in rate is within about half a cent per kWh of the market’s best. Active-duty members establishing new service should also ask about deposit waivers and PCS/early-termination handling before signing any fixed-term contract.
abercrombie-military-discount: All the math below uses one baseline: a $150 apparel order (a typical A&F basket of 2–3 items). Free standard shipping kicks in at $99, so shipping is $0 on this cart. Codes and sale figures move constantly, so every number is illustrative and stamped “as of June 16, 2026” — treat them as a way to compare paths, not as quotes.

Rule 1 — there is no official or online military discount. This is the page’s core correction. The only military-specific discount is an unofficial, in-store, manager’s-discretion ~10–15% that some stores grant with a military ID — present it as a maybe, not a program, and never trust a site quoting a guaranteed “A&F military discount %” or a “15% online via partner portal.”

Rule 2 — A&F codes stack on Sale items, a real edge. Unlike most brands, A&F’s email and influencer codes generally apply on top of “Sale” prices — this is the actual savings engine. But Clearance (ending in $.97/$.99) is excluded, as are Best Brands (third-party), fragrance, body care, and gift cards. Knowing the Sale-vs-Clearance line is what makes the stack work.

Rule 3 — membership compounds. myAbercrombie members get the extra 15% at Black Friday, longer (60-day) VIP returns, points, and the first-order $10 off $50+. It’s free, so joining is the single highest-value action — it layers on top of whatever code and sale you use.

Rule 4 — in-store military discount is an either/or, not a stack. Where a store offers the ~10–15%, it likely won’t combine with a promo code — so weigh it against the live code + Sale price and take the lower. And for this brand, online generally wins, the opposite of auto/tire brands where the discount required an in-store visit.
ruggable-military-discount: Ruggable is a direct-to-consumer washable-rug brand, and its savings are entirely public sale events and codes rather than a group-gated discount. The Offers page is the source of truth: it currently lists a first-order 10% code (email/SMS signup, expires 21 days after signup), a 15% referral credit, a 15% review credit, recurring sitewide sale events advertised up to ~30% off, and a trade program for approved design/industry professionals. None of these is a military, veteran, or first-responder offer, and none requires ID.me or GovX verification.

Because Ruggable states its codes cannot be combined, the smart move is not stacking but choosing the single deepest available offer. Sale pricing generally replaces code discounts, so when a sitewide event is live you take the sale; when it is not, you use one best code — a 15% referral beats a 10% welcome code for a new customer, and a repeat buyer uses a 15% review credit. Cashback portals layer only on a no-code, portal-tracked order, and Ruggable’s 7-day price protection lets you claim a one-time adjustment if your rug drops in price right after you buy.

Be cautious of aggregator pages advertising a "Ruggable Military Discount — up to 30% off" or a "15% ID.me military rate." Those figures are fabricated: the "up to 30%" is simply the public sitewide sale, and "15%" is the public referral or review credit — neither is gated to military status, and there is no Ruggable ID.me store or GovX storefront behind them. Community reports of occasional short "military-only" or holiday promos in past years are unverified signal only; watch for a time-boxed offer around Veterans Day rather than assuming a standing discount exists.
skylight-calendar-military-discount: Multiple coupon pages assert that Skylight "offers military-specific discounts at checkout during major holidays — verify your military status during checkout." This is false. Skylight’s checkout has no military-verification field, the ID.me store page shows no active Skylight military offer (only auto-generated FAQ links and a money-back tile), and the brand publishes no military terms. Some of the same pages simultaneously admit "there is no discount for military members at Skylight" and then invent a generic code that is really a public promo available to anyone. Treat every "military code" for Skylight as a plain public promo, not a service discount.

Because there is no military discount to stack, the real levers are the ones open to every shopper. One public promo code per order is the norm for a direct-to-consumer checkout like Skylight’s, so assume a code and an already-marked-down sale price are not combinable. The reliably stackable layer is credit-card or shopping-portal cashback, which is applied by your card issuer or the portal rather than by Skylight, so it works on top of any price.

On a 15-inch Skylight Calendar (list $299.99), a live public site-wide code (historically ~15%) lands you around $255, while a Black Friday or major holiday event (historically ~25% off) can bring it closer to $225 — the deepest public discount and open to everyone. A friend’s referral link gives a new customer a first-order discount (aggregators cite roughly $20–$40, unverified on the official page), though it generally can’t be combined with other codes. The $79/year Skylight Plus subscription is optional and is a recurring cost, not a device discount.

Bottom line for a service member: want it now, any date — buy at list from Skylight or the cheapest retail partner and put it on a cashback card, since there is no service discount to wait for. Can wait — target Black Friday / Cyber Monday or a major holiday sale. Shopping mid-cycle — apply whatever public code is live and buy through the channel giving you the best card or portal cashback.
margaritaville-military-discount: The single biggest-dollar military benefit in the whole Margaritaville universe is the cruise. Margaritaville at Sea’s "Heroes Sail Free" program — verified through GovX and expanded fleet-wide in August 2024 — gives eligible members a free interior cabin for the first and second guest (you pay only taxes, fees, and port expenses), or an extra 20% off when free cabins aren’t available.

For a land stay, the resort you pick determines the discount. The Heroes rate is set per property: 35% at Fort Myers Beach (code HERO), 30% at Kansas City and Lake Tahoe, 15% (plus a $75 credit) at Hollywood Beach, and 10% at several others. A few properties also publish a government per-diem rate (for example Lake Conroe at $128/night, code PERDIEM) for official government and military travel, which can beat the percentage rate.

Two different verification systems apply. Resort Heroes rates are verified in person — you book the rate and show a qualifying ID at check-in, with no online verification partner. The cruise, the Run, and restaurants verify through GovX, a free account that confirms your status once. There is no confirmed ID.me, SheerID, or WeSalute route for any Margaritaville channel.
allbirds-military-discount: The math below uses one baseline: a $110 pair of Allbirds Wool Runners. On that pair, 15% off works out to $93.50 — a flat, guaranteed win when you’re buying full price.

Allbirds routes military (and healthcare/government/teacher/faculty/staff) verification through GovX; students verify through StudentBeans. You create a free account with the provider, confirm your status, and receive a single-use code. GovX here is verification only — it issues a code for allbirds.com, so there is no separate GovX Allbirds storefront to price against.

The make-or-break rule is that the code “cannot be combined with other codes,” and it can’t be stacked on a sale price. When a public markdown exceeds 15%, the sale wins and the two don’t combine — so you take whichever is cheaper, not both. Because the single-use code makes it a coupon order, it also commonly voids cashback-portal tracking; cashback is safest on a straight no-code sale purchase.

One correction worth making: some aggregators list an “ID.me Allbirds” store and a “10% military” rate. Allbirds’ own Community Offers page routes military verification through GovX, not ID.me, and the verified value is 15%, not 10%. The brand page is the authority.
timberland-military-discount: Timberland uses SheerID on timberland.com: you verify your military, first-responder, healthcare, teacher, or student status, and SheerID issues a single-use 10% promo code tied to that verification. The code is good for one order, and you re-verify every 30 days for a new one. The military tier explicitly covers active-duty, retirees, reservists, veterans, and military spouses and registered dependents across all branches.

A common myth to clear up: several aggregators list Timberland’s verification as ID.me and some claim 20% off military. Both are wrong for the military tier. The verified on-site provider is SheerID (ID.me lists Timberland only as a cash-back/affiliate storefront), and the verified military figure is 10%. The 20% figure floating around is the limited student back-to-school promo (July 9–September 30, 2026), not a military rate — and coupon-site "Timberland military codes" are unverified scraped codes, since the real discount is a personal single-use SheerID code.

Because the discount is small and won’t stack, the honest best path for most shoppers is a retailer substitute or public sale. Foot Locker, Champs, and Zappos carry Timberland 6-inch boots and routinely mark colorways to $110–$170, frequently cheaper than 10% off $198. Timberland also runs public Veterans Day, Memorial Day, and Presidents Day sale pages (open to everyone; the 10% code won’t stack on those prices).

For deeper gated pricing: Timberland has "Timberland" and "Timberland Watches" storefronts on the closed GovX marketplace, and VF-eligible pros may access ExpertVoice (up to 60% off). Both run their own separate membership verification and don’t stack with the SheerID code or public sales.
aaa-military-discount: Verification depends on the channel. On the aaa.com/military online path, AAA uses ID.me, which confirms military status for active duty, Reserves/National Guard, veterans, and (for the broader community) spouses and family members. On the GovX path, AAA uses GovX ID, which verifies current and former service members. In branch or by phone, you show a Military ID or equivalent documentation. ID.me and GovX may require an account and can re-verify status periodically — do not assume a one-time verification is permanent.

Because clubs operate independently, the biggest real-dollar value in the offer is often a free Classic→Plus upgrade (where offered), which increases towing distance and benefits at no added first-year cost. Some clubs add 20% off AAA-branded merchandise and a recurring ~10% membership discount for primary and household members. The GovX "up to 50% off a new membership" may beat a club’s standard military rate in eligible states — compare both aaa.com/military and GovX.com.

AAA Travel separately gives active military, veterans, and families about 10% off vacation packages (no blackout dates) and 10% off the rail portion of rail vacations, with advance AAA Travel reservation required. Because figures vary by club and were read from search extracts of the official pages, confirm the exact first-year dues discount for your region on the live club page before joining.
acme-tools-military-discount: Cashback portals are independent of Acme Tools: Rakuten and TopCashback pay you a percentage for routing your sale, and because Acme’s checkout is unaware of the portal, that cashback stacks on top of any Acme on-site sale price and coupon. Rakuten pays up to 2.5% on eligible brands (2.5% on DEWALT, Metabo HPT, Milwaukee, and Stihl; 2% on brands like EGO, GEARWRENCH, JET, Makita, and Werner; 1.5% on others), while TopCashback pays a flat 1.5%. Rates move, so compare on a monitor like CashbackMonitor before you buy, and note Rakuten pays no cashback on gift cards.

Acme’s 30-day price-match guarantee is a second real lever: if an authorized dealer lists the identical brand and model in stock for less, Acme will match it. But price-match does NOT stack — it excludes auction/eBay and third-party sellers, closeouts, clearance, misprints, giveaways, special promotions, and discount offers, so you take the matched price or a promo, not both. You can still route a price-matched purchase through a cashback portal.

Be cautious of coupon and deal sites that advertise an Acme Tools "military promo code." Some push a 20%-off "military" code, others "up to 50% off" or a "TOOLGUYD" code framed as a military play — none is tied to service, and these aggregator codes expire and are frequently invalid. No primary source confirms any military percentage at Acme Tools, so we deliberately do not assert one. A community-reported in-store courtesy discount (roughly 10%, capped near $150) is manager-discretion only and not a published policy — treat it as YMMV.
sea-life-aquarium-military-discount: SEA LIFE uses ID.me to verify status during online checkout. You create a free ID.me account, confirm eligibility, and the discounted ticket unlocks. Re-verification and support follow ID.me’s rules, and the venue may spot-check physical ID at entry.

The military ticket covers up to 4 people per transaction (dependents allowed), and children age 1 and under are free and do not count toward the 4. Military pricing generally will not stack with other promo codes or combo-pass discounts — pick one.

Aggregator marketing floats "up to 40% off for Military, Veterans, Nurses, Teachers and more." That 40% is ID.me’s general cross-brand headline, not the SEA LIFE military rate — the SEA LIFE-specific figure the storefront shows is "up to 25%," and the real price is location-set and revealed after ID.me verification.
husky-liners-military-discount: The “Husky Liners military discount” you’ll see online is invented. WorthEPenny prints “up to 10%–25% discount to military members” while, on the same page, admitting “there is no official Husky Liners military program” and giving no code and no verification method. Other aggregators (ValueCom, Knoji, thegunzone) variously claim a “consistent 15% via ID.me,” that Husky Liners “uses ID.me, SheerID, or GovX,” or a “military discount at checkout” — all false. Husky Liners has no store on ID.me or GovX and no checkout military field; the GovX results that mention “Husky” are 3Wliners, a seasoning brand, Washington Huskies tickets, and a plush toy — none is Husky Liners.

Because Husky Liners is a RealTruck house brand, its products are MAP-price-protected and sell at a fixed advertised price across retailers, so “shop around for a lower price” rarely moves the number, and there’s no price-match guarantee. The reliable everyday lever on a full-price item is therefore a cashback portal: TopCashback was 4% as of July 15, 2026 (Rakuten doesn’t list a Husky Liners store). Cashback excludes tax, shipping, and fees, requires starting from an empty cart, and is voided by an outside coupon not shown on the portal — but on a full-price item you’re not using a code anyway, so the portal route is clean. The deepest cuts come from Husky Liners’ own public combo/holiday sales, which everyone gets; on the verification date the site showed “no products on sale,” so sales rotate.

If a real military percentage is what you want on floor mats, buy a substitute brand that runs a GovX program. 3Wliners (custom Thorex all-weather mats) and SmartLiner (floor liners/mats) both verify military and first-responder status through free GovX ID and apply a genuine discount — on their own products only, not on Husky Liners items. As a RealTruck brand, Husky Liners’ one veteran tie-in is a donation, not a shopper discount: RealTruck has donated 5% of Veterans Day sales to Building Homes for Heroes. Re-check the brand’s pages before relying on any figure here.
seatgeek-military-discount: The mechanics are the key thing to understand. Unlike most military discounts, SeatGeek does not name a third-party verification provider — no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute for this offer. You open SeatGeek.com, click the chat icon in the bottom-right, type "Military discount," and follow the prompts; SeatGeek says "verification may be required" to confirm eligibility. Because the offer is described as one-time and typically first-purchase, there is no recurring re-verification. ID.me does list SeatGeek — but only for member cash back, and ID.me explicitly states it is not aware of a SeatGeek military discount, so don’t expect to gate this through an ID.me login.

On the amount: SeatGeek genuinely doesn’t publish it. The figures floating around coupon sites — "5% off, up to $20" (WorthEPenny) or "up to 20%" (GrabOn) — are aggregator claims, not SeatGeek terms, and we don’t treat them as facts. The only reliable way to learn your actual offer is to ask in the chat. SeatGeek also doesn’t state whether the discount stacks with public promo codes or sale pricing, or which events count as "eligible," so confirm both in chat before you count on a specific total.

For everyday saving, a few honest options exist. ID.me members can earn modest cash back through the ID.me Shop link (up to ~0.5% for new customers, ~0.2% for existing) — that’s cash back, not a military discount. ID.me also lists a general "$5 off $300+" SeatGeek code open to anyone, and SeatGeek supports public promo codes at checkout. Separately, some leagues and events run their own military ticket policies through SeatGeek (for example event-specific golf military programs) — those are event-by-event, not a SeatGeek-wide discount. If the unpublished amount turns out to be small, it’s worth comparing the same event on Ticketmaster, Vivid Seats, or StubHub before you buy.
le-creuset-military-discount: ID.me’s Le Creuset page is titled "Le Creuset Discounts and Cash Back for Everyone" — a cash-back listing for any ID.me member, not a military-gated discount — and it states plainly that it is not aware of a Le Creuset military offer. Le Creuset’s own promotions, Specials, and Special Markets pages describe no military program and name no verification partner. So there is nothing to verify on lecreuset.com.

The genuine best paths run in order. First, a Factory to Table Sale or outlet markdown is usually live (Dutch ovens have run ~41% off) and beats any nominal military percentage with no verification. Second, if you’re exchange-eligible, the tax-free NEX/AAFES listing is the best military-specific edge on high-ticket pieces — price-check the exact item first. Third, if you’re shopping a physical Le Creuset outlet at full price, ask about the discretionary in-store 15% military offer.

On the 5.5-qt Signature Round Dutch Oven (~$420 MSRP), a typical ~35%-off sale lands near $289 with tax — versus ~$382 for the outlet 15% on a full-price piece — so the public sale is the winner for most shoppers. The exchange wins when you’re eligible and the exchange price is close to retail, because skipping ~7% sales tax on a big-ticket item adds up.
phoenix-zoo-military-discount: Verification is manual and in person: a cashier checks your photo ID for the everyday $5, or your military ID or DD214 for holiday free admission. There is no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute digital verification — everything happens at the gate.

Some discount-directory pages misstate the everyday benefit as "5% off." The zoo’s own discounts page states a flat $5 off general admission, not a percentage, so trust the primary page. The real value is the free-admission holidays: Veterans Day and Memorial Day, when active-duty and veterans enter free with proper ID.

For the best total cost, plan visits around Veterans Day and Memorial Day; if you visit multiple times a year, a household membership beats per-visit discounts; and on non-holidays, weigh the $5 gate discount against the online advance price, which is sometimes lower even without the discount. Also watch for local Arizona-resident or free-day promotions.
american-girl-military-discount: The FAQ language is precise and worth honoring: 15% off for "all active or retired members of the US Armed Forces," valid through 11:59 p.m. Central Time on 12/31/2026, redeemable in store with a military ID or online with a promotion code. Two things the FAQ does not say: it does not explicitly name veterans (separated, non-retired), spouses, or dependents, and it does not state a "$60 maximum discount." That cap appears only on aggregators — treat it as unverified.

The exclusions list is substantial: the Disney Collection, Modern Eras, Create Your Own, Ultimate Collections, the Doll Care Center, salon experiences, parties, dining and food, event tickets, gift cards, gift wrap, and shipping/processing and sales tax are all outside the 15%. The discount is one per household and can’t be combined with other offers, so it’s an either/or against a live sale price.

The tax-free Exchange path is a genuine alternative. The Navy Exchange carries a curated American Girl assortment at about a dozen locations, and select AAFES and MCX locations sell the 14.5-inch dolls — all sales-tax-free. For an excluded line like Create Your Own, or where no promotion code applies, the Exchange (or a public American Girl sale on retiring items) often beats the 15%.
saatva-military-discount: The math below uses one baseline: a $2,000 mattress order (roughly a Saatva Classic queen), pre-tax. A flat $225 on that cart is 11.25% — so any sitewide sale of 15% or better wins on it. The break-even is a $1,500 cart against a 15% sale ($225 = 15% of $1,500): above $1,500 the sale wins, below it the flat $225 wins. On a $1,200 cart, for example, $225 beats the 15% sale’s $180.

Verification runs through ID.me at checkout on saatva.com. It typically takes a few minutes, may require uploading documentation if automatic verification fails, confirms by email, and — per Saatva — is one-time, so future orders won’t need to repeat it. The discount arrives as a unique single-use code.

The same $225-off-$1,000 structure serves several other groups through parallel ID.me tiers: first responders (EMT, paramedic, firefighter, law enforcement, 911 dispatch), teachers (K-12 and professors), healthcare professionals, government employees, and seniors. These tiers don’t stack with each other or with sales — a household only ever uses one, and the buyer must be the verified person.

Two claims to ignore: coupon sites advertising "50% off Saatva" codes — Saatva’s own help center explains it doesn’t do traditional coupon codes — and roundups implying military families qualify. Saatva explicitly excludes spouses and dependents from the military tier; they can still shop the public sale like anyone else. There is also no Saatva GovX storefront, exchange carriage, or pro-deal route.
vortex-optics-military-veteran: Verification depends on the channel you choose. ExpertVoice: create a profile and request to join the military/law-enforcement team; account verification typically completes in 24–72 hours via an emailed link. GovX: verify affiliation when creating a free GovX ID, which is reused across GovX partner offers. Scheels: verify Military/LEO status through ID.me. AAFES: validate shopping eligibility during account creation at shopmyexchange.com.

Because Vortex doesn’t publish one uniform percentage across channels, the effective price on a specific model can differ by program — it’s worth comparing. The 40% off MSRP figure is the one Vortex and Scheels publish for the Scheels channel; treat it as channel-specific rather than a blanket rate.

Re-verification frequency is not stated by Vortex; verification providers (e.g., ID.me, GovX) may re-verify periodically per their own policies. For help, Vortex lists email info@vortexoptics.com and phone 1-800-486-7839.
seaworld-military-discount: The active-duty benefit is the headline: one complimentary single-day admission per year for the service member and as many as three direct dependents, redeemable at SeaWorld, Busch Gardens, or Sesame Place (one park per visit). Dependents can print their own tickets and, once ID.me-verified, may even visit without the member. Discovery Cove and Aquatica are excluded from the free comp. The offer expires December 31, 2026 and renews each calendar year.

For veterans and retirees the picture is different. The most valuable veteran deal is the annual Military Appreciation Month free-admission window in May — in 2026 the national window ran through June 30 to visit, and SeaWorld San Diego’s veteran free admission runs through July 31, 2026. Outside that window, veterans and retirees get 50% off single-day tickets (up to six; San Diego 55%) or the $161 Military Silver Annual Pass. SeaWorld’s veteran free-admission event is tied to May, not Veterans Day — we found no documented November freebie.

A note on how much it saves: each Waves of Honor offer is a standalone entitlement — there’s no coupon code, cashback portal, or public sale to stack. The free or discounted ticket is the price. If you or the family will visit two or more times in a year, the Military Silver Annual Pass (unlimited, no blockouts, free parking, three free guest tickets, up to 20% off in-park) beats repeat single-day buys quickly.
mattress-firm-military-discount: Mattress Firm verifies eligibility through ID.me. You verify your status once on Mattress Firm’s military-discount page, receive a discount code, and apply it online at checkout or present your verified status in a participating store.

Some coupon and aggregator pages headline a flat "20% off Mattress Firm military" rate. The real figure published by Mattress Firm is a range — 10-20% — and the top end is not available on every brand: Purple is reported to be capped at 10%, and a group of premium brands plus clearance, floor models, and adjustable bases are reported to be excluded from the discount entirely.

The ID.me Mattress Firm storefront that hosts the full offer terms and current exclusion list only loads its details behind the live "Verify with ID.me" flow, so the exact brand-tier and exclusion list here reflects a secondary source describing those terms rather than Mattress Firm’s own page directly. Treat the itemized exclusion list as something to re-confirm on the ID.me flow at the time you redeem.

Because the discount is reported to apply only to the already-listed sale price and generally not to combine with other promotions, a big seasonal sale event can sometimes rival or beat the military discount on certain sets — it’s worth price-checking a current public sale against your expected military savings before you commit.
marsupial-gear-military-discount: Verification is manual and human — no instant third-party portal. You send documentation to sales@marsupialgear.com; a staff member confirms your eligibility as an active-duty service member, veteran, or first responder and tags your account. There's no stated re-verification cycle. Because a person reviews it, allow a business day or two during Marsupial's listed hours (Mon–Thu 7:00a–3:30p, Fri 7:00a–1:00p MST).

Ignore the numbers on coupon aggregators. Sites like WorthEPenny, Knoji, and SimplyCodes advertise "up to 25%/30% military discount" figures and scraped "military promo codes" — but Marsupial Gear publishes no percentage and no military code. The verified path is the manual email verification, and the figure Marsupial emails you is the one that governs. Treat any specific percentage from a coupon site as unconfirmed until Marsupial states it.

There's no published stacking policy. As with most single-discount checkouts, assume the verified discount doesn't combine with a public promo code — and since the amount is unpublished, compare it against any live public code (10–15% is typical when one exists) or seasonal sale before ordering, then use whichever is deeper.

One more avenue for qualifying hunters: pro-deal programs like ExpertVoice can run deeper than a standard military percentage — but Marsupial's participation is not confirmed, so verify whether the brand has an active pro store before counting on that path. For most service members, veterans, and first responders, the email-verified discount is the primary lever.
bath-and-body-works-military-discount: How verification works: there’s nothing to verify at Bath & Body Works itself. The only verification in the picture is GovX ID (for the gift-card benefit) — GovX verifies military, first-responder, law-enforcement, medical, government, or education status once, then you log in for gift-card purchases. Exchange eligibility is verified by DoD (base access, or VetVerify for the online veterans benefit), not by the brand.

The honest math on a $100 full-price cart (7% tax modeled, since a tax-free channel competes): doing nothing costs $107. Buy 3 Get 1 Free plus TopCashback lands around $76.62 net — with zero military verification. Adding the GovX 5% gift-card layer as payment brings a similar cart to roughly $76.50, and it keeps working in-store. The Semi-Annual Sale (January and June–July) beats everything at up to 75% off select items when the sale rack has what you want.

The exchange angle nobody covers: the Navy Exchange lists 467 Bath & Body Works items online, AAFES has been opening B&BW (and White Barn) stores on installations since 2021, and shopmyexchange.com’s price-match list explicitly names bathandbodyworks.com — regular prices only, with tax-free checkout as the kicker. The brand’s own promo stack usually saves more, but the exchange wins for APO/FPO shipping and no-coupon simplicity.

Stacking rules worth knowing: most B&BW promos are automatic (no code), so cashback tracks and one portal-listed code can still apply on top. Gift cards are payment, not a coupon — the GovX 5% compounds with any sale. Buying gift cards earns no rewards, and rewards expire 90 days from issue, so redeem promptly.
ford-military-discount: The benefit is structured as an "Exclusive Cash Reward," not a fixed percentage off. Because the amount varies by market and program window, the most reliable way to know your figure is to run the ZIP step on the official site and confirm at the dealer. Dealer and editorial roundups commonly cite around $500 as a base reward, with periodic limited-time "Military Appreciation" bonus cash (often cited near $1,000) around holidays such as Memorial Day, Independence Day, and Veterans Day — but those numbers are not confirmed on Ford’s primary program pages, so treat them as illustrative rather than guaranteed.

Verification runs through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many retailers. You complete it at fordrecognizesu.com/military — Step 1 enters your ZIP, Step 2 confirms your identity and service. ID.me may ask for your SSN and military documentation (for example LES/ERB/ORB for active duty; DD214, NGB Form 22, or a VETERAN-endorsed driver’s license for veterans; retirement orders for retirees; DD Form 1300 for surviving spouses). Ford emails a Certificate you bring to the dealer.

The program window on Ford’s FAQ runs January 6, 2026 through January 4, 2027, and the limit is five eligible new vehicles per household per calendar year. Redemption happens only at an authorized Ford Dealer or Lincoln Retailer; buyers stationed overseas use Ford’s Military AutoSource program instead.
fjallraven-military-discount: The Industry Pro Program is Fjällräven’s pro-deal for full-time outdoor-industry-adjacent professionals, and military and first-responder roles are explicitly listed among its eligible categories. There is no instant verification: Fjällräven’s team manually reviews each application and the employment documentation you upload. Membership "is not guaranteed for any individual," and Fjällräven reserves the right to change the program or cancel membership at any time. If you’re approved, the discount is tagged to your account and applies automatically at checkout — there is no code — and renewal terms arrive in the welcome letter.

The fine print matters. Industry Pro excludes gift cards, Gore-Tex styles, custom Kånken bags, and special collections and collaborations. The program is full-time only — part-time, seasonal, and volunteer roles are not accepted — and students, teachers, media/content creators, coaches, and several other groups are explicitly not accepted. The discount amount itself is not published; it’s disclosed to approved members.

Be skeptical of coupon aggregators claiming a Fjällräven "10–25% military discount" verified via ID.me or SheerID, or a separate "first responder discount." Neither is a published Fjällräven offer. The only verified service-relevant program is Industry Pro — an application-gated pro-deal, not an instant checkbox discount.

Because the Industry Pro percentage is unpublished and the review takes 4–6 weeks, the highest-certainty savings for most shoppers are Fjällräven’s own end-of-season sales and outlet (reported up to ~50–60% off), or buying Fjällräven gear at a retailer that runs an instant ID.me military discount, such as Moosejaw or Backcountry — verify those retailers’ current terms and exclusions before you buy.
mcafee-military-discount: McAfee verifies through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA and the IRS. You create a free ID.me account, prove your military status (government records or uploaded documents such as a DD-214 or military ID), and ID.me passes a verified token to McAfee — at which point the discounted price on 10-Device Total Protection finally appears. ID.me’s Military community generally covers active duty, Guard/Reserve, veterans, retirees, and military family; the offer copy references both US and Canadian military.

About the numbers you’ll see elsewhere: the ID.me Shop store banner’s "special savings of up to 40% off for Military, Veterans, Nurses, Teachers, and more" is ID.me’s network-wide browser-extension banner, not a McAfee-specific rate. And the "McAfee is free for DoD" claim refers to the old DoD Antivirus Home Use Program — free home-use antivirus for DoD personnel — which was discontinued years ago and is not the current ID.me offer.

The structural reason a McAfee military discount rarely wins: subscription-software brands discount the first year aggressively for everyone and make it back at renewal. That means the real competition isn’t "military price vs. full price" — it’s "whatever ID.me reveals vs. an already-halved public intro price with cashback on top." McAfee also has a storefront on GovX (a separate closed marketplace for military and first responders); its live SKU pricing wasn’t captured for this guide, so compare it directly if you’re already a GovX member.
breville-military-discount: Breville runs no military verification — no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, WeSalute, or VerifyPass partnership. Its offers/program page lists Fast-Track, Innovation, Affiliates, and Remanufactured, but no military tier, and ID.me’s Breville page states plainly, "We’re not aware that Breville offers Military discounts." Aggregators invent an offer several ways — a "4% cash back via ID.me," a "BETTERBREW 15% (or 25%) military" code whose percentage even disagrees between sites, and a "Breville GovX military discount" — none of which is verified.

Because there’s no military code to stack, the real question is which substitute path is cheapest. The newsletter welcome code is one-time and single-use and typically excludes already-discounted and remanufactured items. Remanufactured is a separate storefront at an already-cut price, so don’t expect a coupon to stack on top. The exchanges are their own tax-free channel with no breville.com code applying — the lever there is tax plus a price-match, not a coupon.

On the baseline of a Barista Express ($699.95 MSRP new): the Certified Remanufactured store recently ran about $468.95 (roughly $231 off) with a 6-month warranty — usually the cheapest overall; public/Amazon sales land around $499–$549 for a brand-new unit; and the newsletter’s 10–15% brings a full-price direct order to about $595–$630. The exchange row shows the honest trap — NEX’s $749.95 exceeds breville.com, so tax-free only wins if the exchange price-matches a lower quote.
american-trucks-military-discount: Verification runs through SheerID, AmericanTrucks’ third-party provider — you submit your status information and are typically verified in about 90 seconds. The reward is tied to your account rather than applied as an instant checkout discount, so plan around the mechanics rather than expecting money off the current order.

The key mechanic is that AT Cash is delayed, expiring store credit. Rewards are calculated on the price you paid after any coupons or discounts (excluding shipping, fees, and taxes), post within 24 hours of shipment, and expire 90 days from issuance. On a ~$400 order the 5% sitewide tier banks about $20 of credit toward your next order — real recurring value for a repeat modifier, but easy to lose to the 90-day clock for a one-time buyer.

Because rewards are computed after coupons, the smart move is to stack: apply any live sitewide promo code now and earn AT Cash on the post-code price. For higher earn, buy Turn5-owned brands (10%) or Open Box items (20%). Coupon aggregators advertising an "AmericanTrucks military 30% off code" are false — the verified benefit is the AT Cash Rewards store credit, not an instant percentage off.
omaha-steaks-military-discount: Omaha Steaks uses ID.me for verification. You confirm your military status once through ID.me and don’t repeat it on every order; there’s no GovX or SheerID path here. The everyday benefit is a fixed $10 credit on orders of $79 or more, redeemable on the website, the mobile app, and at participating retail locations.

Because the $10 "cannot be combined with any other offers or discounts," it will not stack with a public sale price, a promo code, or the ID.me "Extra 10% off + Free Shipping $139+" offer — it’s an either/or. Meanwhile Omaha Steaks routinely stacks a percentage-off public code and free shipping on an already-marked-down package, and that everyone-path is exactly why the public sale usually beats the fixed $10 on anything with more than about $10 of savings. Verify the live cart both ways and take the lower total.

Two dated exceptions: on Veterans Day (Nov 11) Omaha Steaks has historically run about 10% sitewide plus free shipping on select packages with a troop ID — a richer military-specific deal than the everyday $10, but re-confirm the current-year terms. And ignore coupon-aggregator "Omaha Steaks military discount 20%/50% off" pages — the only verified everyday military term is $10 off $79+ via ID.me, non-combinable.
7-brew-military-discount: Because there is no standing offer, there is nothing to verify online. On Veterans Day, verification is a simple in-person ID check at the window — there is no account, pre-registration, or third-party verifier for the military offer.

The value of the Veterans Day promo is genuinely year-to-year: official 7 Brew posts showed 25% off a drink in 2024 and 50% off any drink for veterans in 2025, and an earlier year offered a free small drink. That is why we do not publish a fixed standing percentage — the aggregator “25% off military” figures presented as permanent policy are not accurate.

The dependable everyday move is 7 Brew Rewards. The free loyalty program earns toward free drinks and adds birthday perks and app flash or holiday offers. Whether the Veterans Day discount combines with Rewards is not stated by 7 Brew, so treat that as unconfirmed.
tumi-military-discount: The GovX route is real but unquantified. GovX runs a TUMI storefront (govx.com/m/1072/tumi) open to verified military, veterans, retirees, Guard & Reserve, spouses and dependents, first responders, and government employees after a free one-time verification. But GovX doesn’t publish its TUMI discount — its "up to 10–25%" marketing is site-wide, not TUMI-specific — and it’s a closed marketplace, so you can’t layer tumi.com promo codes or cashback on a GovX purchase. Treat GovX as a substitute channel to price-check, not a discount to stack: compare its member price against tumi.com’s current sale price every time.

The exchange route is the quiet win for full-price purchases. AAFES (shopmyexchange.com) stocks TUMI Alpha and Voyageur luggage online, tax-free — on a $700 carry-on that’s roughly $49 back at a ~7% sales-tax rate, with free shipping at $49+ or with MILITARY STAR. Honorably discharged veterans can shop online through the Veterans Online Shopping Benefit; active duty, retirees, Guard/Reserve, and dependents also qualify. The catch: AAFES carries a subset of the catalog, and exchange pricing is its own channel — no tumi.com promos or portal cashback apply.

The deepest verified TUMI discount anywhere is public. TUMI’s Semi-Annual Sale runs up to 40% off select styles (20/30/40% tiers, including 19 Degree, Voyageur, and Alpha Bravo) every January and July — the July 2026 edition was live at verification time. Stack a cashback portal on top (Rakuten paid 2% on TUMI as of July 14, 2026; the best portal was ~2.5%) and a $700 bag lands around $420–$560. TUMI Outlet stores run 20–40% off previous-season styles in person, and Black Friday has historically brought ~20–30% off select styles — verify the depth each November. No military-holiday promos were found in TUMI’s history; its calendar is retail-seasonal.

About those "TUMI military discount" codes: coupon aggregators advertise a "40% Off Tumi military discount" and a "Tumi Military Discount — 20% Off Promo Code." Both are fabricated — no such code or program exists on tumi.com or with any verification provider, and ID.me explicitly lists TUMI as having no military discount. The 40% figure is simply lifted from TUMI’s public Semi-Annual Sale tiers. Any "military code + sale" stacking advice for TUMI is fiction, because the code doesn’t exist.
rosetta-stone-military-discount: Rosetta Stone uses WeSalute (formerly Veterans Advantage) as its official military-verification partner. You create or log into a free WeSalute account, verify your service once, and unlock the military price without uploading documents like a military ID. Rosetta Stone is also listed on GovX and ID.me Shop, but those route to a verified price and do not confirm a deeper discount than WeSalute or the public sale. The verified brand-stated consumer rate is a modest 10%; the widely repeated "45–60% off" figure is WeSalute’s marketing measured against the ~$399 list — and it lands at about $149, roughly what anyone pays during a routine Lifetime sale.

On the "free" question: the direct Army–Rosetta Stone contract expired around 2011, and DoD MWR/base libraries offered it for years afterward. Today, most branches’ free digital-library language benefit is Transparent Language Online (Navy/USMC/USCG MWR) or Mango — not Rosetta Stone. Free Rosetta Stone access still exists at some installations through the base library, education center, or unit funding, but it is now the exception, not a DoD-wide benefit. Check with your local MWR or library before assuming it’s free.

The practical verdict: check your base library/MWR for a free language platform first (often Transparent Language, sometimes still Rosetta Stone). If you’re buying Rosetta Stone, take the Lifetime Unlimited public sale (~$149–$199) — the 10% military code is marginal, and the WeSalute $149 lifetime is about the same as the public deal. Rosetta Stone is owned by IXL Learning and controls these terms, prices, and eligibility, which can change at any time.
blade-hq-military-discount: Blade HQ publishes no military discount percentage. The amount depends on the item, and many items get no discount at all. Coupon-site figures like "10%–25%" or storewide "up to 75%–85% off" codes are not from Blade HQ and should not be trusted — knife pricing is MAP-locked, so blanket percentage codes on premium brands are not real.

Verification is manual. There is no confirmed self-serve integration with ID.me, GovX, or SheerID; aggregators name all three inconsistently, which is a red flag. Blade HQ may ask you to email or show proof of Military/LE status, after which a customer-service representative quotes an eligible-item discount. Do not assume an instant online code exists.

The confirmed eligible groups are active-duty military and law enforcement. Broader veteran, retiree, spouse, and dependent eligibility is not confirmed by a Blade HQ primary source. Because Blade HQ controls the terms and can change them at any time, confirm the current wording on bladehq.com/help before you buy.
liberty-university-military-discount: The real maximum-savings play isn’t just the rate — it’s stacking the military rate with your education benefit. Active-duty undergraduates using Tuition Assistance often reach roughly $0 out of pocket because the $250 rate matches the TA cap; veterans and dependents can layer the Post-9/11 GI Bill and Yellow Ribbon, which can cover tuition and add a housing allowance.

Before you enroll, get the free ACE evaluation of your military training for college credit. Credits you don’t have to pay for at any rate are the single biggest lever, and up to 75% of a degree may transfer (with at least 25% completed at Liberty). The application fee is also waived for service members and veterans.

Verification is handled by Liberty’s Office of Military Affairs using your service documentation — orders, DD-214, and/or your military transcript — not a consumer verifier like ID.me. The military rate then applies to eligible LUO tuition, and rates are set per academic year.
hooters-military-discount: The Veterans Day free meal is the one reliably recurring military offer, run annually including in 2024 and 2025. Terms are consistent: one free entrée from a limited special menu, dine-in only, a required beverage purchase, one offer per person, not combinable with other discounts, and a valid military ID or proof of service checked in person.

Hooters uses no third-party verification service and no online account — there is nothing to link and no code to enter. Eligibility is confirmed at the table by staff. Because any everyday discount is location-run, whether it exists, how much it is, and which days it applies are entirely up to each restaurant.

When no military discount applies, the cheapest realistic path is often Hooters’ public food specials — weekday lunch deals and a Monday burger combo (illustratively around $9–$10, varies) that need no ID — or the free HootClub Rewards loyalty program for ongoing points regardless of military status.
ray-ban-military-discount: Ray-Ban’s military savings run through ID.me, a third-party identity and group-verification service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. You create a free ID.me account and verify your community — for example, Military — by submitting accepted documentation such as a military ID, DD-214, or LES. The exact accepted documents are set by ID.me, not Ray-Ban. At ray-ban.com checkout you verify through the ID.me flow and are returned to your cart.

Ray-Ban.com itself is silent on military discounts: its Exclusive Offers page, Terms of Sale, and FAQ contain no mention of a military or veteran discount, ID.me, or a percentage. The only audience discount Ray-Ban documents on its own site is the student program via UNiDAYS. The ID.me Ray-Ban store page confirms an offer exists for "verified Military community members" but renders no percentage, no eligibility sub-groups, and no exclusions — which is why no number can be stated here in good faith.

One thing to watch: numerous coupon and aggregator pages advertise a flat "15% Ray-Ban military discount," some "up to 30%," and several claim "15% off Ray-Ban Meta." None of these are confirmed by Ray-Ban or by ID.me’s rendered terms — and ID.me’s own Ray-Ban Meta page states the opposite, that it is not aware of any Ray-Ban Meta military discount. Treat every percentage as unverified until you confirm it at ID.me checkout.
fanatics-military-discount: Fanatics verifies eligibility through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. At checkout you click Troop ID or First Responder ID, then sign in to or create a free ID.me account to confirm your status. Once verified, ID.me passes the discount to your cart automatically — there is no separate coupon code to enter.

Because Fanatics is an online-only retailer with no physical stores, the discount is redeemed only at Fanatics.com checkout; there is no in-store program. Fanatics does not state whether verification is one-time or must be repeated per order, so treat re-verification as governed by ID.me’s own policies rather than assuming it is permanent.

One thing to watch: the military discount cannot be stacked with Fanatics’ frequent public promo codes and sitewide sales. Those public promos are separate offers, so on a given order it’s worth comparing whether the 15% military discount or the current public sale saves you more.
titan-fitness-military-discount: The "no" comes straight from the source. Titan Fitness’s support center carries a dedicated policy article on military, veteran, and first-responder discounts, and its answer is that no such program currently exists — the article adds that the brand hopes to add a dedicated program in the future, which is exactly the fact this page is re-checked quarterly to catch. There is also no Titan Fitness storefront on GovX (the "Titan" brands listed there — BattleGear, Wellness, Retention — are different companies), no ID.me or SheerID offer, and no Rakuten cashback: the titan.fitness store page on Rakuten returned a 404 on July 14, 2026, so there is no portal layer to manage at all.

Where Titan’s real discounts live is its public sale calendar. The site maintains a dedicated Memorial Day sale collection, and aggregator research reports Black Friday/Cyber Monday as the deepest window of the year, up to about 35% off select equipment. On a $500 strength-equipment order — say a T-3 Series power rack — reported event depths of 15–35% put the effective price around $325–$425. Those depths are reported/historical figures, not a promise of any future promo, but the pattern is the point: if you can wait for an event, waiting is the single biggest lever.

Buying now instead? Sign up for Titan’s email list first: new subscribers reportedly get a welcome code of about 15% off a first order (verify the live percentage at signup — the figure is aggregator-reported). Welcome codes typically apply to full-price items and are one per customer, so treat "code on top of sale price" as not allowed unless checkout accepts it. Titan also publishes a Price Adjustment Policy support article — the one stack-like protection here — but its exact window and terms were not readable at verification time, so confirm them with support before relying on it.

And if a genuine military discount is what matters to you, the honest answer is to cross-shop: Titan simply does not have one, while some competing strength brands and retailers run military programs (for example, REP Fitness and Rogue — verify their current terms on their own pages before assuming). One more channel note: the military exchanges do not carry Titan Fitness, so there is no tax-free path either — every real savings route at Titan is public pricing.
crocs-military-discount: Crocs uses a third-party verification service to confirm your status before issuing a discount code. Crocs’ own military donation page links to SheerID, and Crocs separately maintains an ID.me storefront for its military community — so you may encounter either provider depending on the entry point. Which provider the standing military.html flow uses is not fully clear from Crocs’ pages, so start on Crocs’ military page and follow whichever verification it presents.

You complete the provider’s secure form (never email your military ID directly to the retailer), and on success Crocs issues an instant, single-use coupon code. Because Crocs states it “will verify your eligibility … each time you shop,” expect to re-verify or request a new code per order rather than relying on one permanent code. For problems, use the verification provider’s support and Crocs customer service.

On the rate: 15% is the everyday figure confirmed on Crocs’ military landing page, while the 25% off full-priced styles is confirmed only on Crocs’ Veterans Day donation page as a seasonal Hope for the Warriors promotion. Coupon and aggregator sites often blur the two and headline a flat 25% — treat 15% as the baseline and 25% as a limited-time window.
clear-military-discount: The military/government rate is a standing, year-round price, not a holiday sale — CLEAR offers CLEAR Plus at $125/year to military service members and government employees, versus the $219 standard rate. The official way to claim it is in person at a CLEAR airport enrollment center with a military or government ID; CLEAR verifies your identity biometrically by matching your ID to a live selfie. Membership is annual and renews yearly.

CLEAR does not publish a self-serve online military verification (such as ID.me) for this rate as of July 14, 2026. Coupon and military-discount aggregators claim the CLEAR military rate is redeemed online through an ID.me "Get Offer" button and quote figures like "$90 off" or "$99" — CLEAR’s own pages do not confirm an online military checkout or those numbers. The only official military CLEAR Plus figure is $125/year, and the official enrollment path is in person, so treat the ID.me and $90/$99 claims as unverified.

The most important distinction for active-duty readers: CLEAR Plus is not TSA PreCheck. Service members of all branches and service-academy students already get TSA PreCheck automatically using their 10-digit DoD ID (CAC) as a Known Traveler Number — free. That covers the security-screening benefit without paying CLEAR anything, so decide whether you actually want CLEAR’s separate lanes before you buy. (CLEAR now also enrolls TSA PreCheck, with a $25 spouse discount and free Gold Star family enrollment, but those are PreCheck benefits, not CLEAR Plus discounts.)

Before paying the $125 rate, check whether a card credit makes CLEAR free instead. Amex Platinum, Amex Green, and Hilton Honors Aspire cards reimburse a CLEAR Plus charge up to $219/year as a statement credit (Centurion up to $438/year for two memberships), so paying $125 or the full $219 on that card can net out to $0. Because the credit already covers the full standard fee, the military rate only saves you money if you have no such card. Card-credit and airline-partner terms change, so confirm your card’s current CLEAR credit at the source before relying on it.
us-bank-military-discount: The SCRA track is the strongest thing U.S. Bank offers, and — unusually among big issuers — it’s published policy: “If you obtained your U.S. Bank mortgage, loan, line of credit, or credit card prior to being called to active duty, SCRA allows a cap of 6% on the interest rate and a waiver of all fees while you are on active military service.” It is requested, not automatic — U.S. Bank says plainly that “you’re not automatically covered for all of the protections.” The request is easy: upload orders in the app (Manage cards → “Call to active duty orders”), or go through the Military Service Center by phone (800-934-9555; overseas collect 513-277-5899), email, mail, or fax. The outcome comes by letter. The same published page also covers SCRA auto-lease termination without penalty and mortgage foreclosure protection during service plus one year — worth a call before a PCS or deployment. The statutory floor applies regardless: interest above 6% is forgiven, and the claim window runs through active duty plus 180 days after release.

The MLA track comes with a freshness warning most ranking pages haven’t caught up with. Yes, U.S. Bank reportedly checks applicants’ SSNs against the DoD MLA database and waives annual fees to $0 for covered borrowers — active duty, Guard/Reserve on 30+ day orders, spouses and dependents — mailing an MLA benefits letter that often arrives before the card does. (usbank.com never states this; the figure comes from benefits letters and consistent military-finance reporting, and U.S. Bank may not always waive fees under either program — check your own status at mla.dmdc.osd.mil before applying.) But the card that made the waiver famous, the $400 Altitude Reserve, closed to new applications on November 11, 2024 — existing holders keep it, with benefits cut on December 15, 2025 — and the FlexPerks Gold Amex has quietly disappeared, its usbank.com URL now serving the $0-fee Smartly Visa page. Every currently open flagship consumer card (Smartly Visa, Shield, Altitude Go, Altitude Connect, Cash+) is $0-annual-fee for everyone, so the waiver has almost nothing to act on; annual fees survive mainly on the Korean Air SKYPASS co-brands. The old “you must be an existing U.S. Bank customer” application hurdle was an Altitude-Reserve-era requirement — moot for the closed card and not stated on any current open card page. If the goal is a fee-waived premium travel card while serving, the MLA route lives at American Express and Chase now.

The veteran-honest answer: veterans and retirees not on active duty get no card fee relief at U.S. Bank — the benefit that explicitly includes them is checking. usbank.com states the $12 monthly maintenance fee on Bank Smartly Checking is waived for “active duty military and veterans,” with eligibility worded as “current or former member of the United States Armed Forces,” by self-disclosure — no ID.me, no DD-214 upload step published. The package adds $0 U.S. Bank ATM transaction fees, the first four non-U.S. Bank ATM transactions per statement period fee-free with the first surcharge reimbursed each period, and free cashier’s checks, personal money orders, and stop payments. That’s $144 a year in maintenance fees alone, and it’s one of the few big-bank checking waivers that names veterans explicitly. Unlike Capital One (published 4%) and Chase (reported 4%), U.S. Bank advertises no below-6% SCRA rate — its published benefit is the statutory cap plus the all-fees waiver. Compare the companion issuer guides: Amex publishes its policy openly, Chase’s numbers are letter-confirmed, and Navy Federal and Citi have their own quirks.
bose-military-discount: Verification is handled by ID.me. You verify in your Bose cart using the "Verify with ID.me" button, and the discount applies automatically once verified. An ID.me account is required. Per ID.me’s help center, once you verify a group you generally don’t need to re-verify unless you lose account access or go more than a year without using the account, though ID.me may periodically ask you to re-verify identity for security — so don’t assume verification is permanent. For verification problems, use ID.me support; for order or discount issues at checkout, use Bose customer support.

The two numbers that matter are the 10% rate and the $100 cap. Because savings max out at $100, the discount is proportionally smaller on big-ticket systems, and Bose’s recurring site-wide sales (e.g., "up to 20%" or higher on select products) can beat 10% on a given item — and the page doesn’t confirm the ID.me discount stacks with those, so compare rather than assume. Aviation headsets are the one product line treated differently: excluded for every group except Military, and for a dedicated purchase path, the Bose Military Aviation program is reachable at Military_Headsets@Bose.com.

To stretch value further, Bose Certified Refurbished advertises savings up to roughly 55% on select products, Bose offers a price-match promise and a trade-up program (up to $300 toward new products), and My Bose members get welcome and birthday offers. For audio specifically, some competitors run their own ID.me military offers (Sonos reportedly ~15%, Sony up to ~10%) — confirm each brand’s current terms on its official ID.me storefront before relying on them.
blue-nile-military-discount: Blue Nile’s discount is powered by ID.me, the same identity-verification service used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of major retailers. You verify your military, first-responder, medical, or teacher status once, ID.me issues a promo code, and you enter that code in your Blue Nile cart (or give it over the phone). ID.me community statuses can expire and require periodic re-verification, so don’t assume the access is permanent.

The reason to read the fine print carefully is the exclusion list. The 15% does not apply to loose diamonds, settings, Build Your Own Diamond Jewelry, or preset engagement rings, studs, and solitaire pendants — the exact products most people come to Blue Nile to buy. It’s also void on sale/clearance merchandise and designer lines. Shoppers frequently report that if any ineligible component is in the cart (like a loose diamond in a ring build), the whole code can fail. In practice the 15% only touches a narrow slice of regularly-priced fashion and fine jewelry.

That makes the smartest path situational. For a diamond engagement ring, ignore the military discount and buy into Blue Nile’s frequent public sale events (currently a 250th Anniversary event up to 40% off, with the James Allen Collection up to 50% off), add the $50 email-signup credit, and cross-shop the same stone at sister brand James Allen — both are owned by Signet. The 15% is your best single lever only on regularly-priced, non-diamond jewelry that isn’t on sale. Because Blue Nile controls the terms, confirm the current offer and exclusions on the live ID.me storefront before you buy.
palmetto-state-armory-military-discount: Palmetto State Armory has no online military route. Its official Coupon Code Deals page lists rotating product-specific offers only — no military mechanic — and its Help Center says nothing about a military discount. There is no verification-gated checkout: no ID.me, no GovX ID, no SheerID. ID.me once listed a Palmetto State Armory store, but that page is deactivated and now redirects to the ID.me Shop homepage. The surviving "PSA Outdoors" ID.me listing is affiliate cashback for everyone (up to 2.5%), not a military-gated discount. GovX has no PSA storefront, and PSA’s ExpertVoice page is a program for its own retail employees, not a military benefit.

The one genuine military mechanic is in store and unofficial. On PSA’s own forum, a veteran wrote in November 2023 that "they do offer a military discount in store … I can use it but not online." No PSA staff confirmed terms in the thread, and no percentage is reported — so treat the in-store discount as real but discretionary: ask at the register with ID in hand, and compare whatever you are offered against the online sale price before assuming it wins.

For most readers buying online, the smart move is to ignore the "military discount" chase entirely. PSA’s Daily Deals and clearance pricing are automatic (not a code), so a cashback portal tracks cleanly on top. As of July 7, 2026, BeFrugal listed 7% — the highest rate we found — which on a $479.99 sale-priced rifle nets roughly $446, about $104 under the $549.99 list price, with no code and no verification. Layer a live manufacturer rebate from PSA’s Rebates & Promotions hub when one applies to your item.

Be cautious of coupon and deal sites that advertise a specific PSA "military discount" percentage. One well-known aggregator contradicts itself — its body copy admits there is no official PSA military program while its FAQ claims a 10–25% online military discount. None of it is verifiable on PSA’s site. We deliberately omit those numbers here because repeating them would imply an offer PSA does not run. PSA does run public military-holiday sales (a Veterans Day weekend promo and a Memorial Day sale section), but those are open to everyone — not verified military discounts.
panda-express-military-discount: Panda Express publishes no official military discount anywhere: not in its order FAQ, not in its rewards terms, and not in any corporate page — and it is absent from both the 2024 and 2025 Veterans Day free-meal roundups that list chains like Chipotle and Applebee’s. So there is no company-wide military percentage to claim, no online military code, and no verification partner (no ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute) because there is no formal program.

The "~10% military discount" you will see reported is a discretionary courtesy discount that some individual locations grant at the manager’s discretion. Even the menu-price and coupon sites that mention it note that Panda Express "does not publish or promote an official military discount policy," that it is in-store only with a valid ID at the register, that it varies by store (some report 5–15%), and that it is not stackable with promo codes. Treat it as a YMMV bonus to politely ask about — not a benefit to budget around — and note that some locations reportedly extend the same courtesy to first responders and medical workers.

The reliable, documented savings is the free Panda Rewards program. Its corporate launch release confirms a welcome gift of 25% off your first order (up to $10 off), 10 points earned per $1 on qualifying purchases, redemptions starting at 200 points for free entrées and upgrades, a birthday gift, and a monthly "Good Fortune Gift." On a ~$12.90 Bigger Plate, the 25% welcome gift brings the price to about $9.68 — deeper and more dependable than the ~10% counter discount, and it works on app and online orders where the courtesy discount does not.
rogue-military-discount: The honest core fact: Rogue’s official answer is that it does not run an everyday military discount. Its Military page is a charity-and-shipping page, not a discount page, and the brand explains that it keeps everyday prices low for all customers rather than issue an identity code. That makes the calendar and shipping mechanics — not a coupon — the starting point for any service member shopping Rogue.

The standout brand-run military offer is the Veterans Day sale. Each November, Rogue offers exclusive pricing to logged-in, verified veterans and active US military. Verification is handled inside your Rogue account: log in, verify your status on the account dashboard, and the member pricing appears on the Veterans Day page during the window.
