Because a low-demand date can be cheaper than the flat $2 off, veterans, retirees, and off-season visitors should compare a low-demand advance date against the $2 gate discount, whichever is cheaper.
national-aquarium-military-discount: Verification is entirely in person at the box office — you show a valid military or veteran ID at the time of purchase. The Aquarium spells out the accepted veteran IDs precisely: a DoD identification card, a Veteran Health Identification Card, a Veteran ID Card, or a veteran designation printed on a state-issued driver’s license or ID. Its page names no online verification provider — no ID.me, GovX, or SheerID — and publishes no online military price, so treat any aggregator claim of an "online military code" for this venue as unverified.

One honest caveat about who actually saves: $39.95 is the adult (ages 21–69) rate. Youth (5–20) and seniors (70+) already pay $39.95 as the standard rate, and children 4 and under are free — so the military discount is really a benefit on the 21–69 adult ticket, not an additional cut for other ages. For two adults, that’s about $20 saved per visit.

On Blue Star Museums: the National Aquarium does not advertise participation on its own site and is not confirmed among 2026 participants — it offers its own year-round military price instead. Blue Star (free summer admission for active-duty families, 2026 season May 16–September 7) is a separate NEA program that excludes veterans; verify participation on the official arts.gov map each season before relying on it. A separate "Maryland Mornings" early-entry offer takes $10 off adult and $5 off military timed tickets, but the Aquarium doesn’t address combining it with the military rate — don’t assume stacking.
caesars-military-discount: The room rate is verified online through ID.me: you verify once, choose the Military category, sign in at booking, and Caesars honors the rate. Beware the aggregator "up to 35%" or "up to 50%" headlines — those are a blended marketing ceiling that stacks the base 15%, the extra-10%-off-sale-rates layer, public sale depth, and the fact that Caesars runs the same tier for nurses, first responders, teachers, government employees, students, and seniors. Caesars’ own current headline is up to 25% (the 2026 promo) on top of a standing up to 15% + extra 10% off sale rates.

Room rates are mutually exclusive — you book one rate (the ID.me military rate, the Salute 10% rate, a public sale rate, or a Rewards member offer), not several stacked room discounts, so pick the lowest. The one built-in "stack" is the extra 10% off a flagged sale rate for verified groups. The discount never touches resort fees or room tax, and cashback generally doesn’t help: Rakuten showed no Caesars cash back as of June 2026, and the ID.me gate typically breaks portal tracking.

The durable win is the free Caesars Rewards Salute Card, enrolled in person with a military or veteran ID at a Rewards desk. It grants automatic Platinum status — a loyalty tier, not a rate — so free self/valet parking and presale access apply on top of whatever rate you book, and the parking often outlasts and out-values a single thin room percentage. If you’re flexible on property, price-check MGM Resorts’ 10% room discount (verified in person, no ID.me), though Caesars’ 15–25% usually wins the room. And book direct — OTAs forfeit Caesars Rewards credit, Salute/Platinum perks, and best-rate terms.
prime-military-discount: Coupon and military-info sites keep an "Amazon Prime military discount" alive, and every one of those pages traces back to the same two dead ends: the one-time November 2019 Veterans Day promo ($40 off one year of Prime, November 6–11, 2019 — not repeated in any year since, with nothing announced for 2026), or Amazon’s "military discount" keyword search page, which is just third-party product listings. Amazon’s own plan pages and ID.me both confirm the real answer: no military price exists on any Prime plan, and there is no ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute flow to verify because there is nothing to verify.

The tier that actually fits most junior enlisted is Prime for Young Adults: a 6-month $0 trial, then $7.49/month or $69/year — half the standard price — for anyone aged 18–24 or enrolled in college (including GI Bill and Tuition Assistance students who are enrolled), plus 5% cash back on eligible items while you’re in the program. Amazon verifies age or enrollment at sign-up. The tier that fits assistance-receiving military families is Prime Access at $6.99/month, which qualifies on a government-assistance program (SNAP EBT, Medicaid, WIC, SSI, TANF, and others) or a household income at or below 200% of the Federal Poverty Guideline, reverified every 12 months — being military is neither necessary nor sufficient. Through September 30, 2026, Prime Access also carries a $5/month grocery credit on $25+ eligible grocery orders.

If neither door fits, the honest playbook is simple: take the 30-day free trial, choose the $139 annual plan over $14.99/month (that alone saves $40.88 a year), and share benefits with your household so one membership covers two adults instead of buying twice. Don’t bother routing the membership through a cashback portal — Rakuten’s Amazon offer explicitly excludes subscriptions, so the Prime fee never earns cashback. And if Amazon ever revives a Veterans Day Prime promo, it will appear on amazon.com in early November — worth a glance each year, never worth planning on.
spanx-military-discount: There is no military verification at SPANX because the brand does not participate in ID.me or SheerID military programs. ID.me’s own SPANX store page does not list a military offer, and SheerID does not carry a SPANX military audience. Coupon sites headlining a "SPANX military discount" of "30% off" are describing ordinary public promo codes anyone can use — not a status-gated military benefit.

For a service member, the honest maximum-savings path is a public sitewide sale or promo code stacked with the first-order email/SMS signup offer. SPANX generally allows one promo code per order, so the practical move is to take the largest live public discount and, on a first order, add the signup code where the checkout allows it. On a $68 order, a 20% public code brings it to about $54.

Two more levers: the "On the Sly" clearance section carries marked-down pricing worth checking before you buy at full price, and verified students can occasionally get an offer through UNiDAYS — though that’s a student program, not a military one, and it isn’t always live. There is no GovX, Exchange, or pro-deal channel for SPANX.
dyson-military-discount: Dyson does not use any military verification provider (ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute) for a discount of its own, because it has no such program. For third-party access: GOVX verifies military/government/first-responder/nurse/teacher status before showing gated pricing; WeSalute verifies eligibility as part of a paid membership and issues a WeSalute+ ID card. Each third party sets its own re-verification rules and account requirements — confirm current terms on their sites. NavyWeek does not control and cannot guarantee third-party pricing.

The everyday, primary-source-backed savings are Dyson’s own and open to everyone: Owner Rewards (20% off one selected machine via a one-time code for registered owners), the Dyson Deals page (rotating markdowns, seasonal events), and Dyson Certified Refurbished (Outlet) machines with warranty at lower prices. The 20% Owner Rewards figure is exactly the number that aggregator pages misreport as a "military discount."

Where can military members find the best price on a Dyson? Compare Dyson’s own Deals, Owner Rewards (if you own a Dyson), and the Certified Refurbished outlet against GOVX or WeSalute member pricing — none of the third parties publish their exact percentage publicly, so verify and compare the final price.
govee-military-discount: Govee routes its Key Worker discount through Beans iD, the identity-verification platform run by Student Beans. You create a free Beans iD account, verify your eligibility (military, healthcare, teacher, or first responder) once, and reveal a single-use code that regenerates roughly monthly. There is no confirmed ID.me, SheerID, or GovX verification path for Govee’s military discount — Beans iD is the named partner, and ID.me only offers cashback.

The 10% vs 12% figure depends on the product, not the person: items in Govee’s "12% off" collection get 12%, items in the "10% off" collection get 10%. The code is explicitly non-combinable with any other code, promotion, or sale, so a sitewide sale counts as a "promotion" it will not layer on. In practice you choose the code or the sale — and because Govee discounts deeply and often, the sale usually wins.

Because you enter no discount code on a sale order, portal cashback (e.g. ID.me Shop) can layer on it — but using a Beans iD, WeSalute, or newsletter code turns it into a code order that typically voids or reduces that cashback. The realistic choice is (public sale + cashback) or (Beans iD code alone). Govee’s official Key Worker page is JavaScript-rendered; confirm the current tiers and eligible groups there before you buy.
primary-arms-military-discount: The Heroes Program is “Powered by ID.me.” You link your Primary Arms account to an ID.me profile once; ID.me confirms your military, first-responder, or law-enforcement status, and the Heroes pricing then applies automatically whenever you’re logged in — “no codes to memorize.” Primary Arms launched its ID.me authenticator in 2022.

Because the discount is product-specific and unpublished, the only way to see your real price is to log in and verify. Aggregator figures like a flat “10–25% military discount,” a “GovX” verifier, and stackable “military coupon codes” are not verified Primary Arms facts — the verifier is ID.me, and the coupon terms explicitly say codes cannot combine with the Heroes Program.

Beyond the standard Heroes tier, narrower groups get deeper programs: the Active-Duty Military Discount Program (active-duty only), the Active EMT & Firefighter Program, the once-a-year Premier Savings Program on optics, and the Individual Officer Purchase Program for sworn law enforcement — all ID.me-gated.
tj-maxx-military-discount: All the math below uses one baseline: a $150 mixed cart (apparel plus a home item at T.J. Maxx markdown prices), pre-tax. There is no tax-free or military channel to price in — every real saving here is a layer open to all shoppers.

Two myths, cleared up. First, a "10% T.J. Maxx military discount — register on the site and verify as active-duty, veteran, or family" claim circulates on coupon and QA sites. No such program or verification exists; ID.me confirms none and T.J. Maxx publishes no military page. Second, the WeSalute "T.J. Maxx military offer" is really just the standard free-shipping-over-$89 threshold surfaced through a military-membership site — every shopper already gets it. Neither is a military discount.

The one durable lever. The TJX Rewards credit card earns 5% back in Rewards (5 points per $1) across T.J. Maxx, Marshalls, HomeGoods, HomeSense, and Sierra — a $10 certificate per 1,000 points as store credit — plus 10% off your first purchase, with no annual fee. The open-loop TJX Rewards Platinum Mastercard adds 2% back on gas, grocery, and restaurant purchases elsewhere. On the $150 cart, the card’s 5% is about $7.50 back, and opening the card gets you $15 off (10%) on that first order.

So what wins? A regular TJX shopper’s only durable percentage is the card. A one-time buyer has no discount to chase — just time the markdowns; final yellow-sticker clearance beats any 1.5–5%. Buying online at $89+, take the free shipping (public) and check whether any portal tracks that day (coverage is thin and gift-card-skewed, ~1.5% as of July 8, 2026).
filson-military-discount: When a Filson military offer is live, eligibility is verified through a third-party service — reported to be SheerID, not ID.me — which issues a single-use code tied to that specific promo. It is not a permanent account discount, so you re-verify each time a new offer runs. We say "reported" deliberately: the SheerID provider is not independently pinned to a confirmed Filson program, so treat the mechanic as the best-available report rather than a fixed fact, and confirm the verifier on the live offer.

Be cautious of coupon and deal sites that advertise an "everyday 10-25% Filson military discount via ID.me." That is false on the mechanic — ID.me’s own store page states it isn’t aware Filson offers a military discount and lists only free shipping — and overstated on the rate, because Filson publishes no evergreen percentage. The only brand-stated figure is the Veterans Day 2025 promo (25% off full-price), which was time-boxed. Treat any specific "military code" or "first-responder 40%" figure as unverified.

Filson’s evergreen discount channel is the Pro Program: an application-reviewed program for outdoor-industry professionals — guides, conservation, outdoor media, and industry. Approved pros report roughly 40% off (unverified) for personal use with no resale. It is a professional program with its own eligibility, not a benefit for military service or veteran status, though some community reports suggest active-duty members may qualify — verify that in the application.

Even without an everyday military discount, there are honest ways to save on Filson. Shop the public sale and year-round Men’s/Women’s Outlet — deep seasonal markdowns (Memorial Day, Summer) that are open to everyone and often beat the full-price-only military offer. Sign up for Filson email and VIP texts for a welcome offer (a sitewide code is more cashback-portal-safe than a military code). And cross-shop authorized dealers like REI (a ~10% annual co-op dividend) and Huckberry, which carry Filson and run their own sales and rewards.
sur-la-table-military-discount: Sur La Table’s military benefit is an evergreen in-store ID discount, not a holiday promotion. Verification is manual and in-person: you show a valid military ID to the cashier at a Sur La Table store. There is no online identity-verification path — no ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute military offer for the website — so you should not expect an online code.

Because the discount is channel-locked to physical stores, the smartest route depends on how you shop. In a store, on full-price, non-excluded goods, the 15% military discount is the best single lever. Online, where the identity discount does not exist, you save most by stacking a public sale or promo code with a cashback portal and SLT Perks points. For discontinued or premium excluded items, clearance pricing usually beats every ID discount.

Sur La Table is owned by Marquee Brands (with CSC Generation as operating partner) after a 2020 acquisition out of bankruptcy; its stores and e-commerce are active. As with any brand, terms can change, so confirm the current policy on Sur La Table’s FAQ before you buy.
ninja-military-discount: Ninja’s FAQ is the tell: it routes "military discounts" to ID.me Shop and "student discounts" to UNiDAYS. ID.me Shop is a cashback marketplace where any ID.me member can earn cashback — it is not a verified percentage off at Ninja checkout, and the SharkNinja store page there states plainly that ID.me is not aware of a SharkNinja military offer. There is also no GovX storefront for Ninja Kitchen appliances, so the GovX route that exists for many brands is not available here.

The one genuine Ninja/SharkNinja "military" discount — 9% off — lives on the UK sites (sharkclean.co.uk and ninjakitchen.co.uk) and is verified through GoCertify. It is UK-only, excludes parts, accessories, and certain named products, and cannot be combined with cashback or other codes. It is rejected on the US site, so US coupon pages that advertise a "Ninja military discount" are conflating that UK offer. Treat any US "military code" with caution.

For a US service member the honest best path is a stack of public levers. A certified refurbished unit on ninjakitchen.com is usually the deepest single lever — it sells below new but carries a 90-day limited warranty instead of the standard one year. When a major public sale is live (Memorial Day, July 4, Black Friday), that markdown frequently beats any 10% code. If you are buying a full-price item and no deeper sale is running, the public 10% new-subscriber email code saves about $20 on a $200 appliance. And if you are not applying a code, a cashback portal (roughly 2–3% as of July 8, 2026) adds a few dollars on an un-coded order.

Note the stacking rules: coupon codes typically void cashback on the same order, and codes usually do not combine with sale or clearance pricing — compare and take the lower. Certified refurbished is a substitute price, not something you add a discount on top of. Two identity/welcome levers (the UNiDAYS student 10% and the email 10%) are single-use and not stackable with each other. Finally, buying the same Ninja model at a retailer such as Lowe’s or Home Depot and using that store’s verified military discount can win — but that is the retailer’s program, with its own terms.
sandals-military-discount: The stacking is the headline, and it’s confirmed on both sides: Sandals’ own specials hub calls the program "an additional 10% savings year round," SheerID’s offer page says verified members get "an additional 10% off their special packages," and Sandals’ Best Price Guarantee states the booking engine "will automatically apply all combinable offers." That makes the strategy the opposite of most travel discounts — never choose between the sale and the military rate; take the sale, then add the 10%.

Mechanically, it’s an account-level discount, not a code. You book first (so verification never blocks a sale price), then verify through SheerID under Profile → Service Personnel Discount and apply the discount to your trip before final payment. SheerID’s eligibility list covers US and Canadian active duty, retired military, reserves, US National Guard, US veterans, US Department of Defense personnel, and spouses — though the brand page itself says only "members of the U.S. or Canada military," so treat spouse eligibility as SheerID’s call. Police, firefighters, EMTs, search-and-rescue, and active FEMA members get parallel 10% offers, and Beaches Resorts runs the identical program on a shared account system.

The Veterans Day boost is real but historical: in November 2024 Sandals raised the military discount to 15% (booked November 1–16, 2024, travel through December 31, 2025, across all 17 Sandals and 3 Beaches resorts, with first responders staying at 10%), and editorial coverage reports an up-to-15% window again through November 11, 2025. Don’t blend that into "10–15%" — the standing rate is 10%, and early November is simply the best-known booking window to check.

Skip the detours: GovX’s Sandals page routes members to this same brand program, and WeSalute’s 10% runs through American Airlines Vacations’ private engine with a paid membership and terms that void the discount if a phone rep touches the booking — no better than the free direct path. Rakuten showed 2% cashback on sandals.com as of July 7, 2026, but whether portal tracking pays out alongside the account-applied discount is unverified — treat any cashback as a bonus, not a plan. Editorial sources also report the 10% applies to the resort portion only (not flights), one room per member, and ID at check-in.
true-classic-military-discount: True Classic verifies heroes on its own site through SheerID — a "community verification" widget embedded on the Hero page. Pick your category (military, first responder, medical, teacher, or student), confirm your eligibility through SheerID, and the 20% unlocks at checkout. It also supports GovX ID via a separate GovX storefront. There is no confirmed ID.me, WeSalute, or VerifyPass path for True Classic.

The catch that makes this page more useful than a coupon page: 20% is also True Classic’s near-permanent public price. New subscribers get a 20% email welcome code, sitewide 20% sales run constantly (Memorial Day 2025 was 20% off), and the "We Made Too Much" clearance runs up to about 68% off. So the SheerID Hero 20% usually ties, not beats, what any shopper can already get — and it won’t stack, since only one code applies per order and clearance is excluded.

The Hero discount’s real value is for repeat buyers: the public welcome code is first-order only, while the SheerID code is re-issued each time you verify. If you’re flexible on styles, the "We Made Too Much" outlet often beats both — but no code stacks on top of it.
nfl-plus-military-discount: Verification is handled by ID.me — the same service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. You create or sign in to a free ID.me account and confirm military or first-responder status. NFL issues new promo codes each season and voids prior-season codes, so re-pull a fresh code each year. There is no indication the discount is permanent or auto-renews at the discounted rate — treat it as a per-season code, not a lifetime price.

NFL+ list pricing is $6.99/month or $49.99/year for Basic, and $14.99/month or $99.99/year for Premium (which adds NFL RedZone and full/condensed/All-22 coaches’-film replays). The public preseason 20%-off annual promo brings Premium to about $79.99 and Basic to about $39.99 with no verification. Because the military code and the public sale can’t be combined, verify first, read your revealed code, then compare it to the current public price and take whichever is lower.

If you’re flexible on timing, NFL+ cuts prices deepest in the off-season and around Black Friday — historically as low as $19.99–$29.99/year — which often beats both the public 20% promo and the ID.me code. One more caution: don’t confuse NFL+ with NFL Sunday Ticket. The widely cited "$198 military" price is Sunday Ticket on YouTube, a separate product, not NFL+.
leatherman-military-discount: Verification runs through VerifyPass, a one-time identity check that can take a few hours to clear. Once approved, you get a single-use discount code by email, good for that purchase window — you’ll need to re-verify for a future order, since Leatherman allows only 1 code per person every 365 days and each code expires December 31.

The 20% applies to the original multi-tool price and any custom add-on features, but it explicitly excludes gift cards, limited edition items, and apparel. It also cannot be combined with Leatherman’s own public sale — so when a tool is already marked down 20-50% sitewide, the sale price will often beat the military code, which can’t stack on top of it anyway.

GovX is a separate path worth checking: it’s a free-to-join military and government marketplace that carries Leatherman and advertises 25-50% off MSRP across the brands it sells. GovX doesn’t stack with Leatherman’s code — it’s a substitute marketplace purchase, and its exact price per Leatherman tool is only visible after a free login, so compare it directly against leatherman.com before deciding where to buy.

One figure to watch out for: some sites cite a "40% off" Leatherman military discount. That is not the military rate. Leatherman’s official military-discount page states 20% off for the military tier; a 40% figure has been reported in community discussion tied to Leatherman’s separate special-discount communities (first responders, medical, teachers, students), not the military program, and it is not confirmed against the live military offer.
sport-clips-military-discount: The Sport Clips military benefit is genuinely two-track. The reliable, corporate-level offer is the Veterans Day free haircut: on November 11, participating stores give veterans and active-duty service members a free cut, which the chain bills as its biggest haircut day of the year. Confirm participation each year, since it depends on the individual store.

The second track is the everyday military rate, and this is where honesty matters. Corporate publishes no fixed percentage — the amount, and even whether a rate exists, is set by each independently owned franchise. Community reports cluster around 10% at stores that offer one, but you must confirm it at your location; treat any specific percentage as store-level until you verify it in person.

Verification is entirely in person. Eligibility is shown with a VFW membership card or Military ID at the store — there is no ID.me, SheerID, GovX, WeSalute, or VerifyPass flow, and no online checkout to apply a discount to. Separately, Sport Clips runs its Help A Hero fundraiser (a $2-per-service donation on Nov 11 toward VFW scholarships); that is a charitable mechanic, not a customer discount, so do not treat it as savings.
aritzia-military-discount: All the math below uses one baseline: a $200 apparel cart (say, one Babaton or Wilfred sweater plus a tee), with an illustrative 7% sales tax where noted. There is no tax-free channel that competes.

The debunk matters because the fabrications are wholesale. SavingSays advertises "Aritzia Military Discount – 20% Off," WorthEPenny runs an "Aritzia Military & Veteran Discounts" page, and multiple sites push a code (e.g., "DECORANDDESIGNE for 25% off") framed as a military unlock. None of this is real: Aritzia has no military program, no ID.me/SheerID/GovX military checkout, and no official public promo codes. A random code that happens to "work" is not a military benefit — it usually signals an unauthorized or expired coupon.

The honest maximum-savings path is Aritzia’s own model. Because Aritzia is deliberately full-price, markdowns are funneled into a permanent Sale area, and anything 50%+ off is final sale. So the deepest public price is a 50%+ final-sale item (buy only when you’re sure of size and fit), and the only structured discount is the free Clientele program’s member events. There’s no code layer to add (Aritzia issues none) and no cashback layer (it’s off Rakuten US) — the Sale section, Clientele, and newsletter timing are the whole toolkit.

One substitute note: Aritzia’s core labels are largely exclusive to Aritzia, so there’s no third-party retailer selling the same pieces with a military discount. The resale market (Poshmark, TheRealReal) is the only alternative and carries no military benefit, though it often runs below retail.
harbor-freight-military-discount: Harbor Freight uses no military-status verification because it offers no military discount — there is no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute flow, no account requirement tied to service status, and nothing to re-verify. Its own "How Can I Get A Discount" page lists coupons, the Inside Track Club, the credit card, and email offers as the ways to save, and names no military program.

Any "Harbor Freight military discount %" promoted on coupon aggregators or social posts is not an official program. Some aggregator pages phrase it as "an undetermined discount to veterans who show proof of service on Veterans Day," but no Harbor Freight primary source confirms a proof-of-service military discount — treat the absence as the verified finding.

Harbor Freight does support the veteran community through charitable giving: the Harbor Freight Tools Foundation funds veteran-serving nonprofits such as the National Coalition for Homeless Veterans and The Mission Continues, and associates volunteer with VA hospital programs. That is philanthropy, separate from any customer discount. Veterans seeking tool/auto savings elsewhere can use retailers that do offer a verified military discount, such as AutoZone (10% in-store) or Ace Hardware (varies by participating store).
hoka-military-veteran: All the math below uses one baseline: a full-price HOKA Clifton at $145, shipped to a US address. HOKA offers free shipping and free returns, so shipping is $0 on every path and does not change the ranking — it just makes the percentages directly comparable.

Rule 1 — HOKA’s direct discounts don’t stack with anything. Its terms say the first-responder and medical discounts cannot be combined with other offers, are online only, and exclude sale items and collabs. So the 15%/25% is a substitute for a sale, never an add-on — and an ID.me-gated checkout typically breaks cashback tracking, so do not promise yourself "15% + cashback."

Rule 2 — cashback only survives the right kind of coupon. Portals like Rakuten void your cashback if you use a non-portal "code." A standard sitewide newsletter code is usually fine; a scraped "military code" from a coupon site is exactly what voids it. Always activate the portal before shopping and apply only portal-listed codes.

Rule 3 — the highest cashback portal isn’t always Rakuten. For HOKA right now RebatesMe (~5%) and TopCashback (~4%) beat Rakuten (3%). A real maximize-savings page sends you to the current top portal, not a hard-coded one — and stamps the rate with a date, because these move weekly (rates as of June 16, 2026).
cirque-du-soleil-military-discount: The deepest deal lives at the Las Vegas box office, but it’s narrow: Treasure Island (the Mystère venue) states active military and children under 12 are eligible for a 35% up to 50% discount based on availability, bookable only by phone or in person and not combinable with any other offer. It’s inventory-gated — great seats when a show isn’t sold out, nothing when it is — and the primary source specifies “active military,” so veterans shouldn’t assume the box-office deep rate applies to them.

The dependable, broadly-eligible path is GovX. A free GovX ID verifies active military, veterans, retirees, Guard/Reserve, military family, first responders, government employees, and teachers, then the discounted member price shows automatically on the Cirque store — for touring shows nationwide and Las Vegas resident shows alike. Community and editorial sources peg GovX Cirque savings around 20%, varying by show and date; treat that as a planning estimate, not a fixed rate. Cirque also appears on ID.me Shop with an “up to 30%” tile, but the tile’s exact terms aren’t stated — confirm the actual price before buying.

Beware the aggregator framing. Blogs claim a flat “up to 10–25% military discount, redeemable on cirquedusoleil.com after verifying at 702-894-7722.” That number is 702-894-7722’s box office (phone), the deep discount there is active-military-and-kids, availability-based, box-office only — and there is no self-serve online military percentage on cirquedusoleil.com. The public “up to 20–30%” deals are the fallback everyone already gets; when you have no military status or the military seats are sold out, take that advance-purchase public promo.
kuhl-military-discount: KÜHL.com has no military verification step — no ID.me, SheerID, or GovX military flow — and KÜHL has no GovX storefront (the GovX KÜHL page returns "page not found"). KÜHL’s Pro Sales program sits behind an account login and application; the verification provider and approval criteria are not publicly stated, and military service by itself is not listed as a qualifying basis. KÜHL also appears on ExpertVoice, which is a professional pro-deal platform, not a military-verification service.

The clearest verified savings for the military community is the Exchange. Through ShopMyExchange (AAFES), eligible patrons — active duty, retirees, Reserve/Guard, authorized dependents, and honorably discharged veterans via the Veterans Online Shopping Benefit — buy KÜHL tax-free and can catch Exchange-run promotions. AAFES performs the eligibility verification (military ID, veteran registration, etc.); the benefit is the Exchange’s, not a KÜHL discount, and item-level pricing varies, so check it live before relying on a number.

Be skeptical of coupon-site claims. Figures circulating for a "KÜHL military discount" — 40% off, a "30% off DOESDA" code, 25% off, or a "75% first responder" deal — are not confirmed by any KÜHL primary source, are mutually contradictory, and in at least one case reference an implausible code. The everyday ways to save are open to everyone: KÜHL’s free Mountain Culture Rewards and its seasonal sales. If a confirmed military offer matters more than the specific brand, several outdoor competitors run verified military discounts via GovX/ID.me/SheerID worth comparing.
pep-boys-military-discount: Pep Boys expanded and published this military and first-responder discount on March 11, 2025: a flat 10% off in-store for active, reserve, retired, and veteran service members of all branches, plus first responders, verified with a physical ID at the register — no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute account required.

The catch that makes this discount worth understanding is the no-stacking rule. The 10% cannot be combined with any other offer, coupon, rebate, discount, or promotion — the sole exception being manufacturer rebates (for example, a tire-maker mail-in rebate can ride on top). Because Pep Boys runs frequent public oil-change and tire coupons that also can’t be added to the 10%, the practical move on any given cart is to use the single largest applicable discount, not a stack.

For the most common purchase — an oil change — the biggest recurring win is the Wednesday oil-change special, roughly 50% (up to $50) off a synthetic oil change in the continental U.S. Note the source wording differs slightly: the press release says "50% off Conventional and Platinum Synthetic Oil Changes every Wednesday," while the current terms page reads "$50 off Pennzoil Full Synthetic Oil Change, valid Wednesdays only." Confirm the exact live wording with your local store before booking.

Because Pep Boys controls the terms and can change them at any time, treat the numbers here as a starting point and confirm the current offer on Pep Boys’ official Military Commitment page before you buy.
batteries-plus-military-discount: There is no military verification at Batteries Plus because there is no military discount to unlock. If an official program launches later, expect it to route through ID.me or SheerID — but as of this review, ID.me affirmatively states it is not aware of a Batteries Plus military discount, and coupon-site claims of a "15% off military" code are not supported by any Batteries Plus primary source.

The reliable stack for everyone is a current public coupon plus My Plus Rewards points. Grab a coupon from batteriesplus.com/promotions before every purchase, join the free rewards program, and let points accrue and redeem separately. Coupons generally limit one per transaction and can’t be combined with each other, so the coupon + rewards combination is the real best price.

Two more notes. Because Batteries Plus is a franchise, an individual store manager may extend a small military courtesy at their discretion — it’s fine to ask politely in store, but expect "no" as the published answer. And for commodity batteries (AA/AAA), if you have base access, the tax-free Exchange (AAFES/NEX) is often cheaper than any retail coupon. Separately, Batteries Plus does offer a $10,000 franchise-fee discount to veterans who buy a franchise — that’s for prospective owners, not shoppers.
discount-tire-military-veteran: All the math below uses one baseline: a set of four tires at an $800 subtotal before tax, the typical Discount Tire transaction. Free routine services (lifetime rotations, balancing, and flat repairs) are included on every purchase and free shipping applies to online ship-to-store, so service and shipping are $0 across every path and don’t change the ranking; tax varies by state and applies to all paths roughly equally, so it’s excluded to keep the comparison clean.

Rule 1 — the 5% is combinable, so stacking is the strategy. This is the rare brand where the move is to layer offers on one invoice: military 5% + a manufacturer rebate + any non-card instant savings. Don’t treat the 5% as a substitute for a deal — treat it as one more layer on top of the deal.

Rule 2 — the one wall is the credit card. The military 5% cannot combine with the Discount Tire credit card’s 5%/instant savings or its up-to-15% Visa prepaid rebate. So it’s a true either/or: the military combinable stack vs. the credit-card stack. On a big enough cart the ~15% Visa rebate (about $120 on $800) can beat the military 5% even though the two can’t be used together — so show both totals and let the cart size decide.

Rule 3 — cashback is weak here, and often online-only. Rakuten pays about 1% on Discount Tire (as of June 16, 2026), well below what portals pay elsewhere, and several portals only track the online "ship to store" flow rather than an in-store install — so cashback may not apply to a typical tire installation at all. Treat it as a small bonus on online orders, and use only portal-listed codes so a non-portal code doesn’t void it.

Rule 4 — rebates are mostly mail-in and seasonal. Manufacturer rebates are real money ($50–$150+), but they usually require four matching tires and a rebate form, and they expire — so link the live rebate and watch the deadline. The deepest tire-rebate windows cluster around Memorial Day, July 4, and Black Friday, so timing the purchase to a live rebate matters.

Don’t overlook the competition, honestly: Mavis and Tirebuyer advertise a 10% military discount — double Discount Tire’s base rate. For a shopper near a Mavis, a 10% base discount may beat Discount Tire’s 5% stack depending on the rebates available, so it’s worth a price-check. Discount Tire’s own verified figure is a flat 5%; don’t believe aggregator pages that copy the competitors’ 10% onto Discount Tire.
aventon-military-discount: Aventon’s discount is powered by ID.me, the same identity-verification service used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of major retailers. You verify your military, first-responder, nurse, or teacher status once at checkout, and ID.me issues a one-time 5% code to apply to your order. Students follow a parallel route through Student Beans rather than ID.me.

Because Aventon sells big-ticket e-bikes on thin margins, the standing 5% is real but rarely the deepest savings. Aventon’s public "eBikes for Sale" collection cuts individual models well beyond 5%, and holiday windows — Memorial Day, July 4, Labor Day, and especially Black Friday — are historically the deepest markdowns. Those public sales aren’t military-gated, and you generally can’t stack the 5% code on top of a sale bike.

The honest strategy is timing, not the badge: check whether your exact model is in the Sale collection first. If it is, buy it on sale; if it’s at full price, use the 5% ID.me code. Aventon controls its ID.me program and sale calendar and can change terms anytime, so confirm the current offer at aventon.com/pages/idme before you buy.
amc-military-discount: AMC’s official wording is broad — "no matter how you served, we’re proud to serve you" and "all of our service members" — but AMC does not enumerate which groups qualify. Active-duty service members are clearly covered; whether veterans, retirees, Reserve/National Guard, spouses, or dependents qualify is not stated on AMC’s page, so the safest move is to confirm at the box office before relying on it.

There is no third-party verification provider for this discount. Verification is in person: you present a valid photo military ID at the box office and the associate applies the discount. Because the offer is limited to participating theatres and described as "at least 10%," both availability and the exact amount can vary by location.

A "$1.50" peak-pricing figure circulates on third-party aggregator sites such as military.com, and those sites also list specific eligible groups. Neither the $1.50 figure nor that group breakdown appears on AMC’s official discounts page, so we don’t assert them here. AMC’s own page states only "at least 10% on an evening ticket," at the box office, at participating theatres.
fogo-de-chao-military-discount: The counterintuitive part is that for a two-person meal, Fogo Rewards’ second-visit "complimentary Full Churrasco with the purchase of one at full price" — a free entrée available any day of the year — can beat the Veterans Day 50%-off, because a free full meal for the guest saves more than "50% off yours plus 10% off theirs." Only the solo veteran or a larger party clearly wins with the 50% holiday offer.

Verification is the old-fashioned way: present a valid military ID to your server at a participating restaurant. There is no online account, no promo code, and no third-party verification — ID.me, GovX, SheerID, and WeSalute are not used. The exact dates change each year (Veterans Day ran November 7-11 in 2025), so confirm the current-year terms with your location about two weeks ahead.

Ignore the aggregator noise: claims of an "up to 10-25% everyday military discount" or a "15% off promo code" are not real Fogo offers. The only verified military benefit is the holiday dine-in offer; the everyday value is Fogo Rewards and, when available, below-face-value gift cards used as a payment layer.
true-religion-military-discount: True Religion uses Beans iD (Student Beans’ verification) for its key-worker discounts and Student Beans for students. You verify your eligibility once to receive a 20% code that applies at checkout on full-price items. A GovX storefront serves military and first responders as an alternative marketplace route — it’s a substitute, not a stack, so compare the GovX price against 20% off retail. True Religion does not use ID.me for a military offer.

The 20% “cannot be combined with any other promotional codes or markdowns,” which makes it an either/or against a public sale. Because True Religion runs frequent 25–40% sitewide sales and codes open to everyone, the public price often beats full-price-minus-20% during a sale event — so a verified shopper should check the live cart both ways and take the lower total.

Ignore aggregator “True Religion military 30–40% off” pages: those typically point to True Religion’s public sitewide sales (open to everyone), not a special military code. The verified military benefit is a flat 20% via Beans iD, non-combinable with other codes or markdowns.
sky-zone-military-discount: The reason there is no single answer is structural: Sky Zone locations are independently franchised, and Yelp Q&A threads show the split plainly — some parks confirm a military discount with ID, others say they don’t offer one. Recurring "Military Night" events appear at select parks with discounted weekday passes, but those are transient and local, not a national program.

Because there is no corporate policy, there is nothing to verify nationally. Where a discount exists, it’s a manual ID check at the front desk — there is no chain-wide ID.me or SheerID enrollment for Sky Zone. Aggregators that headline a single "Sky Zone military discount" are presenting one franchise’s local policy as if it were a chain-wide benefit; it isn’t, and it can vanish without notice.

The reliable savings levers don’t require military status. A membership drops the per-visit cost far below any one-time discount for regular jumpers; off-peak weekday passes beat weekend peak pricing; and public coupon codes or Groupon bundles are frequently available and usually cheaper than 10% off a peak pass. Treat a local military night as a bonus, not the plan.
national-car-rental-military-discount: National runs two distinct government/military programs. The leisure rate covers personal, off-duty travel for current federal employees, active-duty military, retired employees, and veterans — booked on nationalcar.com through the Government & Military specials path, with no published percentage. Separately, federal travelers on official orders use the U.S. Government Rental Car Agreement contract rate, which bundles unlimited mileage (CONUS/Canada), physical damage and third-party liability protection, and a full tank at pickup — benefits worth more than any leisure discount, but strictly tied to official-business status.

A word on promo codes: National publishes none for the military rate. Coupon sites circulate contract IDs like GOVRNR and GOVREC as "the National military code," but National’s own military pages publish no such codes — they direct you to book through the government/military specials path or a travel administrator. Treat any pasted contract ID as unverified; a rate booked on someone else’s corporate or contract ID can be rejected at the counter. Similarly, the old "Veterans Advantage 25% off National" claim is stale: WeSalute (formerly Veterans Advantage) now advertises up to 40% off National, redeemed exclusively through a members-only Priceline booking engine — a paid-membership channel that skips nationalcar.com entirely and forfeits Emerald Club perks.

There is no ID.me or SheerID gate on the leisure rate — you simply book through National’s government/military path, and credentials may be checked at the counter (National explicitly reserves ID checks for USAA renters under 25). WeSalute verifies military status at its own membership enrollment; the National savings then live inside its Priceline engine.

Because car-rental pricing is date-driven, none of these rates is always the winner. Quote the military leisure rate, the public rate with any current promo, and — if you are a member — the USAA or WeSalute+/Priceline rate, then book the lowest. Whatever wins, join the free Emerald Club first: it adds counter-skipping, choose-your-own-car access, and free rental days to any direct booking, and Rakuten’s 2.5% cashback (as of July 14, 2026) can layer on clean direct bookings made without outside codes.
canon-military-discount: The "Canon military discount" you may have seen on coupon and aggregator pages (WorthEPenny, Knoji, ValueCom, Dealhack, Swagbucks) is not real. ID.me itself says it is not aware Canon offers a military discount, and Canon support agents in the Canon Community forum tell members there is no military discount and to contact the sales team (1-800-385-2155) for best pricing. The only ID.me-linked Canon code, IDME2025 (~7% off), is a general Canon Shop account promo available to ordinary shoppers — not a military benefit.

Canon’s Refurbished store is the deepest reliable direct saving. Canon U.S.A. sells certified-refurbished cameras and lenses with a 1-year Canon USA warranty, free standard shipping, and periodic Instant Savings — typically running about 15–30% below new. Note it is a different, certified-refurbished SKU, not the new body, and general Canon promo codes usually do not apply to refurb items.

For a military-exclusive edge, the military Exchange is the play coupon pages never mention. AAFES, NEX, and MCX carry cameras and photo gear, and purchases are tax-free for authorized patrons — including honorably discharged veterans shopping online. On an illustrative $1,499 body with ~8% local tax, going tax-free saves roughly $120 on tax alone, before any Exchange markdown. Eligibility is verified by the Exchange (your DoD or veteran status), not by Canon.

A few smaller paths exist. Canon’s free CPS Student membership (enrolled U.S. students 18+) offers member savings on products and services. The Canon Upgrade Program gives a one-time 10% code triggered by a repair estimate (one Upgrade-Program product, 14 days, U.S. only, excludes CarePAK and prior purchases). And WeSalute lists a Canon offer, but it is B&H-fulfilled behind a paid WeSalute+ membership — not a Canon-issued discount. For new gear, the best public windows are seasonal Instant Savings (Memorial Day, July 4, Black Friday) on Canon.com and at B&H, Adorama, and Best Buy, where you can stack card or portal cashback.
razer-military-discount: Razer verifies eligibility through ID.me, the same identity service used by the VA and the IRS. From the Heroes page you sign in to (or create) a free ID.me account, which checks your military records or first-responder/medical credentials; if automatic verification fails, ID.me’s document-upload and support flow applies. Each verification issues one unique code — single-use, valid for one month — and you can re-verify for future purchases under the program terms.

Keep the two tiers straight, because many coupon pages don’t: Razer publishes exactly two rates — 15% on peripherals and accessories, and 5% on desktops and laptops. Aggregators variously quote "5–15% military discount," "10% off PC components," and "5% off gaming chairs and monitors"; none of those extra tiers appear on Razer’s Heroes page, so treat them as unverified. The code is also never valid on the Razer Core, the Tomahawk Gaming Desktop, Gold PIN, or refurbished products.

The honest money math: the Heroes code is strictly either/or with every sale, and Razer promos of 30% or more are routine — historically up to about 50% off select peripherals around Black Friday, and hundreds off Blade laptops. So the 15% wins only on full-priced, non-excluded peripherals with no promo running; on a Blade, the 5% tier ($125 off a $2,500 laptop) is a last resort that public sales almost always beat. Cashback portals pay about 2% on Razer (as of July 14, 2026), but count that only on public purchases — it isn’t a promised stack with the ID.me code.

Two more quirks worth knowing. GovX lists a Razer offer, but it’s a referral that redeems on razer.com — the same program family, not a separate GovX storefront with an extra layer of savings. And despite being a military program, Heroes is US-only with no P.O. Box, APO, FPO, or DPO delivery, so you’ll need a standard US shipping address.
thorne-military-discount: Thorne routes its military discount through GovX (free) and, separately, through WeSalute+ (paid membership). For GovX, you make a free Thorne account, pick the military/first-responder option, and verify once via GovX; GovX confirms your status and unlocks the 20%. There is no confirmed ID.me or SheerID path for Thorne — GovX and WeSalute are the named partners.

Ignore the coupon sites advertising "53%," "40%," "35%," or "up to 25% veteran" codes — the only verified Thorne military figure is 20%. The widely-printed "AMBASSADOR26 / AMBASSADOR2026 = 35% for military" line reads as an ambassador/influencer code, is unverified, and Thorne does not present it as a military discount.
Because Thorne controls the program and can change or end it at any time, confirm the current terms on Thorne’s official GovX page before you buy.
nba-league-pass-military-discount: The military offer is verified through GovX. You verify your eligibility on the GovX NBA League Pass offer page, then receive a unique single-use promo code to enter on NBA.com. It is not a permanent account flag — the discount applies for a defined 12-month promo window, after which standard pricing resumes, so plan to re-verify each season.

Coupon aggregators publish fabricated NBA League Pass "military" codes advertising 20%, 50%, or even 70% off. There is no public military promo code. The only legitimate military code is the single-use code GovX issues after identity verification, and it works only on League Pass Monthly.

On the $16.99/mo standard tier, the 30% discount works out to about $11.89/mo, or roughly $142.73 across 12 months. That beats the $203.88 full-price monthly total, but the public early-season annual promo (about $109.99) and the 40% UNiDAYS student plan (about $10.19/mo) are both cheaper over a full season. Use the GovX military monthly deal mainly for cancel-anytime flexibility.
tuxmat-military-discount: TuxMat handles verification in-house. Instead of an ID.me, GovX, WeSalute, or SheerID gate, you submit proof of service on the Military and Veterans Form and TuxMat confirms eligibility manually — the reply typically arrives within one business day. Because there is no third-party wallet, there’s no "verify once, reuse forever" shortcut; expect a per-request review.

The 20% is effectively the ceiling. TuxMat is a direct-to-consumer Shopify brand: it isn’t sold through AAFES/NEX exchanges or a GovX storefront, no cashback portal reliably survives its checkout, and gift cards aren’t an accepted payment method, so there’s no discounted-gift-card layer. The only other standing offer is the $20 returning-customer credit for repeat buyers, and TuxMat presents the two as separate offers — assume one discount per order.

Ignore the coupon-aggregator claims. Sites advertise stackable "35% off" ("Custom35") and "40% off" TuxMat codes and even frame a "20% off first-responder" tier, but the only military benefit TuxMat’s own site confirms is 20% off with proof of service — and its FAQ says first-time buyers get no general discount. TuxMat does run public seasonal sales open to everyone; a deep enough sale could beat 20%, but assume it can’t be combined with the military discount.

Two fine-print items matter for military buyers: TuxMat does not ship to PO or APO boxes (or Puerto Rico), and payment is limited to Visa, Mastercard, Apple Pay, Google Pay, Shop Pay, and Afterpay — no PayPal, Amex, Visa Debit, or gift cards. Orders come with a 30-day money-back window (TuxMat covers return shipping) and a limited lifetime warranty against manufacturing defects.
no-bull-military-discount: NOBULL uses SheerID for its Community Discount Program and also supports ID.me and GovX. You verify once through your chosen provider and the 20% applies automatically at checkout. The three routes are alternatives — you use one, not all three — and the discount won’t combine with a public sale, a sitewide code, or another offer.

That non-combinable, full-price-only rule is the whole story on maximizing savings. When a 30–50% sale or outlet event is live on the item you want, the public clearance price typically beats full price minus 20%, and you can’t stack the two — so a verified shopper should simply buy the sale item at the public price. If you qualify as a fitness or nutrition professional, check NOBULL’s pro/community tier, which can exceed 20% (personal-use, purchase caps).

Ignore coupon-aggregator “NOBULL military 30–50% off code” pages: those are either public sales open to everyone (not a military code, and not stackable with the 20%) or fabricated. The verified military benefit is a flat 20% on full-price, in-stock items via SheerID, ID.me, or GovX.
menards-military-discount: Menards operates no military-status verification (no ID.me, SheerID, GovX, or WeSalute). No account, military ID, DD-214, or service proof is requested, because there is no military offer to gate. Menards’ own "Military" page at menards.com is a product category for flags and patriotic décor — not a discount program.

The headline savings lever for everyone is the 11% mail-in rebate: on a $1,000 project that’s about $110 back as in-store credit. Other public programs include the BIG Card (2% in-store rebate or promo financing, $0 annual fee), in-store price matching of identical in-stock items at local brick-and-mortar competitors, the weekly ad, and "Ray’s List" clearance.

If you specifically want an instant military price at a home-improvement store, competitors offer verified military discounts — Lowe’s has a standing 10% military discount (year-round, online and in store, via verification) and The Home Depot runs a verification-gated military discount program. Those are the practical alternatives to Menards’ mail-in rebate.
nobull-military-discount: NOBULL runs two parallel verification systems, and it’s worth knowing which is which. The Community Discount Program uses SheerID: you verify your military status on NOBULL’s community page, and once approved the 20% applies automatically at checkout with no code to enter. Separately, NOBULL has an ID.me page where verification happens at checkout and generates a discount code you then apply. The two are mutually exclusive — NOBULL’s FAQ says the community discount "can’t be combined with ID.me" — so pick one path per order. The confirmed 20% figure comes from NOBULL’s FAQ for the SheerID path; NOBULL’s ID.me page only says "eligible % off" without a number, so we don’t assert an ID.me percentage.

On eligibility, NOBULL’s ID.me page spells out the military tier as Service Member, Retiree, and Veteran, and both providers verify a broad set of communities: first responders (EMT, paramedic, firefighter, law enforcement), nurses and medical professionals and hospital employees, teachers, students, and fitness/nutrition professionals. Government employees (federal, state, local) are covered specifically through the ID.me path. What NOBULL does not enumerate is Reserve/National Guard or military spouses and dependents — those are left to what SheerID or ID.me will verify, so the honest guidance is to run the verification rather than assume a spouse or dependent qualifies.

The fine print is standard but strict. The discount is U.S.-only, applied pre-tax and spread evenly across eligible items, and it excludes gift cards, e-gift cards, and shipping. It only works on in-stock items, not previous purchases, and can’t be stacked with any other offer — including NOBULL’s own sales and its "25% off first order" email signup code. That last point is the practical one: because it won’t combine with a sale, compare 20% off full price against the current sale price before checking out. NOBULL doesn’t publish how long verification lasts (SheerID programs are commonly annual, but NOBULL doesn’t say), and it reserves the right to modify or end the offer at any time. Note too that a "30% off military" promo circulating on coupon sites wasn’t found on any NOBULL source, so treat it as stale.
lulus-military-discount: Verification runs through The Beans Group — its consumer service is branded Beans iD, operated by Pion, the company behind Student Beans. You create a free Beans iD account, confirm eligibility, and Beans iD issues a single-use code tied to your account. Lulus notes that you’re providing personal information to Beans iD and that Lulus doesn’t control Beans iD’s privacy practices. Which military sub-groups qualify (veterans, reserve/Guard, retirees, dependents) is decided inside Beans iD’s verification, not spelled out on Lulus’ page.

The math on a $120 full-price order: the 10% military code brings it to $108. The public 15% first-order text offer brings it to $102 — which is why first-timers should take the 15% instead (the two can’t be combined anyway). On repeat full-price orders the military code is the best code you can hold, and a cashback portal can add a separate rebate on top; on Archive Sale and markdown items (often 30%+ off), the public markdown usually beats 10% outright.

Don’t confuse Lulus (the dresses-and-women’s-fashion retailer at Lulus.com) with Lululemon (athletic wear) — they’re different companies with different military discounts, and much of the conflicting information online comes from mixing the two up.
stanley-steemer-military-discount: Because Stanley Steemer operates as a network of independently owned franchises, corporate publishes no national military rate. Any military discount is set location-by-location, so a courtesy, minimum charge, or service area at one branch may differ at another. That is why the honest advice is to call your local franchise and ask directly rather than expect a fixed number — community Q&A reporting is consistent with this, with some locations applying a military discount if you ask and others not.

Be cautious of coupon and deal sites that advertise a flat "Stanley Steemer military discount — 25%, 35%, or 50% off" or codes like "WELCOME." These are generic promo codes or invented figures, not a verified military rate. Stanley Steemer publishes no national military discount, and franchise pricing varies, so treat those numbers with caution.

One important disambiguation: the GovX "Stanley" military store is Stanley 1913 — the drinkware and tumbler brand — not Stanley Steemer. They are completely different companies, so a GovX "Stanley" listing is not a Stanley Steemer military discount.

Even without a company-wide military discount, there are honest ways to lower what you pay: pull your local coupon at stanleysteemer.com/find-local-coupons, grab the email/text sign-up promo, bundle services (carpet plus tile, upholstery, or air-duct) since per-service pricing often improves on a larger job, and book around seasonal specials like July 4 and Black Friday, which are typically the deepest public pricing.
us-mobile-military-discount: There is nothing to verify at US Mobile. It has no military-verification partner — no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute — because it runs no identity-gated discount. Every rate on the site is the public rate, and that public rate is the whole point of an MVNO: it is priced to beat what a single line would cost even on a big carrier’s "military" plan.

So the honest best path for a service member is the same as for everyone. Prepaying annually is the single biggest standing markdown; on one Unlimited line that can take the effective monthly rate from roughly $25 to about $22.50, and lower still on an intro promo. Right-sizing matters even more — if your data use is low, the Light plan (~$8/mo, 2GB) or a By-the-Gig plan can cut most of the bill. Add multi-line pricing for family lines, and stack referral credits (which auto-apply to your bill) with a checkout promo code.

Ignore the coupon-aggregator pages advertising a "US Mobile military discount — 50% off" or a special military promo code. Those are fabricated or are just the ordinary public new-customer promo relabeled. There is no military-specific US Mobile discount, code, or verification program — the only real levers are annual prepay, plan right-sizing, multi-line, referrals, and the public first-cycle promo.
san-diego-safari-park-military-discount: For the active-duty free pass and the dependent 10%, verification is simply showing your military or dependent ID at the park — there’s no online account to set up. Academy cadets and reserves on active orders qualify for the free pass even if their ID doesn’t read "Active."

The accuracy point most pages blur: the free or complimentary admission is active-duty only, and dependents get 10%. Veterans and retirees are not eligible for a direct gate discount. Their routes are base MWR/ITT ticket offices, which set their own package pricing, or the GovX marketplace, which sells discounted Safari Park tickets to verified military (including veterans) and first responders after an online verification.

Don’t conflate the Safari Park in Escondido with the separate San Diego Zoo in Balboa Park — they’re run by the same alliance under the same military policy, but they’re different parks, so check each one’s ticket window. City-wide San Diego military promotions come and go year to year, so re-verify seasonally.
visible-military-discount: Visible is Verizon’s app-based prepaid brand, and its military discount is powered by ID.me group verification — not the ID.me Shop cashback marketplace. You verify your eligibility once through ID.me; the $5/month credit then applies to your account for as long as you keep the line active. ID.me may request re-verification periodically per its standard policy, and support runs through Visible’s in-app chat and community.

The discount is a flat $5/month on every tier: the $25 base plan drops to $20, Visible+ ($35) to $30, and Visible+ Pro ($45) to $40. Because it’s a fixed dollar amount rather than a percentage, and because it will not combine with Visible’s promo codes, the real question for a new customer isn’t which coupon to stack — it’s the military discount versus a limited-time port-in promo.

One point of confusion worth clearing up: the ID.me Shop cashback listing for Visible is inactive and incorrectly states that no military discount exists. That page is a separate product from the ID.me group verification Visible actually runs. The real, verified $5/month offer lives at visible.com/v/idme.
Because Visible controls the terms and can change them at any time, treat the numbers here as a starting point and confirm the current offer on Visible’s official ID.me page before you sign up.
banks-power-military-discount: The program is real and VerifyPass-verified — the page source on Banks’ discount page loads the VerifyPass launcher, and the VerifyPass Banks offer lists two eligibility groups with terms. What isn’t public is the rate: Banks intentionally reveals the percentage only after you verify, which is why we publish the program as real but don’t attach a number to it.

Verification is a one-time VerifyPass check on the discount page; approved users get a checkout code. The terms are consistent across the offer: the code can’t be combined with other discount codes, isn’t applied retroactively, and is one use per customer. Military and first responder/government are separate offers, so you use the one you qualify for.

Because the code won’t stack on a sale, the smart move is to compare your verified code against a live Banks Sale collection price and take the lower. Watch the Banks Promos page for public seasonal offers, use the flat-rate ground shipping offer on qualifying orders to cut shipping, and check authorized dealers, who sometimes run competing promotions on the same part.
bob-evans-military-discount: There is no online verification (no ID.me, SheerID, or GovX). Verification is entirely in-restaurant: you show a valid military/veteran ID or accepted proof of service to your server. This means there is no re-verification cycle and no account to create. Some aggregators claim an online military portal — Bob Evans is a dine-in restaurant, and that claim is fabricated.

The Veterans Day free meal is the longest-running, most reliable offer, recurring annually with a choice of free entrée from a special breakfast/lunch/dinner menu. It is not valid with other offers, discounts, or coupons — it doesn’t stack. The everyday ~10% is unpublished, so treat it as discretionary and don’t assume it combines with coupons, loyalty, or promos.

On the baseline of a roughly $14 dine-in entrée: the Veterans Day offer makes the entrée free (100% off) on Nov 11; the everyday courtesy discount, where honored, brings it to about $12.60 (~10% off); and if a location declines the courtesy, you pay the regular menu price. The biggest win is simple — dine in on Veterans Day.
empire-state-building-military-discount: The baseline for the math below is one adult Main Deck (86th-floor) general-admission ticket. The official starting price is about $44 plus a $5 booking charge — roughly $49 all-in. ESB ticket prices are the amount you actually pay, and no tax-free military channel (exchange) sells ESB tickets, so every route is directly comparable at its listed price. The Top Deck (86th + 102nd floors) starts around $79 + $5 booking (~$84).

Why we won’t print a veteran percentage: the aggregator pages publish mutually contradictory numbers. Military.com and FreeToursByFoot say a veteran shows a military ID onsite to buy a discounted ticket, that it is not available online, and quote roughly "$2–$3 off." One NYC blog claims a flat $40 reduced price you book online by choosing "MILITARY." None of these trace to esbnyc.com — the ESB FAQ states only that active military in uniform receive free admission, names no veteran percentage, and showed no "Military" option on the live buy-tickets flow this pass. Publishing a specific figure would imply an offer the ESB does not confirm.

There is no third-party verification partner (no ID.me, SheerID, or WeSalute) on the ESB site. The active-military perk is verified simply by being in uniform at the door; any veteran rate is a ticket-office ID check at the point of sale, not an online account step. A separate GovX "Empire State Building Observatory" storefront exists for verified military and government members — that is a marketplace route, not an esbnyc.com feature, and its net price should be checked against the NYC Locals and reseller routes before you buy.

Even setting the military question aside, the ESB sells several public discounts that often beat a tiny, uncertain markdown: the New York City Locals ticket at 25% off for NY residents, a senior (62+) rate, free admission for children under 6 and reduced pricing for ages 6–12, and group pricing for parties of 20+. Travel guides also note that the onsite military-ID route "requires ID verification on-site, which can slow down your visit" — a reason a NY resident or multi-attraction visitor may prefer a public ticket or a pass bought ahead.
netflix-military-discount: Netflix publishes only its standard public tiers, confirmed on help.netflix.com: Standard with ads $8.99/month, Standard $19.99/month, and Premium $26.99/month (US). There is no discounted plan tied to military, veteran, first-responder, student, teacher, or government status, and no verification provider gates any plan. The old Basic plan has been discontinued, so Standard with ads is the cheapest standalone tier.

The single most important caveat: any “Netflix military discount — 15% off via SheerID/ID.me” claim you see on coupon or benefits-aggregator sites is fabricated and unverified. The same goes for claimed USAA, Exchange (AAFES), or VetTix subscription-discount partnerships — none are confirmed on netflix.com or help.netflix.com, and Netflix publishes no discounted plan. Treat every such figure as invented.

The genuine saving for many military households is a carrier bundle. Netflix’s own help center states that customers in the United States can sign up for an eligible T-Mobile package that includes a Netflix subscription, or add Netflix to an eligible T-Mobile package. Standard with ads is the included tier; higher tiers cost the price difference. T-Mobile’s own page lists Netflix On Us as available on qualifying plans including Military, 55, and First Responder plans — but eligibility is carrier-set, so confirm current plan terms with T-Mobile, not Netflix.

Netflix updates prices periodically (a May 2026 price-change cycle was reported in trade press), and prices can also vary if you have Netflix through a package or add-on, with taxes applying depending on location. Re-check the current figures on Netflix’s plans-and-pricing page before relying on them.
capital-one-military-discount: The whole page turns on one distinction. Two federal laws protect military borrowers: the SCRA (for debts you already had when you started active duty) and the MLA (for credit extended while you’re serving). Amex and Chase voluntarily zero annual fees on the MLA side, which is why "military fee waiver" lists exist — but the MLA’s own rules (32 CFR 232.4(d)) exclude bona fide, reasonable annual fees from its 36% MAPR cap, so an issuer is never required to waive them. Capital One chooses not to: its official decline criteria list "the account was opened after the active duty start date." Pages that lump Capital One in with the fee-waiver issuers without this distinction cost readers $395 a year.

On the SCRA side, Capital One beats the statute on almost every axis. The law requires a 6% interest cap on pre-service obligations; Capital One caps at 4%. The law lets you invoke benefits up to 180 days after leaving service; Capital One accepts requests up to one year after. Interest above the cap is forgiven, not deferred, relief is retroactive to your active-duty start date (or "order to" date for reservists), and it runs until one year after active duty ends. Since Capital One acquired Discover, one aligned program — and a single request — covers your Capital One and Discover credit cards, auto loans, and personal loans. Verification is your active-duty orders or a commanding-officer letter, reviewed by Capital One directly: no ID.me, SheerID, or GovX, and no code.

The smart plays follow from the dates. If you held any Capital One or Discover account before activating, request SCRA now — online or at 1-855-227-1645 — and collect the retroactive adjustment. If you’re Guard or Reserve, open cards while off orders: each 30+ day activation is a fresh pre-service date for accounts opened before it, effectively a repeatable fee waiver. If you’re already on active duty and want a $0-fee premium travel card, Capital One isn’t the issuer for that — Amex publishes a $0-fee policy for cards opened during service and Chase’s equivalent is letter-confirmed; see our American Express and Amex Platinum guides. Community reports describe product-changing an old pre-service Capital One card into a Venture X and keeping it fee-free under the existing SCRA coverage, but Capital One doesn’t document that path — confirm by phone before counting on it.
waffle-house-military-discount: Waffle House uses no military verification of any kind. There is no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute program, and no online military promo code for ordering or delivery. Any in-store courtesy relies simply on a server or manager eyeballing a military ID and choosing to apply a discount, entirely at their discretion — some locations informally comp around 10%, while others explicitly decline and tell veterans there’s no such policy.

The dependable savings is the Regulars Club, Waffle House’s own free email program. On a ~$12.50 All-Star Special, a single free-item coupon (a free waffle worth around $4, or free hashbrowns or a bacon side) beats even a granted ~10% courtesy (about $1.25) — and it’s official and repeatable. Gift cards are tender rather than a discount, so a "buy $100, get $20" bonus effectively stacks with a coupon because you’re just paying with the card.

Two claims to ignore. The flat "10% Waffle House military discount" repeated by coupon and menu sites (WorthEPenny, militarymarkdown, and similar) has no official source, no published percentage, and no verification mechanism. And Military.com’s "10% military discount" listing is for "The Waffle Experience," an unrelated Sacramento-area waffle chain — not Waffle House. Waffle House is also consistently absent from national Veterans Day free-meal roundups, so any observance is local and not guaranteed.
edible-arrangements-military-discount: A quick debunk. Aggregator pages advertise an Edible "military & veteran" discount — one even dangles a "30% off military" code while admitting "there is no official Edible Arrangements military program." There isn’t. Separately, a stale Military.com listing offering "10% off for members, call 1-877-DO FRUIT" is directly contradicted by Edible’s current statement; don’t treat it as a live consumer discount.

What actually saves money: use whatever public code is live (10% via BLOOM10 as of July 18, 2026), start from Rakuten for ~2% back if it tracks, and join Edible Rewards if you order often. That’s the whole game — there’s no military lever to pull. Remember that delivery and service fees are added on most orders and are never removed by a code, so factor them into the real total.

One nuance to watch: Edible stores are independently owned franchises, and Edible’s own blog notes stores "may run their own in-store promotions." So a local store could, in theory, extend a courtesy on in-store pickup — but that’s a manager’s discretion, never corporate policy, and never a military discount. If a verified military rate on fresh fruit matters most, buy from 1-800-Flowers or FruitBouquets.com instead.
shoe-palace-military-discount: Shoe Palace is a multi-brand sneaker reseller, and its behavior mirrors stores like Foot Locker and Finish Line: tight code exclusions and no identity-based discount. Its footer links only to About, Contact, Careers, Shipping, Returns, App, and Privacy — no military, student, or rewards program. There is no verified-checkout flow (no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, WeSalute, or VerifyPass), so there is no way to unlock a military rate there, because none exists.

The savings Shoe Palace does offer are public: periodic percent-off flash codes and seasonal sale/clearance. The catch is the exclusion list — those codes typically reject Nike, Jordan, adidas new releases, limit-one items, and sale/flash styles. A code that "works" on apparel is rejected the moment a marquee sneaker is in the cart; remove the excluded pair and the code applies to the rest. Codes generally do not stack on already-reduced clearance either. A cashback portal (Rakuten, TopCashback, RebatesMe) can co-exist with a sitewide public code on eligible items, since there is no verified checkout to break portal tracking.

For the sneakers most people actually come for, the genuinely cheaper path is a substitute, not a Shoe Palace order. Nike gives active, reserve, veteran, and retired U.S. military — plus spouses and dependents of active members — 10% off through SheerID on Nike.com and in Nike stores (not Nike Company Stores). You choose your status and branch, enter your name, date of birth, and email, and on approval SheerID issues a single-use code that expires about two weeks after issue; you can re-verify for a new code roughly every 7 days. On a ~$120 Nike/Jordan pair that is about $108 — versus $120 at Shoe Palace, which discounts neither the shoe nor the tax.

The Exchange is the other substitute: AAFES and the Navy Exchange carry many of the same Nike, Jordan, and adidas styles tax-free, with price-match and MILITARY STAR perks, saving roughly 6–10% via sales tax if you have access and they stock the shoe. All honorably discharged veterans can shop the exchanges online; in-store access is limited to active and retired members and specific expanded groups. Shoe Palace only wins when it holds an exclusive colorway or collab you cannot get discounted elsewhere — in which case you will pay full price, so add the highest cashback portal and watch for a deep public sale.
new-balance-military-discount: New Balance uses ID.me to confirm eligibility — the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many major retailers. You create a free ID.me account and verify your community (Military, First Responder, Nurse, Medical Provider, Hospital Employee, Teacher, Government Employee, or Senior 60+), and ID.me issues a unique, one-time-use discount code. You enter that code at checkout on newbalance.com.

New Balance’s own page is unusually explicit about family eligibility: it lists Military as "active duty, veterans, retirees, spouses, dependents, and more." That spouse and dependent coverage is rare to see stated on a brand’s own page. Reserve and National Guard members are not separately named ("and more"); ID.me’s Military community typically covers them, but it’s worth confirming through ID.me.

Because each code is single-use with a one-per-30-days limit, you re-verify or request a new code through ID.me for future orders. New Balance states you will not receive marketing from ID.me or New Balance unless you opt in, and directs shoppers with ID.me account issues to help.id.me.

One thing to watch: several coupon and aggregator pages advertise 25% or 20% off (and one stale summary shows 10%). None of those is the verified military offer — 15% is the only rate confirmed on New Balance’s official idme.html page and on the ID.me store page. Separately, New Balance runs its own sitewide sales on their own codes (for example SUMMER26), but those can’t be combined with the ID.me code.
mission-bbq-military-discount: The reason there’s no “percentage” to quote is that Mission BBQ never ran one — the aggregator “menu” sites that imply an ongoing military discount are wrong. The verifiable benefits are the Veterans Day free sandwich and the May Military Appreciation Week free-sandwich days, both longstanding traditions for this veteran-founded chain.
