Redemption is simple and in-store: tell the team you’re active, retired, or a veteran, and show a military ID if asked. Some stores are generous with informal thanks, but the documented offers are the two event windows. Because there’s no third-party portal, don’t look for an ID.me or GovX flow — there isn’t one.

For ongoing perks, join the Veterans VIP Club in store; it’s a simple sign-up that surfaces periodic offers. The daily noon National Anthem isn’t a discount, but it’s part of why the brand is a favorite among service members. Between events, the everyday menu is regular price.
williams-sonoma-military-discount: The single most reliable way to save is the free Key Rewards program. You join by giving a phone number at checkout and earn 2% back in rewards (2X for the first 30 days), and it earns on top of sale and Outlet prices across eight brands — Williams Sonoma, Williams Sonoma Home, Pottery Barn, Pottery Barn Kids, Pottery Barn Teen, West Elm, Mark & Graham, and Rejuvenation. Because it is a rewards accrual and not a coupon, it does not conflict with markdowns. Frequent buyers of the brand family can step up to the Key Rewards Visa, which pays 10% back for the first 30 days and then 5%, plus free standard shipping and a birthday reward.

The deepest cuts usually come from the Outlet / Open Box section (up to ~75% off, with an extra markdown on open-box items), and from public seasonal sales around Memorial Day, July 4, and Black Friday. None of these is a military benefit, but on marked-down goods they routinely beat the old 15% military rate — and Key Rewards still earns on top. If an email/text welcome code is live, it can add roughly 15% on eligible full-price items, though these public codes commonly exclude sale items, gift cards, and premium brands such as All-Clad and Le Creuset, so always confirm the exclusions at checkout.

It is easy to confuse the Professional Chefs trade program with a discount for service members, but they are different. Professional Chefs gives verified culinary professionals — chefs, restaurateurs, culinary students, and sommeliers — 20% off eligible purchases online and in store, through a separate professional application and verification. It is a trade benefit tied to culinary employment or enrollment, not to military service, and it does not stack with a public welcome code (though it still earns Key Rewards).

Williams Sonoma controls its own terms — Key Rewards rates, sale windows, Professional Chefs eligibility, and welcome codes — and can change them at any time, so treat the numbers here as a starting point and confirm the current details on Williams Sonoma’s official pages before you buy. If Williams Sonoma ever launches a verified military offer, this page will be updated with the official provider and terms.
nectar-military-discount: Nectar’s military benefit is a verified add-on, not the headline sale. The "up to 40–50% off" you see promoted is Nectar’s standard sitewide sale, available to everyone. The military-specific offer is an extra 5% off "our best onsite offer" — meaning it applies on top of whatever sale price is live. On a Queen Nectar Classic priced at $699 during the July sale, the verified 5% brings it to roughly $664.

Verification runs through an on-site "Get Verified" step — a SheerID-style eligibility check — rather than ID.me. You confirm your status once, receive a one-time-use code on-site and by email, and one code can cover your and your family’s orders. First responders (law enforcement, EMTs, paramedics, firefighters) and healthcare professionals each verify on their own Nectar page and receive the same extra 5%.

The stacking rules matter. The 5% stacks on the sale, but it "cannot be combined with any other offer," so you use either the verified code or a public promo code — not both. It covers merchandise only (not shipping, taxes, or packaging), and using it likely voids Rakuten cashback, so treat those as either/or. Nectar’s military page also carries legacy "valid on full-price merchandise only" language that conflicts with the "extra 5% off best onsite offer" wording; the on-sale-plus-5% mechanic matches all three offer pages, but confirm the code applies to the sale price at checkout.

Because Nectar controls the terms and can change them at any time, treat the figures here as a starting point. The single cheapest route for a service member is to buy during a deep seasonal window — Memorial Day, July 4, Labor Day, or Black Friday — where sale depth drives the price far more than the 5% ever will, and add the verified 5% on top.
bank-of-america-military-discount: The reliable, official track is SCRA. On accounts opened before your active-duty start date, Bank of America applies the statutory 6% interest cap to credit cards, lines of credit, and installment loans for your entire active-duty period, with payments reduced to reflect the lower rate — and under the statute, “interest” includes fees, and the excess is forgiven, not deferred. Home loans BofA both owns and services get 4%, the one place BofA publishes a beats-the-statute number, with benefits extending a year past service (HUD-, Fannie Mae-, or Freddie Mac-owned loans may still get 6%). Card and installment-loan benefits are “generally” extended six months after active duty ends. None of it is automatic: request it through the online portal, by phone at 877.345.0693, by fax, or by mail, with your orders or the commanding-officer-signed Military Orders Detail form, during service or within 180 days after. Two published oddities most pages miss: BofA’s form extends SCRA interest-rate benefits to a requesting spouse, domestic partner, or dependent “regardless of whether the Servicemember is liable on the account,” and its benefits page advertises “continued select credit card fees waived for life after military service” — official words with no published details.

The murky track is MLA. BofA’s card agreements acknowledge “credits made in accordance with… the Military Lending Act,” and it runs applicants against Department of Defense records — but it publishes nothing about which fees get credited. Community data points from 2021 through 2026 converge on an unofficial pattern: annual fees over about $100 are credited, fees under are not. The $550 Premium Rewards Elite usually posts its fee and then auto-credits as “MLA CREDIT – ANNUAL FEE” at statement close, no request needed — but at least one covered borrower got only $450 back, and the $95 Premium Rewards and $95 Alaska Airlines cards are reportedly charged in full (an Alaska denial is documented from January 2022). This is lawful: 32 CFR 232.4(d) excludes bona fide, reasonable annual fees from the MLA’s 36% MAPR, so waiving is voluntary — Amex, Chase, and reportedly Citi volunteer fully, Capital One not at all, and BofA volunteers partially and unofficially. Also note the MLA’s credit-card provisions only began October 3, 2017; older accounts are SCRA-only territory.

What to actually do: if you held any BofA card, loan, or mortgage before activating, file one SCRA request with the Military Benefits Unit and let the 6% (or 4%) cap plus deposit-fee waivers work. If you bank at BofA day to day, the published waivers on monthly maintenance, ATM, wire, and replacement-card fees are the dependable win. If you want a premium travel card at a guaranteed $0 fee during service, BofA is the wrong issuer — see our American Express and Chase guides, which document published or letter-confirmed $0-fee practices. And if you want the Premium Rewards Elite anyway, run the math as a civilian would — its $300 airline and $150 lifestyle credits offset the fee for heavy travelers even unwaived — then treat any MLA credit as a bonus, not a plan.
reef-military-discount: All the math below uses one baseline: a $110 reef.com order — a roughly $60 men’s Fanning-class sandal plus a ~$50 second pair or accessory — priced pre-tax (no tax-free channel exists for REEF). On that cart, typical 20–40% public sale markdowns land you around $75–$90, while the flat 2% cashback floor saves only about $2. That gap is why the sale section, not an identity discount, is the headline play.

Rule 1 — GovX is a substitute, never a stack. It’s a closed marketplace: no reef.com codes or cashback portals apply there, member pricing is set per item with no published flat percentage, and its return policies are stricter than reef.com’s. The right way to use it is a per-item price check — compare your exact style and size on GovX against reef.com (especially the sale) and buy on whichever is cheaper.

Rule 2 — codes and cashback don’t mix at reef.com. Rakuten’s REEF terms void cashback on purchases that use coupon codes not listed on Rakuten, influencer codes, or gift cards. A sale-price order with no code is portal-safe; if a first-order welcome code genuinely beats the ~2% cashback, use the code and knowingly give up the cashback. And no "REEF military code + cashback" stack exists, because no REEF military code exists.

Rule 3 — the 20% belongs to students and teachers, not the military. REEF’s only published identity discount on reef.com is 20% off via Student Beans for verified students, teachers, and recent grads (free verification, single-use code). Coupon aggregators recast it — and REEF’s public seasonal sales around Memorial Day, July 4, and Black Friday — as "military deals," but REEF publishes no military offer and no military-holiday promo history. If a student or teacher shares your household, their code is the biggest verified percentage REEF runs.
audi-military-discount: Audi’s archetype here is a manufacturer bonus-cash brand, not a retail percentage discount: the $1,000 is a fixed bonus layered onto whatever price you negotiate. Audi’s own terms name only four programs it will not combine with — Dealer Employee Purchase, Innovator, Corporate Sales, and VIP & Diplomat Sales — and do not list public lease, APR, or customer-cash incentives as incompatible, so in practice the military bonus rides on top of those advertised offers. Confirm the specific stack with your dealer, since an individual advertised offer can carry its own "not combinable" clause.

Eligibility is outsourced to ID.me. You verify your military status once, and ID.me issues a one-time 6-character authorization code tied to you. The code can be used on up to two purchases and is valid through January 4, 2027; it is non-transferable outside your immediate household.

If you’re stationed, deployed, or on a 30+ day TDY overseas (or part of the DoD/diplomatic community serving abroad), compare the Military Select bonus against Military AutoSource (MAS) — the factory-authorized Audi distributor for overseas personnel. Its tax-free (VAT-free) factory-direct pricing and price protection can beat a stateside deal by far more than $1,000. MAS is a separate channel, not something you stack with the CONUS bonus — you choose one path based on where you buy.
figs-military-discount: Verification is handled by ID.me, FIGS’s verification partner and the same identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and many retailers. At checkout you select "Students and Military," choose "Military," and complete ID.me’s military verification. An ID.me account is required, and FIGS does not publish a re-verification schedule — ID.me governs how long a verification stays valid and may ask you to re-verify on its own terms, so don’t assume it’s permanent.

FIGS limits its discounts to students and military: there is no dedicated nurse, first responder, teacher, or government discount, even though FIGS is a medical-apparel brand. Medical professionals save only if they separately qualify as military or as students (a parallel 15% student program runs through ID.me in the U.S. and Student Beans internationally).

One thing to plan around: FIGS rarely deep-discounts core scrubs, so the standing 15% is meaningful on full-price scrub sets, tops, pants, lab coats, and underscrubs. When FIGS runs a sale (such as a Sample Sale up to 40% off), the military discount won’t stack — compare which single price is lower for your cart. Aggregator sites claim the issued code expires after six months, but FIGS does not confirm that, so we don’t state it as fact.
rudis-military-discount: RUDIS uses SheerID, a third-party verification service, with separate programs for military and first responders. You may verify instantly against records, or be asked to upload a document (a military ID or dependent proof, or a first-responder credential) for staff review — the brief notes a review of roughly 20 minutes. The resulting code is personal and single-use, so re-verify to get a new code for a future order. RUDIS does not use GovX or ID.me for this program.

The 10% code is best for a specific current-season item you want at a guaranteed, returnable price. On the baseline $150 adult wrestling-shoe cart (also the free-shipping threshold), 10% brings it to $135. The real competition to the code is the RUDIS Outlet — up to 50% off prior-season shoes, apparel, and gear — which often beats 10% outright, but those sales are final with no returns or exchanges. The single-use code generally won’t stack with other codes or apply on top of Outlet markdowns, and Rewards points redeem separately.

A few channels don’t exist for RUDIS: it doesn’t use GovX or ID.me (SheerID only), it isn’t carried by the AAFES/NEX exchanges, there’s no public individual ExpertVoice/pro-deal program (team and coach buyers go through Custom Team Gear in bulk), and there’s no verified cashback-portal storefront. For a first RUDIS order, check the email-signup “exclusive offer for your first order” — its amount isn’t published, so compare it against the 10% code before you buy.
aarp-military-discount: The military membership rate is verified through ID.me, which confirms military affiliation against authoritative data sources. AARP’s separate online-store "Military and First Responder Discount" — applied to AARP-branded products at aarp.org checkout — is verified through SheerID or ID.me instead. Neither is described as permanent, and re-verification may be required. GovX is not used for AARP membership.

Beyond membership, AARP publishes genuinely useful, largely free veteran resources: a Veteran & Military Spouse Job Center (with Indeed), a Health Benefits Navigator covering VA benefits, PACT Act eligibility, and VA home loans, a Military Caregiving Guide plus a helpline (1-877-333-5885), and a Veteran Fraud Center with the Fraud Watch Network Helpline (877-908-3360). Most of these need no membership at all.

AARP also maintains directories of military discounts at other companies — some supplied through the Veterans Advantage / WeSalute partner program (for example, 1-800-Flowers, Avis/Budget, and CVS offers). Those are the partner brands’ offers, not AARP discounts, and each is governed by that brand’s own terms. Treat AARP’s directory as a jump-off point to each brand’s program, not as an AARP checkout deal.
napa-military-discount: The NAPA military discount is a store-level courtesy, not a company-wide program. Each franchise decides whether to offer it, which IDs it accepts, and what it excludes, so the smart move is to call your local store before you drive over.

There is no online military verification for NAPA — no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute integration. ID.me does list NAPA as a general cash-back store open to everyone, but that is a shopping rebate, not a military discount, and it should not be confused with an identity-verified offer.

A NAPA page advertising “5–20% off via a DD-214 email” could not be verified on a clean fetch and reads like templated SEO copy, so we don’t rely on that figure. The one consistent, verified military-specific benefit is the discretionary ~10% in store.
toyota-military-discount: For the nationwide program, Toyota uses ID.me to confirm military status online before you finalize at the dealer; ID.me re-verification frequency is governed by ID.me, not stated on Toyota’s page. In the five Southeast states (AL, FL, GA, NC, SC), ID.me is not used — instead you present verifiable proof of service directly to your Toyota dealer, and Southeast Toyota Finance administers the rebate. In all cases the rebate is contingent on credit approval from the financing arm.

Acceptable proof documents named in Toyota’s program materials include a Leave and Earning Statement, Military ID card, or DD Form 214 (Certificate of Release or Discharge from Active Duty). Because the $500 is a fixed rebate, negotiate the out-the-door price and APR independently so the rebate is genuinely additive.

Toyota runs a separate $500 College Graduate Rebate for eligible recent or upcoming grads (not combinable with the Military Rebate nationally). Several other automakers run military appreciation or bonus-cash programs — confirm current competitor amounts directly with those brands before deciding.
fedex-military-discount: We checked: Military.com reflects no active FedEx military program, and FedEx’s own small-business pages document FedEx Advantage rather than any military rate. Aggregators that publish a FedEx “military promo code USL200 for 35% off” or a flat “5% veteran discount” are citing figures no FedEx-controlled page confirms — likely conflation with association/USAA rates — so we don’t assert them.

FedEx Advantage attaches the discount to your FedEx account: you enroll once through a partner organization and the negotiated rate applies automatically at label creation, with no code to type. USAA membership is the gate for the enhanced USAA-tier rates; without it you get the standard partner rate. The Advantage rate and FedEx Rewards can coexist — one is a rate discount, the other a loyalty earn.

The practical plan: if you’re USAA-eligible and ship Express or international, enroll through USAA — that’s the biggest military-relevant saver. If not, open a free FedEx account and enroll FedEx Advantage through any partner association you belong to. Either way, never pay the walk-up counter list price, and compare FedEx against USPS/UPS per package since the cheapest carrier shifts by weight and zone.
holiday-inn-express-military-discount: The Military Appreciation Rate is genuine but variable. IHG states a “minimum discount of 5% available at IHG hotels overall,” applied to the Best Flexible Rate, with the actual amount varying by property — and military editorial sites report some hotels running higher, occasionally “up to 20% at some on-post/on-base locations.” Treat anything above 5% as property-specific signal, not an IHG guarantee: the exact number appears at booking for your specific hotel and date. It’s leisure travel only, valid military or veteran ID is required at check-in, and the hotel can deny the rate at the desk if your ID can’t be verified.

For official government or military travel there’s a separate Government Rate: a percentage off the Best Flex Rate that varies by hotel and aligns toward the GSA per-diem cap, verified with official ID or work orders at check-in. It covers federal/state/local government employees, military personnel, Defense or Cost-Reimbursable Contractors, and state-funded universities and healthcare facilities. Like the military rate, it earns IHG One Rewards points, can’t be combined with other offers, and isn’t applicable to group bookings.

The travel-loyalty truth is “status stacks, rates don’t.” The military, government, and Advance Purchase rates are mutually exclusive — you pick one, and there’s no coupon to layer on. But points and status do earn on top of whichever paid rate you book direct, so the real prize is a free IHG One Rewards account: always book through ihg.com or the app (third-party/OTA bookings generally forfeit points and elite benefits), and every stay earns ~10 points per dollar at Holiday Inn Express plus qualifying nights toward status. On any given night, compare the military rate against the Best Flexible, member, and Advance Purchase rates and book the lowest — the 5% floor is frequently not the cheapest.
ghost-golf-military-discount: Verification runs through GovX. You confirm your eligibility (service email or document), and GovX issues a single-use code tied to your order — it’s not a permanent account discount, so you request a fresh code as needed. The code is entered in the promo-code field at ghostgolf.com checkout.

A transparency note: Ghost Golf’s own military-discount page was rate-limited (HTTP 429) on July 20, 2026, so the exact on-page percentage couldn’t be read verbatim. The GovX brand listing shows up to 20% off, and the brand’s own summary describes an "up to 10%–25%" range, so confirm the exact rate during GovX verification. Coupon sites variously claim "up to 25%," "up to 30%," or "10%–25%" — treat those as unverified public-code leads, not the military rate.

Because GovX codes generally don’t stack with public codes (most Shopify stores allow one discount per order), the play is to compare rather than combine. If a live public sitewide code is deeper than the GovX rate, use the public code; otherwise verify with GovX. Sale-priced items may or may not accept the code, so confirm at checkout.
1st-phorm-military-discount: 1st Phorm is a flat-price, direct-to-consumer supplement brand with a deliberately stated no-coupon policy. Rather than gating pricing behind ID.me, GovX, or SheerID, it charges one price 365 days a year "so you can order what you want, when you want, without fear of missing out on the next ‘sale.’" That is why there is no military code to enter and nothing to "stack" on a supplement order — no coupon, no military code, no portal-plus-code play on the brand site.

Be cautious of coupon and deal sites advertising a specific "1st Phorm military discount" percentage or a checkout code. 1st Phorm explicitly states the coupons and codes on other sites are not legitimate, so treat "70% off first responder" and "10% off" claims as fabricated. Community Q&A boards consistently report the same answer service members already suspect: 1st Phorm has no military or first-responder discount.

It is easy to confuse the GovX "TNB x 1st Phorm" listing with a 1st Phorm military discount, but they are different. That listing is The Normal Brand selling a co-branded apparel collaboration — joggers and a hoodie — to verified military and first responders at 25% off through The Normal Brand’s GovX storefront. It is a clothing discount from a separate seller and cannot be applied to 1st Phorm protein, greens, or any supplement.

Even without a military discount, there are honest ways to lower what you pay: batch your order to $150 or more for automatic free shipping and the free-gift tier (the single biggest lever on supplement orders), use autoship on staples you reorder for a small recurring saving, buy pre-built bundles or stacks that can cost less than the same items separately, and rely on the 110% money-back guarantee to try a new product with no risk. None of these is a military benefit, but each is real and open to everyone.
atlantis-military-discount: The official program is straightforward: Atlantis’ military-and-first-responders page headlines up to 30% off Best Available Rates, verified through ID.me’s hosted offer flow. The ID.me Shop listing for the same store says up to 25% for military — a discrepancy worth knowing about, and a reminder that the number is a ceiling that varies by dates and tower, not a guarantee. Coupon sites framing this as a flat 25% or a "30% off sitewide code" are wrong on both counts: no flat rate is promised, and Atlantis runs rate-based offers, not promo codes.

Every path pays the Bahamas’ mandatory charges: 21% on the nightly room rate (VAT plus tourism levies), a $77–$82.50 daily resort fee, and mandatory gratuities. On a 4-night, $400/night stay for two at The Royal, the no-discount total is about $2,356 — a 25% military rate brings it to roughly $1,872, and the full 30% to about $1,775.

Atlantis offers are mutually exclusive — the package terms say offers are "not combined." That matters because the public offers are strong: "every 3rd night free" ties a 25% military rate on a 4-night stay, and the up-to-40% air+hotel bundle (travel August 9 – December 15, 2026, with a $25 daily resort credit) usually wins if you’re flying anyway. Price each path and book the lowest total; historically, a Veterans Day offer (up to 25% off plus $25 daily resort credit) has also appeared around November 11.

The Caesars route is the overlooked prize. Salute membership is free for US active duty, Reserve, Guard, retirees, veterans, and military spouses (enrollment historically in person at a Caesars Rewards desk with ID) and auto-grants Platinum status. Platinum’s 2026 Atlantis partner perk, per AwardWallet’s March 30, 2026 reporting: up to 4 comp nights at The Coral in January, May, June, September, or October (buy-2-get-2 in February, August, November, December; March, April, and July blacked out), booked by phone at 1-888-877-7592, with resort fees and gratuities still due and roughly four hours of casino play expected. On the baseline stay that’s about $420 all-in — but treat the specifics as editorial-reported and verify by phone first.
cracker-barrel-military-discount: Verification is handled by ID.me and linked to your Cracker Barrel Rewards account — use the same email on both. After successful verification, the benefit attaches to your Rewards account, so you don’t re-verify on every visit. The official source doesn’t state a re-verification interval, so don’t assume it’s permanent; ID.me may require periodic re-verification per its own policies. If automatic verification fails, follow ID.me’s support flow and Cracker Barrel Rewards support — the official page doesn’t detail a separate manual fallback.

Two scope points matter. First, this is an in-store benefit: it won’t apply to online, catering, delivery, or takeout orders, and it excludes alcohol, Meals for Two, Take Home Meals, gift cards, taxes, delivery fees, and gratuities. Second, on eligibility, the official restrictions text names active-duty, reserve, retired, and veteran members — it doesn’t separately list National Guard, spouses, or dependents, so verify your specific status in the ID.me flow rather than assuming.

Separately from the everyday discount, Cracker Barrel has run a one-day Veterans Day promotion — a complimentary Sunrise Pancake Special on November 11, 2025, dine-in, with proof of service. That is a limited-time annual promo, not the everyday discount, and the specific item and terms can change year to year, so confirm it closer to Veterans Day. To stretch value, the free Cracker Barrel Rewards program earns Pegs on purchases (separate from the military benefit), and the retail store’s seasonal sales are open to all shoppers and can beat 10% on retail items.
virgin-voyages-military-discount: The rate’s level is set per sailing. Virgin’s official page groups current voyages into 5%, 10%, and 15% lists and says the lineup is "updated frequently" and "dependent on various market factors" — so treat any flat "Virgin Voyages military discount is X%" claim as wrong by construction. Eligibility spans US and Canadian active duty, veterans, spouses, and surviving spouses across all branches including Space Force, National Guard, NOAA Corps, and USPHS, plus firefighters, EMTs, paramedics, and police.

Stacking is the headline. The military offer’s own terms say it is "combinable with select public promotional offers," and Virgin’s promotional T&Cs confirm it from the other side: the 70% Off 2nd Sailor promo (each sailor 35% off, booking window May 29 – July 31, 2026), the Free Balcony Upgrade, and the June Sailor Loot onboard-credit promo each list the Military and First Responders Rate as combinable. Combinability lists change per promo, so check the live promo’s T&C every time.

The wall is reduced-fare programs: casino rates, interline, travel-agent First Mate Rates, any reduced-fare Access Key (including Lock It In GTY), tour operators, and group programs are either/or with the military rate — compute both totals. Also worth knowing: the "must pay in full at booking" claim on some aggregator pages is a misreading; the terms’ "only for paid bookings at full fare" language excludes reduced-fare programs, and Virgin’s separate Pay In Full discount is itself listed as combinable.

Verification really is just an ID at the pier. The "Virgin Voyages" store on ID.me Shop is MemberDeals — a third-party travel seller advertising onboard-cash packages — not Virgin verification; GovX has no dedicated Virgin storefront; and no cashback portal carried Virgin Voyages as of July 7, 2026, so there’s nothing to void by using the code. First-time sailors can layer a Refer a Sailor $150 onboard bar tab on top of any fare promo (non-Lock-It-In cabins).
vons-military-discount: The Vons military benefit is really loyalty-account offer targeting, not a register percentage. You verify as Military through SheerID, a third-party service, and on approval any targeted offers unlock inside your Albertsons for U account. Because that value is account-gated and rotates, there is no fixed “military % plus coupons” stack to promise — the honest framing is “verify, then watch for offers.”

The reliable everyday saver is the free Albertsons for U program, and it is open to every shopper regardless of military status. Digital coupons and personalized for U deals generally stack with each other within program rules (one clip per item), the weekly ad can beat any flat percentage on the right basket, and points convert to grocery and fuel rewards. Layering a grocery cashback app (receipt scan) adds a small extra percentage on top.

One more path matters for eligible patrons: the on-base commissary sells staples at cost plus a 5% surcharge, tax-free, and often beats any supermarket — Vons included. That is a separate grocery channel, not a Vons offer, but for anyone with base access it is frequently the cheapest option for pantry staples.
liberty-mutual-military-discount: Liberty Mutual applies the military discount as a rating factor within your quote; you attest to and may need to document your service status through the agent or quote flow. There is no published ID.me, GovX, or SheerID portal for this discount — it is handled in the insurance application, and the exact savings appear only on the personalized quote.

The military discount is one of several stackable discounts. Liberty Mutual lists it alongside multi-policy, multi-car, RightTrack telematics, claims-free, violation-free, homeowner, early-shopper, good-student, student-away-at-school, preferred-payment, online-purchase, and paperless discounts, and these combine on a single quote. The same "military discount" yields different dollar savings by state, driving record, vehicle, and coverage — there is no fixed percentage.

Carrier choice usually matters more than any single discount. In independent 2026 comparisons, USAA — whose membership is limited to the military community, veterans, and eligible family — frequently prices lowest for eligible service members. The maximum-savings move is to quote Liberty Mutual’s military-discounted rate against USAA (if eligible) and at least one other carrier, rather than assume the military line item makes Liberty Mutual cheapest.

Aggregator sites circulate specific numbers — "12% military discount," "up to 10-25%," a "Military Connect program." None of these appears on Liberty Mutual’s own discounts page. The verified facts are only that a named Military Discount exists for Active, Retired, and Reserve members and that the amount is quote- and state-specific.
montana-knife-company-military-discount: Verification runs through GovX ID, which confirms military/first-responder eligibility and issues a single-use discount code. Re-verification cadence and code lifespan are set by GovX, not MKC. Support runs through GovX for verification issues and MKC for order issues.

MKC does not stack codes — the military code cannot be combined with a referral (a separate public 15%-off-first-order mechanic) or any promo code. Free shipping is automatic on US orders over $200 and applies even when a discount code is used.

MKC’s biggest public price breaks come from its periodic "Expo pricing online" collection and blemished/second drops rather than any coupon, and these can beat the gated GovX percentage. There is no ID.me, SheerID, or WeSalute path — GovX is the sole verification provider.
our-place-military-discount: Our Place uses ID.me — and only ID.me; no GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute listing was found, and there is no Exchange (AAFES/NEX) or pro-deal channel to route around the non-combinable rule. You verify your eligible-group status through ID.me on each visit; once verified, the 10% auto-applies at checkout on orders of $100+. Verification is per-visit, not permanent, and support for verification issues goes to ID.me’s help center, not Our Place.

Run the math on a representative ~$200 cart (say, a Titanium Always Pan Pro plus a small accessory): the ID.me 10% saves $20, while a 30–40% sitewide sale saves $60–$80 — and the two can’t be combined. Our Place’s other levers are also single, non-stacking offers: the Dirty Dishes Club loyalty program (1 point per $1; 100 points = $10 off, redeemable at $50+, not combinable with codes) and a $20 referral/welcome offer on a first $100+ order, which roughly ties the 10% on a ~$200 cart.

Debunks worth knowing: a "20% military discount" claim circulating in search results is false — the verified figure on both the brand page and ID.me is 10%. "Up to 40–45% off for military" conflates the public sale with the military discount. And the "25% off military code 30OPLX2C9XA2" floating around coupon sites is a referral/welcome code, not a military offer — and it’s non-combinable with ID.me anyway.
lenscrafters-military-discount: LensCrafters verifies military status through ID.me, the same free identity service used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of retailers. You create a free ID.me account once, confirm your eligibility, and the 15%/10% unlocks at checkout. There is no confirmed GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute route for LensCrafters — ID.me is the named partner. The military tier sits alongside separate ID.me communities for first responders, government employees, teachers, and nurses.

The category-defining catch is the non-combinable fork: the 15% will not stack with vision insurance or with LensCrafters’ public sales. For anyone with real coverage — TRICARE FEDVIP, EyeMed, or VSP — running the purchase through insurance almost always beats the 15%, and the two are mutually exclusive. Likewise, the near-permanent public sales (about 40% off glasses, 50% off lenses) usually beat the discount, so you pick the single lowest path.

Beware the fabricated figures. "50%/60% off lenses" is the public lens sale or the AAA member deal, "20% off frames" is almost certainly the AAA offer mislabeled as military, and "35% off frames through TRICARE" is invented — TRICARE is federal health coverage, not a LensCrafters frame discount. The only verified military figure is 15% off eyewear / 10% off contacts via ID.me.
royal-caribbean-military-discount: The military rate is applied per stateroom: all guests traveling in the same stateroom receive the rate, but no additional staterooms — only the one occupied by the eligible military person — qualify. Spouses, parents, in-laws, children, other family members, and friends are not eligible for the military rate without the eligible military person occupying the stateroom.

Royal Caribbean verifies the rate by inspecting eligibility documents at check-in, not through an online verification provider on its own website. Each category has a specific accepted ID — for example, active duty shows a WHITE US Uniformed Services ID, retirees a RED or BLUE ID (TAN for 100% disabled), veterans a DD 214 plus a current photo, and spouses a Pink or Tan Dependent Military ID. Royal Caribbean also runs random audits throughout the year, and missing or invalid documentation can revert the fare to full retail or result in denied boarding.

Some shoppers reach the rate through GOVX, a third-party government/military-verification marketplace that markets Royal Caribbean military fares and applies a code at booking. That is a separate channel from Royal Caribbean’s own site, and the at-check-in document requirement still governs. Many aggregator pages also advertise an "up to 50% off" figure and price codes like "MIL" or "PFD," but none of those appear on Royal Caribbean’s official FAQ — treat them as how the trade describes availability, not as Royal Caribbean’s published terms.
jetblue-military-discount: The honest core fact: the biggest, most reliable dollar win is the free-baggage waiver, not the 5% fare cut. On a $300 base fare, 5% is only about $15, while free checked bags can be worth ~$85 or more round-trip for leisure — and $180+ on a duty/PCS move with multiple or overweight bags. JetBlue’s own page states the waiver plainly: 2 free bags (≤50 lbs) for leisure, up to 5 free bags (≤99 lbs) for duty travel.

Active-duty members get the benefit directly. You verify with a DOD Common Access Card at booking (plus travel orders for duty/PCS travel), and dependents on the same reservation share the benefit for leisure travel — for duty travel they can travel on a separate reservation with a Military Dependent ID. Veterans and retirees get the identical 5% + 2 free bags, but only through a paid WeSalute+ membership; WeSalute (not JetBlue) verifies your status, and JetBlue applies the discount against your WeSalute+ Member ID.

A common miss on coupon and aggregator pages: they blur the individual member discount (5% + bags, booked by phone) with JetBlue’s separate GSA/DG government fares — a contract program for federal travelers paying with a U.S. government travel card. They also imply veterans get 5% off for free; in reality the veteran path is gated behind a paid WeSalute+ membership. And most of all, there is no online promo code: the benefit exists only when a JetBlue agent applies it by phone or chat.
grammarly-military-discount: SheerID handles eligibility. Most applicants verify instantly; some are asked to upload a document (military ID, orders, or DD-214), which can take up to seven business days. After verification, you receive a promo link from verify@sheerid.com and can upgrade to Grammarly Pro using any email you like. The discount isn’t tied permanently to your account — it applies to the one subscription period you activate via the promo link.

The catch is the scope. The 50% applies to the first subscription period only and the first seat only; additional seats bill at the standard rate, and at renewal the plan reverts to $144/year unless a new offer is available. Promo offers cannot be combined with other offers or applied to previous purchases, and the discount is not valid through the Apple App Store or Google Play — you must upgrade via the SheerID promo link on the web.

Coupon and affiliate pages assert Grammarly military discounts of "25% off," "40% off for veterans," even "flat 60% off." None matches the primary source — Grammarly’s own support article and the SheerID offer both state 50% off Grammarly Pro. Note also that ID.me’s shop explicitly states it is "not aware that Grammarly offers Military discounts": Grammarly’s program runs through SheerID, not ID.me. If you won’t use Pro daily, the free plan costs nothing; and students, teachers, first responders, or healthcare workers in the household can each claim their own SheerID 50% offer.
opticsplanet-military-discount: OpticsPlanet’s "Honoring Those Who Serve" program is a curated store (about 208 products at the time of check), not a flat sitewide percentage. Availability and depth vary by brand, and MAP-restricted premium brands often yield little or no service discount — which is why the recurring advice is to "call and ask for your specific product."

There is no third-party verification provider for the service discount — it’s handled manually by a phone representative. Do not expect an ID.me, SheerID, or GovX flow on OpticsPlanet’s own checkout. GovX is a separate marketplace where you register once and verify your military or government status online for instant approval on many of the same brands.

Because the discount is placed by phone, cashback portals (roughly 1%–3.25% as of July 2026) and coupon codes generally do not track on it. Those layers only apply to a plain online OpticsPlanet checkout, so the phone service discount and portal cashback effectively do not combine.
maurices-military-discount: The honest picture: ID.me — which partners with hundreds of brands for exactly this kind of offer — explicitly reports it is not aware of a Maurices military program. So there’s no online military verification, and the aggregator claims of “10% off online and in stores” or “up to 25%” aren’t supported by any Maurices primary source. The 25% figure in particular should be disregarded.

What is genuinely supported is a 10% in-store discount at participating stores. Multiple mall store directories (Northpark, Brookfield Square, Hanes Mall) list a Maurices “Military Discount,” and a store social post references an everyday military discount for active and retired members — all redeemed by showing a military ID at the register. Since there are no published corporate terms, treat availability, eligibility, and stacking as store-discretionary and ask before you rely on it.

For most shoppers the bigger savings are online and don’t require military status. Clearance is the deepest single lever; a current public promo code layers on top of it; and mymaurices rewards add points, birthday offers, and members-only prices. That stack beats a flat 10% almost every time, and the maurices VIP credit card can add cardholder perks for frequent buyers.
shark-ninja-military-discount: SharkNinja owns both the Shark and Ninja brands, and neither brand store runs a service-member discount in the US. The clearest primary source is ID.me itself: on its SharkNinja page it states plainly that it is "not aware that SharkNinja offers Military discounts." ID.me still lists SharkNinja, but only as an affiliate cash-back store — a small rebate on qualifying links, not a checkout discount and not a military rate. The generic "up to 40% off for Military" you may see is ID.me marketing for its entire marketplace, not a SharkNinja offer.

The one US path that is genuinely tied to the military community is WeSalute (formerly Veterans Advantage). Through its BenefitHub marketplace, WeSalute+ members occasionally see product-specific SharkNinja deals — for example "$20 off FlexStyle" or "15% off select Facial Pro Glow and hair dryers." WeSalute verifies active duty, retirees, veterans, current and former Guard and Reserve, and immediate family (plus Nurse and Medical members), but these offers require a paid WeSalute+ membership (from $9.99/mo, after a 30-day trial) and cover only select SKUs that rotate. Check whether a live offer covers your exact model before paying the membership just for it.

Multiple coupon aggregators present a "SharkNinja 9% military discount" as if it were a US brand offer. It is not — it is a UK GoCertify program whose eligibility reads "R.A.F, Army, Navy or Armed Forces Dependents," verified by UK payslip, work ID, or work email. It will not validate a US service member, and there is nothing to combine it with on the US brand sites.

For a US buyer, the cheapest real path is almost never a "military" channel. Catch a public site-wide sale (Black Friday and Prime-style events cut the deepest), buy a certified-refurbished Shark or Ninja unit, or compare Amazon — which frequently undercuts the brand sites on these products — and layer a cashback portal. If you are shopping on base, check the exchange (AAFES/NEX/MCX) for a tax-free purchase when it stocks your model.
stetson-military-discount: What we checked: Stetson’s FAQ page and the complete Stetson Help Center, searched in full for "military," "veteran," and "first responder" — zero hits (July 14, 2026). The ID.me Shop store index lists no Stetson store, and the direct Stetson discount-page URL on shop.id.me returns a 404. A site-restricted GovX search surfaces no Stetson products or brand shop. We also found no history of Veterans Day or Memorial Day military promotions from stetson.com — its discounting is seasonal end-of-season clearance, not military-holiday-driven.

About the myth: SemperSave’s "Stetson Military Discount — 10% via ID.me" page (updated January 15, 2025) directly conflicts with reality — Stetson has no ID.me store, and its own help pages publish no military program. The page even hedges that Stetson "does not specify who is eligible in their policy," because there is no policy. WorthEPenny’s "10% with military ID at purchase" is equally unsourced, and shopper Q&A threads (Knoji) flip between "10%" and "none" — the signature of aggregator myth-making, not a real program. Treat every "Stetson military discount %" claim as fabricated until Stetson itself publishes one.

The real military route is a retailer substitute. Boot Barn — an authorized Stetson retailer with the brand’s hats on its shelves — runs an everyday 10% discount for military members and first responders on all full-priced styles, verified through ID.me in the cart online or per the store process in person. On a $150 Stetson that’s $15 off, it works year-round in both channels, and unlike the coupon-site figure, it’s published on Boot Barn’s own page. The catch: full-price styles only, so it never applies to sale or clearance hats.

The deepest real discount, though, is public: Stetson’s end-of-season sale. On July 14, 2026 a "Take 40% Off" EOS collection and an "Extra 25% Off Sale Items" collection were both live — a 40%-off $150 hat lands near $90, crushing the Boot Barn 10% path when your style qualifies. Stacking mechanics to know: sale pricing applies automatically, Stetson’s Help Center allows only one promo code per order, and free ground shipping requires $99+ after discounts (that $90 sale hat falls under the line — add a small item or budget the $10 fee).
american-home-shield-military-discount: The military discount is a standing, evergreen program — publicly (re)announced by AHS via Business Wire in January 2024 and June 2025 — not a seasonal flash sale. On a representative $720/year ShieldGold plan, 20% off is about $144 in year one, then roughly $60/year afterward from the $5/month renewal credit.

AHS verifies military status by having you submit a military email through its military landing page. Unlike many retailers, AHS does not route this through ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute — ID.me’s own shop page states it has no AHS offer, so any site telling you to redeem via ID.me or GovX is wrong. Veterans who lack an active military email should contact AHS sales to ask what documentation (military ID, DD-214, or Veterans ID) they’ll accept, since AHS publishes no self-serve document-upload flow.

Which offer saves you the most depends on your plan and how long you’ll keep it. Because 20% of the annual premium equals $150 at a $750/year premium, the flat public "$150 off first year" is marginally larger in year one on a cheaper sub-$750 plan, while the military 20% wins outright in year one on a pricier ShieldPlatinum plan and wins over any 2+ year horizon thanks to the $5/month renewal credit. The military discount is not combinable with any other offer, so you pick military or a public code, never both.

AHS also publishes a few non-military levers worth knowing: a ~$36 AARP member discount (which AHS names as combinable with other valid public offers, but not with the military discount), a $50 multi-property discount for insuring 2+ homes, and a referral program paying $25 Amazon gift cards to both you and a friend. Ignore aggregator codes like SAVE250 or "50% off" — they’re unverified; the real levers are the military 20% and the standing public first-year offer.
mavis-military-discount: Verification is a manual ID check at the register — there is no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or WeSalute account. The store manager confirms your military ID in person each visit, which also means there is no online military route at all: buying online forfeits the 10% entirely.

The non-combinable rule is the whole story. The 10% "cannot be combined with any other coupons, vouchers, or special offers," and price-match and warranty transactions are excluded. Because Mavis routinely runs manufacturer rebates worth $100–$160 (e.g. Continental $160, Dunlop $150, Bridgestone $130) and service coupons ($30 off oil, up to $80 off brakes) that are usually larger than 10%, the honest advice is to compare: take whichever single number is bigger. On most rebate-eligible tires and coupon-eligible services, the rebate or coupon wins.

One open question worth asking at the counter: Mavis’s rule bars "coupons, vouchers, or special offers," but a tire manufacturer’s mail-in rebate is arguably a separate program paid by the tire maker, not Mavis. The brand page does not explicitly address it, so ask whether you can take the 10% and still send in the manufacturer mail-in. Treat any "yes" as store-level discretion — it is not verified.

The military discount is not tax-free. It comes off the pre-tax subtotal, and tax still applies. The only genuinely tax-free tire route for service members is a base Exchange (AAFES/NEX) car-care or tire center — a substitute channel, not something you stack on the Mavis discount.
cub-cadet-military-discount: Verification happens at claim time through the sbdheroprogram.com portal rather than a storefront ID.me or SheerID gate. You buy the qualifying product from an Independent Dealer, register it within 10 days, then upload proof of service (DD-214 with SSN covered, VA ID card, veteran-designated license, or departmental ID) along with the dealer invoice within 30 days. Military CAC cards are not accepted.

The rebate tiers are model-specific: $300 on ZTX, ZTXS, PRO Z HW 300, and PRO Z 100 series, and $500 on PRO Z 500/700/900 and PRO X series. On a roughly $6,000 PRO Z 500-series zero-turn, the $500 rebate brings the effective price to about $5,500. Homeowner riding mowers and push mowers do not qualify at all.

Two things to plan for. First, the rebate cannot be combined with any other offer, demo, or promotion — so negotiate the dealer price first, since the rebate stacks on top of your agreed price but not on top of other Cub Cadet promotions. Second, coupon aggregators advertising a "Cub Cadet military discount: save up to $500 off your order" at checkout are misleading — the $500 is the maximum rebate tier, paid after purchase, on qualifying PRO equipment only.
reebok-military-discount: Reebok uses ID.me to confirm eligibility at checkout. You sign in to (or create) a free ID.me account and verify your military status; ID.me may request documents proving your status if it can’t verify you automatically. Verification is handled by ID.me, not Reebok — Reebok’s page directs you to choose ID.me at checkout and says the discount then applies automatically. ID.me may require re-verification per its own policies; Reebok does not publish a re-verification frequency, so don’t assume "verify once forever."

One thing to watch: some coupon sites claim "up to 50% off." Reebok’s own terms state 30% off, which is the only rate confirmed on Reebok’s official pages. And because the discount can’t be combined with other promotions and clearance clothing is excluded, it’s worth comparing a current sale price against the 30% military price on the same item.

Reebok runs the same 30% via ID.me for separate communities — first responders, nurses/medical providers, hospital employees, teachers, government employees, and students. If the discount doesn’t appear, make sure you completed ID.me verification at checkout, that your cart excludes clearance clothing, and that you haven’t applied another promo code (offers don’t stack).
golf-galaxy-military-discount: Multiple listings claim "Golf Galaxy offers a 10% military discount via ID.me with the same rules as DICK’s." That is false. ID.me’s own Golf Galaxy military page explicitly says it is "not aware" of any Golf Galaxy military discount, and DICK’s itself has no chain-wide program — only an unguaranteed, manager’s-discretion in-store courtesy some locations grant. Do not expect a 10% military discount at Golf Galaxy checkout.

The only in-store discount discussed anywhere is the DICK’s parent-chain discretionary ~10%, which is not guaranteed, is manager-dependent, and typically excludes sale, clearance, gift cards, and prior purchases. It is corroborated by secondary reporting (The Military Wallet) on DICK’s in-store practice generally, not confirmed specifically at Golf Galaxy locations — treat it as a maybe, not a plan, and ask a manager rather than floor staff.

ID.me cash back (up to ~1% for new members, ~0.5% for existing members) is a rebate paid after purchase, open to any ID.me member — it is not a military-only benefit, but it stacks cleanly with a public sale or clearance price, which is the best no-card savings path for an online order.

For frequent buyers, the DICK’s/Golf Galaxy ScoreRewards credit card’s 10% back in rewards is the largest recurring value, though it is a store rewards program rather than a military discount. Shoppers buying a specific brand — shoes, apparel, a rangefinder — should also check whether that brand runs its own military discount on its own site, which often beats anything available through Golf Galaxy.
lems-military-discount: Lems verifies eligibility through GovX ID (govx.com). Verification is real-time and tied to your GovX ID account, which is reusable across many partner brands. Each order needs a fresh single-use code — you log back in through Lems’ GovX page to generate one, with a limit of one code per day. There is no ID.me, SheerID, WeSalute, or VerifyPass path for Lems.

The percentage is the story here. Lems’ help-center FAQ and aggregators like WorthEPenny and SimplyCodes all repeat "15% via GovX," but the live GovX offer configured for the Lems store on July 18, 2026 was 25% ("type":"percentage","value":25). Treat any fixed 15% claim as outdated, and treat 25% as the current-but-changeable rate — the number you see at checkout governs. Aggregator claims that the discount covers "military family members" or works at "participating retail locations" are also unsupported: Lems’ actual group list reads "Current & former U.S. military," and the mechanic delivers an online checkout code.

Because Shopify checkout takes one code per order, the honest comparison is simple: on a full-price pair the 25% GovX code wins; on a Clearance pair, compare the markdown (often more than 25% off) against 25% off full price and take the lower price. If you don’t qualify for GovX ID, the 10% newsletter/SMS first-order code or a friend’s 10% referral link are the public fallbacks — and qualifying outdoor-industry professionals can apply to the Lems Pro Program, whose rate Lems doesn’t publish.
logitech-military-discount: Logitech uses SheerID, an instant third-party eligibility check. You verify your status on the program page; approval issues a promo code tied to that verification. Codes are typically single-use, so you re-verify for each new order. No permanent "verified account" is implied beyond SheerID’s process.

The military and veteran tier sits alongside parallel SheerID communities for first responders, medical professionals, teachers, and students — all at 20% off. To be clear about a common error: ID.me does not have a Logitech military discount. ID.me’s own shop page states it is "not aware that Logitech offers Military discounts." The free official offer is 20% via SheerID.

A "25%" figure that circulates online is either an aggregator mistake or refers to WeSalute’s paid-membership Logitech G tier ("up to 25%" on original-priced gear), which requires a paid membership and is a separate channel — not the free brand offer.

Because the 20% will not stack on sale prices, the honest cheapest path often is not the code at all. Check Amazon and logitech.com/shop/deals first: the MX line frequently sells below list and below list-minus-20%, and Prime Day/Black Friday go deeper. Logitech Certified Refurbished usually beats a new-unit 20% if you accept the 90-day warranty, and the military Exchanges (AAFES, NEX) carry Logitech tax-free.
rally-house-military-discount: Because no military channel exists, the genuine best path for a service member is the same as for any shopper: stack a public sitewide promo (or email-signup offer) with a cashback portal (Rakuten) and the free Rally Rewards program, and time the order to a major sale event — Memorial Day, Black Friday/Cyber Monday, or Labor Day, historically 20–50% off. That full stack typically lands a $100 team-apparel order somewhere around $74–$78 net, which beats a military discount Rally House does not offer.

Rally Rewards is Rally House’s free loyalty program (the Help Center hosts a "What is Rally Rewards?" article). It provides a birthday coupon and member promos and generally applies on top of sale pricing, though the exact earn/stack mechanics are not confirmed from a primary source — verify in your account. Rakuten cashback is a portal rebate rather than a Rally House discount, so it stacks with a sale price and a promo code on the same order, as long as you enter through the Rakuten link and keep tracking intact.

Be cautious with public promo codes: at apparel retailers they generally do not stack on already-marked-down clearance, and it is safest to assume one code per order unless the code’s own terms say otherwise. If you specifically want a status-based way to buy licensed team gear cheaper, the tax-free military Exchange (AAFES/NEX) sells licensed sports apparel from exchange vendors — a different selection, not the Rally House brand or store.
marcus-theater-military-discount: The box-office rate is verified at the counter with a physical military ID and applies to general admission only — premium formats add surcharges. The electronic-ticket discount is a separate channel (Working Advantage via ID.me/WeSalute) and is not combined with the box-office rate; pick one.

The WeSalute electronic-ticket path widens eligibility to veterans, Guard and Reserve members, and immediate family, whereas the box-office language specifies "active and retired." Confirm veteran acceptance at your local box office.
Because the offer is participating-location, confirm current pricing at your theatre. GovX also lists Marcus tickets for military/government as an alternative marketplace.
32-degrees-military-discount: There is no verification partner because there is no discount to unlock: 32 Degrees uses no ID.me, GovX, SheerID, or VerifyPass military flow, and its Help Center and promotions pages list no military program. Aggregator pages that assert a "32 Degrees 15% military discount for all military members, veterans, reserves and retirees with qualified ID" are unverified — the brand names no verification provider, and shoppers report those codes failing at checkout.

The real savings machine is public. Deal forums repeatedly surface 32 Degrees items at $3.99–$9.99 during flash sales, and the brand runs near-constant one-day and flash events plus deep clearance and BOGO deals. Because these are already 50–75% off, the public-sale path is effectively the "military" path here — a 10–15% military rate, even if it existed, would rarely beat it.

To maximize a single order: buy during a live flash or one-day sale, or from clearance; stack the 15% first-order email code where allowed (one code per order); and route an active cashback portal on top of the final sale price. If a verified service rate is what you’re after, other apparel brands run ID.me or GovX programs — 32 Degrees simply competes on everyday price instead.
la-fitness-military-discount: LA Fitness does not operate its own military verification flow and is not listed as an ID.me partner for a military or first-responder discount. For the WeSalute+ path, WeSalute verifies your service eligibility as part of its paid membership, and the gym rate is then unlocked through GlobalFit — online or by phone, not at the club desk. For any local club offer or a Veterans Day promo, the club itself checks ID at signup or entry (military ID, DD-214, or veteran ID, per the club). There is no published "verify once" national LA Fitness military credential.

Two limits are worth repeating. The WeSalute+/GlobalFit gym rates are not available to anyone who held an LA Fitness membership within the prior 12 months, and they aren’t offered to the general public or at the clubs directly — only through GlobalFit. And the Veterans Day free-access promo is only verifiable for Nov 11–14, 2021; whether it runs in any given year isn’t guaranteed, so treat it as seasonal and re-check each November. Be skeptical of the aggregator "$39.99 first responder, no activation fee" claim — no primary source confirms it, and ID.me reports no LA Fitness first-responder discount.

Because clubs set their own fees, the most effective tactic is often the least technical: use a free guest pass to try a club, then ask at the desk about a waived initiation fee or a service courtesy for military — bring your ID. If your employer (including a government agency) participates in the Corporate Wellness Program, that low corporate rate may beat everything else; have HR request info. For comparison, Anytime Fitness, Gold’s Gym, and 24 Hour Fitness also appear in WeSalute/GlobalFit, and YMCA branches frequently waive enrollment fees and discount dues for service members — compare local pricing before committing.
tidal-military-discount: TIDAL did once run a real military discount: launched in 2022 through SheerID (also usable via VerifyPass), it took roughly 40% off the HiFi and HiFi Plus tiers for verified military and first responders. That ended on June 10, 2024, when TIDAL discontinued both plans and automatically converted those subscribers to the standard $10.99 Individual plan — a change TIDAL announced in emails to affected subscribers. The offer is discontinued, not paused.

That history is why so many coupon pages still get this wrong. Aggregator sites continue to advertise "TIDAL military discount — 40%–50% off" or a "$5.99 Military HiFi" plan. Any page quoting those numbers, or telling you to "verify with SheerID for military," is stale — there is nothing to verify because there is no military plan.

What actually saves money now: if you’re an enrolled student — and many service members studying on the GI Bill or tuition assistance are — the Student plan at $5.49/month is 50% off the Individual rate and the closest thing left to the old military price. A multi-listener household does even better per person on the Family plan: $16.99/month covers up to 6 people, about $2.83 each when fully shared. Solo and not a student? You’ll pay $10.99, but start with the free trial and watch for public promos.

One date to know: TIDAL has a pricing update taking effect August 3, 2026, and alongside it a public Cash App-linked offer giving eligible U.S. Individual customers 25% off for 12 months. That promo is open to everyone who qualifies — it is not military-gated — so verify eligibility at signup, and confirm current plan prices on TIDAL’s support site before subscribing.
banana-republic-military-discount: Banana Republic’s military discount is a discretionary in-store benefit: you present a valid military ID at the register and, where the store participates, get a percentage off. There’s no third-party provider (no ID.me, SheerID, or GovX) and no account to create, so there’s no re-verification cycle — but there’s also nothing to redeem online. Military.com lists it as available to active duty, retirees, veterans, Reserve/National Guard, and dependents, in store only.

The percentage is the honest gap in the record. Banana Republic doesn’t publish it and it varies by location; secondary directories cite roughly 10%, and an older (now-offline) Military.com feature cited 15% off full-price. Treat any specific number as “ask in store,” and ignore coupon-site “military codes,” which aren’t supported by Banana Republic or any verification provider.

Two common mix-ups to correct: the 35% off is the Gap/BR/Old Navy credit-card full-price promo (a card pay-type is required), and the 40% is the public Friends & Family event — neither is a military discount, though both beat one. Separately, the WeSalute “Banana Republic offer” is Rewards free shipping on $50+, not a percentage off the cart.

For most shoppers, timing beats verification. On a $200 cart, Friends & Family (40% off full-price) lands you at $120 and the card 35% at $130, versus roughly $170–$180 with a 10–15% in-store military discount — so plan your purchase around a public event, and use the in-store military discount mainly when nothing deeper is running.
gopro-military-discount: GoPro’s 5% is powered by ID.me, the same identity-verification service used by the VA, the IRS, and dozens of major retailers. You verify your group affiliation once, and the discount then activates on GoPro.com and applies automatically at cart — there is nothing to type and nothing to "stack" code-wise. Re-verification follows ID.me’s own periodic cycle, not every purchase.

Because the 5% is a cart-level percentage, it generally layers on top of the with-subscription price and on bundle sale prices — but GoPro states "Restrictions apply," so sale, clearance, or limited items may be excluded. Confirm the 5% actually reduces your specific cart before paying. The subscription itself is the real discount engine, not a stack partner: the "with a 1-year subscription" camera price is a substitute pricing structure, so you choose the subscription-bundle SKU instead of the camera-only SKU.

The GovX "GoPro Pro Deal" is a closed, separate marketplace: you cannot add the ID.me 5%, a GoPro sale, or a cashback portal on top of a GovX order, and cashback portals can also void on ID.me-gated checkouts. Treat GovX as a standalone alternative to price-check, not a layer. Because GoPro controls the terms and can change them at any time, confirm the current offer on GoPro’s official ID.me page before you buy.
alpha-lion-military-discount: VerifyPass confirms your eligibility — military/veteran, first responder, healthcare, or government — and issues a single-use code without a long detour out of the checkout flow. Codes are one-time per verification, so you reverify each time you want to redeem again. Shoppers report the VerifyPass approval takes about a minute.

The key trade-off is that the 30% applies to non-sale items only and does not stack with other promo codes or sale prices. On a $49.99 full-price tub, the code brings it to $34.99. But because Alpha Lion runs frequent sitewide sales that can reach 30% or more (Black Friday and Cyber Monday especially), a live public sale can equal or beat the military code — and since the two don’t combine, you take whichever single discount is larger.

A couple of accuracy notes: some directories muddy the figure as "10–25%," but the provider-stated rate is 30% off non-sale items. Teachers and students are not listed as eligible on the VerifyPass offer page — the confirmed groups are military/veteran, first responder, healthcare, and government. On top of whichever price you land, a cashback card or portal can add a little more, since those are payment-side rather than code-side.
hbo-max-military-discount: HBO Max has no military or veteran verification flow because there is no military discount to gate — nothing to verify. For its student discount, HBO Max uses UNiDAYS: you create or sign in to a free UNiDAYS account, verify enrollment at a U.S. accredited college or university (ages 18+), receive a unique code, and apply it at HBO Max. Student status must be reverified every 12 months. A veteran hoping to qualify would do so as a student, not as a veteran.

Many coupon, aggregator, and "military discount" listicle pages imply HBO Max has a military rate. It does not. The only verified status-gated discount is for students. We counter this directly so you don’t waste time hunting for a code that doesn’t exist.

For a true "military" angle, the closest route is indirect: Verizon offers its own ID.me-verified military discount on wireless plans, and eligible Verizon customers can add the Netflix & HBO Max perk for $13/month. But that saving comes from Verizon, not from HBO Max — HBO Max itself has no military program. As with most streaming services, a standalone military discount simply isn’t part of the category.
jiffy-lube-military-discount: The documented program uses the WeSalute+ ID Card. WeSalute is a paid membership service (founded as Veterans Advantage) that verifies service status so you don’t have to share your military ID at the point of sale. Enrollment eligibility, per WeSalute: active duty, retiree, veteran, current or former guard & reserve, or an immediate family member. WeSalute membership renews on its own schedule — it isn’t a one-time, permanent verification — and the discount is honored only while your membership is active. For franchise-run discounts that don’t use WeSalute, verification is whatever the individual store accepts (commonly a military ID); there’s no central standard.

Two figures circulate that we deliberately don’t assert as current: a Team Car Care 15% program (still listed by Military.com, but its dedicated Jiffy Lube URL now redirects to the homepage — likely moved or discontinued) and a Heartland Automotive Services 25% program (announced in a November 6, 2015 press release and never re-confirmed). Treat both as historical/unverified unless a local store confirms them today. The honest bottom line: 15% via WeSalute+ is the one brand-level offer we can verify, and everything else is location-specific.

To save more, check jiffylube.com/coupons for nationwide coupons open to everyone (sometimes better than a small percentage), and watch for Veterans Day — location-specific specials in 2025 ranged from free conventional oil changes to 50% off, so check your local store’s social media in early November. A WeSalute+ membership also unlocks other auto and travel discounts (Penske, Avis, Budget) that can offset its cost. Valvoline Instant Oil Change and Take 5 franchises similarly offer location-set military pricing worth comparing. And a practical tip: mention your eligibility and show your ID up front, before service begins — not after the ticket is rung up.
microsoft-military-discount: Verification is different from most retailers here: Microsoft handles it through your personal Microsoft account (the email you use with Outlook.com, Office, OneDrive, Xbox, or Windows) rather than a third-party verifier like ID.me, GovX, or SheerID. You enter your email on Microsoft’s eligibility page; if you’re eligible, you’re approved immediately and discounted prices appear automatically while signed in. Use a personal account, not a work or school account, and note Microsoft "reserves the right to determine eligibility in its discretion."

The "up to 10%" wording matters: it’s a ceiling, not a flat rate, and it effectively applies to consumer Surface hardware and accessories — not to Xbox, software, Windows, or subscriptions. Because the better of the discount or a current sale price applies automatically, it’s worth watching Microsoft Store sales, where a deeper promotion can beat the 10% even on otherwise-excluded categories.

If you’re after Microsoft 365, the Store discount won’t help — Office and Microsoft 365 are excluded. Instead, eligible military families can buy the Microsoft 365 Family "Military Appreciation Edition" for $99.99/year (Microsoft cites about 30% off) through a U.S. military Exchange such as AAFES or the Navy Exchange. That is a separate, Exchange-only offer, not a Microsoft Store discount.
cotopaxi-military-discount: All the math below uses one baseline: a $200 Cotopaxi apparel cart (for example, a Fuego down jacket at about $200 full price), pre-tax. There is no tax-free or military channel to price in — every real saving here is either the ExpertVoice pro store or a public channel open to everyone.

The "40% military discount" confusion, cleared up. Aggregator sites recycle a "40% OFF Cotopaxi Military Discount" headline, and some invent a "$40 in-store military discount" or a "verify via GovX" step. None are verified. ID.me — the actual verification network — states it is not aware that Cotopaxi offers military discounts. The only real ~40% figure is the ExpertVoice pro deal, a pro-purchase program reachable through ExpertVoice’s military door, not a Cotopaxi-run in-house military percentage. There is no military verification step at cotopaxi.com checkout to honor any "military code."

ExpertVoice is the genuine military route. Cotopaxi runs an active ExpertVoice store, and the American Alpine Club’s member-discounts page corroborates "up to 40% off through ExpertVoice at cotopaxi.com." Military members, retirees, veterans, and spouses can reach it by verifying military status with ExpertVoice (a .mil email or DD214/VA card), and outdoor or medical professionals may qualify by occupation. Access is personal-use only, with no resale and purchase caps.

But the honest best deal is often the public Sale. On the $200 baseline, the ExpertVoice pro store lands around $120 (~40% off) on current-season gear, but a comparable past-season item in the Cotopaxi Sale can run roughly $80–$140 (up to ~60% off) — frequently beating the pro deal outright — and Pre-Loved used gear can go deeper still. If you’re a first-time, full-price buyer who isn’t ExpertVoice-eligible, the ~20% welcome code brings a $200 cart to about $160.
louis-vuitton-military-discount: Louis Vuitton is a "never-on-sale" luxury maison: as a matter of brand policy it does not run public discounts, coupon codes, or affinity programs, and the only markdowns are internal employee events. That is why there is no ID.me, SheerID, GovX, WeSalute, or VerifyPass brand page for buying new LV at a discount — no percentage, no code, and no verification flow exists for any group.

Be skeptical of coupon and affinity aggregators (Coupert, lifesaversavings.com, militarymarkdown.com, militarydiscountsaver.com, worthepenny.com) that publish a "10% first responder / military discount" and imply an in-store ID-verified redemption. This is fabricated. Tellingly, several of those same pages simultaneously state that Louis Vuitton does not offer a military discount, contradicting their own coupon headline — a classic SEO-farm pattern. Treat every LV "X% off" affinity claim as false unless it appears on us.louisvuitton.com, which it does not.

The genuinely military-specific saving is the Exchange. The Army & Air Force Exchange Service (shopmyexchange.com) sells LXR-authenticated pre-owned Louis Vuitton tax-free with free shipping, exclusive to eligible military shoppers. On a roughly $2,000-class bag, skipping sales tax and buying authenticated pre-owned instead of new is the only structurally real "military" saving on this brand. Inventory rotates and sells quickly, so treat it as a channel to check rather than a fixed, always-on deal.

If your military status is not essential to the deal, the broader luxury-resale market — Fashionphile, The RealReal, and Rebag — sells the same authenticated pre-owned LV and usually offers the lowest absolute prices, though it is open to everyone and is not a military benefit. Sales tax typically applies there, and a cashback portal can layer a small extra on a resale purchase where the reseller is portal-listed. Whichever route you choose, buy pre-owned only from authenticators — the counterfeit market for Louis Vuitton is heavy.
sonic-military-discount: There is no third-party verification service and no corporate percentage to claim. Where a franchise offers a discount, verification is a simple in-person check of a valid military/veteran ID at the point of order — no account, no online flow, no annual re-verification. If a location declines, there is no corporate appeal; participation is entirely at the franchisee’s discretion. Community and editorial sources commonly report about 10% off at participating locations, but no Sonic primary source confirms any number, so treat it as your-mileage-may-vary rather than a fact.

Coupon and aggregator pages imply a dependable "Sonic 10% military discount." There is no corporate 10% military discount — where it exists it is a per-franchise courtesy at participating locations only, not guaranteed. The recent Veterans Day shake deals were public promos (the 2025 half-price shake reportedly required no military ID), not military-exclusive offers, and prior years ran public food deals (2-for-$5 in 2022, a $0.99 Fritos Chili Cheese Jr. Wrap in 2023). Terms change every year and by location, so re-verify each early November.

The practical savings play is the same for everyone: use the Sonic app / My Sonic Rewards for rotating BOGO, half-price, and $0.99-item offers, and take Sonic’s standing public deals — Happy Hour half-price drinks and slushes (typically 2–4 p.m. daily) and half-price shakes after 8 p.m. These are automatic, need no ID, and usually beat the uncertain ~10% franchise courtesy.
silencer-shop-military-discount: Sound-Off is a call-for-pricing program, archetypally a manual "best price" quote rather than a posted percentage. After Silencer Shop reviews "a range of IDs" — with no named third-party verifier such as ID.me, GovX, or SheerID — you phone the Sound-Off line for a quote on eligible items. Sound-Off comes in an Individual tier for members and an Agency tier for department accounts, and Silencer Shop donates a portion of every Sound-Off order to nonprofits that support first responders and military members.

SilencerCo SPEQ ("Service Proven Equipment") is a separate manufacturer pro-deal. It gives qualified professionals — active, reserve, and retired military, anyone honorably discharged with a DD-214, disabled veterans with a medically-retired ID, active and retired law enforcement, firefighters and EMTs, Federal Flight Deck Officers, and armed private security — a flat, SilencerCo-set discount on SilencerCo suppressors only. Pricing is confidential and delivered after verification, and you buy through a SPEQ dealer rather than silencershop.com directly. Sound-Off and SPEQ are substitutes, not a stack: take the better single quote.

The single biggest 2026 cost change applies to everyone, military or not: the $200 NFA tax stamp dropped to $0 on January 1, 2026 under H.R.1, which dwarfs any percentage discount. Because suppressors are NFA items, the usual money-savers — the GovX marketplace, cashback portals, and the tax-free military exchanges — do not apply, since NFA suppressors are transferred through an FFL/SOT on ATF forms and are not sold through those channels.
mint-mobile-military-discount: Mint’s public 12-month plans (pay 12 months upfront) run $15/mo for 6GB, $20/mo for 17GB, $25/mo for 23GB, and $30/mo for Unlimited, with taxes and fees extra. Mint re-tiered its data buckets in June 2026, raising the 6/17/23GB allotments at the same prices — so a lower tier may now cover your usage. New customers can also take $15 off any 3-month plan as an intro, dropping Unlimited to $25/mo for the first three months before it repriced to the standard rate.
